[p. 407] Al-Tha'labi said: Surat al-An'am is Meccan (makki, revealed in Mecca) except for six verses, which were revealed in Medina: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾ [6:91] to the end of three verses [6:91, 6:93], and ﴿Say: Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ [6:151] to the end of three verses [6:151, 6:153].

Ibn 'Atiyya said: These are the clear verses (al-muhkamat), meaning in this surah.

Al-Qurtubi said: It is Meccan except for two verses: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾, which was revealed concerning Malik ibn al-Sayf and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, the two Jews. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who produced gardens, trellised and untrellised﴾ [6:141], which was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas.

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Surat al-An'am was revealed in Mecca.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him, who said: Surat al-An'am was revealed in Mecca at night, all at once, and around it were seventy thousand angels, raising their voices in glorification of God.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: Surat al-An'am was revealed, accompanied by seventy thousand angels.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Asma', who said: Surat al-An'am was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was traveling, amid a loud chorus of angels, who had arranged themselves between the heaven and the earth.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh reported similarly from Asma' bint Yazid.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Surat al-An'am was revealed to me all at once, accompanied by seventy thousand angels, who had a loud chorus of glorification and praise." This is through the chain of Ibrahim ibn Na'ila, the teacher of al-Tabarani, from Isma'il ibn 'Amr, from Yusuf ibn 'Atiyya ibn 'Awn, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, and then he mentioned it.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from al-Tabarani, from the aforementioned Isma'il, with the same chain.

Al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab reported from Anas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Surat al-An'am was revealed with a procession of angels filling what lies between the two horizons, who had a loud chorus of glorification and sanctification, and the earth was shaking, while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was saying: Glory be to God the Mighty, glory be to God the Mighty."

Al-Hakim, who said: It is sound according to the condition of Muslim, al-Isma'ili in his Mu'jam, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Jabir, who said: When Surat al-An'am was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) glorified God, then said: "Indeed, angels escorted this surah until they filled the horizon."

Al-Bayhaqi, who declared it weak, and al-Khatib in his Tarikh reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "The Qur'an was revealed five verses at a time, and whoever memorizes it five verses at a time will not forget it, except Surat al-An'am, for it was revealed all at once, escorted from every heaven by seventy angels, until they delivered it to the Prophet (ﷺ). It was not recited over a sick person except that God healed him."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar to the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.

Al-Nahhas in his Tarikh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Surat al-An'am was revealed in Mecca all at once, so it is Meccan except for three verses of it that were revealed in Medina: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden﴾ to the completion of the three verses [6:151-153].

Al-Daylami reported with a weak chain (sanad) from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "A caller calls out: O reciter of Surat al-An'am, come to Paradise, because of your love for it and your recitation of it."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Abu Juhayfa, who said: Surat al-An'am was revealed in its entirety, with seventy thousand angels accompanying it. All of it is Meccan except ﴿Even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾ [6:111], which is Medinan.

Abu 'Ubayd in his Fada'il, al-Darimi in his Musnad, Muhammad ibn Nasr in Kitab al-Salat, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: Al-An'am is among the essential parts (nawajib) of the Qur'an.

Muhammad ibn Nasr reported from Ibn Mas'ud something similar.

Al-Salafi reported with a feeble chain from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites, when he prays the morning prayer, the first three verses of Surat al-An'am, up to ﴿and He knows what you earn﴾ [6:3], forty thousand angels will descend to him, and it will be recorded for him the like of their deeds. And a angel from above the seven heavens will descend to him, carrying an iron mace. If Satan whispers any evil into his heart, the angel will strike him a blow until there are seventy veils between him and it. Then, on the Day of Resurrection, God, exalted is He, will say: 'I am your Lord and you are My servant. Walk in My shade, drink from al-Kawthar, bathe in al-Salsabil, and enter Paradise without reckoning or punishment.'"

Al-Daylami reported from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever prays the dawn prayer in congregation, then sits in his place of prayer and recites the first three verses of Surat al-An'am, God will appoint seventy angels to him who will glorify God and seek forgiveness for him until the Day of Resurrection."

Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars said: This surah is the foundation of the argument against the polytheists and others among the innovators, and those who deny the Resurrection and the rising again. This requires that it was revealed all at once, because it is in one single line of argument, though it is expressed in many ways. On it the theologians (al-mutakallimun) built the foundations of religion (usul al-din).

He (glory be to Him) began this surah with "Praise be to Allah," to indicate that all praise belongs to Him, and to establish the proof against those who "ascribe equals to their Lord."

The matter was already covered in Surah al-Fatiha, so there is no need to repeat it here. Then He described Himself as the One "who created the heavens and the earth," informing of His complete power, which necessitates that He alone deserves all praise. Whoever originated and brought these into existence is the one truly worthy of being singled out for praise and of having all commendation directed to Him. The word *khalq* (creation) can mean origination (*ikhtira*) and can also mean determining (*taqdir*), and this has been discussed previously. He used the plural *samawat* (heavens) because of the multiplicity of their layers (*tibaq*), and He mentioned the heavens before the earth because they precede it in existence, as in ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 30].

His words ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾ are coordinated with "created." He mentioned the creation of the substances (*jawahir*) with ﴿created the heavens and the earth﴾, then mentioned the creation of the accidents (*a'rad*) with ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾, because substances cannot do without accidents.

The scholars differed over the intended meaning of "the darknesses and the light." The majority of the commentators said: the darknesses are the blackness of the night, and the light is the brightness of the day.

Al-Hasan said: they are disbelief and faith.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "This is a departure from the apparent meaning."

The better view is that the darknesses include everything to which the name "darkness" applies, and the light includes everything to which the name "light" applies. Thus included within this is the darkness of disbelief and the light of faith, as in ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one who is in darknesses?﴾ [al-An'am: 122]. He used the singular "light" because it is a genus (*jins*) encompassing all its kinds, and He used the plural "darknesses" because of the multiplicity of their causes and the variety of their types.

Al-Nahhas said: "*ja'ala* (made) here means *khalaqa* (created). When it means *khalaqa*, it does not take more than one object."

Al-Qurtubi said: "*ja'ala* here meaning *khalaqa* is the only permissible reading."

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "On this reading, the wording and the meaning agree in the coordination (*nasaq*), so that the plural is coordinated with the plural and the singular with the singular, and the placing of the darknesses before the light is because they are the origin, and for this reason the day was stripped off from the night."

His words ﴿then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾ are coordinated either with "Praise be to Allah" or with "created the heavens and the earth." The "then" (*thumma*) indicates the remoteness of what the disbelievers did, in ascribing equals to their Lord, given what has been made clear: that Allah, glory be to Him, is worthy of praise for creating the heavens, the earth, the darknesses and the light. This requires belief in Him and directing the good praise to Him, not disbelief in Him and taking a partner for Him. The object is placed first for emphasis and for the sake of the rhyme-endings (*fawasil*). The object is omitted because it is evident: that is, they ascribe to Him equals who have no power over anything of what He has power over. This is the utmost folly and the extreme of foolishness, for these blessings come from Him, glory be to Him, and yet disbelief comes from the unbelievers.

His words ﴿It is He who created you from clay﴾: its meaning has two views. The first, which is the more famous and the view of the majority, is that the intended one is Adam, peace be upon him, and the address is given in the general form to all, because they are his offspring and descendants.

The second: that the intended meaning is all of humankind, on the basis that the drop of semen from which they were created was created from clay. Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned the creation of Adam and his children after the creation of the heavens and the earth, following the lesser world (*al-ʿalam al-asghar*) with the greater world (*al-ʿalam al-akbar*). The purpose of mentioning these matters is to repel the disbelief of the unbelievers regarding the Resurrection and to refute their denial with what is witnessed by them, about which they have no doubt.

His words ﴿Then He decreed a term, and there is a specified term with Him﴾: He used the word "then" (*thumma*) because of the difference between their creation and their death.

The early scholars (*salaf*) and those after them differed over the interpretation of the two terms. It was said: "He decreed a term" means death, and "a specified term with Him" means the Resurrection. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Dahhak, Mujahid, ʿIkrima, Zayd ibn Aslam, ʿAtiyya, al-Suddi, Khusayf, Muqatil and others.

It was also said: the first term is what lies between one's creation and one's death, and the second is what lies between one's death and one's resurrection, which is close to the first.

It was said: the first term is the duration of this world, and the second is the lifespan of the human being until the time of his death. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid.

It was said: the first is the taking of souls during sleep, and the second is the taking of the soul at death.

It was said: the first is what is known from the times of the crescent moons and the zodiacal signs and what resembles them, and the second is the term of death.

It was said: the first is for those who have passed away, and the second is for those who remain and for those who will come.

It was said: the first term is the term that is fixed (*mahtum*), and the second is the increase in lifespan for one who keeps the ties of kinship. If he is pious, righteous and joined to his kin, his lifespan is increased; if he severs the ties of kinship, it is not increased for him. This is indicated by the words of the Exalted: ﴿No one is granted a lifespan, nor is anything reduced from his lifespan, except that it is in a Book﴾ [Fatir: 11]. It has been authentically reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that "keeping the ties of kinship (*silat al-rahim*) increases one's lifespan." It has also been reported from him that entering lands in which plague and epidemic have spread is among the causes of death. The indefinite noun is used at the beginning in His words ﴿and a specified term with Him﴾ because it has been made specific by the qualifying description.

His words ﴿Then you doubt﴾: this expresses astonishment at the occurrence of doubt from them, in the presence of what necessitates its absence. That is: how do you doubt the Resurrection when you observe within yourselves from beginning and end what removes and dispels that doubt? He who created you from clay, made you living beings who know and understand, created for you these senses and limbs, then took these away from you so that you became dead and returned to the inanimate state you were in before, is not incapable of resurrecting you, restoring these bodies as they were, and returning to them the souls that had departed from them, by His power and the wondrous perfection of His wisdom.

His words ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and in the earth. He knows your secret and your open, and He knows what you earn﴾: It has been said that "in the heavens and in the earth" is connected to the name "Allah" in terms of what it indicates of His being worshipped, governing and possessing. That is: He is the one worshipped, or the owner, or the one who disposes of affairs in the heavens and the earth, just as you say "Zayd is the caliph in the East and the West," meaning he is the ruler or disposer over both. It has also been said that the meaning is: He is Allah, who knows your secret and your open in the heavens and in the earth, so nothing is hidden from Him, and the governing element for both phrases is what follows them.

Al-Nahhas said: "This is one of the best things said about it."

Ibn Jarir said: "He is Allah in the heavens, and He knows your secret and your open on the earth."

The first view is preferable, and ﴿He knows your secret and your open﴾ is a sentence that confirms the meaning of the first sentence, because His being in the heaven and the earth necessitates His knowledge of the secrets of His servants and their open affairs, and His knowledge of what they earn of good and evil, of bringing benefit and repelling harm.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿAli that this verse, namely from "Praise be to Allah" up to "then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord," was revealed concerning the People of the Book.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abza, from his father, something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid, who said: This verse was revealed concerning the *zanadiqa* (heretics). They said: "Allah did not create darkness, nor beetles, nor scorpions, nor anything ugly; He only creates light and everything beautiful." So this verse was revealed concerning them.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾, that he said: "Disbelief and faith."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatada, who said: "Those who ascribe equals to their Lord are the people of polytheism (*shirk*)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi something similar.

Ibn Abi Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, (p-409) Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid, who said: "*Ya'dilun* (ascribe equals) means they associate partners."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd concerning His words ﴿then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾, that he said: "The gods they worshipped, they ascribed as equals to Allah, though Allah has no equal and no rival, and there is no god with Him, nor has He taken a consort or a son."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding ﴿It is He who created you from clay﴾, meaning Adam; ﴿then He decreed a term﴾, meaning the term of death; ﴿and there is a specified term with Him﴾, the term of the Hour and standing before Allah.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, narrated from him regarding His words ﴿Then He decreed a term﴾ that he said: "The term of this world," and in another wording, "the term of his death." ﴿And there is a specified term with Him﴾: he said, "The Hereafter, which no one knows except Allah."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding "He decreed a term" that he said: "It is the day in which the soul is taken, then it returns to its owner from sleep (*yaqza*)." ﴿And there is a specified term with Him﴾: "It is the term of a person's death."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verse 4–18 (part 1 of 2):

His words: ﴿And no sign comes to them﴾ etc. This is a new statement explaining some of the causes of their disbelief and rebelliousness, namely their turning away from the signs of Allah that come to them, such as the miracles of the prophets and what issues from Allah's overwhelming power, which no one with reason doubts is the act of Allah, Glorified is He. "Turning away" (i'rad) means abandoning reflection on the signs by which they should have reasoned to the Oneness of Allah. The "min" in "min ayatin" (any sign) is extra, for generality (istighraq), and the "min" in "min ayati" (of the signs) is partitive (tab'id). That is: no sign comes to them, from among the signs that are part of the signs of their Lord, except that they turn away from it.

The fa' in ﴿then they have indeed denied﴾ is the answer to an implied condition: meaning, if they turn away from them, then they have denied something greater than that, which is the Truth, ﴿when it came to them﴾. It has been said: the intended meaning of "the Truth" here is the Qur'an. It has also been said: it is Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿So there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock﴾: that is, the reports of the thing they used to mock, which is the Qur'an or Muhammad (ﷺ), with "that which" (ma) being a reference to it, for the sake of magnifying and exalting the matter. That is: they will soon know that this thing at which they mocked is not a fit object for mockery, and that will be at the time Allah's punishment is sent down upon them, just as one says, "Be patient, the news will reach you," at the time of threat and warning. The word "news" (anba') conveys this, for it is only applied to a great report.

His words: ﴿Do they not see how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ This is a new statement explaining what preceded it. The hamza is for denial. "Kam" may be interrogative or declarative, and it suspends the verb "see" from acting on what follows it. "Min qarn" is a specification (tamyiz). "Qarn" is applied to the people of each age, and they were so named because of their being joined together (iqtiran); that is: did they not know, through hearing reports and observing remains, how many nations we destroyed before them, existing in one age after another, because they denied their prophets?

It has been said: "qarn" is a period of time, which is sixty years, or seventy, or eighty, or a hundred, according to differing opinions. Then what is in the verse would be on the assumption of an omitted genitive: that is, "from the people of a generation."

His words: ﴿We had established them in the earth as We have not established you﴾. "Makkana lahu fi al-ard" means He made a place for him in it; "makkanahu fi al-ard" means He established him in it. The clause is a new sentence answering an implied question, as if it were said: "How was that?" It has been said that this clause is a qualifier of "qarn", but the first is preferable. "Ma" in "ma lam numakkin lakum" is an indefinite noun described by what follows it: that is, We established them with an establishment that We did not give you. The meaning: We gave the generations who were before you what We did not give you of worldly life, long lives, and strength of bodies, and We destroyed them all; so your destruction, while you are less than they, is more fitting.

His words: ﴿And We sent the sky upon them in abundance﴾. It means abundant rain. He expressed it by "the sky" because it descends from the sky, and from it is the poet's saying:
"When the sky descended upon the land of a people"
"Midrar" is an intensive form indicating abundance, like "midhkar" for a woman who has borne many males, and "min'th" for one who bears many females. One says "darra al-laban yadurru" when it flows abundantly to the milker. "Midrar" is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal). "The rivers flowing beneath them" means beneath their trees and dwellings: that is, Allah widened blessings upon them after establishing them in the earth, but they disbelieved in them, so Allah destroyed them for their sins. ﴿And We brought into being after them﴾, that is, after their destruction, ﴿other generations﴾, so they became replacements for those who perished. In this is a demonstration of the perfection of His power, Glorified is He, the strength of His dominion, and that He destroys whom He wills and brings into existence whom He wills.

His words: ﴿And had We sent down to you a book upon paper, and they had touched it with their hands, those who disbelieved would have said, "This is nothing but obvious magic."﴾ In this sentence is an explanation of the severity of their stubbornness in disbelief, and that they would not believe even if Allah had sent down to His Messenger a book written on paper, in their sight and presence, ﴿and they touched it with their hands﴾ so that the perception of both senses would be combined for them: the sense of sight and the sense of touch. ﴿Those who disbelieved would have said﴾ among them, ﴿"This is nothing but obvious magic,"﴾ and they would not act upon what they had seen and touched. If this is their state regarding what is seen and perceived by the senses, how then about what is merely revelation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) through an angel that they do not see and do not perceive? "Kitab" is a verbal noun meaning writing, and "qirtas" means a sheet.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verse 4–18 (part 1 of 2):

His words: ﴿And no sign comes to them﴾ etc. This is a new statement explaining some of the causes of their disbelief and rebelliousness, namely their turning away from the signs of Allah that come to them, such as the miracles of the prophets and what issues from Allah's overwhelming power, which no one with reason doubts is the act of Allah, Glorified is He. "Turning away" (i'rad) means abandoning reflection on the signs by which they should have reasoned to the Oneness of Allah. The "min" in "min ayatin" (any sign) is extra, for generality (istighraq), and the "min" in "min ayati" (of the signs) is partitive (tab'id). That is: no sign comes to them, from among the signs that are part of the signs of their Lord, except that they turn away from it.

The fa' in ﴿then they have indeed denied﴾ is the answer to an implied condition: meaning, if they turn away from them, then they have denied something greater than that, which is the Truth, ﴿when it came to them﴾. It has been said: the intended meaning of "the Truth" here is the Qur'an. It has also been said: it is Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿So there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock﴾: that is, the reports of the thing they used to mock, which is the Qur'an or Muhammad (ﷺ), with "that which" (ma) being a reference to it, for the sake of magnifying and exalting the matter. That is: they will soon know that this thing at which they mocked is not a fit object for mockery, and that will be at the time Allah's punishment is sent down upon them, just as one says, "Be patient, the news will reach you," at the time of threat and warning. The word "news" (anba') conveys this, for it is only applied to a great report.

His words: ﴿Do they not see how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ This is a new statement explaining what preceded it. The hamza is for denial. "Kam" may be interrogative or declarative, and it suspends the verb "see" from acting on what follows it. "Min qarn" is a specification (tamyiz). "Qarn" is applied to the people of each age, and they were so named because of their being joined together (iqtiran); that is: did they not know, through hearing reports and observing remains, how many nations we destroyed before them, existing in one age after another, because they denied their prophets?

It has been said: "qarn" is a period of time, which is sixty years, or seventy, or eighty, or a hundred, according to differing opinions. Then what is in the verse would be on the assumption of an omitted genitive: that is, "from the people of a generation."

His words: ﴿We had established them in the earth as We have not established you﴾. "Makkana lahu fi al-ard" means He made a place for him in it; "makkanahu fi al-ard" means He established him in it. The clause is a new sentence answering an implied question, as if it were said: "How was that?" It has been said that this clause is a qualifier of "qarn", but the first is preferable. "Ma" in "ma lam numakkin lakum" is an indefinite noun described by what follows it: that is, We established them with an establishment that We did not give you. The meaning: We gave the generations who were before you what We did not give you of worldly life, long lives, and strength of bodies, and We destroyed them all; so your destruction, while you are less than they, is more fitting.

His words: ﴿And We sent the sky upon them in abundance﴾. It means abundant rain. He expressed it by "the sky" because it descends from the sky, and from it is the poet's saying:
"When the sky descended upon the land of a people"
"Midrar" is an intensive form indicating abundance, like "midhkar" for a woman who has borne many males, and "min'th" for one who bears many females. One says "darra al-laban yadurru" when it flows abundantly to the milker. "Midrar" is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal). "The rivers flowing beneath them" means beneath their trees and dwellings: that is, Allah widened blessings upon them after establishing them in the earth, but they disbelieved in them, so Allah destroyed them for their sins. ﴿And We brought into being after them﴾, that is, after their destruction, ﴿other generations﴾, so they became replacements for those who perished. In this is a demonstration of the perfection of His power, Glorified is He, the strength of His dominion, and that He destroys whom He wills and brings into existence whom He wills.

His words: ﴿And had We sent down to you a book upon paper, and they had touched it with their hands, those who disbelieved would have said, "This is nothing but obvious magic."﴾ In this sentence is an explanation of the severity of their stubbornness in disbelief, and that they would not believe even if Allah had sent down to His Messenger a book written on paper, in their sight and presence, ﴿and they touched it with their hands﴾ so that the perception of both senses would be combined for them: the sense of sight and the sense of touch. ﴿Those who disbelieved would have said﴾ among them, ﴿"This is nothing but obvious magic,"﴾ and they would not act upon what they had seen and touched. If this is their state regarding what is seen and perceived by the senses, how then about what is merely revelation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) through an angel that they do not see and do not perceive? "Kitab" is a verbal noun meaning writing, and "qirtas" means a sheet.

His words: ﴿And they said, "Why was an angel not sent down to him?"﴾ This sentence includes another kind of their denial of his prophethood (ﷺ) and their disbelief in it. That is: they said, "Why did Allah not send down to you an angel that we could see, who would speak to us and declare that he is a prophet, so that we might believe in him and follow him?" Like their saying: ﴿"Why was there not sent down to him an angel to be with him as a warner?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 7].

(p-410) ﴿And had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided﴾: that is, had We sent down an angel in the form they proposed, such that they would see him and address him and he would address them, ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾, that is, We would have destroyed them, since they would not have believed upon his descent and their seeing him. For such a clear sign, namely the descent of an angel in that form, if belief does not follow it, they deserve destruction and punishment. ﴿Then they would not be reprieved﴾: that is, they would not be given respite after its descent and their witnessing of it. It has also been said that the meaning is: if Allah, Glorified is He, sent down a visible angel, their human faculties could not endure remaining alive after witnessing him, but their spirits would be taken at that moment, and thus what Allah sent His messengers for and what He revealed His books for of this obligation with which He charged His servants would be nullified. ﴿That He may try you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [al-Kahf: 7].

His words: ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾: that is, had We made the messenger to the Prophet an angel whom they could see and address, We would have made that angel a man, because they cannot see the angel in his form which Allah created him upon, except after he takes on dense bodily form similar to the bodies of the children of Adam, since every kind is at ease with its own kind. So if Allah, Glorified is He, made the messenger to mankind, or the messenger to His messenger, a visible angel addressing them, they would have fled from him and not been at ease with him, and terror would have overtaken them and fear would have arisen among them that would prevent them from speaking with him and seeing him. This is the least of conditions, so the benefit of sending would not be complete. And when Allah makes him a man, that is, in the form of a man from the children of Adam, so that they might find comfort with him and feel at ease with him, the disbelievers would say, "He is not an angel; he is only a human being," and they would return to the same state in which they were.

His words: ﴿And We would have confused them about that over which they are confused﴾: that is, We would have obscured for them what they obscure for themselves, for when they see him in the form of a human being they say, "This is a human being and not an angel," and if he is cited as evidence that he is an angel, they deny him.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "la-labasna 'alayhim" is: upon their leaders, just as they cause confusion among their weak followers. They used to say to them, "Muhammad is only a human being; there is no difference between him and you," and so they confused them with this and cast doubt upon them. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed that if an angel had descended in the form of a man, they would have found a way to confusion just as they do.

Al-labs means mixing. One says, "labastu 'alayhi al-amr,ult'ibuhu labsan," meaning I mixed it up for him; its origin is concealment by a garment or the like.

Then He, Glorified is He, said, consoling His Prophet (ﷺ) and comforting him: ﴿And messengers before you were certainly mocked, but those who ridiculed them were encompassed by that which they used to mock.﴾ One says, "haqa al-shay'u yahiqu haqan, huyuqan, wa hayaqanan": it descended; that is, what they used to mock descended upon them, and it encompassed them: and that is the Truth, since they were destroyed on account of mocking it.

11. ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth"﴾: that is, say, O Muhammad, to these mockers: travel through the earth and look at the traces of those who were before you, so that you may know what punishments befell them and how their end was after they had been in great bliss that surpasses what you are in. Behold, their dwellings are ruined, their gardens are dust-covered, and their lands are desolate. If their end was this end, then you will follow them and, after their destruction, you too will perish.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah, regarding His words, ﴿And no sign comes to them from among the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it﴾, that he said: no part of the Book of Allah comes to them except that they turn away from it. And regarding His words, ﴿They have denied the Truth when it came to them, so there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock﴾, he said: there will come to them on the Day of Resurrection the news of what they mocked from the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Malik, regarding His words, "from a generation," that he said: "from a nation."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatadah, regarding His words, ﴿We had established them in the earth as We have not established you﴾, that he said: We gave them what We did not give you.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words, ﴿And We sent the sky upon them in abundance﴾, that he said: one after another.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Harun al-Taymi regarding the verse, that he said: the rain in its season.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported, by way of al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words, ﴿And had We sent down to you a book upon paper, and they had touched it with their hands﴾, that he said: even if We had sent down from the sky scrolls containing a book, ﴿and they touched it with their hands﴾, that would have increased them in denial.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid regarding His words, ﴿and they touched it with their hands﴾, that he said: they touched it and looked at it, and still did not believe in it.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called his people to Islam and spoke to them, and he made his case clear to them, as it reached me. Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith ibn Kaladah, Abdah ibn Abd Yaghuth, Ubayy ibn Khalaf ibn Wahb, and al-As ibn Wa'il ibn Hisham said to him: 'If an angel were appointed with you, O Muhammad, to speak on your behalf to the people and be seen with you...' Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatadah regarding His words, ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾, that he said: if Allah had sent down an angel and then they had not believed, He would have hastened punishment upon them.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His words, ﴿And had We sent down an angel﴾, that he said: even if an angel came to them in his own form, ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾, We would have destroyed them, ﴿then they would not be reprieved﴾, they would not be delayed. ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾: he said: if an angel came to them, he would come only in the form of a man, because they cannot endure looking at the angels. ﴿And We would have confused them about that over which they are confused﴾: he said: We would have mixed up for them what they mix up.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid regarding His words, ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾, that he said: in the form of a man, in the creation of a man.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatadah regarding His words, ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾, that he said: in the form of a human being.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Zayd something similar.

"Turning away" (i'rad) means abandoning reflection on the signs by which they should have reasoned to the Oneness of Allah. The "min" in "min ayatin" (any sign) is extra, for generality (istighraq), and the "min" in "min ayati" (of the signs) is partitive (tab'id). That is: no sign comes to them, from among the signs that are part of the signs of their Lord, except that they turn away from it.

The fa' in ﴿then they have indeed denied﴾ is the answer to an implied condition: meaning, if they turn away from them, then they have denied something greater than that, which is the Truth, ﴿when it came to them﴾. It has been said: the intended meaning of "the Truth" here is the Qur'an. It has also been said: it is Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿So there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock﴾: that is, the reports of the thing they used to mock, which is the Qur'an or Muhammad (ﷺ), with "that which" (ma) being a reference to it, for the sake of magnifying and exalting the matter. That is: they will soon know that this thing at which they mocked is not a fit object for mockery, and that will be at the time Allah's punishment is sent down upon them, just as one says, "Be patient, the news will reach you," at the time of threat and warning. The word "news" (anba') conveys this, for it is only applied to a great report.

His words: ﴿Do they not see how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ This is a new statement explaining what preceded it. The hamza is for denial. "Kam" may be interrogative or declarative, and it suspends the verb "see" from acting on what follows it. "Min qarn" is a specification (tamyiz). "Qarn" is applied to the people of each age, and they were so named because of their being joined together (iqtiran); that is: did they not know, through hearing reports and observing remains, how many nations we destroyed before them, existing in one age after another, because they denied their prophets?

It has been said: "qarn" is a period of time, which is sixty years, or seventy, or eighty, or a hundred, according to differing opinions. Then what is in the verse would be on the assumption of an omitted genitive: that is, "from the people of a generation."

His words: ﴿We had established them in the earth as We have not established you﴾. "Makkana lahu fi al-ard" means He made a place for him in it; "makkanahu fi al-ard" means He established him in it. The clause is a new sentence answering an implied question, as if it were said: "How was that?" It has been said that this clause is a qualifier of "qarn", but the first is preferable. "Ma" in "ma lam numakkin lakum" is an indefinite noun described by what follows it: that is, We established them with an establishment that We did not give you. The meaning: We gave the generations who were before you what We did not give you of worldly life, long lives, and strength of bodies, and We destroyed them all; so your destruction, while you are less than they, is more fitting.

His words: ﴿And We sent the sky upon them in abundance﴾. It means abundant rain. He expressed it by "the sky" because it descends from the sky, and from it is the poet's saying:
"When the sky descended upon the land of a people"
"Midrar" is an intensive form indicating abundance, like "midhkar" for a woman who has borne many males, and "min'th" for one who bears many females. One says "darra al-laban yadurru" when it flows abundantly to the milker. "Midrar" is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal). "The rivers flowing beneath them" means beneath their trees and dwellings: that is, Allah widened blessings upon them after establishing them in the earth, but they disbelieved in them, so Allah destroyed them for their sins. ﴿And We brought into being after them﴾, that is, after their destruction, ﴿other generations﴾, so they became replacements for those who perished. In this is a demonstration of the perfection of His power, Glorified is He, the strength of His dominion, and that He destroys whom He wills and brings into existence whom He wills.

His words: ﴿And had We sent down to you a book upon paper, and they had touched it with their hands, those who disbelieved would have said, "This is nothing but obvious magic."﴾ In this sentence is an explanation of the severity of their stubbornness in disbelief, and that they would not believe even if Allah had sent down to His Messenger a book written on paper, in their sight and presence, ﴿and they touched it with their hands﴾ so that the perception of both senses would be combined for them: the sense of sight and the sense of touch. ﴿Those who disbelieved would have said﴾ among them, ﴿"This is nothing but obvious magic,"﴾ and they would not act upon what they had seen and touched. If this is their state regarding what is seen and perceived by the senses, how then about what is merely revelation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) through an angel that they do not see and do not perceive? "Kitab" is a verbal noun meaning writing, and "qirtas" means a sheet.

His words: ﴿And they said, "Why was an angel not sent down to him?"﴾ This sentence includes another kind of their denial of his prophethood (ﷺ) and their disbelief in it. That is: they said, "Why did Allah not send down to you an angel that we could see, who would speak to us and declare that he is a prophet, so that we might believe in him and follow him?" Like their saying: ﴿"Why was there not sent down to him an angel to be with him as a warner?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 7].

(p-410) ﴿And had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided﴾: that is, had We sent down an angel in the form they proposed, such that they would see him and address him and he would address them, ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾, that is, We would have destroyed them, since they would not have believed upon his descent and their seeing him. For such a clear sign, namely the descent of an angel in that form, if belief does not follow it, they deserve destruction and punishment. ﴿Then they would not be reprieved﴾: that is, they would not be given respite after its descent and their witnessing of it. It has also been said that the meaning is: if Allah, Glorified is He, sent down a visible angel, their human faculties could not endure remaining alive after witnessing him, but their spirits would be taken at that moment, and thus what Allah sent His messengers for and what He revealed His books for of this obligation with which He charged His servants would be nullified. ﴿That He may try you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [al-Kahf: 7].

His words: ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾: that is, had We made the messenger to the Prophet an angel whom they could see and address, We would have made that angel a man, because they cannot see the angel in his form which Allah created him upon, except after he takes on dense bodily form similar to the bodies of the children of Adam, since every kind is at ease with its own kind. So if Allah, Glorified is He, made the messenger to mankind, or the messenger to His messenger, a visible angel addressing them, they would have fled from him and not been at ease with him, and terror would have overtaken them and fear would have arisen among them that would prevent them from speaking with him and seeing him. This is the least of conditions, so the benefit of sending would not be complete. And when Allah makes him a man, that is, in the form of a man from the children of Adam, so that they might find comfort with him and feel at ease with him, the disbelievers would say, "He is not an angel; he is only a human being," and they would return to the same state in which they were.

His words: ﴿And We would have confused them about that over which they are confused﴾: that is, We would have obscured for them what they obscure for themselves, for when they see him in the form of a human being they say, "This is a human being and not an angel," and if he is cited as evidence that he is an angel, they deny him.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "la-labasna 'alayhim" is: upon their leaders, just as they cause confusion among their weak followers. They used to say to them, "Muhammad is only a human being; there is no difference between him and you," and so they confused them with this and cast doubt upon them. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed that if an angel had descended in the form of a man, they would have found a way to confusion just as they do.

Al-labs means mixing. One says, "labastu 'alayhi al-amr,ult'ibuhu labsan," meaning I mixed it up for him; its origin is concealment by a garment or the like.

Then He, Glorified is He, said, consoling His Prophet (ﷺ) and comforting him: ﴿And messengers before you were certainly mocked, but those who ridiculed them were encompassed by that which they used to mock.﴾ One says, "haqa al-shay'u yahiqu haqan, huyuqan, wa hayaqanan": it descended; that is, what they used to mock descended upon them, and it encompassed them: and that is the Truth, since they were destroyed on account of mocking it.

11. ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth"﴾: that is, say, O Muhammad, to these mockers: travel through the earth and look at the traces of those who were before you, so that you may know what punishments befell them and how their end was after they had been in great bliss that surpasses what you are in. Behold, their dwellings are ruined, their gardens are dust-covered, and their lands are desolate. If their end was this end, then you will follow them and, after their destruction, you too will perish.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words, ﴿And We sent the sky upon them in abundance﴾, that he said: one after another.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Harun al-Taymi regarding the verse, that he said: the rain in its season.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called his people to Islam and spoke to them, and he made his case clear to them, as it reached me. Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith ibn Kaladah, Abdah ibn Abd Yaghuth, Ubayy ibn Khalaf ibn Wahb, and al-As ibn Wa'il ibn Hisham said to him: 'If an angel were appointed with you, O Muhammad, to speak on your behalf to the people and be seen with you...' So Allah revealed, ﴿And they said, 'Why was an angel not sent down to him?'﴾, the verse."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid regarding His words, ﴿And they said, "Why was an angel not sent down to him?"﴾, that he said: an angel in the form of a man. ﴿And had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided﴾: the Hour would have been established.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatadah regarding His words, ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾, that he said: if Allah had sent down an angel and then they had not believed, He would have hastened punishment upon them.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His words, ﴿And had We sent down an angel﴾, that he said: even if an angel came to them in his own form, ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾, We would have destroyed them, ﴿then they would not be reprieved﴾, they would not be delayed. ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾: he said: if an angel came to them, he would come only in the form of a man, because they cannot endure looking at the angels. ﴿And We would have confused them about that over which they are confused﴾: he said: We would have mixed up for them what they mix up.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid regarding His words, ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾, that he said: in the form of a man, in the creation of a man.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatadah regarding His words, ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾, that he said: in the form of a human being.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Zayd something similar.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿And We would have confused them﴾ that he said: "We would have made them confused (shabbahna ʿalayhim)."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding the verse, that he said: "We would have made confused for them what they confuse for themselves (shabbahna ʿalayhim ma yushabbihuna ʿala anfusihim)."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by, as it reached me, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Umayya ibn Khalaf and Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, and they mocked him (hamazuhu) and ridiculed him (istahza'u bihi), and this angered him. So Allah revealed: ﴿And certainly were messengers mocked before you, but there befell those who mocked them that which they used to mock at﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verse 4–18 (part 1 of 2):

His words: ﴿And no sign comes to them﴾ etc. This is a new statement explaining some of the causes of their disbelief and rebelliousness, namely their turning away from the signs of Allah that come to them, such as the miracles of the prophets and what issues from Allah's overwhelming power, which no one with reason doubts is the act of Allah, Glorified is He. "Turning away" (i'rad) means abandoning reflection on the signs by which they should have reasoned to the Oneness of Allah. The "min" in "min ayatin" (any sign) is extra, for generality (istighraq), and the "min" in "min ayati" (of the signs) is partitive (tab'id). That is: no sign comes to them, from among the signs that are part of the signs of their Lord, except that they turn away from it.

The fa' in ﴿then they have indeed denied﴾ is the answer to an implied condition: meaning, if they turn away from them, then they have denied something greater than that, which is the Truth, ﴿when it came to them﴾. It has been said: the intended meaning of "the Truth" here is the Qur'an. It has also been said: it is Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿So there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock﴾: that is, the reports of the thing they used to mock, which is the Qur'an or Muhammad (ﷺ), with "that which" (ma) being a reference to it, for the sake of magnifying and exalting the matter. That is: they will soon know that this thing at which they mocked is not a fit object for mockery, and that will be at the time Allah's punishment is sent down upon them, just as one says, "Be patient, the news will reach you," at the time of threat and warning. The word "news" (anba') conveys this, for it is only applied to a great report.

His words: ﴿Do they not see how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ This is a new statement explaining what preceded it. The hamza is for denial. "Kam" may be interrogative or declarative, and it suspends the verb "see" from acting on what follows it. "Min qarn" is a specification (tamyiz). "Qarn" is applied to the people of each age, and they were so named because of their being joined together (iqtiran); that is: did they not know, through hearing reports and observing remains, how many nations we destroyed before them, existing in one age after another, because they denied their prophets?

It has been said: "qarn" is a period of time, which is sixty years, or seventy, or eighty, or a hundred, according to differing opinions. Then what is in the verse would be on the assumption of an omitted genitive: that is, "from the people of a generation."

His words: ﴿We had established them in the earth as We have not established you﴾. "Makkana lahu fi al-ard" means He made a place for him in it; "makkanahu fi al-ard" means He established him in it. The clause is a new sentence answering an implied question, as if it were said: "How was that?" It has been said that this clause is a qualifier of "qarn", but the first is preferable. "Ma" in "ma lam numakkin lakum" is an indefinite noun described by what follows it: that is, We established them with an establishment that We did not give you. The meaning: We gave the generations who were before you what We did not give you of worldly life, long lives, and strength of bodies, and We destroyed them all; so your destruction, while you are less than they, is more fitting.

His words: ﴿And We sent the sky upon them in abundance﴾. It means abundant rain. He expressed it by "the sky" because it descends from the sky, and from it is the poet's saying:
"When the sky descended upon the land of a people"
"Midrar" is an intensive form indicating abundance, like "midhkar" for a woman who has borne many males, and "min'th" for one who bears many females. One says "darra al-laban yadurru" when it flows abundantly to the milker. "Midrar" is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal). "The rivers flowing beneath them" means beneath their trees and dwellings: that is, Allah widened blessings upon them after establishing them in the earth, but they disbelieved in them, so Allah destroyed them for their sins. ﴿And We brought into being after them﴾, that is, after their destruction, ﴿other generations﴾, so they became replacements for those who perished. In this is a demonstration of the perfection of His power, Glorified is He, the strength of His dominion, and that He destroys whom He wills and brings into existence whom He wills.

His words: ﴿And had We sent down to you a book upon paper, and they had touched it with their hands, those who disbelieved would have said, "This is nothing but obvious magic."﴾ In this sentence is an explanation of the severity of their stubbornness in disbelief, and that they would not believe even if Allah had sent down to His Messenger a book written on paper, in their sight and presence, ﴿and they touched it with their hands﴾ so that the perception of both senses would be combined for them: the sense of sight and the sense of touch. ﴿Those who disbelieved would have said﴾ among them, ﴿"This is nothing but obvious magic,"﴾ and they would not act upon what they had seen and touched. If this is their state regarding what is seen and perceived by the senses, how then about what is merely revelation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) through an angel that they do not see and do not perceive? "Kitab" is a verbal noun meaning writing, and "qirtas" means a sheet.

His words: ﴿And they said, "Why was an angel not sent down to him?"﴾ This sentence includes another kind of their denial of his prophethood (ﷺ) and their disbelief in it. That is: they said, "Why did Allah not send down to you an angel that we could see, who would speak to us and declare that he is a prophet, so that we might believe in him and follow him?" Like their saying: ﴿"Why was there not sent down to him an angel to be with him as a warner?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 7].

(p-410) ﴿And had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided﴾: that is, had We sent down an angel in the form they proposed, such that they would see him and address him and he would address them, ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾, that is, We would have destroyed them, since they would not have believed upon his descent and their seeing him. For such a clear sign, namely the descent of an angel in that form, if belief does not follow it, they deserve destruction and punishment. ﴿Then they would not be reprieved﴾: that is, they would not be given respite after its descent and their witnessing of it. It has also been said that the meaning is: if Allah, Glorified is He, sent down a visible angel, their human faculties could not endure remaining alive after witnessing him, but their spirits would be taken at that moment, and thus what Allah sent His messengers for and what He revealed His books for of this obligation with which He charged His servants would be nullified. ﴿That He may try you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [al-Kahf: 7].

His words: ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾: that is, had We made the messenger to the Prophet an angel whom they could see and address, We would have made that angel a man, because they cannot see the angel in his form which Allah created him upon, except after he takes on dense bodily form similar to the bodies of the children of Adam, since every kind is at ease with its own kind. So if Allah, Glorified is He, made the messenger to mankind, or the messenger to His messenger, a visible angel addressing them, they would have fled from him and not been at ease with him, and terror would have overtaken them and fear would have arisen among them that would prevent them from speaking with him and seeing him. This is the least of conditions, so the benefit of sending would not be complete. And when Allah makes him a man, that is, in the form of a man from the children of Adam, so that they might find comfort with him and feel at ease with him, the disbelievers would say, "He is not an angel; he is only a human being," and they would return to the same state in which they were.

His words: ﴿And We would have confused them about that over which they are confused﴾: that is, We would have obscured for them what they obscure for themselves, for when they see him in the form of a human being they say, "This is a human being and not an angel," and if he is cited as evidence that he is an angel, they deny him.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "la-labasna 'alayhim" is: upon their leaders, just as they cause confusion among their weak followers. They used to say to them, "Muhammad is only a human being; there is no difference between him and you," and so they confused them with this and cast doubt upon them. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed that if an angel had descended in the form of a man, they would have found a way to confusion just as they do.

Al-labs means mixing. One says, "labastu 'alayhi al-amr,ult'ibuhu labsan," meaning I mixed it up for him; its origin is concealment by a garment or the like.

Then He, Glorified is He, said, consoling His Prophet (ﷺ) and comforting him: ﴿And messengers before you were certainly mocked, but those who ridiculed them were encompassed by that which they used to mock.﴾ One says, "haqa al-shay'u yahiqu haqan, huyuqan, wa hayaqanan": it descended; that is, what they used to mock descended upon them, and it encompassed them: and that is the Truth, since they were destroyed on account of mocking it.

11. ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth"﴾: that is, say, O Muhammad, to these mockers: travel through the earth and look at the traces of those who were before you, so that you may know what punishments befell them and how their end was after they had been in great bliss that surpasses what you are in. Behold, their dwellings are ruined, their gardens are dust-covered, and their lands are desolate. If their end was this end, then you will follow them and, after their destruction, you too will perish.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah, regarding His words, ﴿And no sign comes to them from among the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it﴾, that he said: no part of the Book of Allah comes to them except that they turn away from it. And regarding His words, ﴿They have denied the Truth when it came to them, so there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock﴾, he said: there will come to them on the Day of Resurrection the news of what they mocked from the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Malik, regarding His words, "from a generation," that he said: "from a nation."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatadah, regarding His words, ﴿We had established them in the earth as We have not established you﴾, that he said: We gave them what We did not give you.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words, ﴿And We sent the sky upon them in abundance﴾, that he said: one after another.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Harun al-Taymi regarding the verse, that he said: the rain in its season.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verse 19–21 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Say: "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?"﴾ This is an argument against them and a rebuke to them.

The meaning: Say to them this statement, and if they say, "To Allah," then say it. Once it is established that to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, either by their acknowledgment or by the establishment of proof against them, Allah is able to hasten punishment upon them. But He has prescribed for Himself mercy, meaning He has promised it out of His bounty and generosity. The mention of "Himself" here is an expression of the emphasis of His promise and the absence of intermediaries besides Him. In the speech there is an encouragement for those who turn away from Him to come back to Him, and a calming of their hearts by (the fact) that He is merciful to His servants, does not hasten punishment upon them, and accepts from them repentance and turning back. Among His mercy to them is the sending of messengers, the sending down of books, and the setting up of proofs.

His saying: ﴿He will surely gather you unto the Day of Resurrection﴾. The lam is the answer to an implied oath.

Al-Farra' and others said: It is possible that the complete sentence ends at His saying "mercy," and what follows it is a fresh statement by way of explanation, so the meaning would be: He will surely gather you, i.e., He will grant you respite and delay your gathering.

It was said: The meaning is: He will surely gather you in the graves until the day that you denied.

It was said: "ilā" here means "fī" (in): i.e., He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection.

It was said: It is possible that the position of "la-yajma'annakum" is in the accusative as a substitute for "mercy," so the lam would have the meaning of "an" (that).

The meaning: Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy, that He will gather you, as they said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him﴾ [Yusuf: 35], i.e., that they should imprison him. It was said: The clause "la-yajma'annakum" is brought for intimidation after encouragement, and for warning after promise: i.e., if He grants you respite by His mercy, He will requite you by gathering you to punish those among the disobedient who deserve His punishment. The pronoun in ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ refers either to the Day or to the gathering.

His saying: ﴿Those who have lost their souls, they will not believe﴾.

Al-Zajjaj said: The relative pronoun is in the nominative as the subject, and what follows it is its predicate, as you say: "He who honours me, for him is a dirham," so the fa' is because the subject includes the meaning of a conditional.

Al-Akhfash said: If you wish, "alladhina" may be in the accusative position as a substitute for the kaf and mim in "la-yajma'annakum," i.e., He will surely gather the polytheists who have lost their souls. Al-Mubarrad rejected this and claimed that it is an error, because one does not substitute from the addressee nor from the addressed. One does not say: "I passed by you, Zayd," nor "you passed by me, Zayd." It was said that "alladhina" may be in the genitive as a substitute for "the deniers" mentioned earlier, or as an adjective for them. It was said that it is a vocative with the particle of address implied.

His saying: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever dwells in the night and the day﴾. That is, to Allah. He singled out "dwells" for mention because what is characterized by stillness is more numerous than what is characterized by motion. It was said: The meaning is: whatever dwells in them or moves, and he suffices with one of the two opposites over the other. This is part of the argument against the disbelievers.

His saying: ﴿Say: "Shall I take other than Allah as a protector?"﴾ The interrogative is for denial. He said this to them when they invited him to worship idols. Since the denial was of taking other than Allah as a protector, not of taking a protector in general, the hamza entered upon the object and not upon the verb.

What is meant by "protector" here is "one worshipped," i.e., how can I take other than Allah as an object of worship? "Originator of the heavens and the earth" is in the genitive as an adjective of the name of Allah. Al-Akhfash permitted the nominative by supposing an implied subject, al-Zajjaj permitted the accusative by way of praise, and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi permitted its accusative by an implied verb, as if it were said: "Shall I abandon the originator of the heavens and the earth?!"

His saying: ﴿And He feeds but is not fed﴾. The majority read with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the 'ayn in the first, and with a damma and a fatha on the 'ayn in the second, i.e., He provides sustenance and is not provided for. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and al-A'mash read with a fatha on the yā' in the second and a fatha on the 'ayn. It was also read with a fatha on the yā' and 'ayn in the first, and a damma and kasra on the 'ayn in the second, on the basis that the pronoun returns to the protector mentioned. He singled out feeding from among the other kinds of favour because the need for it is more pressing.

His saying: ﴿Say: "I have been commanded to be the first to submit"﴾. After the prohibition of taking other than Allah as a protector, He commanded him to say to them that he is commanded to be the first of those who submit his face to Allah from among his people, and the most sincere from his community. It was said: The meaning of "aslama" is "istaslama" (to surrender) to the command of Allah. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, forbade him to be among the polytheists.

The meaning: I have been commanded to be the first to submit, and I have been forbidden from association: i.e., he says this to them.

Then He commanded him to say: ﴿Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day﴾, i.e., if I disobey Him by worshipping another or by opposing His command or prohibition.

Fear is the anticipation of something disliked. It was said: it has the meaning of knowledge, i.e., I know that if I disobey my Lord, there is for me a great punishment.

His saying: ﴿Whoever is averted from it on that day, He has had mercy upon him﴾.

The people of Medina, the people of Mecca and Ibn 'Amir read in the passive voice, i.e., whoever is averted from the punishment; Sibawayh chose this reading. The Kufans read in the active voice, which is the choice of Abu Hatim, so the pronoun in this reading refers to Allah.

The meaning of "on that day" is the day of the great punishment. ﴿He has had mercy upon him﴾ means Allah saved him, bestowed favour upon him and admitted him to Paradise. The demonstrative "that" refers either to the averting or to the mercy: i.e., that averting or mercy is ﴿the clear triumph﴾, meaning the manifest and evident. Ubayy read: "Whoever Allah averts from it."

His saying: ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm﴾, i.e., if Allah sends down upon you harm from poverty or sickness, ﴿there is no remover of it but Him﴾, i.e., there is none able to remove it besides Him. ﴿And if He touches you with good﴾ from ease or well-being, ﴿then He is over all things competent﴾. Touching with harm and with good is included in this.

His saying: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾. Al-qahr is domination, and al-qahir is the dominant one, and "uqhira al-rajul" means when a man becomes subdued and humiliated. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Husayn wished to rule Khuza'a, but Husayn became humiliated and subdued."

The meaning of ﴿over His servants﴾ is the superiority of dominance through subjugation and victory over them, not spatial above, as one says: "The sultan is above his subjects," i.e., in rank and elevation.

In subjugation there is an additional meaning not found in power, namely preventing others from reaching their desire. ﴿And He is the Wise﴾ in His command, ﴿the Acquainted﴾ with the deeds of His servants.

His saying: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?"﴾ "Ayy" is the subject, "akbar" is its predicate, and "shahadatan" is a specification. The word "shay'" (thing) is applied to the eternal and the originated, the impossible and the possible.

The meaning: which witness is greatest in testimony? So "shay'" was placed in the position of "witness." It was said: "shay'" here is placed in the position of the name of Allah.

The meaning: Allah is greatest in testimony, i.e., His singularity in lordship and the establishment of proofs for His unity is the greatest testimony and the most mighty. He is a witness between me and you. It was said: His saying "Allah is a witness between me and you" is the answer, because if the witness is between him and them, He is the greatest testimony for him, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. It was said: The answer is complete at His saying "Say: Allah," meaning Allah is the greatest testimony, then He began and said: "He is a witness between me and you," i.e., He is a witness between me and you.

His saying: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby and whoever it reaches﴾. That is, Allah revealed to me this Qur'an which I have recited to you, in order that I may warn you by it and warn by it whoever it reaches, i.e., everyone it reaches of those existing and non-existing who will exist in future times. In this verse there is an indication that the rulings of the Qur'an extend to those who will exist just as they extend to those who were already existing at the time of revelation, without any need for those absurdities mentioned in the science of the principles of jurisprudence. Abu Nuhayk read "wa-ūḥiya" in the active voice, and all others read it in the passive voice.

His saying: ﴿Do you indeed testify that with Allah there are other gods?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach according to the reading of whoever reads with two hamzas on the original, or with the second changed. As for whoever reads it as a statement, he has affirmed their polytheism against them. He said "other gods" because "gods" is a plural, and the plural may take the feminine. Al-Farra' said this, and similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names﴾ [al-A'raf: 180], and He said: ﴿Then what is the state of the former generations?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 51]. ﴿Say: "I do not testify"﴾, i.e., "I do not testify with you," and it is omitted because the sentence indicates it, since this testimony is false. Similar to it is ﴿If they testify, do not testify with them﴾ [al-An'am: 150]. The "mā" in ﴿of what you associate﴾ is either relative or verbal-masdar: i.e., of the idols you make gods, or of your associating others with Allah.

His saying: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Scripture know him as they know their sons﴾. "Al-kitab" is generic, so it includes the Torah, the Gospel and others. I.e., they know the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. This was said by a group of the early generations, and al-Zajjaj adopted it. It was said: the pronoun returns to the Book, i.e., they know it with a certain knowledge such that nothing in it is obscure to them, and "as they know their sons" is an explanation of the certainty of that knowledge, its perfection, and the absence of any doubt in it, for the knowledge of fathers of their sons is the one that reaches the utmost degree of mastery in general and in detail.

His saying: ﴿Those who have lost their souls, they will not believe﴾. It is in the place of nominative as subject, and its predicate is ﴿they will not believe﴾. The entry of the fa' into the predicate is because the subject includes the meaning of a conditional. It was said: the relative pronoun is the predicate of an implied subject; it was said: it is an adjective of the first relative pronoun.

On the last two views, ﴿they will not believe﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿those to whom We have given the Scripture﴾.

The meaning according to the first view is that the disbelievers who have lost their souls through their obstinacy and rebellion do not believe in what the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, brought. According to the last two views, those whom Allah gave the Book are those who have lost their souls because of their falling into distance from the truth and not acting upon the knowledge established for them, so they do not believe.

His saying: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies His signs?﴾ That is, he invents lies against Allah, saying that the Torah or the Gospel contains what is not in them, ﴿or denies His signs﴾ that require belief in them, the clear and manifest miracle. He combined being a liar against Allah and a denier of what Allah commanded him to believe in, and whoever is like this, no one among Allah's servants is more unjust than him. The pronoun in ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾ refers to the matter (the situation).

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Salman al-Farisi, who said: "We find in the Torah that Allah created the heavens and the earth, then made one hundred mercies before He created creation. Then He created creation and placed among them one mercy, and held back with Himself ninety-nine mercies. By them they show mercy, by them they show compassion, by them they share, by them they visit one another, and by them the she-camel yearns, by them the cow gives birth, by them the sheep bleats, by them birds follow one another, and by them fish follow one another in the sea. When the Day of Resurrection comes, He will gather that mercy to what is with Him, and His mercy is better and more extensive."

Muslim, Ahmad and others related from Salman, from the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, who said: "On the day Allah created the heavens and the earth, He created one hundred mercies: of them is one mercy by which creation shows mercy, and ninety-nine for the Day of Resurrection. When the Day of Resurrection comes, He will complete them with this mercy."

And it is established in the two Sahihs and others, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, said: "When Allah had decreed creation, He wrote a book which He placed with Him above the Throne: Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath."

It has been narrated through other chains with similar meaning.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verse 19–21 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever rests in the night and the day﴾, that he said: "What is settled (istaqarra) in the night and the day." And regarding His words: ﴿Say: Shall I take other than Allah as a protector (waliyy)?﴾ he said: "As for the waliyy, it is the one who takes charge of him and acknowledges His lordship (rububiyyah)."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿Originator (Fatir) of the heavens and the earth﴾, that he said: "Badi' (the Originator) of the heavens and the earth."

Abu Ubayd in his Fada'il, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Anbari narrated from him, who said: "I did not know what 'fatara' (originated/created) the heavens and the earth, until two Bedouins came to me disputing over a well, and one of them said: 'I am the one who fatarahā (originated it),' meaning: 'I began it (ibtada'tuhā).'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words: ﴿And He feeds but is not fed﴾, that he said: "He provides sustenance and is not provided for."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿Whoever is turned away from it﴾, that he said: "Whoever is turned away from it, the punishment is turned away from him."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words: ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm﴾, he said: "With well-being (ʿafiyah)."

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "al-Nammam ibn Zayd, Qardam ibn Ka'b and Bahri ibn Amr came and said: 'O Muhammad, do you know of any god besides Allah?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'There is no god but Allah. With this I have been sent, and to this I call.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: What thing is greatest in testimony?﴾ — the verse."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby﴾, that he said: "It means the people of Makkah, and whoever reaches (balagha) — meaning whoever among the people this Qur'an reaches — for him it is a warner."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to Khosrow, Caesar, the Negus and every tyrant, calling them to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. (He was not the Negus upon whom the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed the funeral prayer.)"

Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, al-Khatib and Ibn al-Najjar narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever the Qur'an reaches, it is as if I have spoken to him directly with it," then he recited: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby and whoever it reaches﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: "Whoever the Qur'an reaches, it is as if he has seen the Prophet (ﷺ)." And in another wording: "Whoever the Qur'an reaches, until he understands it and comprehends it, is like one who witnessed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and spoke with him."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby﴾, that he said: "The Arabs, and whoever reaches" — he said: "the non-Arabs (ʿajam)."
