Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verse 19–21 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Say: "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?"﴾ This is an argument against them and a rebuke to them.

The meaning: Say to them this statement, and if they say, "To Allah," then say it. Once it is established that to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, either by their acknowledgment or by the establishment of proof against them, Allah is able to hasten punishment upon them. But He has prescribed for Himself mercy, meaning He has promised it out of His bounty and generosity. The mention of "Himself" here is an expression of the emphasis of His promise and the absence of intermediaries besides Him. In the speech there is an encouragement for those who turn away from Him to come back to Him, and a calming of their hearts by (the fact) that He is merciful to His servants, does not hasten punishment upon them, and accepts from them repentance and turning back. Among His mercy to them is the sending of messengers, the sending down of books, and the setting up of proofs.

His saying: ﴿He will surely gather you unto the Day of Resurrection﴾. The lam is the answer to an implied oath.

Al-Farra' and others said: It is possible that the complete sentence ends at His saying "mercy," and what follows it is a fresh statement by way of explanation, so the meaning would be: He will surely gather you, i.e., He will grant you respite and delay your gathering.

It was said: The meaning is: He will surely gather you in the graves until the day that you denied.

It was said: "ilā" here means "fī" (in): i.e., He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection.

It was said: It is possible that the position of "la-yajma'annakum" is in the accusative as a substitute for "mercy," so the lam would have the meaning of "an" (that).

The meaning: Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy, that He will gather you, as they said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him﴾ [Yusuf: 35], i.e., that they should imprison him. It was said: The clause "la-yajma'annakum" is brought for intimidation after encouragement, and for warning after promise: i.e., if He grants you respite by His mercy, He will requite you by gathering you to punish those among the disobedient who deserve His punishment. The pronoun in ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ refers either to the Day or to the gathering.

His saying: ﴿Those who have lost their souls, they will not believe﴾.

Al-Zajjaj said: The relative pronoun is in the nominative as the subject, and what follows it is its predicate, as you say: "He who honours me, for him is a dirham," so the fa' is because the subject includes the meaning of a conditional.

Al-Akhfash said: If you wish, "alladhina" may be in the accusative position as a substitute for the kaf and mim in "la-yajma'annakum," i.e., He will surely gather the polytheists who have lost their souls. Al-Mubarrad rejected this and claimed that it is an error, because one does not substitute from the addressee nor from the addressed. One does not say: "I passed by you, Zayd," nor "you passed by me, Zayd." It was said that "alladhina" may be in the genitive as a substitute for "the deniers" mentioned earlier, or as an adjective for them. It was said that it is a vocative with the particle of address implied.

His saying: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever dwells in the night and the day﴾. That is, to Allah. He singled out "dwells" for mention because what is characterized by stillness is more numerous than what is characterized by motion. It was said: The meaning is: whatever dwells in them or moves, and he suffices with one of the two opposites over the other. This is part of the argument against the disbelievers.

His saying: ﴿Say: "Shall I take other than Allah as a protector?"﴾ The interrogative is for denial. He said this to them when they invited him to worship idols. Since the denial was of taking other than Allah as a protector, not of taking a protector in general, the hamza entered upon the object and not upon the verb.

What is meant by "protector" here is "one worshipped," i.e., how can I take other than Allah as an object of worship? "Originator of the heavens and the earth" is in the genitive as an adjective of the name of Allah. Al-Akhfash permitted the nominative by supposing an implied subject, al-Zajjaj permitted the accusative by way of praise, and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi permitted its accusative by an implied verb, as if it were said: "Shall I abandon the originator of the heavens and the earth?!"

His saying: ﴿And He feeds but is not fed﴾. The majority read with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the 'ayn in the first, and with a damma and a fatha on the 'ayn in the second, i.e., He provides sustenance and is not provided for. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and al-A'mash read with a fatha on the yā' in the second and a fatha on the 'ayn. It was also read with a fatha on the yā' and 'ayn in the first, and a damma and kasra on the 'ayn in the second, on the basis that the pronoun returns to the protector mentioned. He singled out feeding from among the other kinds of favour because the need for it is more pressing.

His saying: ﴿Say: "I have been commanded to be the first to submit"﴾. After the prohibition of taking other than Allah as a protector, He commanded him to say to them that he is commanded to be the first of those who submit his face to Allah from among his people, and the most sincere from his community. It was said: The meaning of "aslama" is "istaslama" (to surrender) to the command of Allah. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, forbade him to be among the polytheists.

The meaning: I have been commanded to be the first to submit, and I have been forbidden from association: i.e., he says this to them.

Then He commanded him to say: ﴿Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day﴾, i.e., if I disobey Him by worshipping another or by opposing His command or prohibition.

Fear is the anticipation of something disliked. It was said: it has the meaning of knowledge, i.e., I know that if I disobey my Lord, there is for me a great punishment.

His saying: ﴿Whoever is averted from it on that day, He has had mercy upon him﴾.

The people of Medina, the people of Mecca and Ibn 'Amir read in the passive voice, i.e., whoever is averted from the punishment; Sibawayh chose this reading. The Kufans read in the active voice, which is the choice of Abu Hatim, so the pronoun in this reading refers to Allah.

The meaning of "on that day" is the day of the great punishment. ﴿He has had mercy upon him﴾ means Allah saved him, bestowed favour upon him and admitted him to Paradise. The demonstrative "that" refers either to the averting or to the mercy: i.e., that averting or mercy is ﴿the clear triumph﴾, meaning the manifest and evident. Ubayy read: "Whoever Allah averts from it."

His saying: ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm﴾, i.e., if Allah sends down upon you harm from poverty or sickness, ﴿there is no remover of it but Him﴾, i.e., there is none able to remove it besides Him. ﴿And if He touches you with good﴾ from ease or well-being, ﴿then He is over all things competent﴾. Touching with harm and with good is included in this.

His saying: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾. Al-qahr is domination, and al-qahir is the dominant one, and "uqhira al-rajul" means when a man becomes subdued and humiliated. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Husayn wished to rule Khuza'a, but Husayn became humiliated and subdued."

The meaning of ﴿over His servants﴾ is the superiority of dominance through subjugation and victory over them, not spatial above, as one says: "The sultan is above his subjects," i.e., in rank and elevation.

In subjugation there is an additional meaning not found in power, namely preventing others from reaching their desire. ﴿And He is the Wise﴾ in His command, ﴿the Acquainted﴾ with the deeds of His servants.

His saying: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?"﴾ "Ayy" is the subject, "akbar" is its predicate, and "shahadatan" is a specification. The word "shay'" (thing) is applied to the eternal and the originated, the impossible and the possible.

The meaning: which witness is greatest in testimony? So "shay'" was placed in the position of "witness." It was said: "shay'" here is placed in the position of the name of Allah.

The meaning: Allah is greatest in testimony, i.e., His singularity in lordship and the establishment of proofs for His unity is the greatest testimony and the most mighty. He is a witness between me and you. It was said: His saying "Allah is a witness between me and you" is the answer, because if the witness is between him and them, He is the greatest testimony for him, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. It was said: The answer is complete at His saying "Say: Allah," meaning Allah is the greatest testimony, then He began and said: "He is a witness between me and you," i.e., He is a witness between me and you.

His saying: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby and whoever it reaches﴾. That is, Allah revealed to me this Qur'an which I have recited to you, in order that I may warn you by it and warn by it whoever it reaches, i.e., everyone it reaches of those existing and non-existing who will exist in future times. In this verse there is an indication that the rulings of the Qur'an extend to those who will exist just as they extend to those who were already existing at the time of revelation, without any need for those absurdities mentioned in the science of the principles of jurisprudence. Abu Nuhayk read "wa-ūḥiya" in the active voice, and all others read it in the passive voice.

His saying: ﴿Do you indeed testify that with Allah there are other gods?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach according to the reading of whoever reads with two hamzas on the original, or with the second changed. Among His mercy to them is the sending of messengers, the sending down of books, and the setting up of proofs.

His saying: ﴿He will surely gather you unto the Day of Resurrection﴾. The lam is the answer to an implied oath.

Al-Farra' and others said: It is possible that the complete sentence ends at His saying "mercy," and what follows it is a fresh statement by way of explanation, so the meaning would be: He will surely gather you, i.e., He will grant you respite and delay your gathering.

It was said: The meaning is: He will surely gather you in the graves until the day that you denied.

It was said: "ilā" here means "fī" (in): i.e., He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection.

It was said: It is possible that the position of "la-yajma'annakum" is in the accusative as a substitute for "mercy," so the lam would have the meaning of "an" (that).

The meaning: Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy, that He will gather you, as they said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs, that they should imprison him﴾ [Yusuf: 35], i.e., that they should imprison him. It was said: The clause "la-yajma'annakum" is brought for intimidation after encouragement, and for warning after promise: i.e., if He grants you respite by His mercy, He will requite you by gathering you to punish those among the disobedient who deserve His punishment. The pronoun in ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ refers either to the Day or to the gathering.

His saying: ﴿Those who have lost their souls, they will not believe﴾.

Al-Zajjaj said: The relative pronoun is in the nominative as the subject, and what follows it is its predicate, as you say: "He who honours me, for him is a dirham," so the fa' is because the subject includes the meaning of a conditional.

Al-Akhfash said: If you wish, "alladhina" may be in the accusative position as a substitute for the kaf and mim in "la-yajma'annakum," i.e., He will surely gather the polytheists who have lost their souls. Al-Mubarrad rejected this and claimed that it is an error, because one does not substitute from the addressee nor from the addressed. One does not say: "I passed by you, Zayd," nor "you passed by me, Zayd." It was said that "alladhina" may be in the genitive as a substitute for "the deniers" mentioned earlier, or as an adjective for them. It was said that it is a vocative with the particle of address implied.

His saying: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever dwells in the night and the day﴾. That is, to Allah. He singled out "dwells" for mention because what is characterized by stillness is more numerous than what is characterized by motion. It was said: The meaning is: whatever dwells in them or moves, and he suffices with one of the two opposites over the other. This is part of the argument against the disbelievers.

His saying: ﴿Say: "Shall I take other than Allah as a protector?"﴾ The interrogative is for denial. He said this to them when they invited him to worship idols. Since the denial was of taking other than Allah as a protector, not of taking a protector in general, the hamza entered upon the object and not upon the verb.

What is meant by "protector" here is "one worshipped," i.e., how can I take other than Allah as an object of worship? "Originator of the heavens and the earth" is in the genitive as an adjective of the name of Allah. Al-Akhfash permitted the nominative by supposing an implied subject, al-Zajjaj permitted the accusative by way of praise, and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi permitted its accusative by an implied verb, as if it were said: "Shall I abandon the originator of the heavens and the earth?!"

His saying: ﴿And He feeds but is not fed﴾. The majority read with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the 'ayn in the first, and with a damma and a fatha on the 'ayn in the second, i.e., He provides sustenance and is not provided for. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and al-A'mash read with a fatha on the yā' in the second and a fatha on the 'ayn. It was also read with a fatha on the yā' and 'ayn in the first, and a damma and kasra on the 'ayn in the second, on the basis that the pronoun returns to the protector mentioned. He singled out feeding from among the other kinds of favour because the need for it is more pressing.

His saying: ﴿Say: "I have been commanded to be the first to submit"﴾. After the prohibition of taking other than Allah as a protector, He commanded him to say to them that he is commanded to be the first of those who submit his face to Allah from among his people, and the most sincere from his community. It was said: The meaning of "aslama" is "istaslama" (to surrender) to the command of Allah. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, forbade him to be among the polytheists.

The meaning: I have been commanded to be the first to submit, and I have been forbidden from association: i.e., he says this to them.

Then He commanded him to say: ﴿Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day﴾, i.e., if I disobey Him by worshipping another or by opposing His command or prohibition.

Fear is the anticipation of something disliked. It was said: it has the meaning of knowledge, i.e., I know that if I disobey my Lord, there is for me a great punishment.

His saying: ﴿Whoever is averted from it on that day, He has had mercy upon him﴾.

The people of Medina, the people of Mecca and Ibn 'Amir read in the passive voice, i.e., whoever is averted from the punishment; Sibawayh chose this reading. The Kufans read in the active voice, which is the choice of Abu Hatim, so the pronoun in this reading refers to Allah.

The meaning of "on that day" is the day of the great punishment. ﴿He has had mercy upon him﴾ means Allah saved him, bestowed favour upon him and admitted him to Paradise. The demonstrative "that" refers either to the averting or to the mercy: i.e., that averting or mercy is ﴿the clear triumph﴾, meaning the manifest and evident. Ubayy read: "Whoever Allah averts from it."

His saying: ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm﴾, i.e., if Allah sends down upon you harm from poverty or sickness, ﴿there is no remover of it but Him﴾, i.e., there is none able to remove it besides Him. ﴿And if He touches you with good﴾ from ease or well-being, ﴿then He is over all things competent﴾. Touching with harm and with good is included in this.

His saying: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾. Al-qahr is domination, and al-qahir is the dominant one, and "uqhira al-rajul" means when a man becomes subdued and humiliated. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Husayn wished to rule Khuza'a, but Husayn became humiliated and subdued."

The meaning of ﴿over His servants﴾ is the superiority of dominance through subjugation and victory over them, not spatial above, as one says: "The sultan is above his subjects," i.e., in rank and elevation.

In subjugation there is an additional meaning not found in power, namely preventing others from reaching their desire. ﴿And He is the Wise﴾ in His command, ﴿the Acquainted﴾ with the deeds of His servants.

His saying: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?"﴾ "Ayy" is the subject, "akbar" is its predicate, and "shahadatan" is a specification. The word "shay'" (thing) is applied to the eternal and the originated, the impossible and the possible.

The meaning: which witness is greatest in testimony? So "shay'" was placed in the position of "witness." It was said: "shay'" here is placed in the position of the name of Allah.

The meaning: Allah is greatest in testimony, i.e., His singularity in lordship and the establishment of proofs for His unity is the greatest testimony and the most mighty. He is a witness between me and you. It was said: His saying "Allah is a witness between me and you" is the answer, because if the witness is between him and them, He is the greatest testimony for him, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. It was said: The answer is complete at His saying "Say: Allah," meaning Allah is the greatest testimony, then He began and said: "He is a witness between me and you," i.e., He is a witness between me and you.

His saying: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby and whoever it reaches﴾. That is, Allah revealed to me this Qur'an which I have recited to you, in order that I may warn you by it and warn by it whoever it reaches, i.e., everyone it reaches of those existing and non-existing who will exist in future times. In this verse there is an indication that the rulings of the Qur'an extend to those who will exist just as they extend to those who were already existing at the time of revelation, without any need for those absurdities mentioned in the science of the principles of jurisprudence. Abu Nuhayk read "wa-ūḥiya" in the active voice, and all others read it in the passive voice.

His saying: ﴿Do you indeed testify that with Allah there are other gods?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach according to the reading of whoever reads with two hamzas on the original, or with the second changed. As for whoever reads it as a statement, he has affirmed their polytheism against them. He said "other gods" because "gods" is a plural, and the plural may take the feminine. Al-Farra' said this, and similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names﴾ [al-A'raf: 180], and He said: ﴿Then what is the state of the former generations?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 51]. ﴿Say: "I do not testify"﴾, i.e., "I do not testify with you," and it is omitted because the sentence indicates it, since this testimony is false. Similar to it is ﴿If they testify, do not testify with them﴾ [al-An'am: 150]. The "mā" in ﴿of what you associate﴾ is either relative or verbal-masdar: i.e., of the idols you make gods, or of your associating others with Allah.

His saying: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Scripture know him as they know their sons﴾. "Al-kitab" is generic, so it includes the Torah, the Gospel and others. I.e., they know the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. This was said by a group of the early generations, and al-Zajjaj adopted it. It was said: the pronoun returns to the Book, i.e., they know it with a certain knowledge such that nothing in it is obscure to them, and "as they know their sons" is an explanation of the certainty of that knowledge, its perfection, and the absence of any doubt in it, for the knowledge of fathers of their sons is the one that reaches the utmost degree of mastery in general and in detail.

His saying: ﴿Those who have lost their souls, they will not believe﴾. It is in the place of nominative as subject, and its predicate is ﴿they will not believe﴾. The entry of the fa' into the predicate is because the subject includes the meaning of a conditional. It was said: the relative pronoun is the predicate of an implied subject; it was said: it is an adjective of the first relative pronoun.

On the last two views, ﴿they will not believe﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿those to whom We have given the Scripture﴾.

The meaning according to the first view is that the disbelievers who have lost their souls through their obstinacy and rebellion do not believe in what the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, brought. According to the last two views, those whom Allah gave the Book are those who have lost their souls because of their falling into distance from the truth and not acting upon the knowledge established for them, so they do not believe.

His saying: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies His signs?﴾ That is, he invents lies against Allah, saying that the Torah or the Gospel contains what is not in them, ﴿or denies His signs﴾ that require belief in them, the clear and manifest miracle. He combined being a liar against Allah and a denier of what Allah commanded him to believe in, and whoever is like this, no one among Allah's servants is more unjust than him. The pronoun in ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾ refers to the matter (the situation).

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Salman al-Farisi, who said: "We find in the Torah that Allah created the heavens and the earth, then made one hundred mercies before He created creation. Then He created creation and placed among them one mercy, and held back with Himself ninety-nine mercies. By them they show mercy, by them they show compassion, by them they share, by them they visit one another, and by them the she-camel yearns, by them the cow gives birth, by them the sheep bleats, by them birds follow one another, and by them fish follow one another in the sea. When the Day of Resurrection comes, He will gather that mercy to what is with Him, and His mercy is better and more extensive."

Muslim, Ahmad and others related from Salman, from the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, who said: "On the day Allah created the heavens and the earth, He created one hundred mercies: of them is one mercy by which creation shows mercy, and ninety-nine for the Day of Resurrection. When the Day of Resurrection comes, He will complete them with this mercy."

And it is established in the two Sahihs and others, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, said: "When Allah had decreed creation, He wrote a book which He placed with Him above the Throne: Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath."

It has been narrated through other chains with similar meaning.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verse 19–21 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever rests in the night and the day﴾, that he said: "What is settled (istaqarra) in the night and the day." And regarding His words: ﴿Say: Shall I take other than Allah as a protector (waliyy)?﴾ he said: "As for the waliyy, it is the one who takes charge of him and acknowledges His lordship (rububiyyah)."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿Originator (Fatir) of the heavens and the earth﴾, that he said: "Badi' (the Originator) of the heavens and the earth."

Abu Ubayd in his Fada'il, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Anbari narrated from him, who said: "I did not know what 'fatara' (originated/created) the heavens and the earth, until two Bedouins came to me disputing over a well, and one of them said: 'I am the one who fatarahā (originated it),' meaning: 'I began it (ibtada'tuhā).'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words: ﴿And He feeds but is not fed﴾, that he said: "He provides sustenance and is not provided for."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿Whoever is turned away from it﴾, that he said: "Whoever is turned away from it, the punishment is turned away from him."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words: ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm﴾, he said: "With well-being (ʿafiyah)."

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "al-Nammam ibn Zayd, Qardam ibn Ka'b and Bahri ibn Amr came and said: 'O Muhammad, do you know of any god besides Allah?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'There is no god but Allah. With this I have been sent, and to this I call.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: What thing is greatest in testimony?﴾ — the verse."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby﴾, that he said: "It means the people of Makkah, and whoever reaches (balagha) — meaning whoever among the people this Qur'an reaches — for him it is a warner."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to Khosrow, Caesar, the Negus and every tyrant, calling them to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. (He was not the Negus upon whom the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed the funeral prayer.)"

Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, al-Khatib and Ibn al-Najjar narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever the Qur'an reaches, it is as if I have spoken to him directly with it," then he recited: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby and whoever it reaches﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: "Whoever the Qur'an reaches, it is as if he has seen the Prophet (ﷺ)." And in another wording: "Whoever the Qur'an reaches, until he understands it and comprehends it, is like one who witnessed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and spoke with him."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby﴾, that he said: "The Arabs, and whoever reaches" — he said: "the non-Arabs (ʿajam)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ikrimah, who said: al-Nadr, who was from the Banu Abd al-Dar, said: "On the Day of Resurrection, al-Lat and al-Uzza will intercede for me." So Allah revealed: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾ — the verse.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 22–32 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying: ﴿And the Day We will gather them﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read the two verbs with the nun (first person plural). It was also read with the ya' (third person) in both. The adverbial complement of time (nasib al-zarf) is an implied, delayed element: "On the Day We gather them, such-and-such will happen." The interrogative in ﴿Where are your partners﴾ is for reproach and rebuke of the polytheists.

He attributed the "partners" to them, because they were not in reality partners of God. Rather, since they named them partners, they were attributed to them. They are what they used to worship besides God, or what they worshipped alongside God.

His saying: ﴿whom you used to claim﴾, meaning, you used to claim them to be partners. Both objects are omitted together. The reason the interrogation carries rebuke is that their objects of worship were absent from them at that time, or were present but of no benefit to them in any way. Thus their existence was like their non-existence.

His saying: ﴿Then their trial would be only that they said, "By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾

Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj) said: The interpretation of this verse is that God, Mighty and Majestic, informed of the accounts of the polytheists and their being tested by their polytheism. Then He informed that their trial was not, until they saw the realities, except that they disowned polytheism. A parallel in the language is that you see a person who loves a deviant, and when he falls into ruin he disavows him, so you say: "Your love for him was only that you would disown him." End.

So the meaning of "trial" here is their disbelief: that is, the outcome of their disbelief, in which they took pride and for which they fought, was nothing but the denial and oath of disavowal in his saying: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists.﴾ It has also been said: the meaning of "trial" here is their answer. That is, their answer was nothing but denial and disavowal, so this answer was a trial because it was a lie. The clause ﴿Then their trial was not﴾ is coordinated with the governing element of the implied temporal adverb, as has passed. The exception is an incomplete exception (istithna' mufarragh), i.e., one in which the excepted element takes the role of the omitted subject or object. "Trial" (fitnatuhum) has been read in the nominative and accusative, and "yakun" and "takun" (both "was/were" forms) are read; the reading is clear.

It was also read: "wa ma kana fitnatuhum." And "rabbana" was read in the accusative as a vocative (nida').

﴿See how they lied against themselves﴾ by denying what they had done of polytheism in the world. ﴿And lost from them is what they used to invent﴾, meaning their invention departed, vanished, dissipated, and was nullified: what they used to presume, that the partners would bring them closer to God. This is on the basis that "ma" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah). It has also been said that it is a relative pronoun referring to the deities: that is, what they used to worship besides God departed from them, so it gave them no benefit at all. This is an expression of wonder for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at their varied conditions and contradictory claims. It has also been said: it is not possible that they would lie in the Hereafter, because it is an abode in which nothing but truth takes place. So the meaning of ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ is the denial of their polytheism in their own selves and in their belief. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they will not conceal from God any statement﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:42].

His saying: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾. This is a new statement explaining what some of the polytheists used to do in the world. The pronoun refers to "those who associated partners." That is: some of those who associated partners listen to you when you recite the Qur'an. ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾, meaning We did that to them as recompense for their disbelief. "Akinnah" are coverings, plural of "kinan," like "asinnah" and "sinan." One says "kanantu al-shay' fi kunhin" when you put a thing into something, and "akננtuhu" when you hide it. The clause ﴿We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾ is either a fresh statement informing of its content, or in a place of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal): that is, while We have placed over their hearts coverings, out of aversion to their understanding the Qur'an, or lest they understand it. "Waqr" is deafness; it is said: "wuqirat udhunuhu, yaqirru waqran," meaning, his ear became deaf.

Talhah ibn Musarrif read "wiqran" with a kasra on the waw, meaning: He placed in their ears what blocked them from hearing speech, by analogy with the load (wiqr) of a camel, which is the amount it is able to carry. The mention of the coverings and the deafness is a parable for the extreme remoteness of their hearts from understanding and hearing the truth, as though their hearts do not reason and their ears do not perceive. ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾, meaning they will not believe in any of the signs they see, such as miracles and the like, because of their obstinacy and rebelliousness.

His saying: ﴿Until, when they come to you disputing with you, those who disbelieve say, "This is not but the legends of the former peoples."﴾ Here "hatta" is the inceptive "hatta" which is followed by sentences. The clause "yujadilunaka" (disputing with you) is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause. The meaning: they reached such a degree of disbelief and obstinacy that when they come to you disputing, they do not suffice with merely not believing, but they say, "This is not but the legends of the former peoples." It has also been said: "hatta" here is the prepositional "hatta" (until), and what follows is in the genitive place. The meaning: until the time of their coming disputing, they say, "This is not but the legends of the former peoples." This is the utmost of denial and the extremity of obstinacy.

"Al-asatir" (legends):
Al-Zajjaj said: its singular is "asfar."
Al-Akhfash said: "usturah."
Abu Ubaydah said: "asarah."
Al-Nahhas said: "ustur."
Al-Qushayri said: "usteer."
It has also been said: it is a plural with no singular, like "aba'id" and "ababil." The meaning: what the former peoples inscribed in books of stories and narratives.

Al-Jawhari said: "al-asatir" are falsehoods and trifles.

His saying: ﴿And they forbid it and keep away from it﴾, meaning the polytheists forbid people from believing in the Qur'an or in Muhammad (ﷺ), and they themselves keep far from it in their own selves.

It has also been said: it was revealed concerning Abu Talib, for he used to forbid the disbelievers from harming the Prophet (ﷺ), while he himself kept away from responding to him. ﴿And they destroy none but themselves, and they perceive not﴾, meaning they destroy none but themselves by what they do of forbidding and keeping away, exposing themselves to the punishment and wrath of God, while they are unaware that they have brought this calamity upon themselves.

His saying: ﴿If you could but see when they are made to stand before the Fire﴾. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or to everyone who is able to see. He expressed the future Day of Resurrection with the past tense to alert to the certainty of its occurrence, as the scholars of semantics (ulama' al-ma'ani) mentioned. "Wuqifu" means they were detained. One says "waqaftuhu waqfan" and "waqafa wuqufan." It has also been said: the meaning of ﴿they were made to stand before the Fire﴾ is that they were made to enter it, so "ala" is in the sense of "fi" (in). It has also been said: it is in the sense of "ba'" (with): that is, they were made to stand by the Fire, that is, near it, witnessing it. The object of "tara" (you see) is omitted, and the apodosis of "law" (if) is omitted so that the hearer may go in every direction. The estimate is: if you could see them when they are made to stand before the Fire, you would see a dreadful sight and a horrible state. ﴿Then they will say, "Oh, if only we could be returned"﴾, meaning to the world, ﴿and not deny the signs of our Lord﴾, meaning those which His Messenger (ﷺ) brought to us, ﴿and be among the believers﴾ in them, acting upon what is in them. The three verbs fall under the wish (tamanni): that is, they wished to be returned, and not to deny, and to be among the believers. The three verbs are with the nominative, as is the reading of al-Kisa'i, the people of Madinah, Shu'bah, Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr.

Hafs and Hamzah read "naku<u>dh</u>iba" and "nakuna" in the accusative, by implying "an" after the waw, in answer to the wish. Sibawayh preferred the cutting-off (qat') in "wa la nukadhdhibu," so that it is not included in the wish, and the estimate is: "while we do not deny," in the sense of persisting in not denying: that is, "do not deny, whether we were returned or not." He said: it is like "da'ni wa la a'ud" (leave me, and I will not return): that is, I will not return in any state, whether you leave me or do not leave me.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' used as evidence for its being outside the wish His saying: ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾, because lying does not occur in a wish.

Ibn 'Amir read "wa nakuna" in the accusative and included the first two verbs in the wish.

Ubayy read "wa la nukadhdhibu bi-ayati rabbina abadan" (and we would never deny the signs of our Lord).

He and Ibn Mas'ud read "ya laytana nuraddu fa la nukadhdhiba" with the fa' and the accusative. The fa' is one with which the accusative occurs in the answer to the wish, just as it occurs with the waw, as al-Zajjaj said. Most of the Basrans said: the answer is only with the fa'.

His saying: ﴿Rather, there has appeared to them what they used to conceal before﴾. This is a turning away (idrab) from what the wish indicates of promise of belief and affirmation: that is, that wish did not come from them with sincere intention and pure conviction; rather, it is for another reason, namely that there appeared to them what they used to conceal, that is, what they used to deny of polytheism, and they knew that they would perish because of their polytheism, so they turned to wishing and false promises. It has also been said: there appeared to them what they used to conceal of hypocrisy and disbelief, as attested by their own limbs against them. It has also been said: there appeared to them what they used to hide of their ugly deeds, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And there will appear to them from God that which they had not been reckoning﴾ [al-Zumar 39:47].

Al-Mubarrad said: there appeared to them the recompense of their disbelief which they used to conceal, and this is like the first statement. It has also been said: the meaning is that there became apparent to those who followed the misguided leaders what the leaders used to conceal from them regarding the matter of the Resurrection and the Last Day; and if they were returned to the world as they wished, they would return to doing what they had been forbidden of ugly deeds, the chief of which is polytheism, just as Iblis witnessed what he witnessed of God's signs and then was obstinate. ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾, that is, they are characterized by this attribute and do not depart from it in any state, even if they witnessed what they witnessed. It has also been said: the meaning is: and indeed they are liars in what they report about themselves of truthfulness and belief.

Yahya ibn Wathhab read "wa law ridduu" with a kasra on the ra' because the original is "radadu," so the kasra of the dal was transferred to the ra'. The clause ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the coordinated element, which is ﴿and they said﴾, and the element coordinated with, which is ﴿they would have returned﴾: that is, they would have returned to what they had been forbidden.

﴿And they said, "There is not but our worldly life"﴾, meaning: there is not but our worldly life, and we will not be resurrected after death. This is from the extremity of their rebelliousness and obstinacy, since they say this statement on the assumption that they had returned to the world after witnessing the Resurrection.

His saying: ﴿And if you could but see when they are made to stand before their Lord﴾. Its explanation has already preceded in his saying: ﴿And if you could but see when they are made to stand before the Fire﴾ [al-An'am 6:27]: that is, they were detained for what will be decided for them by their Lord. It has also been said: "ala" is in the sense of "'inda" (before). The apodosis of "law" is omitted: that is, you would witness a tremendous matter. The interrogative in ﴿Is this not the truth?﴾ is for reproach and rebuke: that is, is not this Resurrection, which they deny, existent and occurring, and this recompense, which they reject, present?

They say, "Yes, by our Lord." They acknowledged what they had denied, and confirmed their acknowledgment with an oath. He said: ﴿So taste the punishment, for what you used to disbelieve﴾, that is, the punishment of the Fire, which you witness, because of your disbelief in Him, or for everything you were commanded to believe in during the life of the world.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 22–32 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying: ﴿And the Day We will gather them﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read the two verbs with the nun (first person plural). It was also read with the ya' (third person) in both. The adverbial complement of time (nasib al-zarf) is an implied, delayed element: "On the Day We gather them, such-and-such will happen." The interrogative in ﴿Where are your partners﴾ is for reproach and rebuke of the polytheists.

He attributed the "partners" to them, because they were not in reality partners of God. Rather, since they named them partners, they were attributed to them. They are what they used to worship besides God, or what they worshipped alongside God.

His saying: ﴿whom you used to claim﴾, meaning, you used to claim them to be partners. Both objects are omitted together. The reason the interrogation carries rebuke is that their objects of worship were absent from them at that time, or were present but of no benefit to them in any way. Thus their existence was like their non-existence.

His saying: ﴿Then their trial would be only that they said, "By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾

Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj) said: The interpretation of this verse is that God, Mighty and Majestic, informed of the accounts of the polytheists and their being tested by their polytheism. Then He informed that their trial was not, until they saw the realities, except that they disowned polytheism. A parallel in the language is that you see a person who loves a deviant, and when he falls into ruin he disavows him, so you say: "Your love for him was only that you would disown him." End.

So the meaning of "trial" here is their disbelief: that is, the outcome of their disbelief, in which they took pride and for which they fought, was nothing but the denial and oath of disavowal in his saying: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists.﴾ It has also been said: the meaning of "trial" here is their answer. That is, their answer was nothing but denial and disavowal, so this answer was a trial because it was a lie. The clause ﴿Then their trial was not﴾ is coordinated with the governing element of the implied temporal adverb, as has passed. The exception is an incomplete exception (istithna' mufarragh), i.e., one in which the excepted element takes the role of the omitted subject or object. "Trial" (fitnatuhum) has been read in the nominative and accusative, and "yakun" and "takun" (both "was/were" forms) are read; the reading is clear.

It was also read: "wa ma kana fitnatuhum." And "rabbana" was read in the accusative as a vocative (nida').

﴿See how they lied against themselves﴾ by denying what they had done of polytheism in the world. ﴿And lost from them is what they used to invent﴾, meaning their invention departed, vanished, dissipated, and was nullified: what they used to presume, that the partners would bring them closer to God. This is on the basis that "ma" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah). It has also been said that it is a relative pronoun referring to the deities: that is, what they used to worship besides God departed from them, so it gave them no benefit at all. This is an expression of wonder for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at their varied conditions and contradictory claims. It has also been said: it is not possible that they would lie in the Hereafter, because it is an abode in which nothing but truth takes place. So the meaning of ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ is the denial of their polytheism in their own selves and in their belief. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they will not conceal from God any statement﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:42].

His saying: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾. This is a new statement explaining what some of the polytheists used to do in the world. The pronoun refers to "those who associated partners." That is: some of those who associated partners listen to you when you recite the Qur'an. ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾, meaning We did that to them as recompense for their disbelief. "Akinnah" are coverings, plural of "kinan," like "asinnah" and "sinan." One says "kanantu al-shay' fi kunhin" when you put a thing into something, and "akננtuhu" when you hide it. The clause ﴿We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾ is either a fresh statement informing of its content, or in a place of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal): that is, while We have placed over their hearts coverings, out of aversion to their understanding the Qur'an, or lest they understand it. "Waqr" is deafness; it is said: "wuqirat udhunuhu, yaqirru waqran," meaning, his ear became deaf.

Talhah ibn Musarrif read "wiqran" with a kasra on the waw, meaning: He placed in their ears what blocked them from hearing speech, by analogy with the load (wiqr) of a camel, which is the amount it is able to carry. The mention of the coverings and the deafness is a parable for the extreme remoteness of their hearts from understanding and hearing the truth, as though their hearts do not reason and their ears do not perceive. ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾, meaning they will not believe in any of the signs they see, such as miracles and the like, because of their obstinacy and rebelliousness.

His saying: ﴿Until, when they come to you disputing with you, those who disbelieve say, "This is not but the legends of the former peoples."﴾ Here "hatta" is the inceptive "hatta" which is followed by sentences. The clause "yujadilunaka" (disputing with you) is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause. The meaning: they reached such a degree of disbelief and obstinacy that when they come to you disputing, they do not suffice with merely not believing, but they say, "This is not but the legends of the former peoples." It has also been said: "hatta" here is the prepositional "hatta" (until), and what follows is in the genitive place. The meaning: until the time of their coming disputing, they say, "This is not but the legends of the former peoples." This is the utmost of denial and the extremity of obstinacy.

"Al-asatir" (legends):
Al-Zajjaj said: its singular is "asfar."
Al-Akhfash said: "usturah."
Abu Ubaydah said: "asarah."
Al-Nahhas said: "ustur."
Al-Qushayri said: "usteer."
It has also been said: it is a plural with no singular, like "aba'id" and "ababil." The meaning: what the former peoples inscribed in books of stories and narratives.

Al-Jawhari said: "al-asatir" are falsehoods and trifles.

His saying: ﴿And they forbid it and keep away from it﴾, meaning the polytheists forbid people from believing in the Qur'an or in Muhammad (ﷺ), and they themselves keep far from it in their own selves.

It has also been said: it was revealed concerning Abu Talib, for he used to forbid the disbelievers from harming the Prophet (ﷺ), while he himself kept away from responding to him. ﴿And they destroy none but themselves, and they perceive not﴾, meaning they destroy none but themselves by what they do of forbidding and keeping away, exposing themselves to the punishment and wrath of God, while they are unaware that they have brought this calamity upon themselves.

His saying: ﴿If you could but see when they are made to stand before the Fire﴾. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or to everyone who is able to see. He expressed the future Day of Resurrection with the past tense to alert to the certainty of its occurrence, as the scholars of semantics (ulama' al-ma'ani) mentioned. "Wuqifu" means they were detained. One says "waqaftuhu waqfan" and "waqafa wuqufan." It has also been said: the meaning of ﴿they were made to stand before the Fire﴾ is that they were made to enter it, so "ala" is in the sense of "fi" (in). It has also been said: it is in the sense of "ba'" (with): that is, they were made to stand by the Fire, that is, near it, witnessing it. The object of "tara" (you see) is omitted, and the apodosis of "law" (if) is omitted so that the hearer may go in every direction. The estimate is: if you could see them when they are made to stand before the Fire, you would see a dreadful sight and a horrible state. ﴿Then they will say, "Oh, if only we could be returned"﴾, meaning to the world, ﴿and not deny the signs of our Lord﴾, meaning those which His Messenger (ﷺ) brought to us, ﴿and be among the believers﴾ in them, acting upon what is in them. The three verbs fall under the wish (tamanni): that is, they wished to be returned, and not to deny, and to be among the believers. The three verbs are with the nominative, as is the reading of al-Kisa'i, the people of Madinah, Shu'bah, Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr.

Hafs and Hamzah read "naku<u>dh</u>iba" and "nakuna" in the accusative, by implying "an" after the waw, in answer to the wish. Sibawayh preferred the cutting-off (qat') in "wa la nukadhdhibu," so that it is not included in the wish, and the estimate is: "while we do not deny," in the sense of persisting in not denying: that is, "do not deny, whether we were returned or not." He said: it is like "da'ni wa la a'ud" (leave me, and I will not return): that is, I will not return in any state, whether you leave me or do not leave me.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' used as evidence for its being outside the wish His saying: ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾, because lying does not occur in a wish.

Ibn 'Amir read "wa nakuna" in the accusative and included the first two verbs in the wish.

Ubayy read "wa la nukadhdhibu bi-ayati rabbina abadan" (and we would never deny the signs of our Lord).

He and Ibn Mas'ud read "ya laytana nuraddu fa la nukadhdhiba" with the fa' and the accusative. The fa' is one with which the accusative occurs in the answer to the wish, just as it occurs with the waw, as al-Zajjaj said. Most of the Basrans said: the answer is only with the fa'.

His saying: ﴿Rather, there has appeared to them what they used to conceal before﴾. This is a turning away (idrab) from what the wish indicates of promise of belief and affirmation: that is, that wish did not come from them with sincere intention and pure conviction; rather, it is for another reason, namely that there appeared to them what they used to conceal, that is, what they used to deny of polytheism, and they knew that they would perish because of their polytheism, so they turned to wishing and false promises. "Trial" (fitnatuhum) has been read in the nominative and accusative, and "yakun" and "takun" (both "was/were" forms) are read; the reading is clear.

It was also read: "wa ma kana fitnatuhum." And "rabbana" was read in the accusative as a vocative (nida').

﴿See how they lied against themselves﴾ by denying what they had done of polytheism in the world. ﴿And lost from them is what they used to invent﴾, meaning their invention departed, vanished, dissipated, and was nullified: what they used to presume, that the partners would bring them closer to God. This is on the basis that "ma" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah). It has also been said that it is a relative pronoun referring to the deities: that is, what they used to worship besides God departed from them, so it gave them no benefit at all. This is an expression of wonder for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at their varied conditions and contradictory claims. It has also been said: it is not possible that they would lie in the Hereafter, because it is an abode in which nothing but truth takes place. So the meaning of ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ is the denial of their polytheism in their own selves and in their belief. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they will not conceal from God any statement﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:42].

His saying: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾. This is a new statement explaining what some of the polytheists used to do in the world. The pronoun refers to "those who associated partners." That is: some of those who associated partners listen to you when you recite the Qur'an. ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾, meaning We did that to them as recompense for their disbelief. "Waqr" is deafness; it is said: "wuqirat udhunuhu, yaqirru waqran," meaning, his ear became deaf.

Talhah ibn Musarrif read "wiqran" with a kasra on the waw, meaning: He placed in their ears what blocked them from hearing speech, by analogy with the load (wiqr) of a camel, which is the amount it is able to carry. The mention of the coverings and the deafness is a parable for the extreme remoteness of their hearts from understanding and hearing the truth, as though their hearts do not reason and their ears do not perceive. ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾, meaning they will not believe in any of the signs they see, such as miracles and the like, because of their obstinacy and rebelliousness.

The clause "yujadilunaka" (disputing with you) is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause. The meaning: they reached such a degree of disbelief and obstinacy that when they come to you disputing, they do not suffice with merely not believing, but they say, "This is not but the legends of the former peoples." It has also been said: "hatta" here is the prepositional "hatta" (until), and what follows is in the genitive place. Al-Zajjaj said: its singular is "asfar."
Al-Akhfash said: "usturah."
Abu Ubaydah said: "asarah."
Al-Nahhas said: "ustur."
Al-Qushayri said: "usteer."
It has also been said: it is a plural with no singular, like "aba'id" and "ababil." The meaning: what the former peoples inscribed in books of stories and narratives.

Al-Jawhari said: "al-asatir" are falsehoods and trifles.

His saying: ﴿And they forbid it and keep away from it﴾, meaning the polytheists forbid people from believing in the Qur'an or in Muhammad (ﷺ), and they themselves keep far from it in their own selves.

It has also been said: it was revealed concerning Abu Talib, for he used to forbid the disbelievers from harming the Prophet (ﷺ), while he himself kept away from responding to him. ﴿And they destroy none but themselves, and they perceive not﴾, meaning they destroy none but themselves by what they do of forbidding and keeping away, exposing themselves to the punishment and wrath of God, while they are unaware that they have brought this calamity upon themselves.

He expressed the future Day of Resurrection with the past tense to alert to the certainty of its occurrence, as the scholars of semantics (ulama' al-ma'ani) mentioned. It has also been said: the meaning of ﴿they were made to stand before the Fire﴾ is that they were made to enter it, so "ala" is in the sense of "fi" (in). It has also been said: it is in the sense of "ba'" (with): that is, they were made to stand by the Fire, that is, near it, witnessing it. The object of "tara" (you see) is omitted, and the apodosis of "law" (if) is omitted so that the hearer may go in every direction. The estimate is: if you could see them when they are made to stand before the Fire, you would see a dreadful sight and a horrible state. ﴿Then they will say, "Oh, if only we could be returned"﴾, meaning to the world, ﴿and not deny the signs of our Lord﴾, meaning those which His Messenger (ﷺ) brought to us, ﴿and be among the believers﴾ in them, acting upon what is in them. The three verbs fall under the wish (tamanni): that is, they wished to be returned, and not to deny, and to be among the believers. The three verbs are with the nominative, as is the reading of al-Kisa'i, the people of Madinah, Shu'bah, Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr.

Hafs and Hamzah read "naku<u>dh</u>iba" and "nakuna" in the accusative, by implying "an" after the waw, in answer to the wish. Sibawayh preferred the cutting-off (qat') in "wa la nukadhdhibu," so that it is not included in the wish, and the estimate is: "while we do not deny," in the sense of persisting in not denying: that is, "do not deny, whether we were returned or not." He said: it is like "da'ni wa la a'ud" (leave me, and I will not return): that is, I will not return in any state, whether you leave me or do not leave me.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' used as evidence for its being outside the wish His saying: ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾, because lying does not occur in a wish.

Ibn 'Amir read "wa nakuna" in the accusative and included the first two verbs in the wish.

Ubayy read "wa la nukadhdhibu bi-ayati rabbina abadan" (and we would never deny the signs of our Lord).

His saying: ﴿Rather, there has appeared to them what they used to conceal before﴾. This is a turning away (idrab) from what the wish indicates of promise of belief and affirmation: that is, that wish did not come from them with sincere intention and pure conviction; rather, it is for another reason, namely that there appeared to them what they used to conceal, that is, what they used to deny of polytheism, and they knew that they would perish because of their polytheism, so they turned to wishing and false promises. It has also been said: there appeared to them what they used to conceal of hypocrisy and disbelief, as attested by their own limbs against them. It has also been said: there appeared to them what they used to hide of their ugly deeds, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And there will appear to them from God that which they had not been reckoning﴾ [al-Zumar 39:47].

Al-Mubarrad said: there appeared to them the recompense of their disbelief which they used to conceal, and this is like the first statement. It has also been said: the meaning is that there became apparent to those who followed the misguided leaders what the leaders used to conceal from them regarding the matter of the Resurrection and the Last Day; and if they were returned to the world as they wished, they would return to doing what they had been forbidden of ugly deeds, the chief of which is polytheism, just as Iblis witnessed what he witnessed of God's signs and then was obstinate. ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾, that is, they are characterized by this attribute and do not depart from it in any state, even if they witnessed what they witnessed. It has also been said: the meaning is: and indeed they are liars in what they report about themselves of truthfulness and belief.

Yahya ibn Wathhab read "wa law ridduu" with a kasra on the ra' because the original is "radadu," so the kasra of the dal was transferred to the ra'. The clause ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the coordinated element, which is ﴿and they said﴾, and the element coordinated with, which is ﴿they would have returned﴾: that is, they would have returned to what they had been forbidden.

﴿And they said, "There is not but our worldly life"﴾, meaning: there is not but our worldly life, and we will not be resurrected after death. This is from the extremity of their rebelliousness and obstinacy, since they say this statement on the assumption that they had returned to the world after witnessing the Resurrection.

His saying: ﴿And if you could but see when they are made to stand before their Lord﴾. Its explanation has already preceded in his saying: ﴿And if you could but see when they are made to stand before the Fire﴾ [al-An'am 6:27]: that is, they were detained for what will be decided for them by their Lord. It has also been said: "ala" is in the sense of "'inda" (before). The apodosis of "law" is omitted: that is, you would witness a tremendous matter. The interrogative in ﴿Is this not the truth?﴾ is for reproach and rebuke: that is, is not this Resurrection, which they deny, existent and occurring, and this recompense, which they reject, present?

They say, "Yes, by our Lord." They acknowledged what they had denied, and confirmed their acknowledgment with an oath. He said: ﴿So taste the punishment, for what you used to disbelieve﴾, that is, the punishment of the Fire, which you witness, because of your disbelief in Him, or for everything you were commanded to believe in during the life of the world.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding his saying: ﴿Then their trial would not be﴾, that he said: "their excuse."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him: ﴿Then their trial would not be﴾, he said: "their argument," ﴿except that they said, "By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists"﴾, meaning the hypocrites and the polytheists, who said while they were in the Fire: "Come, let us lie, perhaps it will benefit us." So God said: ﴿See how they lied against themselves and lost from them﴾ on the Day of Resurrection ﴿what they used to invent﴾, meaning what they used to lie about in the world.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him regarding his saying: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾, then He said: ﴿and they will not conceal from God any statement﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:42]. He said: "by their limbs."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah: ﴿See how they lied against themselves﴾, he said: "by their false excuse." ﴿And lost from them what they used to invent﴾, he said: "what they used to associate (with God)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding his saying: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾, he said: "the Quraysh." And regarding his saying: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾, he said: "like the quiver for arrows."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah regarding his saying: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness﴾, he said: "They hear it with their ears but retain nothing of it, like the beast that does not hear the call and does not understand what is said to it."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi that he said: "The covering (al-ghita') is what shut their hearts so that they could not understand it. The deafness (al-waqr) is deafness. Asatir al-awwalin (the tales of the ancients) are the idle words (asajii') of the ancients."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Asatir al-awwalin: the stories (ahadith) of the ancients."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada that he said: "Asatir al-awwalin: the lies (kadhib) of the ancients and their falsehood (batil)."

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il (Proofs of Prophethood) related from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿and they forbid it and keep away from it﴾, that he said: "It was revealed concerning Abu Talib. He used to forbid the polytheists from harming the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he would keep away from what he had brought."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymira a similar report.

Ibn Jarir related from Ata' a similar report as well.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas, concerning the verse, that he said: "They forbid people from it, from believing in it, and they keep away from it: they distance themselves."

Ibn Jarir related through al-Awfi from him that he said: "They do not meet it (the Messenger), and they do not let anyone who would come to him go."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya concerning the verse that he said: "The disbelievers of Makkah used to push people away from him and not respond to him."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid a similar report.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada that he said: "They forbid the Qur'an and the Prophet (ﷺ), and they keep away from it: they distance themselves from it."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal concerning the verse that he said: "It was revealed concerning the paternal uncles of the Prophet (ﷺ), and they were ten. They were the most supportive of people towards him in public, and the most hostile of people towards him in private."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada, concerning His saying ﴿Rather, there has appeared to them what they used to conceal before﴾, that he said: "From their deeds." ﴿And even if they were returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden﴾ means: "Even if Allah were to grant them a worldly life like the worldly life they had before, they would return to their deeds, the evil deeds they had been forbidden from."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Allah, glorified is He, informed that if they were returned, they would not be able to attain guidance. So He said: ﴿Even if they were returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden﴾, meaning: even if they were returned to the world, guidance would be barred between them and themselves just as it was barred between them and it the first time, while they were in the world."

Yahya ibn Wathhab read "wa law ridduu" with a kasra on the ra' because the original is "radadu," so the kasra of the dal was transferred to the ra'. The clause ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the coordinated element, which is ﴿and they said﴾, and the element coordinated with, which is ﴿they would have returned﴾: that is, they would have returned to what they had been forbidden.

﴿And they said, "There is not but our worldly life"﴾, meaning: there is not but our worldly life, and we will not be resurrected after death. This is from the extremity of their rebelliousness and obstinacy, since they say this statement on the assumption that they had returned to the world after witnessing the Resurrection.

His saying: ﴿And if you could but see when they are made to stand before their Lord﴾. Its explanation has already preceded in his saying: ﴿And if you could but see when they are made to stand before the Fire﴾ [al-An'am 6:27]: that is, they were detained for what will be decided for them by their Lord. It has also been said: "ala" is in the sense of "'inda" (before). The apodosis of "law" is omitted: that is, you would witness a tremendous matter. The interrogative in ﴿Is this not the truth?﴾ is for reproach and rebuke: that is, is not this Resurrection, which they deny, existent and occurring, and this recompense, which they reject, present?

They say, "Yes, by our Lord." They acknowledged what they had denied, and confirmed their acknowledgment with an oath. He said: ﴿So taste the punishment, for what you used to disbelieve﴾, that is, the punishment of the Fire, which you witness, because of your disbelief in Him, or for everything you were commanded to believe in during the life of the world.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding his saying: ﴿Then their trial would not be﴾, that he said: "their excuse."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 22–32 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying: ﴿And the Day We will gather them﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read the two verbs with the nun (first person plural). It was also read with the ya' (third person) in both. The adverbial complement of time (nasib al-zarf) is an implied, delayed element: "On the Day We gather them, such-and-such will happen." The interrogative in ﴿Where are your partners﴾ is for reproach and rebuke of the polytheists.

He attributed the "partners" to them, because they were not in reality partners of God. Rather, since they named them partners, they were attributed to them. They are what they used to worship besides God, or what they worshipped alongside God.

His saying: ﴿whom you used to claim﴾, meaning, you used to claim them to be partners. Both objects are omitted together. The reason the interrogation carries rebuke is that their objects of worship were absent from them at that time, or were present but of no benefit to them in any way. Thus their existence was like their non-existence.

His saying: ﴿Then their trial would be only that they said, "By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists."﴾

Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj) said: The interpretation of this verse is that God, Mighty and Majestic, informed of the accounts of the polytheists and their being tested by their polytheism. Then He informed that their trial was not, until they saw the realities, except that they disowned polytheism. A parallel in the language is that you see a person who loves a deviant, and when he falls into ruin he disavows him, so you say: "Your love for him was only that you would disown him." End.

So the meaning of "trial" here is their disbelief: that is, the outcome of their disbelief, in which they took pride and for which they fought, was nothing but the denial and oath of disavowal in his saying: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists.﴾ It has also been said: the meaning of "trial" here is their answer. That is, their answer was nothing but denial and disavowal, so this answer was a trial because it was a lie. The clause ﴿Then their trial was not﴾ is coordinated with the governing element of the implied temporal adverb, as has passed. The exception is an incomplete exception (istithna' mufarragh), i.e., one in which the excepted element takes the role of the omitted subject or object. "Trial" (fitnatuhum) has been read in the nominative and accusative, and "yakun" and "takun" (both "was/were" forms) are read; the reading is clear.

It was also read: "wa ma kana fitnatuhum." And "rabbana" was read in the accusative as a vocative (nida').

﴿See how they lied against themselves﴾ by denying what they had done of polytheism in the world. ﴿And lost from them is what they used to invent﴾, meaning their invention departed, vanished, dissipated, and was nullified: what they used to presume, that the partners would bring them closer to God. This is on the basis that "ma" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah). It has also been said that it is a relative pronoun referring to the deities: that is, what they used to worship besides God departed from them, so it gave them no benefit at all. This is an expression of wonder for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at their varied conditions and contradictory claims. It has also been said: it is not possible that they would lie in the Hereafter, because it is an abode in which nothing but truth takes place. So the meaning of ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ is the denial of their polytheism in their own selves and in their belief. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they will not conceal from God any statement﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:42].

His saying: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾. This is a new statement explaining what some of the polytheists used to do in the world. The pronoun refers to "those who associated partners." That is: some of those who associated partners listen to you when you recite the Qur'an. ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾, meaning We did that to them as recompense for their disbelief. "Akinnah" are coverings, plural of "kinan," like "asinnah" and "sinan." One says "kanantu al-shay' fi kunhin" when you put a thing into something, and "akננtuhu" when you hide it. The clause ﴿We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾ is either a fresh statement informing of its content, or in a place of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal): that is, while We have placed over their hearts coverings, out of aversion to their understanding the Qur'an, or lest they understand it. "Waqr" is deafness; it is said: "wuqirat udhunuhu, yaqirru waqran," meaning, his ear became deaf.

Talhah ibn Musarrif read "wiqran" with a kasra on the waw, meaning: He placed in their ears what blocked them from hearing speech, by analogy with the load (wiqr) of a camel, which is the amount it is able to carry. The mention of the coverings and the deafness is a parable for the extreme remoteness of their hearts from understanding and hearing the truth, as though their hearts do not reason and their ears do not perceive. ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾, meaning they will not believe in any of the signs they see, such as miracles and the like, because of their obstinacy and rebelliousness.

His saying: ﴿Until, when they come to you disputing with you, those who disbelieve say, "This is not but the legends of the former peoples."﴾ Here "hatta" is the inceptive "hatta" which is followed by sentences. The clause "yujadilunaka" (disputing with you) is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause. The meaning: they reached such a degree of disbelief and obstinacy that when they come to you disputing, they do not suffice with merely not believing, but they say, "This is not but the legends of the former peoples." It has also been said: "hatta" here is the prepositional "hatta" (until), and what follows is in the genitive place. The meaning: until the time of their coming disputing, they say, "This is not but the legends of the former peoples." This is the utmost of denial and the extremity of obstinacy.

"Al-asatir" (legends):
Al-Zajjaj said: its singular is "asfar."
Al-Akhfash said: "usturah."
Abu Ubaydah said: "asarah."
Al-Nahhas said: "ustur."
Al-Qushayri said: "usteer."
It has also been said: it is a plural with no singular, like "aba'id" and "ababil." The meaning: what the former peoples inscribed in books of stories and narratives.

Al-Jawhari said: "al-asatir" are falsehoods and trifles.

His saying: ﴿And they forbid it and keep away from it﴾, meaning the polytheists forbid people from believing in the Qur'an or in Muhammad (ﷺ), and they themselves keep far from it in their own selves.

It has also been said: it was revealed concerning Abu Talib, for he used to forbid the disbelievers from harming the Prophet (ﷺ), while he himself kept away from responding to him. ﴿And they destroy none but themselves, and they perceive not﴾, meaning they destroy none but themselves by what they do of forbidding and keeping away, exposing themselves to the punishment and wrath of God, while they are unaware that they have brought this calamity upon themselves.

His saying: ﴿If you could but see when they are made to stand before the Fire﴾. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or to everyone who is able to see. He expressed the future Day of Resurrection with the past tense to alert to the certainty of its occurrence, as the scholars of semantics (ulama' al-ma'ani) mentioned. "Wuqifu" means they were detained. One says "waqaftuhu waqfan" and "waqafa wuqufan." It has also been said: the meaning of ﴿they were made to stand before the Fire﴾ is that they were made to enter it, so "ala" is in the sense of "fi" (in). It has also been said: it is in the sense of "ba'" (with): that is, they were made to stand by the Fire, that is, near it, witnessing it. The object of "tara" (you see) is omitted, and the apodosis of "law" (if) is omitted so that the hearer may go in every direction. The estimate is: if you could see them when they are made to stand before the Fire, you would see a dreadful sight and a horrible state. ﴿Then they will say, "Oh, if only we could be returned"﴾, meaning to the world, ﴿and not deny the signs of our Lord﴾, meaning those which His Messenger (ﷺ) brought to us, ﴿and be among the believers﴾ in them, acting upon what is in them. The three verbs fall under the wish (tamanni): that is, they wished to be returned, and not to deny, and to be among the believers. The three verbs are with the nominative, as is the reading of al-Kisa'i, the people of Madinah, Shu'bah, Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr.

Hafs and Hamzah read "naku<u>dh</u>iba" and "nakuna" in the accusative, by implying "an" after the waw, in answer to the wish. Sibawayh preferred the cutting-off (qat') in "wa la nukadhdhibu," so that it is not included in the wish, and the estimate is: "while we do not deny," in the sense of persisting in not denying: that is, "do not deny, whether we were returned or not." He said: it is like "da'ni wa la a'ud" (leave me, and I will not return): that is, I will not return in any state, whether you leave me or do not leave me.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' used as evidence for its being outside the wish His saying: ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾, because lying does not occur in a wish.

Ibn 'Amir read "wa nakuna" in the accusative and included the first two verbs in the wish.

Ubayy read "wa la nukadhdhibu bi-ayati rabbina abadan" (and we would never deny the signs of our Lord).

He and Ibn Mas'ud read "ya laytana nuraddu fa la nukadhdhiba" with the fa' and the accusative. The fa' is one with which the accusative occurs in the answer to the wish, just as it occurs with the waw, as al-Zajjaj said. Most of the Basrans said: the answer is only with the fa'.

His saying: ﴿Rather, there has appeared to them what they used to conceal before﴾. This is a turning away (idrab) from what the wish indicates of promise of belief and affirmation: that is, that wish did not come from them with sincere intention and pure conviction; rather, it is for another reason, namely that there appeared to them what they used to conceal, that is, what they used to deny of polytheism, and they knew that they would perish because of their polytheism, so they turned to wishing and false promises. Al-Mubarrad said: there appeared to them the recompense of their disbelief which they used to conceal, and this is like the first statement. ﴿And they said, "There is not but our worldly life"﴾, meaning: there is not but our worldly life, and we will not be resurrected after death. This is from the extremity of their rebelliousness and obstinacy, since they say this statement on the assumption that they had returned to the world after witnessing the Resurrection.

His saying: ﴿And if you could but see when they are made to stand before their Lord﴾. It has also been said: "ala" is in the sense of "'inda" (before). The apodosis of "law" is omitted: that is, you would witness a tremendous matter. The interrogative in ﴿Is this not the truth?﴾ is for reproach and rebuke: that is, is not this Resurrection, which they deny, existent and occurring, and this recompense, which they reject, present?

They say, "Yes, by our Lord." They acknowledged what they had denied, and confirmed their acknowledgment with an oath. He said: ﴿So taste the punishment, for what you used to disbelieve﴾, that is, the punishment of the Fire, which you witness, because of your disbelief in Him, or for everything you were commanded to believe in during the life of the world.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding his saying: ﴿Then their trial would not be﴾, that he said: "their excuse."
