﴿And He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾: creating them with truth, or while the creation is in truth. So how do you worship idols, which are themselves created?

He said: ﴿And the day He says, "Be," and it is, [His word is the truth]﴾. ﴿His word is the truth﴾ means: remember the day when He says, "Be," and it is; or, fear the day when He says, "Be," and it is. It was also said that it is a conjunction (ʿatf) with the pronoun in *wa-ittaquhu* (﴿and fear Him﴾). It was also said that *yawma* (the day) is an adverbial of time (ẓarf) governed by the sense of the clause ﴿His word is the truth﴾, and the meaning is: His command, which relates to things. *Al-Ḥaqq* (the truth) means: the one for whom it is witnessed that it is true. It was also said that *qawluhu* (His word) is the subject (mubtadaʾ), *al-ḥaqq* is its qualifier (ṣifah), and ﴿and the day He says, "Be," and it is﴾ is its predicate (khabar), placed before it. The meaning is: His word, qualified by truth, exists on the day when He says, "Be," and it is. It was also said that *qawluhu* is raised by *yakūnu* (it is), and *al-ḥaqq* is its qualifier, that is: on the day He says "Be," His word, the truth, will be.

Ibn ʿĀmir read *fa-nakūnu* with the nūn (we), and this indicates the speed of the reckoning. The rest read it with the yāʾ (he), which is the correct reading.

He said: ﴿And His is the dominion on the day the Trumpet is blown﴾. The adverbial (ẓarf) is in the accusative, governed by what precedes it, that is: His is the dominion on this day. It was also said that it is a substitution (badal) for the first *yawm* (day). *Al-Ṣūr* (the Trumpet) is a horn into which the first blast is blown for annihilation and the second for re-creation. Al-Jawharī likewise said that *al-ṣūr* is the horn. The rajaz poet said:

*"We struck them on the morning of the two hosts, a violent strike, not like the strike of the two horns."*

*Al-Ṣūr* is pronounced with a ḍammah or a kasrah on the ṣād, as dialectal forms. It is reported from ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd that he read *yawma yunfakhu fī al-ṣuwar* with the wāw vowelled, as the plural of *ṣūrah* (form), and the intended meaning is creation. Abū ʿUbaydah said: this, although possible, is rejected by what is in the Book and the Sunnah. Al-Farrāʾ said: *kun fa-yakūn* is said to refer to the Trumpet specifically, that is: and on the day He says to the Trumpet, "Be," and it is.

He said: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. *ʿĀlimu* is raised because it is a qualifier of *alladhī khalaqa al-samāwāti wa-al-arḍ* (He who created the heavens and the earth). It is also permissible that it be raised by supposing an implied subject: that is, He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed. It is reported from some of them that he read *yanfukhu* with the active form, and on this reading the subject may be ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾. It is also permissible that it be raised by an implied verb, as Sībawayh cited:

*"At your call, Yazid, a suppliant for a dispute, and one who is struck by what the calamities cast down."*

That is: *yubkīhi mukhtabiṭun* (one who is struck weeps for him).

Al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿmash read *ʿālimi* in the genitive, as a substitution (badal) for the pronoun in *lahu al-mulk* (His is the dominion). ﴿And He is the Wise﴾ in all that proceeds from Him, ﴿the Aware of everything﴾.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddī, regarding His saying ﴿And your people denied it﴾: he said, Quraysh denied the Qur'an. ﴿And it is the truth﴾. As for *al-wakīl* (the guardian), it means the one who preserves. As for ﴿For every news there is a fixed time﴾, the news of the people became fixed on the day of Badr by what He had promised them of punishment.

An-Naḥḥās narrated in his work on abrogation (naskh) from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying ﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾: he said, this verse was abrogated by the verse of the sword (*āyat al-sayf*): ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5].

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding ﴿For every news there is a fixed time﴾: he said, it means a reality (ḥaqīqah).

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from al-Ḥasan that he said regarding ﴿For every news there is a fixed time﴾: its punishment is withheld until its sin is committed, then its punishment is released.

Ibn Jarīr narrated through al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding ﴿For every news there is a fixed time﴾: he said, it is an action and a reality, both what occurred of it in this world and what occurred of it in the Hereafter.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses, turn away from them﴾ and similar in the Qur'an: he said, Allah commanded the believers to unity, forbade them from disagreement and division, and informed them that those before them were destroyed only through contention and disputes concerning the religion of Allah.

Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Mujāhid regarding ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses﴾: he said, they mock them. He forbade Muḥammad (ﷺ) to sit with them, except if he forgets; when reminded, he should stand up. That is the saying of Allah: ﴿So do not sit after the reminder with the wrongdoing people﴾.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn that he held that this verse was revealed concerning the people of desires (ahl al-ahwāʾ).

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr and Abū Nuʿaym in *al-Ḥilyah* narrated from Abū Jaʿfar, who said: Do not sit with the people of disputes, for they are those who engage in vain talk concerning the verses of Allah.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, who said: the companions of desires are among those who engage in vain talk concerning the verses of Allah.

Abū al-Shaykh narrated from Muqātil, who said: when the polytheists in Mecca heard the Qur'an from the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), they engaged in vain talk and mocked. The Muslims said: their company is not suitable for us, we fear that we would go out when we hear their words and sit with them, and then we would not blame them. So Allah revealed this verse.

Abū al-Shaykh also narrated from al-Suddī that he said: this verse is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

An-Naḥḥās narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding ﴿And upon those who fear Allah there is nothing of their reckoning﴾: he said, this Meccan verse was abrogated by the Medinan verse, which is His saying: ﴿And He has already sent down to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah being rejected and mocked, do not sit with them﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 140], and so on.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from Mujāhid regarding ﴿And upon those who fear Allah there is nothing of their reckoning﴾: if they sit, but they should not sit.

Ibn Abī Shaybah narrated from Hishām ibn ʿUrwah, from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, that a group was brought to him who had sat drinking with a man who was fasting. He struck them and said: do not sit with them until they engage in talk other than that.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from Mujāhid regarding His saying ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and diversion﴾: he said, it is like His saying: ﴿Leave Me with whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11], meaning it is for threat (tahdīd).

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Abū Dāwūd in his work on abrogation narrated from Qatādah regarding this verse: he said, it was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from him regarding ﴿amusement and diversion﴾: he said, eating and drinking.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿lest a soul be delivered to ruin (an tubsala)﴾: he said, lest it be disgraced. And regarding ﴿they were delivered to ruin (ubsilū)﴾: he said, they were disgraced.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from him regarding ﴿They were delivered to ruin for what they earned﴾: he said, they were handed over for their misdeeds.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also narrated from him regarding ﴿Say, "Shall we call upon other than Allah"﴾: he said, this is a parable that Allah struck for the idols and for the callers who call to other than Allah.

As for His saying ﴿like one whom the devils have lured in the earth﴾: it means they misled him. They are the ghouls (ghīlān) who call him by his name and his father's name and his grandfather's name, so he follows them and thinks he is in something, and in the morning they have cast him into destruction. Perhaps they eat him, or they cast him into a desert wasteland where he perishes of thirst. This is the likeness of one who answers the gods that are worshipped other than Allah.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also narrated from him regarding ﴿like one whom the devils have lured﴾: he said, it is the man who does not respond to the guidance of Allah. He is the man who obeys the devil, acts in the earth with disobedience, deviates from the truth and strays from it. ﴿He has companions who call him to guidance﴾ and claim that what they command him is guidance. Allah says this about their allies among mankind: ﴿Indeed, the guidance is the guidance of Allah﴾, and misguidance is what the jinn call to.

Ibn al-Mubārak in *al-Zuhd*, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī (who graded it ḥasan), al-Nasāʾī, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Baʿth* narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the Trumpet, and he said: it is a horn into which it is blown." The narrations concerning the manner of the blowing are established in the books of hadith, and we have no need to cite them here.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾: he means that the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed is the One who blows into the Trumpet.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 74–83 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿To his father, Azar﴾. Al-Jawhari said: Azar is a non-Arabic name, and it is derived from "Azara fulan fulanan" when he assisted him, so he is the one who supports his people in worshipping idols.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it is derived from "strength" (al-quwwa).

Al-Juwayni said in his book al-Nukat min al-Tafsir: There is no disagreement among people that the name of Ibrahim's father was Tarikh, and what is in the Qur'an indicates that his name was Azar.

The claim of consensus has been challenged by what is narrated from Ibn Ishaq, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi, that he had two names: Azar and Tarikh.

Muqatil said: Azar is a title (laqab), and Tarikh is a name.

Sulayman al-Taymi said: Azar means "reproach and rebuke," and its meaning in their speech is "the crooked one."

Al-Dahhak said: the meaning of Azar is "the old man, the grieved one" in Persian.

Al-Farra' said: it is an epithet of blame in their language, as if he said: "O you who err."

The same was narrated from al-Zajjaj.

Mujahid said: it is the name of an idol.

On this view, the application of the name of an idol to his father is either by way of addressing him as one whose god it is, or by an ellipsis of a noun: i.e., he said to his father, "Worshipper of Azar," or "Do you worship Azar?" with the verb omitted.

Ibn 'Abbas read "A'izar" with two hamzas, the first fatha and the second kasra, and it is narrated from him that he read with two fathas.

The position of "idh qala" is in the accusative, by way of the estimated phrase "and mention when Ibrahim said," and this estimated phrase is coordinated with ﴿Say: Shall we call upon other than Allah﴾. It has also been said that it is coordinated with ﴿and warn by it lest a soul be delivered to ruin﴾, and "Azar" is in apposition (ʿatf bayan).

His saying: ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾ The interrogation is for denunciation: i.e., do you make them gods for yourself to worship? ﴿Indeed I see you and your people﴾ who follow you in the worship of idols ﴿in manifest error﴾, clearly away from the path of truth.

His saying: ﴿And thus did We show Ibrahim﴾: i.e., and like that vision We showed Ibrahim. The sentence is parenthetical (mu'tarida), and ﴿the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth﴾ means their sovereignty. The taa' and the waw were added for emphasis in the description, and like it are "raghabut" and "rahabut," for emphasis in desire and fear.

It has been said: he meant by the dominion of the heavens and the earth what is in them of creation. It has been said: Allah uncovered that for him until he saw up to the Throne and down to the lowest of the earths. It has been said: he saw from the dominion of the heavens and the earth what Allah related in this verse. It has been said: the intended meaning of their dominion is lordship and divinity: i.e., We showed him that and enabled him to know it through the way of inference that he followed. The meaning of "nuri" is "We showed him," a narration of a past state.

His saying: ﴿And that he might be among the certain (al-muqinin)﴾ is connected to an estimated element: i.e., We showed him that so that he might be among the certain. Azar and his people were worshipping idols, stars, the sun and the moon, so he wanted to alert them to the error. It has been said that he was born in a cave (sarab), and his provision was placed on the tips of his fingers, so he would suck them.

The reason for placing him in the cave is that Nimrod saw a dream that his kingdom would be lost at the hands of a boy, so he ordered the killing of every boy. And Allah knows best.

His saying: ﴿So when the night covered him﴾: i.e., it concealed him with its darkness. From it come "al-janna" (garden/shield), "al-mijann" (shield), and "al-jinn," all from concealment. The poet said:

"And had it not been for the darkness of the night, 'Iyad ibn Thabit would have overtaken our running at Dhi al-Ramth and al-Artam."

The fa' is for coordination with "qala Ibrahim": i.e., and mention when he said, and when the night covered him. This is a separate story from the story of the presentation of the dominion to him. The response of "lamma" is ﴿he saw a star﴾. It has been said he saw it through a crack in the rock placed over the top of the cave he was in. It has been said he saw it when his father brought him out of the cave, and it was the time of the setting of the sun. It has been said he saw Jupiter, and it has been said Venus.

His saying: ﴿This is my lord﴾ is a resumed sentence, an answer to an estimated question, as if it was said: "What did he say when he saw the star?" It has been said: this was from him when his sight was limited, for he was in the time of childhood. It has been said: he intended the establishment of proof against his people, as one who recounts what is among them and what they believe, in order to bind them. The second view was held by al-Zajjaj. It has been said: it is with the omission of the interrogative particle: i.e., "Is this my lord?" and its meaning is a denial that such a thing could be a lord. Similar is His saying: ﴿So if you die, will they be immortal?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 34], i.e., "Will they be immortal?" Similar is the saying of al-Hudhali:

"They enchanted me and said, 'O Khuwaylid, do not be frightened,' so I said, denying the faces: 'They are they.'"

i.e., "Are they they?" And the saying of another:

"By your life, I do not know, though I am knowledgeable, whether with seven they threw the coals or with eight."

i.e., "with seven?" It has been said the meaning is: "And you say, 'This is my lord,'" so the saying is implied. It has been said the meaning, with an omitted noun, is: "This is the proof of my lord."

﴿So when it set﴾: i.e., it went down. Ibrahim said: "I do not love the setting ones," i.e., the gods that set, for setting is a change from one state to another, and it is an indication of having come into being (huduth).

﴿So when he saw the moon rising﴾: i.e., ascending. It is said: "bazagha al-qamar" when it began to rise. And al-bazgh is the splitting; it was splitting the darkness with its light. ﴿So when it set, he said: "Unless my lord guides me﴾: i.e., unless He keeps me firm upon guidance and enables me to the proof ﴿I will surely be among the people who are astray﴾, those who are not guided to the truth, so they wrong themselves and deprive themselves of their share of good.

78. ﴿So when he saw the sun rising﴾: "bazigha" and "bazigatan" are both in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal), because the seeing is visual. He said "This is my lord" although the sun is feminine, because his intention was "this rising one," as said by al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash. It has been said: "this light." It has been said: "this body," "this is greater," i.e., than what preceded it of the star and the moon. ﴿He said: "O my people, indeed I am free of what you associate﴾: i.e., of the things you make partners with Allah and worship. "Ma" is either relative or verbal-masdariyya. He said this when it became clear to him that these things are created, and neither benefit nor harm, deducing this from their setting, which is an indication of their having come into being.

79. ﴿Indeed I have turned my face﴾: i.e., I directed my worship and monotheism to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He mentioned the face because it is the organ by which a person is recognized, or because it is used for the whole person, as already explained. The meaning of "fatara al-samawati wa al-ard" has already been explained: "hanifan," inclining toward the true religion.

80. His saying: ﴿And his people argued with him﴾: i.e., they argued with him about monotheism, with what indicates their claim that what they associate with Allah and worship of idols are gods. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, answered with what Allah related of him: he said, ﴿Do you argue with me concerning Allah?﴾: i.e., concerning His being without partner, without equal, without opposite.

Nafi' read "Atuhajjunni" with lightening of the nun; the rest read it with doubling, by assimilating the plural nun into the protective nun. Nafi' lightened it by deleting one of the two nuns, and Sibawayh permitted that. It is related from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' that Nafi''s reading is a solecism (lahn).

The sentence ﴿and He has already guided me﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: i.e., He guided me to His monotheism, while you want me to be like you in error, ignorance, and lack of guidance.

His saying: ﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him﴾. He said this when they frightened him with their gods, that they would be angry with him and afflict him with some harm. I.e., I do not fear what is a created thing among Allah's creatures that neither harms nor benefits. The pronoun in "bihi" may refer back to Allah, or to their worshipped things understood from "what you associate with Him." ﴿Except that my Lord should will something﴾: i.e., except at the time of my Lord's will, that He afflicts me with some harm for a sin I have committed; the affair is with Him, and that is from Him, not from your false gods that neither harm nor benefit.

The meaning: a negation of harm from their gods in every state, and an affirmation that harm and benefit belong to Allah, glorified is He, and proceed from His will. Then He gave the reason in His saying: ﴿My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾: i.e., His knowledge encompasses everything, so when He wills good, it is according to His will, and when He wills to send some evil upon me, it occurs; what Allah wills occurs and what He does not will does not occur. Then he said to them, completing the proof against them and repelling what they frightened him with:

﴿And how should I fear what you have associated, while you do not fear that you have associated with Allah what He has not sent down any authority for?﴾: i.e., how should I fear what does not harm, benefit, create, or provide, while you do not fear what has issued from you of associating with Allah, who is the Harmer, the Benefactor, the Creator, the Provider. He presented to them this argument of compulsion from which they find no escape or deviation. The interrogation is for denunciation and rebuke. "Ma" in ﴿what He has not sent down any authority for﴾ is the object of "ashraktum": i.e., you do not fear that you made the things for which He has not sent down any authority partners with Allah. Or the meaning is that Allah, glorified is He, did not permit their being made partners with Him, nor did He send down to them any proof by which they could argue for associating them; so how did they worship them, take them as gods, and make them partners with Allah, glorified is He?

His saying: ﴿So which of the two parties is more deserving of security?﴾ The two parties are the party of the believers and the party of the polytheists: (p-431) i.e., if the matter is as previously stated, that my object of worship is Allah, characterized by those attributes, and your object of worship is those created things, how do you frighten me with them, and how should I fear them? They are in such a station, while you do not fear your associating with Allah, glorified is He. After this, inform me: which of the two parties is more deserving of security and freedom from fear ﴿if you know﴾ the true state of affairs and recognize the sound proofs and distinguish them from false doubts.

Then Allah, glorified is He, said, judging between them and clarifying for them: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾: i.e., they are more deserving of security than those who associated. It has been said this is part of Ibrahim's speech; it has been said it is from the speech of Ibrahim's people. The meaning of "did not mix their belief with wrongdoing" is that they did not blend it with wrongdoing. The wrongdoing intended is shirk, as is established in the two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When this verse was revealed, it was hard on the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they said: 'Which of us has not wronged himself?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'It is not as you think; it is as Luqman said: "O my son, do not associate anything with Allah; indeed, association is a great wrong" [Luqman: 13].'" It is strange that the author of al-Kashshaf, in commenting on this verse, says: he rejected interpreting "wrongdoing" as "disbelief" in order to dispel ambiguity, while he does not know that the truthful one whose word is confirmed has explained it this way. When Allah's river comes, the river of Ma'qil is nullified. The reference in His saying "ulaika" is to the relative clause described by what preceded, and ﴿for them is security﴾ is a sentence functioning as the predicate of the demonstrative. This is the clearest of what has been said, with the possibility of other aspects. ﴿And they are guided﴾ to the truth, firm upon it, while others are in error and ignorance.

The reference in His saying ﴿And that was Our argument﴾ is to the proofs previously presented by Ibrahim to them: i.e., those proofs that Ibrahim presented to them from His saying ﴿So when the night covered him﴾ to His saying ﴿and they are guided﴾.

﴿Our argument, We gave it to Ibrahim﴾: i.e., We gave it to him and guided him to it. The clause ﴿We gave it to Ibrahim﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, or in the nominative position as a second predicate of the demonstrative. ﴿Against his people﴾: i.e., as a proof against his people. ﴿We raise in degrees whom We will﴾ through guidance and direction to the truth and instruction in proof, or by what is more general than that. ﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise, Knowing﴾: i.e., Wise in everything that proceeds from Him, Knowing of the state of His servants, and that among them are those who deserve elevation and those who do not.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said regarding His saying, ﴿And when Ibrahim said to his father Azar﴾: "Azar is the idol. The father of Ibrahim was named Ya'zar, his mother was named Mithla, his wife was named Sarah, and his concubine, the mother of Isma'il, was named Hajar."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: "Azar was not his father; rather it is the name of an idol."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "His father's name was Tarakh, and the idol's name was Azar."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated a similar report from Ibn Juraij.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sulayman al-Taymi that he recited ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾ and said: "It has reached me that it is 'a'waj' (crooked, harsh), and that it is the harshest word Abraham ever said to his father."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Abraham's father was not named Azar; his name was Tarakh."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* narrated from him regarding the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ that he said: "The sun, the moon, and the stars."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him concerning the verse, that he said: "He (Abraham) had the heavens uncovered until he saw them, [with the earth resting] on a rock, the rock on a fish, namely the fish from which people's food comes, the fish on a chain, and the chain on the Seal of Majesty (Khatam al-'Izzah)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid concerning the verse that he said: "Their authority (sultanuhuma)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Rabi' ibn Anas concerning the words ﴿And his people argued with him﴾ that he said: "They disputed with him."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning the words ﴿Do you argue with me﴾ that he said: "Do you dispute with me?"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) that he interpreted ﴿and did not mix their faith with wrongdoing﴾ as "with polytheism (shirk)." Abu al-Shaykh likewise narrated this from Umar ibn al-Khattab. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Abu al-Shaykh likewise narrated it from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir likewise narrated it from Salman al-Farisi. The two of them also narrated it from Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh likewise narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated a similar report from him (Ibn Abbas) through another chain. Similar reports have also been transmitted from a group of the Tabi'un (Successors). What we have already cited from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in explaining the verse suffices in place of all of these, as is established in the Sahihayn (the two Sahih collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim) and other works.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij concerning the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people﴾ that he said: "Their adversary."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning the words ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾ that he said: "By knowledge."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: "Indeed, the scholars have degrees like the degrees of the martyrs."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 74–83 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿To his father, Azar﴾. Al-Jawhari said: Azar is a non-Arabic name, and it is derived from "Azara fulan fulanan" when he assisted him, so he is the one who supports his people in worshipping idols.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it is derived from "strength" (al-quwwa).

Al-Juwayni said in his book al-Nukat min al-Tafsir: There is no disagreement among people that the name of Ibrahim's father was Tarikh, and what is in the Qur'an indicates that his name was Azar.

The claim of consensus has been challenged by what is narrated from Ibn Ishaq, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi, that he had two names: Azar and Tarikh.

Muqatil said: Azar is a title (laqab), and Tarikh is a name.

Sulayman al-Taymi said: Azar means "reproach and rebuke," and its meaning in their speech is "the crooked one."

Al-Dahhak said: the meaning of Azar is "the old man, the grieved one" in Persian.

Al-Farra' said: it is an epithet of blame in their language, as if he said: "O you who err."

The same was narrated from al-Zajjaj.

Mujahid said: it is the name of an idol.

On this view, the application of the name of an idol to his father is either by way of addressing him as one whose god it is, or by an ellipsis of a noun: i.e., he said to his father, "Worshipper of Azar," or "Do you worship Azar?" with the verb omitted.

Ibn 'Abbas read "A'izar" with two hamzas, the first fatha and the second kasra, and it is narrated from him that he read with two fathas.

The position of "idh qala" is in the accusative, by way of the estimated phrase "and mention when Ibrahim said," and this estimated phrase is coordinated with ﴿Say: Shall we call upon other than Allah﴾. It has also been said that it is coordinated with ﴿and warn by it lest a soul be delivered to ruin﴾, and "Azar" is in apposition (ʿatf bayan).

His saying: ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾ The interrogation is for denunciation: i.e., do you make them gods for yourself to worship? ﴿Indeed I see you and your people﴾ who follow you in the worship of idols ﴿in manifest error﴾, clearly away from the path of truth.

His saying: ﴿And thus did We show Ibrahim﴾: i.e., and like that vision We showed Ibrahim. The sentence is parenthetical (mu'tarida), and ﴿the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth﴾ means their sovereignty. The taa' and the waw were added for emphasis in the description, and like it are "raghabut" and "rahabut," for emphasis in desire and fear.

It has been said: he meant by the dominion of the heavens and the earth what is in them of creation. It has been said: Allah uncovered that for him until he saw up to the Throne and down to the lowest of the earths. It has been said: he saw from the dominion of the heavens and the earth what Allah related in this verse. It has been said: the intended meaning of their dominion is lordship and divinity: i.e., We showed him that and enabled him to know it through the way of inference that he followed. The meaning of "nuri" is "We showed him," a narration of a past state.

His saying: ﴿And that he might be among the certain (al-muqinin)﴾ is connected to an estimated element: i.e., We showed him that so that he might be among the certain. Azar and his people were worshipping idols, stars, the sun and the moon, so he wanted to alert them to the error. It has been said that he was born in a cave (sarab), and his provision was placed on the tips of his fingers, so he would suck them.

The reason for placing him in the cave is that Nimrod saw a dream that his kingdom would be lost at the hands of a boy, so he ordered the killing of every boy. And Allah knows best.

His saying: ﴿So when the night covered him﴾: i.e., it concealed him with its darkness. From it come "al-janna" (garden/shield), "al-mijann" (shield), and "al-jinn," all from concealment. The poet said:

"And had it not been for the darkness of the night, 'Iyad ibn Thabit would have overtaken our running at Dhi al-Ramth and al-Artam."

The fa' is for coordination with "qala Ibrahim": i.e., and mention when he said, and when the night covered him. This is a separate story from the story of the presentation of the dominion to him. The response of "lamma" is ﴿he saw a star﴾. It has been said he saw it through a crack in the rock placed over the top of the cave he was in. It has been said he saw it when his father brought him out of the cave, and it was the time of the setting of the sun. It has been said he saw Jupiter, and it has been said Venus.

His saying: ﴿This is my lord﴾ is a resumed sentence, an answer to an estimated question, as if it was said: "What did he say when he saw the star?" It has been said: this was from him when his sight was limited, for he was in the time of childhood. It has been said: he intended the establishment of proof against his people, as one who recounts what is among them and what they believe, in order to bind them. The second view was held by al-Zajjaj. It has been said: it is with the omission of the interrogative particle: i.e., "Is this my lord?" and its meaning is a denial that such a thing could be a lord. Similar is His saying: ﴿So if you die, will they be immortal?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 34], i.e., "Will they be immortal?" Similar is the saying of al-Hudhali:

"They enchanted me and said, 'O Khuwaylid, do not be frightened,' so I said, denying the faces: 'They are they.'"

i.e., "Are they they?" And the saying of another:

"By your life, I do not know, though I am knowledgeable, whether with seven they threw the coals or with eight."

i.e., "with seven?" It has been said the meaning is: "And you say, 'This is my lord,'" so the saying is implied. It has been said the meaning, with an omitted noun, is: "This is the proof of my lord."

﴿So when it set﴾: i.e., it went down. Ibrahim said: "I do not love the setting ones," i.e., the gods that set, for setting is a change from one state to another, and it is an indication of having come into being (huduth).

﴿So when he saw the moon rising﴾: i.e., ascending. It is said: "bazagha al-qamar" when it began to rise. And al-bazgh is the splitting; it was splitting the darkness with its light. ﴿So when it set, he said: "Unless my lord guides me﴾: i.e., unless He keeps me firm upon guidance and enables me to the proof ﴿I will surely be among the people who are astray﴾, those who are not guided to the truth, so they wrong themselves and deprive themselves of their share of good.

78. ﴿So when he saw the sun rising﴾: "bazigha" and "bazigatan" are both in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal), because the seeing is visual. He said "This is my lord" although the sun is feminine, because his intention was "this rising one," as said by al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash. It has been said: "this light." It has been said: "this body," "this is greater," i.e., than what preceded it of the star and the moon. ﴿He said: "O my people, indeed I am free of what you associate﴾: i.e., of the things you make partners with Allah and worship. "Ma" is either relative or verbal-masdariyya. He said this when it became clear to him that these things are created, and neither benefit nor harm, deducing this from their setting, which is an indication of their having come into being.

79. ﴿Indeed I have turned my face﴾: i.e., I directed my worship and monotheism to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He mentioned the face because it is the organ by which a person is recognized, or because it is used for the whole person, as already explained. The meaning of "fatara al-samawati wa al-ard" has already been explained: "hanifan," inclining toward the true religion.

80. His saying: ﴿And his people argued with him﴾: i.e., they argued with him about monotheism, with what indicates their claim that what they associate with Allah and worship of idols are gods. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, answered with what Allah related of him: he said, ﴿Do you argue with me concerning Allah?﴾: i.e., concerning His being without partner, without equal, without opposite.

Nafi' read "Atuhajjunni" with lightening of the nun; the rest read it with doubling, by assimilating the plural nun into the protective nun. Nafi' lightened it by deleting one of the two nuns, and Sibawayh permitted that. It is related from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' that Nafi''s reading is a solecism (lahn).

The sentence ﴿and He has already guided me﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: i.e., He guided me to His monotheism, while you want me to be like you in error, ignorance, and lack of guidance.

His saying: ﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him﴾. He said this when they frightened him with their gods, that they would be angry with him and afflict him with some harm. I.e., I do not fear what is a created thing among Allah's creatures that neither harms nor benefits. The pronoun in "bihi" may refer back to Allah, or to their worshipped things understood from "what you associate with Him." ﴿Except that my Lord should will something﴾: i.e., except at the time of my Lord's will, that He afflicts me with some harm for a sin I have committed; the affair is with Him, and that is from Him, not from your false gods that neither harm nor benefit.

The meaning: a negation of harm from their gods in every state, and an affirmation that harm and benefit belong to Allah, glorified is He, and proceed from His will. Then He gave the reason in His saying: ﴿My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾: i.e., His knowledge encompasses everything, so when He wills good, it is according to His will, and when He wills to send some evil upon me, it occurs; what Allah wills occurs and what He does not will does not occur. Then he said to them, completing the proof against them and repelling what they frightened him with:

﴿And how should I fear what you have associated, while you do not fear that you have associated with Allah what He has not sent down any authority for?﴾: i.e., how should I fear what does not harm, benefit, create, or provide, while you do not fear what has issued from you of associating with Allah, who is the Harmer, the Benefactor, the Creator, the Provider. He presented to them this argument of compulsion from which they find no escape or deviation. The interrogation is for denunciation and rebuke. "Ma" in ﴿what He has not sent down any authority for﴾ is the object of "ashraktum": i.e., you do not fear that you made the things for which He has not sent down any authority partners with Allah. Or the meaning is that Allah, glorified is He, did not permit their being made partners with Him, nor did He send down to them any proof by which they could argue for associating them; so how did they worship them, take them as gods, and make them partners with Allah, glorified is He?

His saying: ﴿So which of the two parties is more deserving of security?﴾ The two parties are the party of the believers and the party of the polytheists: (p-431) i.e., if the matter is as previously stated, that my object of worship is Allah, characterized by those attributes, and your object of worship is those created things, how do you frighten me with them, and how should I fear them? They are in such a station, while you do not fear your associating with Allah, glorified is He. After this, inform me: which of the two parties is more deserving of security and freedom from fear ﴿if you know﴾ the true state of affairs and recognize the sound proofs and distinguish them from false doubts.

Then Allah, glorified is He, said, judging between them and clarifying for them: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾: i.e., they are more deserving of security than those who associated. It has been said this is part of Ibrahim's speech; it has been said it is from the speech of Ibrahim's people. The meaning of "did not mix their belief with wrongdoing" is that they did not blend it with wrongdoing. The wrongdoing intended is shirk, as is established in the two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When this verse was revealed, it was hard on the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they said: 'Which of us has not wronged himself?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'It is not as you think; it is as Luqman said: "O my son, do not associate anything with Allah; indeed, association is a great wrong" [Luqman: 13].'" It is strange that the author of al-Kashshaf, in commenting on this verse, says: he rejected interpreting "wrongdoing" as "disbelief" in order to dispel ambiguity, while he does not know that the truthful one whose word is confirmed has explained it this way. When Allah's river comes, the river of Ma'qil is nullified. The reference in His saying "ulaika" is to the relative clause described by what preceded, and ﴿for them is security﴾ is a sentence functioning as the predicate of the demonstrative. This is the clearest of what has been said, with the possibility of other aspects. ﴿And they are guided﴾ to the truth, firm upon it, while others are in error and ignorance.

The reference in His saying ﴿And that was Our argument﴾ is to the proofs previously presented by Ibrahim to them: i.e., those proofs that Ibrahim presented to them from His saying ﴿So when the night covered him﴾ to His saying ﴿and they are guided﴾.

﴿Our argument, We gave it to Ibrahim﴾: i.e., We gave it to him and guided him to it. The clause ﴿We gave it to Ibrahim﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, or in the nominative position as a second predicate of the demonstrative. ﴿Against his people﴾: i.e., as a proof against his people. ﴿We raise in degrees whom We will﴾ through guidance and direction to the truth and instruction in proof, or by what is more general than that. ﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise, Knowing﴾: i.e., Wise in everything that proceeds from Him, Knowing of the state of His servants, and that among them are those who deserve elevation and those who do not.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said regarding His saying, ﴿And when Ibrahim said to his father Azar﴾: "Azar is the idol. The father of Ibrahim was named Ya'zar, his mother was named Mithla, his wife was named Sarah, and his concubine, the mother of Isma'il, was named Hajar."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: "Azar was not his father; rather it is the name of an idol."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "His father's name was Tarakh, and the idol's name was Azar."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated a similar report from Ibn Juraij.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sulayman al-Taymi that he recited ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾ and said: "It has reached me that it is 'a'waj' (crooked, harsh), and that it is the harshest word Abraham ever said to his father."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Abraham's father was not named Azar; his name was Tarakh."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* narrated from him regarding the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ that he said: "The sun, the moon, and the stars."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him concerning the verse, that he said: "He (Abraham) had the heavens uncovered until he saw them, [with the earth resting] on a rock, the rock on a fish, namely the fish from which people's food comes, the fish on a chain, and the chain on the Seal of Majesty (Khatam al-'Izzah)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid concerning the verse that he said: "Their authority (sultanuhuma)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Rabi' ibn Anas concerning the words ﴿And his people argued with him﴾ that he said: "They disputed with him."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning the words ﴿Do you argue with me﴾ that he said: "Do you dispute with me?"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) that he interpreted ﴿and did not mix their faith with wrongdoing﴾ as "with polytheism (shirk)." Abu al-Shaykh likewise narrated this from Umar ibn al-Khattab. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Abu al-Shaykh likewise narrated it from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir likewise narrated it from Salman al-Farisi. The two of them also narrated it from Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh likewise narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated a similar report from him (Ibn Abbas) through another chain. Similar reports have also been transmitted from a group of the Tabi'un (Successors). What we have already cited from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in explaining the verse suffices in place of all of these, as is established in the Sahihayn (the two Sahih collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim) and other works.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij concerning the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people﴾ that he said: "Their adversary."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning the words ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾ that he said: "By knowledge."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: "Indeed, the scholars have degrees like the degrees of the martyrs."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 74–83 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿To his father, Azar﴾. Al-Jawhari said: Azar is a non-Arabic name, and it is derived from "Azara fulan fulanan" when he assisted him, so he is the one who supports his people in worshipping idols.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it is derived from "strength" (al-quwwa).

Al-Juwayni said in his book al-Nukat min al-Tafsir: There is no disagreement among people that the name of Ibrahim's father was Tarikh, and what is in the Qur'an indicates that his name was Azar.

The claim of consensus has been challenged by what is narrated from Ibn Ishaq, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi, that he had two names: Azar and Tarikh.

Muqatil said: Azar is a title (laqab), and Tarikh is a name.

Sulayman al-Taymi said: Azar means "reproach and rebuke," and its meaning in their speech is "the crooked one."

Al-Dahhak said: the meaning of Azar is "the old man, the grieved one" in Persian.

Al-Farra' said: it is an epithet of blame in their language, as if he said: "O you who err."

The same was narrated from al-Zajjaj.

Mujahid said: it is the name of an idol.

On this view, the application of the name of an idol to his father is either by way of addressing him as one whose god it is, or by an ellipsis of a noun: i.e., he said to his father, "Worshipper of Azar," or "Do you worship Azar?" with the verb omitted.

Ibn 'Abbas read "A'izar" with two hamzas, the first fatha and the second kasra, and it is narrated from him that he read with two fathas.

The position of "idh qala" is in the accusative, by way of the estimated phrase "and mention when Ibrahim said," and this estimated phrase is coordinated with ﴿Say: Shall we call upon other than Allah﴾. It has also been said that it is coordinated with ﴿and warn by it lest a soul be delivered to ruin﴾, and "Azar" is in apposition (ʿatf bayan).

His saying: ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾ The interrogation is for denunciation: i.e., do you make them gods for yourself to worship? ﴿Indeed I see you and your people﴾ who follow you in the worship of idols ﴿in manifest error﴾, clearly away from the path of truth.

His saying: ﴿And thus did We show Ibrahim﴾: i.e., and like that vision We showed Ibrahim. The sentence is parenthetical (mu'tarida), and ﴿the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth﴾ means their sovereignty. The taa' and the waw were added for emphasis in the description, and like it are "raghabut" and "rahabut," for emphasis in desire and fear.

It has been said: he meant by the dominion of the heavens and the earth what is in them of creation. It has been said: Allah uncovered that for him until he saw up to the Throne and down to the lowest of the earths. It has been said: he saw from the dominion of the heavens and the earth what Allah related in this verse. It has been said: the intended meaning of their dominion is lordship and divinity: i.e., We showed him that and enabled him to know it through the way of inference that he followed. The meaning of "nuri" is "We showed him," a narration of a past state.

His saying: ﴿And that he might be among the certain (al-muqinin)﴾ is connected to an estimated element: i.e., We showed him that so that he might be among the certain. Azar and his people were worshipping idols, stars, the sun and the moon, so he wanted to alert them to the error. It has been said that he was born in a cave (sarab), and his provision was placed on the tips of his fingers, so he would suck them.

The reason for placing him in the cave is that Nimrod saw a dream that his kingdom would be lost at the hands of a boy, so he ordered the killing of every boy. And Allah knows best.

His saying: ﴿So when the night covered him﴾: i.e., it concealed him with its darkness. From it come "al-janna" (garden/shield), "al-mijann" (shield), and "al-jinn," all from concealment. The poet said:

"And had it not been for the darkness of the night, 'Iyad ibn Thabit would have overtaken our running at Dhi al-Ramth and al-Artam."

The fa' is for coordination with "qala Ibrahim": i.e., and mention when he said, and when the night covered him. This is a separate story from the story of the presentation of the dominion to him. The response of "lamma" is ﴿he saw a star﴾. It has been said he saw it through a crack in the rock placed over the top of the cave he was in. It has been said he saw it when his father brought him out of the cave, and it was the time of the setting of the sun. It has been said he saw Jupiter, and it has been said Venus.

His saying: ﴿This is my lord﴾ is a resumed sentence, an answer to an estimated question, as if it was said: "What did he say when he saw the star?" It has been said: this was from him when his sight was limited, for he was in the time of childhood. It has been said: he intended the establishment of proof against his people, as one who recounts what is among them and what they believe, in order to bind them. The second view was held by al-Zajjaj. It has been said: it is with the omission of the interrogative particle: i.e., "Is this my lord?" and its meaning is a denial that such a thing could be a lord. Similar is His saying: ﴿So if you die, will they be immortal?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 34], i.e., "Will they be immortal?" Similar is the saying of al-Hudhali:

"They enchanted me and said, 'O Khuwaylid, do not be frightened,' so I said, denying the faces: 'They are they.'"

i.e., "Are they they?" And the saying of another:

"By your life, I do not know, though I am knowledgeable, whether with seven they threw the coals or with eight."

i.e., "with seven?" It has been said the meaning is: "And you say, 'This is my lord,'" so the saying is implied. It has been said the meaning, with an omitted noun, is: "This is the proof of my lord."

﴿So when it set﴾: i.e., it went down. Ibrahim said: "I do not love the setting ones," i.e., the gods that set, for setting is a change from one state to another, and it is an indication of having come into being (huduth).

﴿So when he saw the moon rising﴾: i.e., ascending. It is said: "bazagha al-qamar" when it began to rise. And al-bazgh is the splitting; it was splitting the darkness with its light. ﴿So when it set, he said: "Unless my lord guides me﴾: i.e., unless He keeps me firm upon guidance and enables me to the proof ﴿I will surely be among the people who are astray﴾, those who are not guided to the truth, so they wrong themselves and deprive themselves of their share of good.

78. ﴿So when he saw the sun rising﴾: "bazigha" and "bazigatan" are both in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal), because the seeing is visual. He said "This is my lord" although the sun is feminine, because his intention was "this rising one," as said by al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash. It has been said: "this light." It has been said: "this body," "this is greater," i.e., than what preceded it of the star and the moon. ﴿He said: "O my people, indeed I am free of what you associate﴾: i.e., of the things you make partners with Allah and worship. "Ma" is either relative or verbal-masdariyya. He said this when it became clear to him that these things are created, and neither benefit nor harm, deducing this from their setting, which is an indication of their having come into being.

79. ﴿Indeed I have turned my face﴾: i.e., I directed my worship and monotheism to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He mentioned the face because it is the organ by which a person is recognized, or because it is used for the whole person, as already explained. The meaning of "fatara al-samawati wa al-ard" has already been explained: "hanifan," inclining toward the true religion.

80. His saying: ﴿And his people argued with him﴾: i.e., they argued with him about monotheism, with what indicates their claim that what they associate with Allah and worship of idols are gods. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, answered with what Allah related of him: he said, ﴿Do you argue with me concerning Allah?﴾: i.e., concerning His being without partner, without equal, without opposite.

Nafi' read "Atuhajjunni" with lightening of the nun; the rest read it with doubling, by assimilating the plural nun into the protective nun. Nafi' lightened it by deleting one of the two nuns, and Sibawayh permitted that. It is related from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' that Nafi''s reading is a solecism (lahn).

The sentence ﴿and He has already guided me﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: i.e., He guided me to His monotheism, while you want me to be like you in error, ignorance, and lack of guidance.

His saying: ﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him﴾. He said this when they frightened him with their gods, that they would be angry with him and afflict him with some harm. I.e., I do not fear what is a created thing among Allah's creatures that neither harms nor benefits. The pronoun in "bihi" may refer back to Allah, or to their worshipped things understood from "what you associate with Him." ﴿Except that my Lord should will something﴾: i.e., except at the time of my Lord's will, that He afflicts me with some harm for a sin I have committed; the affair is with Him, and that is from Him, not from your false gods that neither harm nor benefit.

The meaning: a negation of harm from their gods in every state, and an affirmation that harm and benefit belong to Allah, glorified is He, and proceed from His will. Then He gave the reason in His saying: ﴿My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾: i.e., His knowledge encompasses everything, so when He wills good, it is according to His will, and when He wills to send some evil upon me, it occurs; what Allah wills occurs and what He does not will does not occur. Then he said to them, completing the proof against them and repelling what they frightened him with:

﴿And how should I fear what you have associated, while you do not fear that you have associated with Allah what He has not sent down any authority for?﴾: i.e., how should I fear what does not harm, benefit, create, or provide, while you do not fear what has issued from you of associating with Allah, who is the Harmer, the Benefactor, the Creator, the Provider. He presented to them this argument of compulsion from which they find no escape or deviation. The interrogation is for denunciation and rebuke. "Ma" in ﴿what He has not sent down any authority for﴾ is the object of "ashraktum": i.e., you do not fear that you made the things for which He has not sent down any authority partners with Allah. Or the meaning is that Allah, glorified is He, did not permit their being made partners with Him, nor did He send down to them any proof by which they could argue for associating them; so how did they worship them, take them as gods, and make them partners with Allah, glorified is He?

His saying: ﴿So which of the two parties is more deserving of security?﴾ The two parties are the party of the believers and the party of the polytheists: (p-431) i.e., if the matter is as previously stated, that my object of worship is Allah, characterized by those attributes, and your object of worship is those created things, how do you frighten me with them, and how should I fear them? They are in such a station, while you do not fear your associating with Allah, glorified is He. After this, inform me: which of the two parties is more deserving of security and freedom from fear ﴿if you know﴾ the true state of affairs and recognize the sound proofs and distinguish them from false doubts.

Then Allah, glorified is He, said, judging between them and clarifying for them: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾: i.e., they are more deserving of security than those who associated. It has been said this is part of Ibrahim's speech; it has been said it is from the speech of Ibrahim's people. The meaning of "did not mix their belief with wrongdoing" is that they did not blend it with wrongdoing. The wrongdoing intended is shirk, as is established in the two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When this verse was revealed, it was hard on the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they said: 'Which of us has not wronged himself?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'It is not as you think; it is as Luqman said: "O my son, do not associate anything with Allah; indeed, association is a great wrong" [Luqman: 13].'" It is strange that the author of al-Kashshaf, in commenting on this verse, says: he rejected interpreting "wrongdoing" as "disbelief" in order to dispel ambiguity, while he does not know that the truthful one whose word is confirmed has explained it this way. When Allah's river comes, the river of Ma'qil is nullified. The reference in His saying "ulaika" is to the relative clause described by what preceded, and ﴿for them is security﴾ is a sentence functioning as the predicate of the demonstrative. This is the clearest of what has been said, with the possibility of other aspects. ﴿And they are guided﴾ to the truth, firm upon it, while others are in error and ignorance.

The reference in His saying ﴿And that was Our argument﴾ is to the proofs previously presented by Ibrahim to them: i.e., those proofs that Ibrahim presented to them from His saying ﴿So when the night covered him﴾ to His saying ﴿and they are guided﴾.

﴿Our argument, We gave it to Ibrahim﴾: i.e., We gave it to him and guided him to it. The clause ﴿We gave it to Ibrahim﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, or in the nominative position as a second predicate of the demonstrative. ﴿Against his people﴾: i.e., as a proof against his people. ﴿We raise in degrees whom We will﴾ through guidance and direction to the truth and instruction in proof, or by what is more general than that. ﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise, Knowing﴾: i.e., Wise in everything that proceeds from Him, Knowing of the state of His servants, and that among them are those who deserve elevation and those who do not.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said regarding His saying, ﴿And when Ibrahim said to his father Azar﴾: "Azar is the idol. The father of Ibrahim was named Ya'zar, his mother was named Mithla, his wife was named Sarah, and his concubine, the mother of Isma'il, was named Hajar."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: "Azar was not his father; rather it is the name of an idol."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "His father's name was Tarakh, and the idol's name was Azar."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated a similar report from Ibn Juraij.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sulayman al-Taymi that he recited ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾ and said: "It has reached me that it is 'a'waj' (crooked, harsh), and that it is the harshest word Abraham ever said to his father."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Abraham's father was not named Azar; his name was Tarakh."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* narrated from him regarding the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ that he said: "The sun, the moon, and the stars."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him concerning the verse, that he said: "He (Abraham) had the heavens uncovered until he saw them, [with the earth resting] on a rock, the rock on a fish, namely the fish from which people's food comes, the fish on a chain, and the chain on the Seal of Majesty (Khatam al-'Izzah)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid concerning the verse that he said: "Their authority (sultanuhuma)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Rabi' ibn Anas concerning the words ﴿And his people argued with him﴾ that he said: "They disputed with him."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning the words ﴿Do you argue with me﴾ that he said: "Do you dispute with me?"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) that he interpreted ﴿and did not mix their faith with wrongdoing﴾ as "with polytheism (shirk)." Abu al-Shaykh likewise narrated this from Umar ibn al-Khattab. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Abu al-Shaykh likewise narrated it from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir likewise narrated it from Salman al-Farisi. The two of them also narrated it from Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh likewise narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated a similar report from him (Ibn Abbas) through another chain. Similar reports have also been transmitted from a group of the Tabi'un (Successors). What we have already cited from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in explaining the verse suffices in place of all of these, as is established in the Sahihayn (the two Sahih collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim) and other works.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij concerning the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people﴾ that he said: "Their adversary."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning the words ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾ that he said: "By knowledge."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: "Indeed, the scholars have degrees like the degrees of the martyrs."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 74–83 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿To his father, Azar﴾. Al-Jawhari said: Azar is a non-Arabic name, and it is derived from "Azara fulan fulanan" when he assisted him, so he is the one who supports his people in worshipping idols.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it is derived from "strength" (al-quwwa).

Al-Juwayni said in his book al-Nukat min al-Tafsir: There is no disagreement among people that the name of Ibrahim's father was Tarikh, and what is in the Qur'an indicates that his name was Azar.

The claim of consensus has been challenged by what is narrated from Ibn Ishaq, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi, that he had two names: Azar and Tarikh.

Muqatil said: Azar is a title (laqab), and Tarikh is a name.

Sulayman al-Taymi said: Azar means "reproach and rebuke," and its meaning in their speech is "the crooked one."

Al-Dahhak said: the meaning of Azar is "the old man, the grieved one" in Persian.

Al-Farra' said: it is an epithet of blame in their language, as if he said: "O you who err."

The same was narrated from al-Zajjaj.

Mujahid said: it is the name of an idol.

On this view, the application of the name of an idol to his father is either by way of addressing him as one whose god it is, or by an ellipsis of a noun: i.e., he said to his father, "Worshipper of Azar," or "Do you worship Azar?" with the verb omitted.

Ibn 'Abbas read "A'izar" with two hamzas, the first fatha and the second kasra, and it is narrated from him that he read with two fathas.

The position of "idh qala" is in the accusative, by way of the estimated phrase "and mention when Ibrahim said," and this estimated phrase is coordinated with ﴿Say: Shall we call upon other than Allah﴾. It has also been said that it is coordinated with ﴿and warn by it lest a soul be delivered to ruin﴾, and "Azar" is in apposition (ʿatf bayan).

His saying: ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾ The interrogation is for denunciation: i.e., do you make them gods for yourself to worship? ﴿Indeed I see you and your people﴾ who follow you in the worship of idols ﴿in manifest error﴾, clearly away from the path of truth.

His saying: ﴿And thus did We show Ibrahim﴾: i.e., and like that vision We showed Ibrahim. The sentence is parenthetical (mu'tarida), and ﴿the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth﴾ means their sovereignty. The taa' and the waw were added for emphasis in the description, and like it are "raghabut" and "rahabut," for emphasis in desire and fear.

It has been said: he meant by the dominion of the heavens and the earth what is in them of creation. It has been said: Allah uncovered that for him until he saw up to the Throne and down to the lowest of the earths. It has been said: he saw from the dominion of the heavens and the earth what Allah related in this verse. It has been said: the intended meaning of their dominion is lordship and divinity: i.e., We showed him that and enabled him to know it through the way of inference that he followed. The meaning of "nuri" is "We showed him," a narration of a past state.

His saying: ﴿And that he might be among the certain (al-muqinin)﴾ is connected to an estimated element: i.e., We showed him that so that he might be among the certain. Azar and his people were worshipping idols, stars, the sun and the moon, so he wanted to alert them to the error. It has been said that he was born in a cave (sarab), and his provision was placed on the tips of his fingers, so he would suck them.

The reason for placing him in the cave is that Nimrod saw a dream that his kingdom would be lost at the hands of a boy, so he ordered the killing of every boy. And Allah knows best.

His saying: ﴿So when the night covered him﴾: i.e., it concealed him with its darkness. From it come "al-janna" (garden/shield), "al-mijann" (shield), and "al-jinn," all from concealment. The poet said:

"And had it not been for the darkness of the night, 'Iyad ibn Thabit would have overtaken our running at Dhi al-Ramth and al-Artam."

The fa' is for coordination with "qala Ibrahim": i.e., and mention when he said, and when the night covered him. This is a separate story from the story of the presentation of the dominion to him. The response of "lamma" is ﴿he saw a star﴾. It has been said he saw it through a crack in the rock placed over the top of the cave he was in. It has been said he saw it when his father brought him out of the cave, and it was the time of the setting of the sun. It has been said he saw Jupiter, and it has been said Venus.

His saying: ﴿This is my lord﴾ is a resumed sentence, an answer to an estimated question, as if it was said: "What did he say when he saw the star?" It has been said: this was from him when his sight was limited, for he was in the time of childhood. It has been said: he intended the establishment of proof against his people, as one who recounts what is among them and what they believe, in order to bind them. The second view was held by al-Zajjaj. It has been said: it is with the omission of the interrogative particle: i.e., "Is this my lord?" and its meaning is a denial that such a thing could be a lord. Similar is His saying: ﴿So if you die, will they be immortal?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 34], i.e., "Will they be immortal?" Similar is the saying of al-Hudhali:

"They enchanted me and said, 'O Khuwaylid, do not be frightened,' so I said, denying the faces: 'They are they.'"

i.e., "Are they they?" And the saying of another:

"By your life, I do not know, though I am knowledgeable, whether with seven they threw the coals or with eight."

i.e., "with seven?" It has been said the meaning is: "And you say, 'This is my lord,'" so the saying is implied. It has been said the meaning, with an omitted noun, is: "This is the proof of my lord."

﴿So when it set﴾: i.e., it went down. Ibrahim said: "I do not love the setting ones," i.e., the gods that set, for setting is a change from one state to another, and it is an indication of having come into being (huduth).

﴿So when he saw the moon rising﴾: i.e., ascending. It is said: "bazagha al-qamar" when it began to rise. And al-bazgh is the splitting; it was splitting the darkness with its light. ﴿So when it set, he said: "Unless my lord guides me﴾: i.e., unless He keeps me firm upon guidance and enables me to the proof ﴿I will surely be among the people who are astray﴾, those who are not guided to the truth, so they wrong themselves and deprive themselves of their share of good.

78. ﴿So when he saw the sun rising﴾: "bazigha" and "bazigatan" are both in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal), because the seeing is visual. He said "This is my lord" although the sun is feminine, because his intention was "this rising one," as said by al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash. It has been said: "this light." It has been said: "this body," "this is greater," i.e., than what preceded it of the star and the moon. ﴿He said: "O my people, indeed I am free of what you associate﴾: i.e., of the things you make partners with Allah and worship. "Ma" is either relative or verbal-masdariyya. He said this when it became clear to him that these things are created, and neither benefit nor harm, deducing this from their setting, which is an indication of their having come into being.

79. ﴿Indeed I have turned my face﴾: i.e., I directed my worship and monotheism to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He mentioned the face because it is the organ by which a person is recognized, or because it is used for the whole person, as already explained. The meaning of "fatara al-samawati wa al-ard" has already been explained: "hanifan," inclining toward the true religion.

80. His saying: ﴿And his people argued with him﴾: i.e., they argued with him about monotheism, with what indicates their claim that what they associate with Allah and worship of idols are gods. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, answered with what Allah related of him: he said, ﴿Do you argue with me concerning Allah?﴾: i.e., concerning His being without partner, without equal, without opposite.

Nafi' read "Atuhajjunni" with lightening of the nun; the rest read it with doubling, by assimilating the plural nun into the protective nun. Nafi' lightened it by deleting one of the two nuns, and Sibawayh permitted that. It is related from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' that Nafi''s reading is a solecism (lahn).

The sentence ﴿and He has already guided me﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: i.e., He guided me to His monotheism, while you want me to be like you in error, ignorance, and lack of guidance.

His saying: ﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him﴾. He said this when they frightened him with their gods, that they would be angry with him and afflict him with some harm. I.e., I do not fear what is a created thing among Allah's creatures that neither harms nor benefits. The pronoun in "bihi" may refer back to Allah, or to their worshipped things understood from "what you associate with Him." ﴿Except that my Lord should will something﴾: i.e., except at the time of my Lord's will, that He afflicts me with some harm for a sin I have committed; the affair is with Him, and that is from Him, not from your false gods that neither harm nor benefit.

The meaning: a negation of harm from their gods in every state, and an affirmation that harm and benefit belong to Allah, glorified is He, and proceed from His will. Then He gave the reason in His saying: ﴿My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾: i.e., His knowledge encompasses everything, so when He wills good, it is according to His will, and when He wills to send some evil upon me, it occurs; what Allah wills occurs and what He does not will does not occur. Then he said to them, completing the proof against them and repelling what they frightened him with:

﴿And how should I fear what you have associated, while you do not fear that you have associated with Allah what He has not sent down any authority for?﴾: i.e., how should I fear what does not harm, benefit, create, or provide, while you do not fear what has issued from you of associating with Allah, who is the Harmer, the Benefactor, the Creator, the Provider. He presented to them this argument of compulsion from which they find no escape or deviation. The interrogation is for denunciation and rebuke. "Ma" in ﴿what He has not sent down any authority for﴾ is the object of "ashraktum": i.e., you do not fear that you made the things for which He has not sent down any authority partners with Allah. Or the meaning is that Allah, glorified is He, did not permit their being made partners with Him, nor did He send down to them any proof by which they could argue for associating them; so how did they worship them, take them as gods, and make them partners with Allah, glorified is He?

His saying: ﴿So which of the two parties is more deserving of security?﴾ The two parties are the party of the believers and the party of the polytheists: (p-431) i.e., if the matter is as previously stated, that my object of worship is Allah, characterized by those attributes, and your object of worship is those created things, how do you frighten me with them, and how should I fear them? They are in such a station, while you do not fear your associating with Allah, glorified is He. After this, inform me: which of the two parties is more deserving of security and freedom from fear ﴿if you know﴾ the true state of affairs and recognize the sound proofs and distinguish them from false doubts.

Then Allah, glorified is He, said, judging between them and clarifying for them: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾: i.e., they are more deserving of security than those who associated. It has been said this is part of Ibrahim's speech; it has been said it is from the speech of Ibrahim's people. The meaning of "did not mix their belief with wrongdoing" is that they did not blend it with wrongdoing. The wrongdoing intended is shirk, as is established in the two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When this verse was revealed, it was hard on the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they said: 'Which of us has not wronged himself?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'It is not as you think; it is as Luqman said: "O my son, do not associate anything with Allah; indeed, association is a great wrong" [Luqman: 13].'" It is strange that the author of al-Kashshaf, in commenting on this verse, says: he rejected interpreting "wrongdoing" as "disbelief" in order to dispel ambiguity, while he does not know that the truthful one whose word is confirmed has explained it this way. When Allah's river comes, the river of Ma'qil is nullified. The reference in His saying "ulaika" is to the relative clause described by what preceded, and ﴿for them is security﴾ is a sentence functioning as the predicate of the demonstrative. This is the clearest of what has been said, with the possibility of other aspects. ﴿And they are guided﴾ to the truth, firm upon it, while others are in error and ignorance.

The reference in His saying ﴿And that was Our argument﴾ is to the proofs previously presented by Ibrahim to them: i.e., those proofs that Ibrahim presented to them from His saying ﴿So when the night covered him﴾ to His saying ﴿and they are guided﴾.

﴿Our argument, We gave it to Ibrahim﴾: i.e., We gave it to him and guided him to it. The clause ﴿We gave it to Ibrahim﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, or in the nominative position as a second predicate of the demonstrative. ﴿Against his people﴾: i.e., as a proof against his people. ﴿We raise in degrees whom We will﴾ through guidance and direction to the truth and instruction in proof, or by what is more general than that. ﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise, Knowing﴾: i.e., Wise in everything that proceeds from Him, Knowing of the state of His servants, and that among them are those who deserve elevation and those who do not.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said regarding His saying, ﴿And when Ibrahim said to his father Azar﴾: "Azar is the idol. The father of Ibrahim was named Ya'zar, his mother was named Mithla, his wife was named Sarah, and his concubine, the mother of Isma'il, was named Hajar."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: "Azar was not his father; rather it is the name of an idol."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "His father's name was Tarakh, and the idol's name was Azar."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated a similar report from Ibn Juraij.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sulayman al-Taymi that he recited ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾ and said: "It has reached me that it is 'a'waj' (crooked, harsh), and that it is the harshest word Abraham ever said to his father."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Abraham's father was not named Azar; his name was Tarakh."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* narrated from him regarding the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ that he said: "The sun, the moon, and the stars."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him concerning the verse, that he said: "He (Abraham) had the heavens uncovered until he saw them, [with the earth resting] on a rock, the rock on a fish, namely the fish from which people's food comes, the fish on a chain, and the chain on the Seal of Majesty (Khatam al-'Izzah)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid concerning the verse that he said: "Their authority (sultanuhuma)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Rabi' ibn Anas concerning the words ﴿And his people argued with him﴾ that he said: "They disputed with him."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning the words ﴿Do you argue with me﴾ that he said: "Do you dispute with me?"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) that he interpreted ﴿and did not mix their faith with wrongdoing﴾ as "with polytheism (shirk)." Abu al-Shaykh likewise narrated this from Umar ibn al-Khattab. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Abu al-Shaykh likewise narrated it from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir likewise narrated it from Salman al-Farisi. The two of them also narrated it from Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh likewise narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated a similar report from him (Ibn Abbas) through another chain. Similar reports have also been transmitted from a group of the Tabi'un (Successors). What we have already cited from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in explaining the verse suffices in place of all of these, as is established in the Sahihayn (the two Sahih collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim) and other works.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij concerning the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people﴾ that he said: "Their adversary."
