Then he said to them, completing the proof against them and repelling what they frightened him with:

﴿And how should I fear what you have associated, while you do not fear that you have associated with Allah what He has not sent down any authority for?﴾: i.e., how should I fear what does not harm, benefit, create, or provide, while you do not fear what has issued from you of associating with Allah, who is the Harmer, the Benefactor, the Creator, the Provider. He presented to them this argument of compulsion from which they find no escape or deviation. The interrogation is for denunciation and rebuke. "Ma" in ﴿what He has not sent down any authority for﴾ is the object of "ashraktum": i.e., you do not fear that you made the things for which He has not sent down any authority partners with Allah. Or the meaning is that Allah, glorified is He, did not permit their being made partners with Him, nor did He send down to them any proof by which they could argue for associating them; so how did they worship them, take them as gods, and make them partners with Allah, glorified is He?

His saying: ﴿So which of the two parties is more deserving of security?﴾ The two parties are the party of the believers and the party of the polytheists: (p-431) i.e., if the matter is as previously stated, that my object of worship is Allah, characterized by those attributes, and your object of worship is those created things, how do you frighten me with them, and how should I fear them? They are in such a station, while you do not fear your associating with Allah, glorified is He. After this, inform me: which of the two parties is more deserving of security and freedom from fear ﴿if you know﴾ the true state of affairs and recognize the sound proofs and distinguish them from false doubts.

Then Allah, glorified is He, said, judging between them and clarifying for them: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾: i.e., they are more deserving of security than those who associated. It has been said this is part of Ibrahim's speech; it has been said it is from the speech of Ibrahim's people. The meaning of "did not mix their belief with wrongdoing" is that they did not blend it with wrongdoing. The wrongdoing intended is shirk, as is established in the two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When this verse was revealed, it was hard on the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they said: 'Which of us has not wronged himself?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'It is not as you think; it is as Luqman said: "O my son, do not associate anything with Allah; indeed, association is a great wrong" [Luqman: 13].'" It is strange that the author of al-Kashshaf, in commenting on this verse, says: he rejected interpreting "wrongdoing" as "disbelief" in order to dispel ambiguity, while he does not know that the truthful one whose word is confirmed has explained it this way. When Allah's river comes, the river of Ma'qil is nullified. The reference in His saying "ulaika" is to the relative clause described by what preceded, and ﴿for them is security﴾ is a sentence functioning as the predicate of the demonstrative. This is the clearest of what has been said, with the possibility of other aspects. ﴿And they are guided﴾ to the truth, firm upon it, while others are in error and ignorance.

The reference in His saying ﴿And that was Our argument﴾ is to the proofs previously presented by Ibrahim to them: i.e., those proofs that Ibrahim presented to them from His saying ﴿So when the night covered him﴾ to His saying ﴿and they are guided﴾.

﴿Our argument, We gave it to Ibrahim﴾: i.e., We gave it to him and guided him to it. The clause ﴿We gave it to Ibrahim﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, or in the nominative position as a second predicate of the demonstrative. ﴿Against his people﴾: i.e., as a proof against his people. ﴿We raise in degrees whom We will﴾ through guidance and direction to the truth and instruction in proof, or by what is more general than that. ﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise, Knowing﴾: i.e., Wise in everything that proceeds from Him, Knowing of the state of His servants, and that among them are those who deserve elevation and those who do not.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said regarding His saying, ﴿And when Ibrahim said to his father Azar﴾: "Azar is the idol. The father of Ibrahim was named Ya'zar, his mother was named Mithla, his wife was named Sarah, and his concubine, the mother of Isma'il, was named Hajar."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: "Azar was not his father; rather it is the name of an idol."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "His father's name was Tarakh, and the idol's name was Azar."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated a similar report from Ibn Juraij.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sulayman al-Taymi that he recited ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾ and said: "It has reached me that it is 'a'waj' (crooked, harsh), and that it is the harshest word Abraham ever said to his father."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Abraham's father was not named Azar; his name was Tarakh."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* narrated from him regarding the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ that he said: "The sun, the moon, and the stars."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him concerning the verse, that he said: "He (Abraham) had the heavens uncovered until he saw them, [with the earth resting] on a rock, the rock on a fish, namely the fish from which people's food comes, the fish on a chain, and the chain on the Seal of Majesty (Khatam al-'Izzah)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid concerning the verse that he said: "Their authority (sultanuhuma)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Rabi' ibn Anas concerning the words ﴿And his people argued with him﴾ that he said: "They disputed with him."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning the words ﴿Do you argue with me﴾ that he said: "Do you dispute with me?"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) that he interpreted ﴿and did not mix their faith with wrongdoing﴾ as "with polytheism (shirk)." Abu al-Shaykh likewise narrated this from Umar ibn al-Khattab. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Abu al-Shaykh likewise narrated it from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir likewise narrated it from Salman al-Farisi. The two of them also narrated it from Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh likewise narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated a similar report from him (Ibn Abbas) through another chain. Similar reports have also been transmitted from a group of the Tabi'un (Successors). What we have already cited from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in explaining the verse suffices in place of all of these, as is established in the Sahihayn (the two Sahih collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim) and other works.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij concerning the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people﴾ that he said: "Their adversary."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning the words ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾ that he said: "By knowledge."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: "Indeed, the scholars have degrees like the degrees of the martyrs."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 74–83 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿To his father, Azar﴾. Al-Jawhari said: Azar is a non-Arabic name, and it is derived from "Azara fulan fulanan" when he assisted him, so he is the one who supports his people in worshipping idols.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it is derived from "strength" (al-quwwa).

Al-Juwayni said in his book al-Nukat min al-Tafsir: There is no disagreement among people that the name of Ibrahim's father was Tarikh, and what is in the Qur'an indicates that his name was Azar.

The claim of consensus has been challenged by what is narrated from Ibn Ishaq, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi, that he had two names: Azar and Tarikh.

Muqatil said: Azar is a title (laqab), and Tarikh is a name.

Sulayman al-Taymi said: Azar means "reproach and rebuke," and its meaning in their speech is "the crooked one."

Al-Dahhak said: the meaning of Azar is "the old man, the grieved one" in Persian.

Al-Farra' said: it is an epithet of blame in their language, as if he said: "O you who err."

The same was narrated from al-Zajjaj.

Mujahid said: it is the name of an idol.

On this view, the application of the name of an idol to his father is either by way of addressing him as one whose god it is, or by an ellipsis of a noun: i.e., he said to his father, "Worshipper of Azar," or "Do you worship Azar?" with the verb omitted.

Ibn 'Abbas read "A'izar" with two hamzas, the first fatha and the second kasra, and it is narrated from him that he read with two fathas.

The position of "idh qala" is in the accusative, by way of the estimated phrase "and mention when Ibrahim said," and this estimated phrase is coordinated with ﴿Say: Shall we call upon other than Allah﴾. It has also been said that it is coordinated with ﴿and warn by it lest a soul be delivered to ruin﴾, and "Azar" is in apposition (ʿatf bayan).

His saying: ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾ The interrogation is for denunciation: i.e., do you make them gods for yourself to worship? ﴿Indeed I see you and your people﴾ who follow you in the worship of idols ﴿in manifest error﴾, clearly away from the path of truth.

His saying: ﴿And thus did We show Ibrahim﴾: i.e., and like that vision We showed Ibrahim. The sentence is parenthetical (mu'tarida), and ﴿the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth﴾ means their sovereignty. The taa' and the waw were added for emphasis in the description, and like it are "raghabut" and "rahabut," for emphasis in desire and fear.

It has been said: he meant by the dominion of the heavens and the earth what is in them of creation. It has been said: Allah uncovered that for him until he saw up to the Throne and down to the lowest of the earths. It has been said: he saw from the dominion of the heavens and the earth what Allah related in this verse. It has been said: the intended meaning of their dominion is lordship and divinity: i.e., We showed him that and enabled him to know it through the way of inference that he followed. The meaning of "nuri" is "We showed him," a narration of a past state.

His saying: ﴿And that he might be among the certain (al-muqinin)﴾ is connected to an estimated element: i.e., We showed him that so that he might be among the certain. Azar and his people were worshipping idols, stars, the sun and the moon, so he wanted to alert them to the error. It has been said that he was born in a cave (sarab), and his provision was placed on the tips of his fingers, so he would suck them.

The reason for placing him in the cave is that Nimrod saw a dream that his kingdom would be lost at the hands of a boy, so he ordered the killing of every boy. And Allah knows best.

His saying: ﴿So when the night covered him﴾: i.e., it concealed him with its darkness. From it come "al-janna" (garden/shield), "al-mijann" (shield), and "al-jinn," all from concealment. The poet said:

"And had it not been for the darkness of the night, 'Iyad ibn Thabit would have overtaken our running at Dhi al-Ramth and al-Artam."

The fa' is for coordination with "qala Ibrahim": i.e., and mention when he said, and when the night covered him. This is a separate story from the story of the presentation of the dominion to him. The response of "lamma" is ﴿he saw a star﴾. It has been said he saw it through a crack in the rock placed over the top of the cave he was in. It has been said he saw it when his father brought him out of the cave, and it was the time of the setting of the sun. It has been said he saw Jupiter, and it has been said Venus.

His saying: ﴿This is my lord﴾ is a resumed sentence, an answer to an estimated question, as if it was said: "What did he say when he saw the star?" It has been said: this was from him when his sight was limited, for he was in the time of childhood. It has been said: he intended the establishment of proof against his people, as one who recounts what is among them and what they believe, in order to bind them. The second view was held by al-Zajjaj. It has been said: it is with the omission of the interrogative particle: i.e., "Is this my lord?" and its meaning is a denial that such a thing could be a lord. Similar is His saying: ﴿So if you die, will they be immortal?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 34], i.e., "Will they be immortal?" Similar is the saying of al-Hudhali:

"They enchanted me and said, 'O Khuwaylid, do not be frightened,' so I said, denying the faces: 'They are they.'"

i.e., "Are they they?" And the saying of another:

"By your life, I do not know, though I am knowledgeable, whether with seven they threw the coals or with eight."

i.e., "with seven?" It has been said the meaning is: "And you say, 'This is my lord,'" so the saying is implied. It has been said the meaning, with an omitted noun, is: "This is the proof of my lord."

﴿So when it set﴾: i.e., it went down. Ibrahim said: "I do not love the setting ones," i.e., the gods that set, for setting is a change from one state to another, and it is an indication of having come into being (huduth).

﴿So when he saw the moon rising﴾: i.e., ascending. It is said: "bazagha al-qamar" when it began to rise. And al-bazgh is the splitting; it was splitting the darkness with its light. ﴿So when it set, he said: "Unless my lord guides me﴾: i.e., unless He keeps me firm upon guidance and enables me to the proof ﴿I will surely be among the people who are astray﴾, those who are not guided to the truth, so they wrong themselves and deprive themselves of their share of good.

78. ﴿So when he saw the sun rising﴾: "bazigha" and "bazigatan" are both in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal), because the seeing is visual. He said "This is my lord" although the sun is feminine, because his intention was "this rising one," as said by al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash. It has been said: "this light." It has been said: "this body," "this is greater," i.e., than what preceded it of the star and the moon. ﴿He said: "O my people, indeed I am free of what you associate﴾: i.e., of the things you make partners with Allah and worship. "Ma" is either relative or verbal-masdariyya. He said this when it became clear to him that these things are created, and neither benefit nor harm, deducing this from their setting, which is an indication of their having come into being.

79. ﴿Indeed I have turned my face﴾: i.e., I directed my worship and monotheism to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He mentioned the face because it is the organ by which a person is recognized, or because it is used for the whole person, as already explained. The meaning of "fatara al-samawati wa al-ard" has already been explained: "hanifan," inclining toward the true religion.

80. His saying: ﴿And his people argued with him﴾: i.e., they argued with him about monotheism, with what indicates their claim that what they associate with Allah and worship of idols are gods. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, answered with what Allah related of him: he said, ﴿Do you argue with me concerning Allah?﴾: i.e., concerning His being without partner, without equal, without opposite.

Nafi' read "Atuhajjunni" with lightening of the nun; the rest read it with doubling, by assimilating the plural nun into the protective nun. Nafi' lightened it by deleting one of the two nuns, and Sibawayh permitted that. It is related from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' that Nafi''s reading is a solecism (lahn).

The sentence ﴿and He has already guided me﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: i.e., He guided me to His monotheism, while you want me to be like you in error, ignorance, and lack of guidance.

His saying: ﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him﴾. He said this when they frightened him with their gods, that they would be angry with him and afflict him with some harm. I.e., I do not fear what is a created thing among Allah's creatures that neither harms nor benefits. The pronoun in "bihi" may refer back to Allah, or to their worshipped things understood from "what you associate with Him." ﴿Except that my Lord should will something﴾: i.e., except at the time of my Lord's will, that He afflicts me with some harm for a sin I have committed; the affair is with Him, and that is from Him, not from your false gods that neither harm nor benefit.

The meaning: a negation of harm from their gods in every state, and an affirmation that harm and benefit belong to Allah, glorified is He, and proceed from His will. Then He gave the reason in His saying: ﴿My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾: i.e., His knowledge encompasses everything, so when He wills good, it is according to His will, and when He wills to send some evil upon me, it occurs; what Allah wills occurs and what He does not will does not occur. Then he said to them, completing the proof against them and repelling what they frightened him with:

﴿And how should I fear what you have associated, while you do not fear that you have associated with Allah what He has not sent down any authority for?﴾: i.e., how should I fear what does not harm, benefit, create, or provide, while you do not fear what has issued from you of associating with Allah, who is the Harmer, the Benefactor, the Creator, the Provider. He presented to them this argument of compulsion from which they find no escape or deviation. The interrogation is for denunciation and rebuke. "Ma" in ﴿what He has not sent down any authority for﴾ is the object of "ashraktum": i.e., you do not fear that you made the things for which He has not sent down any authority partners with Allah. Or the meaning is that Allah, glorified is He, did not permit their being made partners with Him, nor did He send down to them any proof by which they could argue for associating them; so how did they worship them, take them as gods, and make them partners with Allah, glorified is He?

His saying: ﴿So which of the two parties is more deserving of security?﴾ The two parties are the party of the believers and the party of the polytheists: (p-431) i.e., if the matter is as previously stated, that my object of worship is Allah, characterized by those attributes, and your object of worship is those created things, how do you frighten me with them, and how should I fear them? They are in such a station, while you do not fear your associating with Allah, glorified is He. After this, inform me: which of the two parties is more deserving of security and freedom from fear ﴿if you know﴾ the true state of affairs and recognize the sound proofs and distinguish them from false doubts.

Then Allah, glorified is He, said, judging between them and clarifying for them: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾: i.e., they are more deserving of security than those who associated. It has been said this is part of Ibrahim's speech; it has been said it is from the speech of Ibrahim's people. The meaning of "did not mix their belief with wrongdoing" is that they did not blend it with wrongdoing. The wrongdoing intended is shirk, as is established in the two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When this verse was revealed, it was hard on the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they said: 'Which of us has not wronged himself?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'It is not as you think; it is as Luqman said: "O my son, do not associate anything with Allah; indeed, association is a great wrong" [Luqman: 13].'" It is strange that the author of al-Kashshaf, in commenting on this verse, says: he rejected interpreting "wrongdoing" as "disbelief" in order to dispel ambiguity, while he does not know that the truthful one whose word is confirmed has explained it this way. When Allah's river comes, the river of Ma'qil is nullified. The reference in His saying "ulaika" is to the relative clause described by what preceded, and ﴿for them is security﴾ is a sentence functioning as the predicate of the demonstrative. This is the clearest of what has been said, with the possibility of other aspects. ﴿And they are guided﴾ to the truth, firm upon it, while others are in error and ignorance.

The reference in His saying ﴿And that was Our argument﴾ is to the proofs previously presented by Ibrahim to them: i.e., those proofs that Ibrahim presented to them from His saying ﴿So when the night covered him﴾ to His saying ﴿and they are guided﴾.

﴿Our argument, We gave it to Ibrahim﴾: i.e., We gave it to him and guided him to it. The clause ﴿We gave it to Ibrahim﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, or in the nominative position as a second predicate of the demonstrative. ﴿Against his people﴾: i.e., as a proof against his people. ﴿We raise in degrees whom We will﴾ through guidance and direction to the truth and instruction in proof, or by what is more general than that. ﴿Indeed your Lord is Wise, Knowing﴾: i.e., Wise in everything that proceeds from Him, Knowing of the state of His servants, and that among them are those who deserve elevation and those who do not.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said regarding His saying, ﴿And when Ibrahim said to his father Azar﴾: "Azar is the idol. The father of Ibrahim was named Ya'zar, his mother was named Mithla, his wife was named Sarah, and his concubine, the mother of Isma'il, was named Hajar."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: "Azar was not his father; rather it is the name of an idol."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "His father's name was Tarakh, and the idol's name was Azar."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated a similar report from Ibn Juraij.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sulayman al-Taymi that he recited ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾ and said: "It has reached me that it is 'a'waj' (crooked, harsh), and that it is the harshest word Abraham ever said to his father."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Abraham's father was not named Azar; his name was Tarakh."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* narrated from him regarding the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ that he said: "The sun, the moon, and the stars."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him concerning the verse, that he said: "He (Abraham) had the heavens uncovered until he saw them, [with the earth resting] on a rock, the rock on a fish, namely the fish from which people's food comes, the fish on a chain, and the chain on the Seal of Majesty (Khatam al-'Izzah)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid concerning the verse that he said: "Their authority (sultanuhuma)."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Rabi' ibn Anas concerning the words ﴿And his people argued with him﴾ that he said: "They disputed with him."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning the words ﴿Do you argue with me﴾ that he said: "Do you dispute with me?"

Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) that he interpreted ﴿and did not mix their faith with wrongdoing﴾ as "with polytheism (shirk)." Abu al-Shaykh likewise narrated this from Umar ibn al-Khattab. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Abu al-Shaykh likewise narrated it from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir likewise narrated it from Salman al-Farisi. The two of them also narrated it from Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh likewise narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated a similar report from him (Ibn Abbas) through another chain. Similar reports have also been transmitted from a group of the Tabi'un (Successors). What we have already cited from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in explaining the verse suffices in place of all of these, as is established in the Sahihayn (the two Sahih collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim) and other works.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij concerning the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave Abraham against his people﴾ that he said: "Their adversary."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam concerning the words ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾ that he said: "By knowledge."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: "Indeed, the scholars have degrees like the degrees of the martyrs."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 84–90:

His words, ﴿And We bestowed upon him﴾, are coordinated (ma'tuf) with the clause ﴿And that was Our argument﴾ [al-An'am: 83]. He coordinated a verbal clause with a nominal clause. It has also been said that it is coordinated with "ataynaha" (We gave it), but the first view is preferable.

The meaning is: We bestowed upon him that as a reward for his arguing about the religion and his giving of himself for it. (p-432) ﴿Each of them We guided﴾: the accusative of "kullan" (each) is because it is the object of the verb that follows it, placed before it for restriction (qasr). That is, each one of them We guided. Likewise, "Nuhan" (Noah) is in the accusative by "hadayna" (We guided) the second, or by a hidden verb that the following words explain. ﴿And from his offspring﴾: that is, from the offspring of Abraham. Al-Farra' said: from the offspring of Noah.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, al-Qushayri and Ibn 'Atiyya preferred this second view. Al-Zajjaj preferred the first. It has been objected to it that he counted among this offspring Yunus and Lut, and they were not from the offspring of Abraham, since Lut was the son of Abraham's brother. "Dawud" and "Sulayman" are in the accusative by a hidden verb, meaning: and We guided from his offspring Dawud and Sulayman. The same applies to what follows them. God, glorified be He, counted the guidance of these prophets among the blessings He enumerated for Abraham, because the honour of sons is connected to that of fathers.

The meaning of "min qabl" (before) in His words ﴿and Noah We guided before﴾ is: before Abraham. The reference in His words "wa-kadhalika" (and likewise) to the verbal noun of the verb that comes later is: and a reward like that ﴿We reward the good-doers﴾.

And Ilyas (Elias).

Al-Dahhak said: he is from the descendants of Isma'il. Al-Qutaybi said: he is from the tribe of Yusha' ibn Nun.

Al-A'raj, al-Hasan and Qatada read "wa-l-yasa'" with the hamza of the definite article (al-) pronounced as a connecting hamza (wasl).

The people of the two sanctuaries (Ahl al-Haramayn), Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read "al-yasa'" with a single lam and lightened (mukhaffafan).

The Kufans, except 'Asim, read it with two lams. Al-Kisa'i also read so, and he rejected the first reading. There is no basis for the rejection, for it is a foreign (a'jami) name, and foreignness is not subject to analogy but is transmitted as it was heard. It is not impossible that the name has two forms among the non-Arabs, or that the Arabs changed it in two ways.

Al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads with one lam, the name is "yasa'" and the alif and lam are extra, as in the saying of the poet:

"I saw al-Walid ibn Yazid blessed,
his shoulder heavy with the burdens of the caliphate."

Whoever reads with two lams, the name is "Layasa'". Some people thought that al-Yasa' is Ilyas, and this is a mistake, for God mentioned each of them separately.

Wahb said: al-Yasa' was the companion of Ilyas, and they were before Yahya, 'Isa and Zakariyya. It has also been said that Ilyas is Idris, but this is not correct, for Idris was the grandfather of Noah and Ilyas was from his descendants. It has also been said that Ilyas is al-Khidr, and it has been said: no, rather al-Yasa' is al-Khidr. ﴿And each of them We preferred over the worlds﴾: that is, each one of them We preferred by prophethood over the worlds of his time. The clause is parenthetical (mu'tarida).

His words ﴿And from their fathers and their offspring and their brothers﴾: that is, We guided. "Min" (from) is partitive: that is, We guided some of their fathers, offspring and brothers. ﴿And We chose them﴾ is coordinated with "faddalna" (We preferred). "Ijtiba'" (choosing) means selection, or purification, or preference, and it is derived from "jaba'tu al-ma' fi al-hawd" (I gathered the water in the pool), meaning I collected it. So "ijtiba'" is joining what you choose to your special possession.

Al-Kisa'i said: "jaba'tu al-ma' fi al-hawd" is a verb with a short form "jaby" (gathering), and "al-jabiya" is the pool. The poet said:

"Like the pool of the Iraqi shaykh, overflowing."

The reference in His words ﴿That is the guidance of God﴾ is to the guidance, the preference, and the choosing understood from the preceding verbs. ﴿He guides by it﴾, God, ﴿whom He wills of His servants﴾, and they are those whom He granted success for good and for following the truth. ﴿And had they associated﴾: that is, these mentioned ones, by worshipping other than God, ﴿their deeds would have been nullified from them﴾ of their good works. ﴿That which they used to do﴾. Ihbat (nullification) means invalidation.

Its verification was discussed previously in al-Baqarah.

The reference in His words ﴿Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book﴾ is to the prophets mentioned earlier. That is, the genus of the Book, so that it applies to everything revealed to these mentioned ones, and the judgement (hukm), the knowledge ('ilm), the prophethood (nubuwwa), the messengership (risala), or what is more general than that. ﴿So if these disbelieve in them﴾: the pronoun in "bihā" (in them) refers to the judgement, the prophethood and the Book, or to prophethood alone. The reference by "these" is to the disbelieving Quraysh, the obstinate opponents of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). ﴿Then We have entrusted with them a people﴾: this is the answer to the conditional: that is, We have assigned to belief in them a people ﴿who are not disbelievers in them﴾. They are the Emigrants (Muhajirun) and the Helpers (Ansar), or the prophets mentioned earlier.

This second view is preferable because of His words afterwards: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾. For the reference is to the mentioned prophets, not to the Emigrants and Helpers, since it would not be correct for the Prophet (ﷺ) to be commanded to follow their guidance. And placing "bi-hudahum" (by their guidance) before the verb indicates the restriction of their guidance to being followed. "Iqtida'" (following) is seeking to conform to another's action.

It has been said: the meaning is: be patient as they were patient. It has been said: follow them in monotheism (tawhid), even though the particulars of the laws differ. In it there is evidence that he (ﷺ) is commanded to follow the prophets before him in matters for which no explicit text was revealed to him.

His words ﴿Say: I do not ask you for a reward for it﴾: God commanded him to tell them that he does not ask them for a reward for the Qur'an, and to say to them: it is nothing but a reminder (dhikra), meaning the Qur'an, ﴿to the worlds﴾, that is, an admonition and a reminder for all creation, those present at its revelation and those who will exist after them.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: "the maternal uncle is a father, and the paternal uncle is a father." God attributed 'Isa to his maternal relatives, saying: ﴿And from his offspring﴾ until His words: ﴿Zakariyya and Yahya and 'Isa﴾.

Abu al-Shaykh and al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi reported from 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr, who said: Yahya ibn Ya'mar entered upon al-Hajjaj and mentioned al-Husayn. Al-Hajjaj said: he was not from the offspring of the Prophet. Yahya said: you lie. Al-Hajjaj said: you must bring me evidence for what you say. So he recited ﴿And from his offspring﴾ up to His words "'Isa", and God informed that 'Isa was from the offspring of Adam through his mother. Al-Hajjaj said: you have spoken truly.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Harb ibn Abi al-Aswad, who said: al-Hajjaj sent for Yahya ibn Ya'mar and said: I have been informed that you claim al-Hasan and al-Husayn are from the offspring of the Prophet; you will find it in the Book of God, and I have read it from its beginning to its end and did not find it. Yahya ibn Ya'mar mentioned something similar to what preceded.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿and We chose them﴾, that he said: we purified them.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Zayd, regarding His words ﴿And had they associated, their deeds would have been nullified from them﴾, that he said: he means these whom We guided and upon whom We bestowed favour.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid, who said: "al-hukm" is intellect (al-lubb).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿So if these disbelieve in them﴾, that he said: meaning the people of Makkah; he says: if they disbelieve in the Qur'an ﴿then We have entrusted with them a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾, meaning the people of Madinah and the Helpers.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿Then We have entrusted with them a people﴾, that he said: they are the eighteen prophets about whom God said: (p-433) ﴿so follow their guidance﴾. Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi, who said regarding the verse: they are the angels. Al-Bukhari, al-Nasa'i and others reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿so follow their guidance﴾, that he said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was commanded to follow their guidance, and he used to prostrate in Sad. The wording of Ibn Abi Hatim from Mujahid is: I asked Ibn 'Abbas about the prostration in Sad, and he recited this verse and said: your Prophet was commanded to follow Dawud (peace be upon him).

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Say: I do not ask you for a reward for it﴾, that he said: say to them, O Muhammad: I do not ask you for anything in return for what I call you to, a passing benefit of the goods of this world.

His words, ﴿And We bestowed upon him﴾, are coordinated (ma'tuf) with the clause ﴿And that was Our argument﴾ [al-An'am: 83]. He coordinated a verbal clause with a nominal clause. It has also been said that it is coordinated with "ataynaha" (We gave it), but the first view is preferable.

The meaning is: We bestowed upon him that as a reward for his arguing about the religion and his giving of himself for it. (p-432) ﴿Each of them We guided﴾: the accusative of "kullan" (each) is because it is the object of the verb that follows it, placed before it for restriction (qasr). That is, each one of them We guided. Likewise, "Nuhan" (Noah) is in the accusative by "hadayna" (We guided) the second, or by a hidden verb that the following words explain. ﴿And from his offspring﴾: that is, from the offspring of Abraham. Al-Farra' said: from the offspring of Noah.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, al-Qushayri and Ibn 'Atiyya preferred this second view. Al-Zajjaj preferred the first. It has been objected to it that he counted among this offspring Yunus and Lut, and they were not from the offspring of Abraham, since Lut was the son of Abraham's brother. "Dawud" and "Sulayman" are in the accusative by a hidden verb, meaning: and We guided from his offspring Dawud and Sulayman. The same applies to what follows them. God, glorified be He, counted the guidance of these prophets among the blessings He enumerated for Abraham, because the honour of sons is connected to that of fathers.

The meaning of "min qabl" (before) in His words ﴿and Noah We guided before﴾ is: before Abraham. The reference in His words "wa-kadhalika" (and likewise) to the verbal noun of the verb that comes later is: and a reward like that ﴿We reward the good-doers﴾.

And Ilyas (Elias).

Al-Dahhak said: he is from the descendants of Isma'il. Al-Qutaybi said: he is from the tribe of Yusha' ibn Nun.

Al-A'raj, al-Hasan and Qatada read "wa-l-yasa'" with the hamza of the definite article (al-) pronounced as a connecting hamza (wasl).

The people of the two sanctuaries (Ahl al-Haramayn), Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read "al-yasa'" with a single lam and lightened (mukhaffafan).

The Kufans, except 'Asim, read it with two lams. Al-Kisa'i also read so, and he rejected the first reading. There is no basis for the rejection, for it is a foreign (a'jami) name, and foreignness is not subject to analogy but is transmitted as it was heard. It is not impossible that the name has two forms among the non-Arabs, or that the Arabs changed it in two ways.

Al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads with one lam, the name is "yasa'" and the alif and lam are extra, as in the saying of the poet:

"I saw al-Walid ibn Yazid blessed,
his shoulder heavy with the burdens of the caliphate."

Whoever reads with two lams, the name is "Layasa'". Some people thought that al-Yasa' is Ilyas, and this is a mistake, for God mentioned each of them separately.

Wahb said: al-Yasa' was the companion of Ilyas, and they were before Yahya, 'Isa and Zakariyya. It has also been said that Ilyas is Idris, but this is not correct, for Idris was the grandfather of Noah and Ilyas was from his descendants. It has also been said that Ilyas is al-Khidr, and it has been said: no, rather al-Yasa' is al-Khidr. ﴿And each of them We preferred over the worlds﴾: that is, each one of them We preferred by prophethood over the worlds of his time. The clause is parenthetical (mu'tarida).

His words ﴿And from their fathers and their offspring and their brothers﴾: that is, We guided. "Min" (from) is partitive: that is, We guided some of their fathers, offspring and brothers. ﴿And We chose them﴾ is coordinated with "faddalna" (We preferred). "Ijtiba'" (choosing) means selection, or purification, or preference, and it is derived from "jaba'tu al-ma' fi al-hawd" (I gathered the water in the pool), meaning I collected it. So "ijtiba'" is joining what you choose to your special possession.

Al-Kisa'i said: "jaba'tu al-ma' fi al-hawd" is a verb with a short form "jaby" (gathering), and "al-jabiya" is the pool. The poet said:

"Like the pool of the Iraqi shaykh, overflowing."

The reference in His words ﴿That is the guidance of God﴾ is to the guidance, the preference, and the choosing understood from the preceding verbs. ﴿He guides by it﴾, God, ﴿whom He wills of His servants﴾, and they are those whom He granted success for good and for following the truth. ﴿And had they associated﴾: that is, these mentioned ones, by worshipping other than God, ﴿their deeds would have been nullified from them﴾ of their good works. ﴿That which they used to do﴾. Ihbat (nullification) means invalidation.

Its verification was discussed previously in al-Baqarah.

The reference in His words ﴿Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book﴾ is to the prophets mentioned earlier. That is, the genus of the Book, so that it applies to everything revealed to these mentioned ones, and the judgement (hukm), the knowledge ('ilm), the prophethood (nubuwwa), the messengership (risala), or what is more general than that. ﴿So if these disbelieve in them﴾: the pronoun in "bihā" (in them) refers to the judgement, the prophethood and the Book, or to prophethood alone. The reference by "these" is to the disbelieving Quraysh, the obstinate opponents of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). ﴿Then We have entrusted with them a people﴾: this is the answer to the conditional: that is, We have assigned to belief in them a people ﴿who are not disbelievers in them﴾. They are the Emigrants (Muhajirun) and the Helpers (Ansar), or the prophets mentioned earlier.

This second view is preferable because of His words afterwards: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾. For the reference is to the mentioned prophets, not to the Emigrants and Helpers, since it would not be correct for the Prophet (ﷺ) to be commanded to follow their guidance. And placing "bi-hudahum" (by their guidance) before the verb indicates the restriction of their guidance to being followed. "Iqtida'" (following) is seeking to conform to another's action.

It has been said: the meaning is: be patient as they were patient. It has been said: follow them in monotheism (tawhid), even though the particulars of the laws differ. In it there is evidence that he (ﷺ) is commanded to follow the prophets before him in matters for which no explicit text was revealed to him.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 6, verses 91–94 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿They did not measure God with the true measure of His worth.﴾ *Qadartu al-shay'* and *qadartuhu* mean "I knew its measure." Its root meaning is "concealment," and it was then used for knowing a thing. The sense is: they did not know Him with the true knowledge of Him, since they denied that He sends messengers and sends down Books.

It was also said that the meaning is: they did not measure the blessings of God with their true measure.

Abu Hamzah read *wa-ma qadarū Allāha ḥaqqa qadarihi* with a fatḥah on the *dal* (*qadar*). This is a dialectal form (*lughah*). When this denial came from them, and they were Jews, God commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to present them with an argument they could not repel. So He said: ﴿Say: Who sent down the Book which Moses brought?﴾ They acknowledged this and submitted to it. In this there was a rebuke and reproach to them beyond measure, while compelling them to admit what they had denied: that God sent down revelation to humans, namely the prophets (peace be upon them). Thus their denial was refuted and the corruption of their denial was made clear.

It was also said that those who uttered this statement were the disbelievers of Quraysh. In that case, the argument that God sent down the Book to Moses is addressed to them on the basis that they acknowledged it and knew it from reports from the Jews, whom they used to believe.

﴿Light and guidance﴾ are both in the accusative as circumstantial qualifiers (*ḥāl*). ﴿For the people﴾ is attached to an omitted element which is a qualifier of *hudan* (guidance), meaning: existing for the people.

His saying: ﴿You make it into scrolls.﴾ That is: you make the Book which Moses brought into scrolls, in which you write it, so that what you want of alteration, substitution, and concealment of the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned in it may be accomplished for you. This is a censure of them. The pronoun in ﴿you disclose them﴾ refers to the scrolls, and the pronoun in ﴿you make it﴾ refers to the Book. The clause ﴿you make it﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier. The clause ﴿you disclose them﴾ is a qualifier of *qarāṭīs* (scrolls). ﴿And you conceal much﴾ is coordinated with ﴿you disclose them﴾, meaning: and you conceal much of them.

The address in ﴿And you were taught what you did not know, you nor your fathers﴾ is to the Jews, meaning: while you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew. It is possible that this clause is a new sentence confirming what precedes it. What they came to know is what our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) informed them of, from the matters revealed to him by God, for these included what was not known to them from their Books, nor through the words of their prophets, nor known to their fathers. It is also possible that *mā* in ﴿what you did not know﴾ refers to what they knew from the Torah, in which case it is a favour (*mann*) bestowed upon them by sending down the Torah.

It was also said that the address is to the polytheists of Quraysh and others, so *mā* refers to what they came to know from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Then God commanded His Messenger to answer this argument which He had imposed on them when He said: ﴿Who sent down the Book which Moses brought?﴾ So He said: ﴿Say: God.﴾ That is, God sent it down. ﴿Then leave them in their discourse, playing.﴾ That is, leave them in their falsehood while they play, meaning they behave like children who play.

His saying: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed.﴾ This is part of the refutation of them in their saying: ﴿God has not sent down anything upon a human.﴾ He informed them that God sent down the Torah to Moses, and followed it with: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down,﴾ meaning upon Muhammad (ﷺ). So how can you say: ﴿God has not sent down anything upon a human?﴾ ﴿Blessed﴾ and ﴿confirming﴾ are two qualifiers of *kitāb* (Book). *Mubārak* is abundant in blessing, and *muṣaddiq* is abundant in confirmation. ﴿What is between its hands﴾ refers to the Books God sent down to the prophets before it, such as the Torah and the Gospel. It agrees with them in calling to God and to His unity, even if it differs with them in some rulings.

His saying: ﴿And that you may warn﴾. It was said that it is coordinated with what is indicated by *mubārak*, as if it were said: We sent it down for blessings and that you may warn. He specified the Mother of Cities, which is Mecca, because it is the greatest of the cities in standing, because it is the first house set up for people, and because it is the qiblah of this community and the place of their pilgrimage. So warning its people entails warning all the people of the earth. The intended meaning of ﴿those around it﴾ is all the people of the earth. The intended meaning of warning the Mother of Cities is warning its people and the people of the rest of the earth, so this is by way of an omitted genitive construction, like ﴿ask the town﴾.

﴿Those who believe in the Hereafter﴾ is a subject (*mubtada'*), and ﴿they believe in it﴾ is its predicate. The meaning: it is incumbent upon whoever affirms the Last Abode to believe in this Book, affirm it, and act upon what is in it, because affirming the Hereafter requires accepting one who calls people to what brings its good and averts its harm. The clause ﴿and they guard over their prayer﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier. He singled out guarding the prayer from among all the obligations because it is its pillar and is like the head to the body.

His saying: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates against God a lie?﴾ This clause confirms the content of what preceded of the argument against them, that God sent down Books to His messengers. That is: how can you say: ﴿God has not sent down anything upon a human,﴾ and that entails denying the prophets (peace be upon them)? And none is more unjust than one who fabricates against God a lie, claiming to be a prophet when he is not one, or who lies about God concerning anything. ﴿Or says: It has been revealed to me,﴾ while nothing has been revealed to him. That is, while the true state is that nothing was revealed to him. God has protected His prophets from what you claim about them. This is only the way of the great liars, leaders of misguidance, such as Musaylimah the Liar, al-Aswad al-'Ansi, and Sajah.

His saying: ﴿And who says: I will send down the like of what God has sent down.﴾ This is coordinated with *man iftara* (one who fabricates). That is: and who is more unjust than one who fabricates, or than one who says: It has been revealed to me when nothing has been revealed to him, or than one who says: I will send down the like of what God has sent down. They are those who say: ﴿If we willed, we would say the like of this﴾ [al-Anfal: 31].

It was also said: "He is 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh, for he used to write the revelation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The Messenger of God (ﷺ) dictated to him: ﴿Then We produced it as another creation,﴾ and 'Abd Allah said: ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators.﴾ The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Thus it was revealed.' 'Abd Allah then doubted and said: If Muhammad is truthful, then it was revealed to me as it was revealed to him; and if he is lying, then I have said as he said.' Then he apostatized from Islam and joined the polytheists, then he embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest," as is well known.

His saying: ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death.﴾ The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or to everyone suited to it. The intended meaning is every wrongdoer, and it includes, primarily, those who deny what God has sent down and those who claim prophethood by fabricating against God. The answer to *law* (if) is omitted: that is, you would see a tremendous matter. *Al-ghamarāt* is the plural of *ghamrah*, meaning hardship. Its original sense is a thing that overwhelms (*yaghmuru*) things and covers them, as in *ghamrat al-mā'* (the flood of water). Then it was used for hardships, as in *ghamrat al-ḥarb* (the surge of battle).

Al-Jawhari said: *al-ghamrah* means hardship, and its plural is *ghumar*, like *nawbah* and *nawab*.

His saying: ﴿And the angels stretch out their hands﴾ is in the accusative position: that is, while the angels stretch out their hands to seize the souls of the disbelievers. It was also said: for punishment, and in their hands are iron hammers. A similar statement is God's saying: ﴿If you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieved, striking their faces and their backs﴾ [al-Anfal: 50].

His saying: ﴿Bring out your souls.﴾ That is, saying to them: bring out your souls from these agonies into which you have fallen, or bring out your souls from our hands and free them from punishment, or bring out your souls from your bodies and surrender them to us so that we may seize them. ﴿Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation.﴾ That is, the day on which your souls are seized. Or they meant by "today" the time in which they are punished, whose beginning is the punishment of the grave. *Al-hūn* and *al-hawān* have the same meaning: that is, today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation, by which you will be in disgrace and abasement after what you were in of arrogance and self-exaltation. The *bā'* in ﴿because you used to say about God other than the truth﴾ indicates cause: that is, because of your saying this, denying that God sent down His Books to His messengers, and associating others with Him. ﴿And you used to be arrogant toward His signs﴾, refusing to affirm them and to act upon them. So what you were recompensed with of the punishment of humiliation was ﴿a fitting recompense﴾ [al-Naba': 26].

His saying (94): ﴿And you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time.﴾

Abu Haywah read *furādan* with tanwin, which is the dialect of Tamim. The rest read it with the feminine *alif* for the plural, so it does not take tanwin.

Tha'lab related *furād* without tanwin, like *thalāth* and *rubā'*. *Furādā* is the plural of *fard*, like *sukārā* the plural of *sakrān*, and *kusālā* the plural of *kaslān*. The meaning: you have come to Us individually, one by one, each of you alone, apart from his family and his wealth, and from what he used to worship besides God, so he benefited nothing from any of that. ﴿As We created you the first time﴾: that is, in the state in which you were when you came out from your mothers' wombs. The *kāf* (as) is a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun: that is, you have come to Us a coming like your coming when We created you; or it is a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in *furādā*: that is, resembling the beginning of Our creating you. ﴿And you left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾: that is, what We gave you. *Al-khawl* is what God gives a person of worldly goods. That is, you left that behind you and did not bring any of it to Us, nor did you benefit from it in any way. ﴿And We do not see with you your intercessors whom﴾ you worshipped and said: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to God in position﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], and ﴿you claimed that they were among you partners﴾ of God, deserving worship from you as He deserves it.

His saying: ﴿Certainly your bonds have been severed.﴾

Nafi', al-Kisa'i, and Hafs read *baynakum* with a fatḥah, as an adverbial of place (*ẓarfiyyah*). The subject of *taqaṭṭaʿa* is omitted: that is, the connection between you and your partners has been severed, as indicated by ﴿and We do not see with you your intercessors.﴾

The rest read it with a ḍammah, attributing the severing to *al-bayn* (the space between): that is, the severing occurred between you. It is possible that the meaning of the reading with fatḥah is the same as the meaning of the reading with ḍammah, in attributing the verb to the adverb. It was given the fatḥah because it is frequently used as an adverb.

Ibn Mas'ud read: *laqad taqaṭṭaʿa mā baynakum*, attributing the verb to *mā*: that is, what was between you. ﴿And what you used to claim has gone astray from you﴾ of the partners and of the association, and you were prevented from them and they from you.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿They did not measure God with the true measure of His worth,﴾ that he said: They are the disbelievers who did not believe in God's power. Whoever believes that God is over all things powerful has measured God with the true measure of His worth, and whoever does not believe in that has not measured God with the true measure of His worth, when they said: ﴿God has not sent down anything upon a human.﴾

"The Jews said: O Muhammad, has God sent down a Book to you? He said: Yes. They said: By God, God has not sent down any Book from heaven. So God sent down: Say, O Muhammad: Who sent down the Book which Moses brought?" up to the end of the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, regarding ﴿They did not measure God with the true measure of His worth, when they said: God has not sent down anything upon a human,﴾ that it was said by the polytheists of Quraysh.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi, who said: Finhas the Jew said: God has not sent down anything upon Muhammad, and then it was revealed.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from 'Ikrimah, who said: It was revealed concerning Malik ibn al-Sayf.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 91–94 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "A man from the Jews called Malik ibn al-Sayf came and disputed with the Prophet (ﷺ). The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'I adjure you by He who sent down the Torah to Musa: Do you find in the Torah that God hates the fat rabbi?' He was a fat rabbi, so he became angry and said: 'By God, God has not sent down anything upon any human being.' His companions said to him: 'Woe to you! Not even upon Musa?' He said: 'God has not sent down anything upon any human being.' Then this was revealed."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid concerning God's words, ﴿You make it into scattered pages﴾, that he said: "(It refers to) the Jews." And concerning His words (p-435) ﴿And you were taught what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers﴾, he said: "This is addressed to the Muslims."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada concerning God's words, ﴿And you were taught what you did not know﴾, that he said: "They are the Jews. God gave them knowledge, but they did not follow it, did not act upon it, and did not practise it, so God censured them for that knowledge."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada concerning God's words, ﴿And this is a blessed Book which We have sent down﴾, that he said: "It is the Qur'an which God sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from him, saying concerning ﴿confirming what came before it﴾: "That is, of the Books that passed before it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning God's words, ﴿that you may warn the Mother of the Cities﴾, that he said: "Makkah and those around it."

He said: "He means the towns around it, to the east and to the west."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "It was called the Mother of the Cities only because the first House was founded in it."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatada concerning God's words, ﴿that you may warn the Mother of the Cities﴾, that he said: "It is Makkah." He said: "And it has reached me that the earth was spread out from Makkah."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated similarly from Ata' ibn Dinar.

Al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak narrated from Shurahbil ibn Sa'd, who said: "It was revealed concerning Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh, (the verse) ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God, or says, 'It has been revealed to me,' when nothing has been revealed to him﴾, to the end of the verse. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered Makkah, he fled to Uthman, his foster brother, and Uthman hid him with himself until the people of Makkah were reassured. Then he sought safe conduct for him."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Khalaf al-A'mā that it was revealed concerning Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh. Ibn Abi Hatim likewise narrated from al-Suddi.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij concerning God's words, ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God, or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him﴾, that he said: "It was revealed concerning Musaylima the Liar and those like him who called to what he called to. (And) ﴿or who says, "I will send down the like of what God has sent down"﴾, it was revealed concerning Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated similarly from Ikrimah.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ikrimah that when (the verses) ﴿By those sent forth in succession﴾ and ﴿By those that blow violently﴾ [al-Mursalat: 1–2] were revealed, al-Nadr, who was from the Banu Abd al-Dar, said: "And by those that grind, grinding, and those that knead, kneading," with much (other) speech. So God revealed ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God﴾, to the end of the verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning God's words, ﴿in the agonies of death﴾, that he said: "The throes of death."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning God's words, ﴿and the angels will stretch out their hands﴾, that he said: "This is at the time of death. And the stretching out (basṭ) is striking." (Compare) ﴿striking their faces and their backs﴾ [al-Anfal: 50; Muhammad: 27].

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him, saying: "In the verse, this is the Angel of Death (peace be upon him)."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Dahhak concerning God's words, ﴿and the angels will stretch out their hands﴾, that he said: "With punishment."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid concerning God's words, ﴿the punishment of humiliation﴾, that he said: "The humiliation."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ikrimah, who said: "al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said: 'Al-Lat and al-Uzza will intercede for me.' So (the verse) was revealed: ﴿And you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾, to the end of the verse."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning God's words, ﴿And you have come to Us alone﴾, to the end of the verse, that he said: "(It is) like the day you were born: everything that was taken from you on the day you were born will be returned to you."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi concerning God's words, ﴿And you have left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾, that he said: "Of wealth and servants." (Concerning) ﴿behind your backs﴾, he said: "In this world."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatada concerning God's words, ﴿Now your bonds have been cut off from you﴾, that he said: "(It means) what had been between them of connection."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid concerning God's words, ﴿Now your bonds have been cut off from you﴾, that he said: "Your association with one another in this world."
