The meaning: you have come to Us individually, one by one, each of you alone, apart from his family and his wealth, and from what he used to worship besides God, so he benefited nothing from any of that. ﴿As We created you the first time﴾: that is, in the state in which you were when you came out from your mothers' wombs. The *kāf* (as) is a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun: that is, you have come to Us a coming like your coming when We created you; or it is a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in *furādā*: that is, resembling the beginning of Our creating you. ﴿And you left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾: that is, what We gave you. *Al-khawl* is what God gives a person of worldly goods. That is, you left that behind you and did not bring any of it to Us, nor did you benefit from it in any way. ﴿And We do not see with you your intercessors whom﴾ you worshipped and said: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to God in position﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], and ﴿you claimed that they were among you partners﴾ of God, deserving worship from you as He deserves it.

His saying: ﴿Certainly your bonds have been severed.﴾

Nafi', al-Kisa'i, and Hafs read *baynakum* with a fatḥah, as an adverbial of place (*ẓarfiyyah*). The subject of *taqaṭṭaʿa* is omitted: that is, the connection between you and your partners has been severed, as indicated by ﴿and We do not see with you your intercessors.﴾

The rest read it with a ḍammah, attributing the severing to *al-bayn* (the space between): that is, the severing occurred between you. It is possible that the meaning of the reading with fatḥah is the same as the meaning of the reading with ḍammah, in attributing the verb to the adverb. It was given the fatḥah because it is frequently used as an adverb.

Ibn Mas'ud read: *laqad taqaṭṭaʿa mā baynakum*, attributing the verb to *mā*: that is, what was between you. ﴿And what you used to claim has gone astray from you﴾ of the partners and of the association, and you were prevented from them and they from you.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿They did not measure God with the true measure of His worth,﴾ that he said: They are the disbelievers who did not believe in God's power. Whoever believes that God is over all things powerful has measured God with the true measure of His worth, and whoever does not believe in that has not measured God with the true measure of His worth, when they said: ﴿God has not sent down anything upon a human.﴾

"The Jews said: O Muhammad, has God sent down a Book to you? He said: Yes. They said: By God, God has not sent down any Book from heaven. So God sent down: Say, O Muhammad: Who sent down the Book which Moses brought?" up to the end of the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, regarding ﴿They did not measure God with the true measure of His worth, when they said: God has not sent down anything upon a human,﴾ that it was said by the polytheists of Quraysh.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi, who said: Finhas the Jew said: God has not sent down anything upon Muhammad, and then it was revealed.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from 'Ikrimah, who said: It was revealed concerning Malik ibn al-Sayf.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 91–94 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "A man from the Jews called Malik ibn al-Sayf came and disputed with the Prophet (ﷺ). The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'I adjure you by He who sent down the Torah to Musa: Do you find in the Torah that God hates the fat rabbi?' He was a fat rabbi, so he became angry and said: 'By God, God has not sent down anything upon any human being.' His companions said to him: 'Woe to you! Not even upon Musa?' He said: 'God has not sent down anything upon any human being.' Then this was revealed."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid concerning God's words, ﴿You make it into scattered pages﴾, that he said: "(It refers to) the Jews." And concerning His words (p-435) ﴿And you were taught what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers﴾, he said: "This is addressed to the Muslims."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada concerning God's words, ﴿And you were taught what you did not know﴾, that he said: "They are the Jews. God gave them knowledge, but they did not follow it, did not act upon it, and did not practise it, so God censured them for that knowledge."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada concerning God's words, ﴿And this is a blessed Book which We have sent down﴾, that he said: "It is the Qur'an which God sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from him, saying concerning ﴿confirming what came before it﴾: "That is, of the Books that passed before it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning God's words, ﴿that you may warn the Mother of the Cities﴾, that he said: "Makkah and those around it."

He said: "He means the towns around it, to the east and to the west."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "It was called the Mother of the Cities only because the first House was founded in it."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatada concerning God's words, ﴿that you may warn the Mother of the Cities﴾, that he said: "It is Makkah." He said: "And it has reached me that the earth was spread out from Makkah."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated similarly from Ata' ibn Dinar.

Al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak narrated from Shurahbil ibn Sa'd, who said: "It was revealed concerning Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh, (the verse) ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God, or says, 'It has been revealed to me,' when nothing has been revealed to him﴾, to the end of the verse. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered Makkah, he fled to Uthman, his foster brother, and Uthman hid him with himself until the people of Makkah were reassured. Then he sought safe conduct for him."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Khalaf al-A'mā that it was revealed concerning Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh. Ibn Abi Hatim likewise narrated from al-Suddi.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij concerning God's words, ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God, or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him﴾, that he said: "It was revealed concerning Musaylima the Liar and those like him who called to what he called to. (And) ﴿or who says, "I will send down the like of what God has sent down"﴾, it was revealed concerning Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated similarly from Ikrimah.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ikrimah that when (the verses) ﴿By those sent forth in succession﴾ and ﴿By those that blow violently﴾ [al-Mursalat: 1–2] were revealed, al-Nadr, who was from the Banu Abd al-Dar, said: "And by those that grind, grinding, and those that knead, kneading," with much (other) speech. So God revealed ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God﴾, to the end of the verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning God's words, ﴿in the agonies of death﴾, that he said: "The throes of death."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning God's words, ﴿and the angels will stretch out their hands﴾, that he said: "This is at the time of death. And the stretching out (basṭ) is striking." (Compare) ﴿striking their faces and their backs﴾ [al-Anfal: 50; Muhammad: 27].

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him, saying: "In the verse, this is the Angel of Death (peace be upon him)."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Dahhak concerning God's words, ﴿and the angels will stretch out their hands﴾, that he said: "With punishment."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid concerning God's words, ﴿the punishment of humiliation﴾, that he said: "The humiliation."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ikrimah, who said: "al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said: 'Al-Lat and al-Uzza will intercede for me.' So (the verse) was revealed: ﴿And you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾, to the end of the verse."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning God's words, ﴿And you have come to Us alone﴾, to the end of the verse, that he said: "(It is) like the day you were born: everything that was taken from you on the day you were born will be returned to you."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi concerning God's words, ﴿And you have left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾, that he said: "Of wealth and servants." (Concerning) ﴿behind your backs﴾, he said: "In this world."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatada concerning God's words, ﴿Now your bonds have been cut off from you﴾, that he said: "(It means) what had been between them of connection."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid concerning God's words, ﴿Now your bonds have been cut off from you﴾, that he said: "Your association with one another in this world."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 6, verses 91–94 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿They did not measure God with the true measure of His worth.﴾ *Qadartu al-shay'* and *qadartuhu* mean "I knew its measure." Its root meaning is "concealment," and it was then used for knowing a thing. The sense is: they did not know Him with the true knowledge of Him, since they denied that He sends messengers and sends down Books.

It was also said that the meaning is: they did not measure the blessings of God with their true measure.

Abu Hamzah read *wa-ma qadarū Allāha ḥaqqa qadarihi* with a fatḥah on the *dal* (*qadar*). This is a dialectal form (*lughah*). When this denial came from them, and they were Jews, God commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to present them with an argument they could not repel. So He said: ﴿Say: Who sent down the Book which Moses brought?﴾ They acknowledged this and submitted to it. In this there was a rebuke and reproach to them beyond measure, while compelling them to admit what they had denied: that God sent down revelation to humans, namely the prophets (peace be upon them). Thus their denial was refuted and the corruption of their denial was made clear.

It was also said that those who uttered this statement were the disbelievers of Quraysh. In that case, the argument that God sent down the Book to Moses is addressed to them on the basis that they acknowledged it and knew it from reports from the Jews, whom they used to believe.

﴿Light and guidance﴾ are both in the accusative as circumstantial qualifiers (*ḥāl*). ﴿For the people﴾ is attached to an omitted element which is a qualifier of *hudan* (guidance), meaning: existing for the people.

His saying: ﴿You make it into scrolls.﴾ That is: you make the Book which Moses brought into scrolls, in which you write it, so that what you want of alteration, substitution, and concealment of the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned in it may be accomplished for you. This is a censure of them. The pronoun in ﴿you disclose them﴾ refers to the scrolls, and the pronoun in ﴿you make it﴾ refers to the Book. The clause ﴿you make it﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier. The clause ﴿you disclose them﴾ is a qualifier of *qarāṭīs* (scrolls). ﴿And you conceal much﴾ is coordinated with ﴿you disclose them﴾, meaning: and you conceal much of them.

The address in ﴿And you were taught what you did not know, you nor your fathers﴾ is to the Jews, meaning: while you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew. It is possible that this clause is a new sentence confirming what precedes it. What they came to know is what our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) informed them of, from the matters revealed to him by God, for these included what was not known to them from their Books, nor through the words of their prophets, nor known to their fathers. It is also possible that *mā* in ﴿what you did not know﴾ refers to what they knew from the Torah, in which case it is a favour (*mann*) bestowed upon them by sending down the Torah.

It was also said that the address is to the polytheists of Quraysh and others, so *mā* refers to what they came to know from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Then God commanded His Messenger to answer this argument which He had imposed on them when He said: ﴿Who sent down the Book which Moses brought?﴾ So He said: ﴿Say: God.﴾ That is, God sent it down. ﴿Then leave them in their discourse, playing.﴾ That is, leave them in their falsehood while they play, meaning they behave like children who play.

His saying: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed.﴾ This is part of the refutation of them in their saying: ﴿God has not sent down anything upon a human.﴾ He informed them that God sent down the Torah to Moses, and followed it with: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down,﴾ meaning upon Muhammad (ﷺ). So how can you say: ﴿God has not sent down anything upon a human?﴾ ﴿Blessed﴾ and ﴿confirming﴾ are two qualifiers of *kitāb* (Book). *Mubārak* is abundant in blessing, and *muṣaddiq* is abundant in confirmation. ﴿What is between its hands﴾ refers to the Books God sent down to the prophets before it, such as the Torah and the Gospel. It agrees with them in calling to God and to His unity, even if it differs with them in some rulings.

His saying: ﴿And that you may warn﴾. It was said that it is coordinated with what is indicated by *mubārak*, as if it were said: We sent it down for blessings and that you may warn. He specified the Mother of Cities, which is Mecca, because it is the greatest of the cities in standing, because it is the first house set up for people, and because it is the qiblah of this community and the place of their pilgrimage. So warning its people entails warning all the people of the earth. The intended meaning of ﴿those around it﴾ is all the people of the earth. The intended meaning of warning the Mother of Cities is warning its people and the people of the rest of the earth, so this is by way of an omitted genitive construction, like ﴿ask the town﴾.

﴿Those who believe in the Hereafter﴾ is a subject (*mubtada'*), and ﴿they believe in it﴾ is its predicate. The meaning: it is incumbent upon whoever affirms the Last Abode to believe in this Book, affirm it, and act upon what is in it, because affirming the Hereafter requires accepting one who calls people to what brings its good and averts its harm. The clause ﴿and they guard over their prayer﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier. He singled out guarding the prayer from among all the obligations because it is its pillar and is like the head to the body.

His saying: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates against God a lie?﴾ This clause confirms the content of what preceded of the argument against them, that God sent down Books to His messengers. That is: how can you say: ﴿God has not sent down anything upon a human,﴾ and that entails denying the prophets (peace be upon them)? And none is more unjust than one who fabricates against God a lie, claiming to be a prophet when he is not one, or who lies about God concerning anything. ﴿Or says: It has been revealed to me,﴾ while nothing has been revealed to him. That is, while the true state is that nothing was revealed to him. God has protected His prophets from what you claim about them. This is only the way of the great liars, leaders of misguidance, such as Musaylimah the Liar, al-Aswad al-'Ansi, and Sajah.

His saying: ﴿And who says: I will send down the like of what God has sent down.﴾ This is coordinated with *man iftara* (one who fabricates). That is: and who is more unjust than one who fabricates, or than one who says: It has been revealed to me when nothing has been revealed to him, or than one who says: I will send down the like of what God has sent down. They are those who say: ﴿If we willed, we would say the like of this﴾ [al-Anfal: 31].

It was also said: "He is 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh, for he used to write the revelation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The Messenger of God (ﷺ) dictated to him: ﴿Then We produced it as another creation,﴾ and 'Abd Allah said: ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators.﴾ The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Thus it was revealed.' 'Abd Allah then doubted and said: If Muhammad is truthful, then it was revealed to me as it was revealed to him; and if he is lying, then I have said as he said.' Then he apostatized from Islam and joined the polytheists, then he embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest," as is well known.

His saying: ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death.﴾ The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or to everyone suited to it. The intended meaning is every wrongdoer, and it includes, primarily, those who deny what God has sent down and those who claim prophethood by fabricating against God. The answer to *law* (if) is omitted: that is, you would see a tremendous matter. *Al-ghamarāt* is the plural of *ghamrah*, meaning hardship. Its original sense is a thing that overwhelms (*yaghmuru*) things and covers them, as in *ghamrat al-mā'* (the flood of water). Then it was used for hardships, as in *ghamrat al-ḥarb* (the surge of battle).

Al-Jawhari said: *al-ghamrah* means hardship, and its plural is *ghumar*, like *nawbah* and *nawab*.

His saying: ﴿And the angels stretch out their hands﴾ is in the accusative position: that is, while the angels stretch out their hands to seize the souls of the disbelievers. It was also said: for punishment, and in their hands are iron hammers. A similar statement is God's saying: ﴿If you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieved, striking their faces and their backs﴾ [al-Anfal: 50].

His saying: ﴿Bring out your souls.﴾ That is, saying to them: bring out your souls from these agonies into which you have fallen, or bring out your souls from our hands and free them from punishment, or bring out your souls from your bodies and surrender them to us so that we may seize them. ﴿Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation.﴾ That is, the day on which your souls are seized. Or they meant by "today" the time in which they are punished, whose beginning is the punishment of the grave. *Al-hūn* and *al-hawān* have the same meaning: that is, today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation, by which you will be in disgrace and abasement after what you were in of arrogance and self-exaltation. The *bā'* in ﴿because you used to say about God other than the truth﴾ indicates cause: that is, because of your saying this, denying that God sent down His Books to His messengers, and associating others with Him. ﴿And you used to be arrogant toward His signs﴾, refusing to affirm them and to act upon them. So what you were recompensed with of the punishment of humiliation was ﴿a fitting recompense﴾ [al-Naba': 26].

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning God's words, ﴿in the agonies of death﴾, that he said: "The throes of death."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning God's words, ﴿and the angels will stretch out their hands﴾, that he said: "This is at the time of death. And the stretching out (basṭ) is striking." (Compare) ﴿striking their faces and their backs﴾ [al-Anfal: 50; Muhammad: 27].

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him, saying: "In the verse, this is the Angel of Death (peace be upon him)."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Dahhak concerning God's words, ﴿and the angels will stretch out their hands﴾, that he said: "With punishment."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid concerning God's words, ﴿the punishment of humiliation﴾, that he said: "The humiliation."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ikrimah, who said: "al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said: 'Al-Lat and al-Uzza will intercede for me.' So (the verse) was revealed: ﴿And you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾, to the end of the verse."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning God's words, ﴿And you have come to Us alone﴾, to the end of the verse, that he said: "(It is) like the day you were born: everything that was taken from you on the day you were born will be returned to you."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi concerning God's words, ﴿And you have left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾, that he said: "Of wealth and servants." (Concerning) ﴿behind your backs﴾, he said: "In this world."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatada concerning God's words, ﴿Now your bonds have been cut off from you﴾, that he said: "(It means) what had been between them of connection."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid concerning God's words, ﴿Now your bonds have been cut off from you﴾, that he said: "Your association with one another in this world."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 6, verses 91–94 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying: ﴿They did not measure God with the true measure of His worth.﴾ *Qadartu al-shay'* and *qadartuhu* mean "I knew its measure." Its root meaning is "concealment," and it was then used for knowing a thing. The sense is: they did not know Him with the true knowledge of Him, since they denied that He sends messengers and sends down Books.

It was also said that the meaning is: they did not measure the blessings of God with their true measure.

Abu Hamzah read *wa-ma qadarū Allāha ḥaqqa qadarihi* with a fatḥah on the *dal* (*qadar*). This is a dialectal form (*lughah*). When this denial came from them, and they were Jews, God commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to present them with an argument they could not repel. So He said: ﴿Say: Who sent down the Book which Moses brought?﴾ They acknowledged this and submitted to it. In this there was a rebuke and reproach to them beyond measure, while compelling them to admit what they had denied: that God sent down revelation to humans, namely the prophets (peace be upon them). Thus their denial was refuted and the corruption of their denial was made clear.

It was also said that those who uttered this statement were the disbelievers of Quraysh. In that case, the argument that God sent down the Book to Moses is addressed to them on the basis that they acknowledged it and knew it from reports from the Jews, whom they used to believe.

﴿Light and guidance﴾ are both in the accusative as circumstantial qualifiers (*ḥāl*). ﴿For the people﴾ is attached to an omitted element which is a qualifier of *hudan* (guidance), meaning: existing for the people.

His saying: ﴿You make it into scrolls.﴾ That is: you make the Book which Moses brought into scrolls, in which you write it, so that what you want of alteration, substitution, and concealment of the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned in it may be accomplished for you. This is a censure of them. The pronoun in ﴿you disclose them﴾ refers to the scrolls, and the pronoun in ﴿you make it﴾ refers to the Book. The clause ﴿you make it﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier. The clause ﴿you disclose them﴾ is a qualifier of *qarāṭīs* (scrolls). ﴿And you conceal much﴾ is coordinated with ﴿you disclose them﴾, meaning: and you conceal much of them.

The address in ﴿And you were taught what you did not know, you nor your fathers﴾ is to the Jews, meaning: while you were taught what neither you nor your fathers knew. It is possible that this clause is a new sentence confirming what precedes it. What they came to know is what our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) informed them of, from the matters revealed to him by God, for these included what was not known to them from their Books, nor through the words of their prophets, nor known to their fathers. It is also possible that *mā* in ﴿what you did not know﴾ refers to what they knew from the Torah, in which case it is a favour (*mann*) bestowed upon them by sending down the Torah.

It was also said that the address is to the polytheists of Quraysh and others, so *mā* refers to what they came to know from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Then God commanded His Messenger to answer this argument which He had imposed on them when He said: ﴿Who sent down the Book which Moses brought?﴾ So He said: ﴿Say: God.﴾ That is, God sent it down. ﴿Then leave them in their discourse, playing.﴾ That is, leave them in their falsehood while they play, meaning they behave like children who play.

His saying: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed.﴾ This is part of the refutation of them in their saying: ﴿God has not sent down anything upon a human.﴾ He informed them that God sent down the Torah to Moses, and followed it with: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down,﴾ meaning upon Muhammad (ﷺ). So how can you say: ﴿God has not sent down anything upon a human?﴾ ﴿Blessed﴾ and ﴿confirming﴾ are two qualifiers of *kitāb* (Book). *Mubārak* is abundant in blessing, and *muṣaddiq* is abundant in confirmation. ﴿What is between its hands﴾ refers to the Books God sent down to the prophets before it, such as the Torah and the Gospel. It agrees with them in calling to God and to His unity, even if it differs with them in some rulings.

His saying: ﴿And that you may warn﴾. It was said that it is coordinated with what is indicated by *mubārak*, as if it were said: We sent it down for blessings and that you may warn. He specified the Mother of Cities, which is Mecca, because it is the greatest of the cities in standing, because it is the first house set up for people, and because it is the qiblah of this community and the place of their pilgrimage. So warning its people entails warning all the people of the earth. The intended meaning of ﴿those around it﴾ is all the people of the earth. The intended meaning of warning the Mother of Cities is warning its people and the people of the rest of the earth, so this is by way of an omitted genitive construction, like ﴿ask the town﴾.

﴿Those who believe in the Hereafter﴾ is a subject (*mubtada'*), and ﴿they believe in it﴾ is its predicate. The meaning: it is incumbent upon whoever affirms the Last Abode to believe in this Book, affirm it, and act upon what is in it, because affirming the Hereafter requires accepting one who calls people to what brings its good and averts its harm. The clause ﴿and they guard over their prayer﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier. He singled out guarding the prayer from among all the obligations because it is its pillar and is like the head to the body.

His saying: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates against God a lie?﴾ This clause confirms the content of what preceded of the argument against them, that God sent down Books to His messengers. That is: how can you say: ﴿God has not sent down anything upon a human,﴾ and that entails denying the prophets (peace be upon them)? And none is more unjust than one who fabricates against God a lie, claiming to be a prophet when he is not one, or who lies about God concerning anything. ﴿Or says: It has been revealed to me,﴾ while nothing has been revealed to him. That is, while the true state is that nothing was revealed to him. God has protected His prophets from what you claim about them. This is only the way of the great liars, leaders of misguidance, such as Musaylimah the Liar, al-Aswad al-'Ansi, and Sajah.

His saying: ﴿And who says: I will send down the like of what God has sent down.﴾ This is coordinated with *man iftara* (one who fabricates). That is: and who is more unjust than one who fabricates, or than one who says: It has been revealed to me when nothing has been revealed to him, or than one who says: I will send down the like of what God has sent down. They are those who say: ﴿If we willed, we would say the like of this﴾ [al-Anfal: 31].

It was also said: "He is 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh, for he used to write the revelation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The Messenger of God (ﷺ) dictated to him: ﴿Then We produced it as another creation,﴾ and 'Abd Allah said: ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators.﴾ The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Thus it was revealed.' 'Abd Allah then doubted and said: If Muhammad is truthful, then it was revealed to me as it was revealed to him; and if he is lying, then I have said as he said.' Then he apostatized from Islam and joined the polytheists, then he embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest," as is well known.

His saying: ﴿If you could see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death.﴾ The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or to everyone suited to it. The intended meaning is every wrongdoer, and it includes, primarily, those who deny what God has sent down and those who claim prophethood by fabricating against God. The answer to *law* (if) is omitted: that is, you would see a tremendous matter. *Al-ghamarāt* is the plural of *ghamrah*, meaning hardship. Its original sense is a thing that overwhelms (*yaghmuru*) things and covers them, as in *ghamrat al-mā'* (the flood of water). Then it was used for hardships, as in *ghamrat al-ḥarb* (the surge of battle).

Al-Jawhari said: *al-ghamrah* means hardship, and its plural is *ghumar*, like *nawbah* and *nawab*.

His saying: ﴿And the angels stretch out their hands﴾ is in the accusative position: that is, while the angels stretch out their hands to seize the souls of the disbelievers. It was also said: for punishment, and in their hands are iron hammers. A similar statement is God's saying: ﴿If you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieved, striking their faces and their backs﴾ [al-Anfal: 50].

His saying: ﴿Bring out your souls.﴾ That is, saying to them: bring out your souls from these agonies into which you have fallen, or bring out your souls from our hands and free them from punishment, or bring out your souls from your bodies and surrender them to us so that we may seize them. ﴿Today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation.﴾ That is, the day on which your souls are seized. Or they meant by "today" the time in which they are punished, whose beginning is the punishment of the grave. *Al-hūn* and *al-hawān* have the same meaning: that is, today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation, by which you will be in disgrace and abasement after what you were in of arrogance and self-exaltation. The *bā'* in ﴿because you used to say about God other than the truth﴾ indicates cause: that is, because of your saying this, denying that God sent down His Books to His messengers, and associating others with Him. ﴿And you used to be arrogant toward His signs﴾, refusing to affirm them and to act upon them. So what you were recompensed with of the punishment of humiliation was ﴿a fitting recompense﴾ [al-Naba': 26].

His saying (94): ﴿And you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time.﴾

Abu Haywah read *furādan* with tanwin, which is the dialect of Tamim. The rest read it with the feminine *alif* for the plural, so it does not take tanwin.

Tha'lab related *furād* without tanwin, like *thalāth* and *rubā'*. *Furādā* is the plural of *fard*, like *sukārā* the plural of *sakrān*, and *kusālā* the plural of *kaslān*. The meaning: you have come to Us individually, one by one, each of you alone, apart from his family and his wealth, and from what he used to worship besides God, so he benefited nothing from any of that. ﴿As We created you the first time﴾: that is, in the state in which you were when you came out from your mothers' wombs. The *kāf* (as) is a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun: that is, you have come to Us a coming like your coming when We created you; or it is a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in *furādā*: that is, resembling the beginning of Our creating you. ﴿And you left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾: that is, what We gave you. *Al-khawl* is what God gives a person of worldly goods. That is, you left that behind you and did not bring any of it to Us, nor did you benefit from it in any way. ﴿And We do not see with you your intercessors whom﴾ you worshipped and said: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to God in position﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], and ﴿you claimed that they were among you partners﴾ of God, deserving worship from you as He deserves it.

His saying: ﴿Certainly your bonds have been severed.﴾

Nafi', al-Kisa'i, and Hafs read *baynakum* with a fatḥah, as an adverbial of place (*ẓarfiyyah*). The subject of *taqaṭṭaʿa* is omitted: that is, the connection between you and your partners has been severed, as indicated by ﴿and We do not see with you your intercessors.﴾

The rest read it with a ḍammah, attributing the severing to *al-bayn* (the space between): that is, the severing occurred between you. It is possible that the meaning of the reading with fatḥah is the same as the meaning of the reading with ḍammah, in attributing the verb to the adverb. It was given the fatḥah because it is frequently used as an adverb.

Ibn Mas'ud read: *laqad taqaṭṭaʿa mā baynakum*, attributing the verb to *mā*: that is, what was between you. ﴿And what you used to claim has gone astray from you﴾ of the partners and of the association, and you were prevented from them and they from you.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿They did not measure God with the true measure of His worth,﴾ that he said: They are the disbelievers who did not believe in God's power. Whoever believes that God is over all things powerful has measured God with the true measure of His worth, and whoever does not believe in that has not measured God with the true measure of His worth, when they said: ﴿God has not sent down anything upon a human.﴾

"The Jews said: O Muhammad, has God sent down a Book to you? He said: Yes. They said: By God, God has not sent down any Book from heaven. So God sent down: Say, O Muhammad: Who sent down the Book which Moses brought?" up to the end of the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, regarding ﴿They did not measure God with the true measure of His worth, when they said: God has not sent down anything upon a human,﴾ that it was said by the polytheists of Quraysh.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi, who said: Finhas the Jew said: God has not sent down anything upon Muhammad, and then it was revealed.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from 'Ikrimah, who said: It was revealed concerning Malik ibn al-Sayf.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 91–94 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "A man from the Jews called Malik ibn al-Sayf came and disputed with the Prophet (ﷺ). The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'I adjure you by He who sent down the Torah to Musa: Do you find in the Torah that God hates the fat rabbi?' He was a fat rabbi, so he became angry and said: 'By God, God has not sent down anything upon any human being.' His companions said to him: 'Woe to you! Not even upon Musa?' He said: 'God has not sent down anything upon any human being.' Then this was revealed."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid concerning God's words, ﴿You make it into scattered pages﴾, that he said: "(It refers to) the Jews." And concerning His words (p-435) ﴿And you were taught what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers﴾, he said: "This is addressed to the Muslims."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada concerning God's words, ﴿And you were taught what you did not know﴾, that he said: "They are the Jews. God gave them knowledge, but they did not follow it, did not act upon it, and did not practise it, so God censured them for that knowledge."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada concerning God's words, ﴿And this is a blessed Book which We have sent down﴾, that he said: "It is the Qur'an which God sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from him, saying concerning ﴿confirming what came before it﴾: "That is, of the Books that passed before it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning God's words, ﴿that you may warn the Mother of the Cities﴾, that he said: "Makkah and those around it."

He said: "He means the towns around it, to the east and to the west."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, who said: "It was called the Mother of the Cities only because the first House was founded in it."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatada concerning God's words, ﴿that you may warn the Mother of the Cities﴾, that he said: "It is Makkah." He said: "And it has reached me that the earth was spread out from Makkah."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated similarly from Ata' ibn Dinar.

Al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak narrated from Shurahbil ibn Sa'd, who said: "It was revealed concerning Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh, (the verse) ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God, or says, 'It has been revealed to me,' when nothing has been revealed to him﴾, to the end of the verse. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered Makkah, he fled to Uthman, his foster brother, and Uthman hid him with himself until the people of Makkah were reassured. Then he sought safe conduct for him."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Khalaf al-A'mā that it was revealed concerning Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh. Ibn Abi Hatim likewise narrated from al-Suddi.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij concerning God's words, ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God, or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him﴾, that he said: "It was revealed concerning Musaylima the Liar and those like him who called to what he called to. (And) ﴿or who says, "I will send down the like of what God has sent down"﴾, it was revealed concerning Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated similarly from Ikrimah.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ikrimah that when (the verses) ﴿By those sent forth in succession﴾ and ﴿By those that blow violently﴾ [al-Mursalat: 1–2] were revealed, al-Nadr, who was from the Banu Abd al-Dar, said: "And by those that grind, grinding, and those that knead, kneading," with much (other) speech. And the stretching out (basṭ) is striking." (Compare) ﴿striking their faces and their backs﴾ [al-Anfal: 50; Muhammad: 27].

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 95–99 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾. This begins an enumeration of the wonders of His creation and a mention of what their gods are unable to do even in the smallest matter. Al-falq (splitting) means al-shaqq (cleaving): that is, He, glorified is He, splits the grain so that vegetation emerges from it, and splits the date-stone so that the tree emerges from it. It has been said that the meaning of ﴿Splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾ is the cleft that is in them from their original creation. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿Splitter﴾ is Creator.

Al-nawa (date-stones) is the plural of nawah, applied to everything that has a hard pit, such as dates, apricots and peaches.

His saying: ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾. This clause is a predicate following a predicate, so it is in the place of nominative case (raf'). It has been said that it is a clause explaining what precedes it, since its meaning is the same as its meaning. The first view is preferable, for the meaning of ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾ is that He brings forth the animal from something like a sperm-drop or an egg, which is dead.

The meaning of ﴿and brings forth the dead from the living﴾ is that He brings forth the sperm-drop and the egg, which are dead, from the living. The clause ﴿and brings forth the dead from the living﴾ is conjoined to ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾, a nominal clause conjoined to a verbal clause, and there is no harm in that. It has been said that it is conjoined to ﴿Splitter﴾, on the assumption that the clause ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾ explains what precedes it; but the first view is preferable. The demonstrative ﴿That is﴾ refers to the Doer of that amazing act mentioned earlier, and ﴿Allah﴾ is its predicate. The meaning is: the Doer of this amazing act is the One who possesses every perfection, the One who bestows every grace, and the One who deserves all praise and exaltation. ﴿How then are you turned away?﴾ That is, how are you diverted from the truth, given what you see of His wondrous creation and the perfection of His power?

His saying: ﴿Splitter of the dawn﴾. It is in the nominative case as one of the predicates of inna in ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾ (p-436). It has also been said that it is an adjective of the noble name in ﴿That is Allah﴾. Al-Hasan and Isa ibn Umar read "fāliq al-aṣbāḥ" with a fatha on the hamza, while the majority read it with a kasra. On the reading with fatha it is the plural of ṣubḥ, and on the reading with kasra it is the verbal noun of aṣbaḥa. Al-ṣubḥ and al-ṣabāḥ are the beginning of the day, and likewise al-iṣbāḥ. Al-Nakha'i read "falaqa al-iṣbāḥa" with a verb and a kasra on the hamza.

The meaning of ﴿Splitter of the dawn﴾ is that He cleaves the light from the darkness and uncovers it; or the meaning, by omitting a modifier, is: Splitter of the darkness of the dawn, which is the first grey of light; or Splitter of the column of dawn from the whiteness of day, because it appears mixed with darkness and then becomes pure white.

Al-Hasan, Isa ibn Umar, Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "and He made the night a resting-place" (ja'ala al-layla sakanan), taking it according to the sense of fāliq (for Hamzah and al-Kisa'i), while for al-Hasan and Isa it is conjoined to falaqa.

The majority read "wa jā'iluʾ" (and the Maker) conjoined to "fāliq". It was also read "fāliqa" and "jā'ila" in the accusative, as praise.

Ya'qub read "wa jā'iluʾ al-layli sākinan".

Al-sakan is the place of rest, from sakana ilayhi, when one is at ease with it, because people rest in it from movement in their livelihood and are relieved of fatigue and toil.

His saying: ﴿And the sun and the moon as a reckoning﴾. It is in the accusative by supposing a verb: that is, and He made the sun and the moon; and in the nominative on the basis of the inchoative, with the predicate omitted, its estimate being: and the sun and the moon are made as a reckoning; and in the genitive, conjoined to "the night", according to the reading of the one who read "wa ja'ala al-layla".

Al-Akhfash said: al-ḥusbān is the plural of ḥisāb, like shuhbān and shihāb.

Ya'qub said: ḥusbān is the verbal noun of ḥasibtu al-shay' uḥsubuhu, ḥasban and ḥusbānan.

Al-ḥisāb is the noun; it has been said that al-ḥusbān with a damma is the verbal noun of ḥasaba with a fatha, and al-ḥisbān with a kasra is the verbal noun of ḥasiba.

The meaning: He made them a measure of reckoning upon which the interests of the servants depend, and He set them in motion upon a measure that neither increases nor decreases, so that He might show His servants by this the greatness of His power and the wondrous perfection of His creation. It has been said that al-ḥusbān is light; and in one usage al-ḥusbān is fire, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He sends upon it a ḥusbān from the heaven﴾ [al-Kahf: 40]. The demonstrative in ﴿That is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾ refers to the making implied by the doer or by the making, according to the two readings.

Al-ʿAzīz: the Overpowering, the Victorious.

Al-ʿAlīm: the One of abundant knowledge, and among the things He knows is setting them in motion under this firm ordinance.

His saying: ﴿And it is He who made the stars for you, that you may be guided by them﴾. That is, He created them for guidance by them ﴿in the darknesses﴾, that is, of the night, when travelling ﴿on land and sea﴾. The attribution of "darknesses" to land and sea is because they are associated with them. Or the intended meaning of the darknesses is the confusion of their paths, in which one is not guided except by the stars. This is one of the benefits of the stars for which Allah created them. Among them is what Allah mentioned in His saying: ﴿And a guard against every rebellious devil﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 7], ﴿and We have made them missiles against the devils﴾ [al-Mulk: 5]. Among them is that He made them an adornment for the heaven. Whoever claims other benefits than these has greatly fabricated against Allah. ﴿We have detailed the signs﴾, which We have explained in full detail, so that they may be more effective in admonition, ﴿for a people who know﴾ what is in these signs of the proof of Allah's power, His greatness and the wondrous wisdom of His design.

His saying: 98. ﴿And it is He who produced you from a single soul﴾, that is, Adam, peace be upon him, as has passed. This is another kind of His wondrous creation, which indicates the perfection of His power. ﴿Then a lodging place and a deposit place﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥasan, Abū ʿAmr, ʿĪsā, al-Aʿraj and al-Nakhaʿī read it with a kasra on the qāf, while the rest read it with a fatha. Both are nominative, as inchoatives whose predicate is omitted, the estimate being: then from you is a lodging place, or then for you is a lodging place. The first estimate is on the first reading, the second on the second: that is, then from you is a lodging place upon the back of the earth, or then for you is a lodging place upon it; and from you is a deposit place in the womb, or in the bottom of the earth, or in the loins. It has been said that the lodging place is in the womb and the deposit place is in the earth; it has been said that the lodging place is in the grave.

Al-Qurṭubī said: Most of the people of tafsir say: the lodging place is what is in the womb, and the deposit place is what is in the loins. It has been said that the lodging place is one who has been created and the deposit place is one who has not yet been created. It has been said that the idea of deposit is an indication of their being in graves until the resurrection.

What indicates that lodging place is explained as dwelling upon the earth is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And for you on the earth is a lodging place and enjoyment for a time﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36]. Here He, glorified is He, mentioned ﴿understand﴾ (yafqahūn), and before it ﴿know﴾ (yaʿlamūn), because in the production of souls from one soul, and in making some of them a lodging place and some a deposit place, there is a subtlety and fineness not found in the creation of the stars for guidance; so the mention of understanding (fiqh) is fitting, since it suggests greater precision and deeper reflection.

His saying: ﴿And it is He who sent down water from the heaven﴾. This is another kind of His wondrous creatures.

The water is rain water. In ﴿So We brought forth by it﴾ there is a shift from the third person to the first person, to show concern for this creature and what results from it. The pronoun in ﴿by it﴾ refers to the water. ﴿The vegetation of every thing﴾ means every kind of the varied types of vegetation. It has been said that the meaning is the provision of every thing; but the first interpretation is preferable.

Then He detailed this general statement, saying: ﴿So We brought forth from it green shoots﴾.

Al-Akhfash said: that is, green (akhḍar).

Al-khiḍr: the moist herbs, which branch out from the stalks emerging from the grain. It has been said: it means wheat, barley, maize, rice and all the other grains. ﴿We bring forth from it grain piled up﴾: this clause is an adjective of khiḍr, that is: We bring forth from the green stalks grain arranged in layers, that is, composed one upon another as in the ears of grain. ﴿And from the palm-tree﴾ is a fronted predicate, and ﴿from its spathe﴾ is a substitute for it. On the reading of the one who read "yakhruju minhu ḥabbun", the raising of "qinwānun" is by its being conjoined to "ḥabb". Al-Farrā' permitted, outside the Qur'an, "qinwānan" conjoined to "ḥabban" in the accusative; and Tamim say "qinyān".

It was read with a damma and a fatha on the qāf, according to the difference of the two dialects: the dialect of Qays and the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz.

Al-ṭalʿ: the sheath before it splits open over the spadix, and the spadix is also called ṭalʿ.

Al-qinwān: the plural of qinw, and the difference between its plural and its dual is that the dual has a kasra on the nūn, while the plural follows what the case requires; similar is ṣinwān.

Al-qinw: the cluster (ʿidhq).

The meaning: that qinwān originates from ṭalʿ. The ʿidhq is the cluster of the palm-tree; it has been said that qinwān are the hearts (jimār) of the palm.

Al-dāniya: the near one, which is within reach of the one standing or sitting.

Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is "from them is near, and from them is far", and it is elided; similar is ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Naḥl: 81]. The near is specified by mention because the purpose of the verse is to show measure and favour, and what is within easy reach is more abundant.

His saying: ﴿And gardens of grapevines﴾.

Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Layla, al-Aʿmash and ʿĀṣim in his authentic transmission from him read "jannātun" with a nominative; the rest read it in the accusative.

Abū ʿUbayda and Abū Ḥātim rejected the first reading, until Abū Ḥātim said: it is impossible, because gardens do not come from palm-trees.

Al-Naḥḥās said: the nominative is not interpreted in this way, but it is a nominative as an inchoative whose predicate is omitted: that is, and for them are gardens, as a group of reciters read "wa ḥūrun ʿīn" [al-Wāqiʿa: 22]. Sībawayh, al-Kisā'ī and al-Farrā' permitted the like of this. As for the accusative, it has been said that it is conjoined to "nabāta kulli shay'" — that is, We brought forth by it gardens of grapevines — or it is accusative by a verb to be supposed later: that is, and gardens of grapevines We brought forth; and the same view holds for the accusative of "zaytūn" and "rummān". It has also been said that they are accusative by specification, since they are esteemed. "Mushtabihan" is accusative as a circumstantial state: that is, each of them resembles the other in some of its attributes and does not resemble it in others. It has been said that one of them resembles the other in leaf, considering its covering of the whole branch and its size, but does not resemble it in taste. It has also been said that zaytūn and rummān are singled out because their habitats are close to the Arabs, as in the saying of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ [al-Ghāshiya: 17]. Then He, glorified is He, commanded them to look with the gaze of consideration at its fruit when it bears fruit, and at its ripeness when it ripens.

Al-thamar in the language is the produce of the tree.

Al-yāniʿ: the ripe one, which has reached maturity and whose time for picking has come.

Ibn al-Anbārī said: al-yanʿ is the plural of yāniʿ, like rakb and rākib.

Al-Farrā' said: aynaʿa means it turned red.

Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read "thamarihi" with a damma on the thā' and the mīm; the rest read it with fatha, except al-Aʿmash, who read "thumrihi" with a damma on the thā' and a sukūn on the mīm, for lightness.

Muhammad ibn al-Samaifaʿ, Ibn Muḥayṣin and Ibn Abī Isḥāq read "yunʿahu" with a damma on the yā' of the present tense.

Al-Farrā' said: it is the dialect of some people of Najd.

The rest read it with a fatha. The indication in His saying ﴿Indeed in that﴾ refers to what has been mentioned previously, both in summary and in detail: ﴿there are indeed signs for a people who believe﴾ in Allah, reasoning from what they witness of His wondrous creatures which He has recounted to them.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾, that he said: He created the grain and the date-stone.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh transmitted from Qatādah, who said: He splits the grain and the date-stone to bring forth vegetation.

Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh transmitted from Mujāhid, who said: "the two halves that are in them."

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Abū Mālik something similar.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh transmitted from him regarding His saying: ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾, that he said: the palm-tree from the date-stone and the ear of grain from the grain; ﴿and brings forth the dead from the living﴾, that he said: the date-stone from the palm-tree and the grain from the ear.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Mujāhid: ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead and brings forth the dead from the living﴾, that he said: people, the living, from sperm-drops, and the sperm-drop is dead, coming out from living people; and likewise from livestock and plants.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿So how are you turned away?﴾ that it means: how then do you deny?

He also related from al-Hasan that he said: "How are you diverted?"

He also related from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿Splitter of the dawn﴾ that he said: "He created the night and the day."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said: "By dawn (al-Isbah) is meant the light of the sun by day and the light of the moon by night."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid regarding ﴿Splitter of the dawn﴾ that he said: "The brightening of the dawn."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿Splitter of the dawn﴾, that he said: "Splitter of the morning (al-Subh)."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And He made the night a resting-place﴾, that he said: "Every bird and beast rests in it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And the sun and the moon as a reckoning﴾, that he said: "That is, the count of days, months and years."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And it is He who placed for you the stars that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of the land and the sea﴾, that he said: "A man may go astray while he is in darkness, and the path may be lost to him through deviation."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Khatib in his Book of the Stars related from Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "Learn from the stars what you are guided by on your land and your sea, then stop. By Allah, they were created only as an adornment for the heaven, as missiles against the devils, and as signs by which one is guided."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib related from Ibn Umar that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Learn from the stars what you are guided by in the darknesses of the land and the sea, then desist."

There are reports regarding the recommendation of observing the sun and the moon for the remembrance of Allah, the Glorified, and not for anything else. Among them is that al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Abu Hurayrah that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The dearest of Allah's servants to Allah are those who observe the sun and the moon for the remembrance of Allah."

Ibn Shahin, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim and al-Khatib related from Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and he mentioned something similar.

Ahmad in al-Zuhd and al-Khatib related from Abu al-Darda' something similar.

al-Khatib in his Book of the Stars related from Abu Hurayrah, as a marfu' report, something similar to his first hadith.

al-Hakim in his History and al-Daylami, with a weak chain, related also from Abu Hurayrah that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three will be shaded by Allah in His shade on a day when there is no shade but His: the trustworthy merchant, the just ruler, and the one who observes the sun by day."

Abd Allah ibn Ahmad, in the Zawa'id of al-Zuhd, related from Salman al-Farisi that he said: "Seven are in the shade of Allah on a day when there is no shade but His," and he mentioned among them the man who observes the sun for the times of prayer.

These hadiths are therefore restricted to observing these for the remembrance of Allah and for prayer, and not for anything else.

Allah has made the end of the time of the Fajr prayer the rising of the sun, the beginning of the Zuhr prayer its decline, the time of 'Asr as long as the sun remains white and pure, and the time of Maghrib the setting of (p. 438) the sun.

It is reported regarding the 'Isha prayer that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to pray it at the time of the setting of the moon on the third night of the month." By this the beginnings, middles and ends of the months are known. Whoever observes the sun and the moon in these matters is the one the Prophet (ﷺ) intended, and whoever observes them for other than this is not intended by what has been reported. The same applies to the stars. The prohibition of looking into them has been reported, as Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib related "from Ali, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade me from looking into the stars."

Ibn Mardawayh, al-Marhabi and al-Khatib related "from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade looking into the stars." al-Khatib related from Aisha, as a marfu' report, something similar.

al-Tabarani, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah and al-Khatib related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When my companions are mentioned, then hold back; when divine decree (al-qadar) is mentioned, then hold back; and when the stars are mentioned, then hold back."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas that he said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever acquires knowledge from the stars has acquired a branch of magic, to whatever extent he acquires." These hadiths are therefore understood as referring to looking into the stars for purposes other than guidance, reflection and taking lessons.

What is reported permitting the study of the stars is restricted to guidance, reflection and taking lessons, as the earlier hadith of Ibn Umar indicates. On this basis is to be understood what is reported from Ikrimah, in what al-Khatib related from him: that he asked a man about the calculation of the stars, and the man hesitated to inform him. Ikrimah said: "I heard Ibn Abbas say: It is a knowledge that people are unable to attain, and I wish I knew it."

Abu Dawud and al-Khatib related from Samurah ibn Jundub that he delivered a sermon and mentioned a hadith from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Amma ba'du. Some people claim that the eclipse of this sun, the eclipse of this moon, and the displacement of these stars from their places are due to the death of great men of the earth. They have lied. Rather, these are among the signs of Allah by which He makes His servants take heed, so that He may see what repentance arises in them."

It is established in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others, regarding the eclipses of the sun and the moon, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "They do not eclipse for the death of anyone nor for his life, but Allah causes His servants to fear through them."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Umamah as a marfu' report: "Allah set Adam before Himself, then struck his left shoulder, and his offspring came out from his loins until they filled the earth." This hadith is the meaning of what is in the verse: ﴿And it is He who produced you from a single soul﴾.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related through several chains from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿then a lodging place and a place of storage﴾, that he said: "The lodging place is what is in the womb, and the place of storage is what is deposited in the loins of men and animals."

In another wording: "The lodging place is what is in the womb and on the surface of the earth and in its belly, of what is living and of what has died."

In another wording: "The lodging place is what is in the earth, and the place of storage is what is in the loins."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Mas'ud regarding the verse that he said: "Its lodging place is in this world, and its place of storage is in the Hereafter."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "The lodging place is the womb, and the place of storage is the place where one dies."

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan and Qatadah regarding the verse, that they both said: "A lodging place in the grave and a place of storage in this world, which will soon join its companion."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿We bring forth from it grain piled up﴾, that he said: "This is the ear of grain (al-sunbul)."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Bara' ibn Azib regarding ﴿clusters hanging low﴾ that he said: "Near."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿clusters hanging low﴾ that he said: "The short palm trees whose bunches cling to the ground."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from him: "The clusters (qinwan) are the unripe dates (al-kabais), and the hanging low (al-daniyah) is the one set upright."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also, regarding ﴿clusters hanging low﴾, that he said: "The drooping of the bunches of the spathe."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿resembling one another and not resembling﴾, that he said: "Their leaves resemble one another while their fruit differs."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi regarding His saying ﴿Look at its fruit when it bears fruit﴾, that he said: "Its dates and its grapes."

Abu Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Bara' regarding "and its ripening (yan'ihi)" that he said: "Its ripening."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 95–99 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾. This begins an enumeration of the wonders of His creation and a mention of what their gods are unable to do even in the smallest matter. Al-falq (splitting) means al-shaqq (cleaving): that is, He, glorified is He, splits the grain so that vegetation emerges from it, and splits the date-stone so that the tree emerges from it. It has been said that the meaning of ﴿Splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾ is the cleft that is in them from their original creation. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿Splitter﴾ is Creator.

Al-nawa (date-stones) is the plural of nawah, applied to everything that has a hard pit, such as dates, apricots and peaches.

His saying: ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾. This clause is a predicate following a predicate, so it is in the place of nominative case (raf'). It has been said that it is a clause explaining what precedes it, since its meaning is the same as its meaning. The first view is preferable, for the meaning of ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾ is that He brings forth the animal from something like a sperm-drop or an egg, which is dead.

The meaning of ﴿and brings forth the dead from the living﴾ is that He brings forth the sperm-drop and the egg, which are dead, from the living. The clause ﴿and brings forth the dead from the living﴾ is conjoined to ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾, a nominal clause conjoined to a verbal clause, and there is no harm in that. It has been said that it is conjoined to ﴿Splitter﴾, on the assumption that the clause ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾ explains what precedes it; but the first view is preferable. The demonstrative ﴿That is﴾ refers to the Doer of that amazing act mentioned earlier, and ﴿Allah﴾ is its predicate. The meaning is: the Doer of this amazing act is the One who possesses every perfection, the One who bestows every grace, and the One who deserves all praise and exaltation. ﴿How then are you turned away?﴾ That is, how are you diverted from the truth, given what you see of His wondrous creation and the perfection of His power?

His saying: ﴿Splitter of the dawn﴾. It is in the nominative case as one of the predicates of inna in ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾ (p-436). It has also been said that it is an adjective of the noble name in ﴿That is Allah﴾. Al-Hasan and Isa ibn Umar read "fāliq al-aṣbāḥ" with a fatha on the hamza, while the majority read it with a kasra. On the reading with fatha it is the plural of ṣubḥ, and on the reading with kasra it is the verbal noun of aṣbaḥa. Al-ṣubḥ and al-ṣabāḥ are the beginning of the day, and likewise al-iṣbāḥ. Al-Nakha'i read "falaqa al-iṣbāḥa" with a verb and a kasra on the hamza.

The meaning of ﴿Splitter of the dawn﴾ is that He cleaves the light from the darkness and uncovers it; or the meaning, by omitting a modifier, is: Splitter of the darkness of the dawn, which is the first grey of light; or Splitter of the column of dawn from the whiteness of day, because it appears mixed with darkness and then becomes pure white.

Al-Hasan, Isa ibn Umar, Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "and He made the night a resting-place" (ja'ala al-layla sakanan), taking it according to the sense of fāliq (for Hamzah and al-Kisa'i), while for al-Hasan and Isa it is conjoined to falaqa.

The majority read "wa jā'iluʾ" (and the Maker) conjoined to "fāliq". It was also read "fāliqa" and "jā'ila" in the accusative, as praise.

Ya'qub read "wa jā'iluʾ al-layli sākinan".

Al-sakan is the place of rest, from sakana ilayhi, when one is at ease with it, because people rest in it from movement in their livelihood and are relieved of fatigue and toil.

His saying: ﴿And the sun and the moon as a reckoning﴾. It is in the accusative by supposing a verb: that is, and He made the sun and the moon; and in the nominative on the basis of the inchoative, with the predicate omitted, its estimate being: and the sun and the moon are made as a reckoning; and in the genitive, conjoined to "the night", according to the reading of the one who read "wa ja'ala al-layla".

Al-Akhfash said: al-ḥusbān is the plural of ḥisāb, like shuhbān and shihāb.

Ya'qub said: ḥusbān is the verbal noun of ḥasibtu al-shay' uḥsubuhu, ḥasban and ḥusbānan.

Al-ḥisāb is the noun; it has been said that al-ḥusbān with a damma is the verbal noun of ḥasaba with a fatha, and al-ḥisbān with a kasra is the verbal noun of ḥasiba.

The meaning: He made them a measure of reckoning upon which the interests of the servants depend, and He set them in motion upon a measure that neither increases nor decreases, so that He might show His servants by this the greatness of His power and the wondrous perfection of His creation. It has been said that al-ḥusbān is light; and in one usage al-ḥusbān is fire, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He sends upon it a ḥusbān from the heaven﴾ [al-Kahf: 40]. The demonstrative in ﴿That is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾ refers to the making implied by the doer or by the making, according to the two readings.

Al-ʿAzīz: the Overpowering, the Victorious.

Al-ʿAlīm: the One of abundant knowledge, and among the things He knows is setting them in motion under this firm ordinance.

His saying: ﴿And it is He who made the stars for you, that you may be guided by them﴾. That is, He created them for guidance by them ﴿in the darknesses﴾, that is, of the night, when travelling ﴿on land and sea﴾. The attribution of "darknesses" to land and sea is because they are associated with them. Or the intended meaning of the darknesses is the confusion of their paths, in which one is not guided except by the stars. This is one of the benefits of the stars for which Allah created them. Among them is what Allah mentioned in His saying: ﴿And a guard against every rebellious devil﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 7], ﴿and We have made them missiles against the devils﴾ [al-Mulk: 5]. Among them is that He made them an adornment for the heaven. Whoever claims other benefits than these has greatly fabricated against Allah. ﴿We have detailed the signs﴾, which We have explained in full detail, so that they may be more effective in admonition, ﴿for a people who know﴾ what is in these signs of the proof of Allah's power, His greatness and the wondrous wisdom of His design.

His saying: 98. ﴿And it is He who produced you from a single soul﴾, that is, Adam, peace be upon him, as has passed. This is another kind of His wondrous creation, which indicates the perfection of His power. ﴿Then a lodging place and a deposit place﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, al-Ḥasan, Abū ʿAmr, ʿĪsā, al-Aʿraj and al-Nakhaʿī read it with a kasra on the qāf, while the rest read it with a fatha. Both are nominative, as inchoatives whose predicate is omitted, the estimate being: then from you is a lodging place, or then for you is a lodging place. The first estimate is on the first reading, the second on the second: that is, then from you is a lodging place upon the back of the earth, or then for you is a lodging place upon it; and from you is a deposit place in the womb, or in the bottom of the earth, or in the loins. It has been said that the lodging place is in the womb and the deposit place is in the earth; it has been said that the lodging place is in the grave.

Al-Qurṭubī said: Most of the people of tafsir say: the lodging place is what is in the womb, and the deposit place is what is in the loins. It has been said that the lodging place is one who has been created and the deposit place is one who has not yet been created. It has been said that the idea of deposit is an indication of their being in graves until the resurrection.

What indicates that lodging place is explained as dwelling upon the earth is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And for you on the earth is a lodging place and enjoyment for a time﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36]. Here He, glorified is He, mentioned ﴿understand﴾ (yafqahūn), and before it ﴿know﴾ (yaʿlamūn), because in the production of souls from one soul, and in making some of them a lodging place and some a deposit place, there is a subtlety and fineness not found in the creation of the stars for guidance; so the mention of understanding (fiqh) is fitting, since it suggests greater precision and deeper reflection.

His saying: ﴿And it is He who sent down water from the heaven﴾. This is another kind of His wondrous creatures.

The water is rain water. In ﴿So We brought forth by it﴾ there is a shift from the third person to the first person, to show concern for this creature and what results from it. The pronoun in ﴿by it﴾ refers to the water. ﴿The vegetation of every thing﴾ means every kind of the varied types of vegetation. It has been said that the meaning is the provision of every thing; but the first interpretation is preferable.

Then He detailed this general statement, saying: ﴿So We brought forth from it green shoots﴾.

Al-Akhfash said: that is, green (akhḍar).

Al-khiḍr: the moist herbs, which branch out from the stalks emerging from the grain. It has been said: it means wheat, barley, maize, rice and all the other grains. ﴿We bring forth from it grain piled up﴾: this clause is an adjective of khiḍr, that is: We bring forth from the green stalks grain arranged in layers, that is, composed one upon another as in the ears of grain. ﴿And from the palm-tree﴾ is a fronted predicate, and ﴿from its spathe﴾ is a substitute for it. On the reading of the one who read "yakhruju minhu ḥabbun", the raising of "qinwānun" is by its being conjoined to "ḥabb". Al-Farrā' permitted, outside the Qur'an, "qinwānan" conjoined to "ḥabban" in the accusative; and Tamim say "qinyān".

It was read with a damma and a fatha on the qāf, according to the difference of the two dialects: the dialect of Qays and the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz.

Al-ṭalʿ: the sheath before it splits open over the spadix, and the spadix is also called ṭalʿ.

Al-qinwān: the plural of qinw, and the difference between its plural and its dual is that the dual has a kasra on the nūn, while the plural follows what the case requires; similar is ṣinwān.

Al-qinw: the cluster (ʿidhq).

The meaning: that qinwān originates from ṭalʿ. The ʿidhq is the cluster of the palm-tree; it has been said that qinwān are the hearts (jimār) of the palm.

Al-dāniya: the near one, which is within reach of the one standing or sitting.

Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is "from them is near, and from them is far", and it is elided; similar is ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Naḥl: 81]. The near is specified by mention because the purpose of the verse is to show measure and favour, and what is within easy reach is more abundant.

His saying: ﴿And gardens of grapevines﴾.

Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Layla, al-Aʿmash and ʿĀṣim in his authentic transmission from him read "jannātun" with a nominative; the rest read it in the accusative.

Abū ʿUbayda and Abū Ḥātim rejected the first reading, until Abū Ḥātim said: it is impossible, because gardens do not come from palm-trees.

Al-Naḥḥās said: the nominative is not interpreted in this way, but it is a nominative as an inchoative whose predicate is omitted: that is, and for them are gardens, as a group of reciters read "wa ḥūrun ʿīn" [al-Wāqiʿa: 22]. Sībawayh, al-Kisā'ī and al-Farrā' permitted the like of this. As for the accusative, it has been said that it is conjoined to "nabāta kulli shay'" — that is, We brought forth by it gardens of grapevines — or it is accusative by a verb to be supposed later: that is, and gardens of grapevines We brought forth; and the same view holds for the accusative of "zaytūn" and "rummān". It has also been said that they are accusative by specification, since they are esteemed. "Mushtabihan" is accusative as a circumstantial state: that is, each of them resembles the other in some of its attributes and does not resemble it in others. It has been said that one of them resembles the other in leaf, considering its covering of the whole branch and its size, but does not resemble it in taste. It has also been said that zaytūn and rummān are singled out because their habitats are close to the Arabs, as in the saying of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾ [al-Ghāshiya: 17]. Then He, glorified is He, commanded them to look with the gaze of consideration at its fruit when it bears fruit, and at its ripeness when it ripens.

Al-thamar in the language is the produce of the tree.

Al-yāniʿ: the ripe one, which has reached maturity and whose time for picking has come.

Ibn al-Anbārī said: al-yanʿ is the plural of yāniʿ, like rakb and rākib.

Al-Farrā' said: aynaʿa means it turned red.

Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read "thamarihi" with a damma on the thā' and the mīm; the rest read it with fatha, except al-Aʿmash, who read "thumrihi" with a damma on the thā' and a sukūn on the mīm, for lightness.

Muhammad ibn al-Samaifaʿ, Ibn Muḥayṣin and Ibn Abī Isḥāq read "yunʿahu" with a damma on the yā' of the present tense.

Al-Farrā' said: it is the dialect of some people of Najd.

The rest read it with a fatha. The indication in His saying ﴿Indeed in that﴾ refers to what has been mentioned previously, both in summary and in detail: ﴿there are indeed signs for a people who believe﴾ in Allah, reasoning from what they witness of His wondrous creatures which He has recounted to them.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾, that he said: He created the grain and the date-stone.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh transmitted from Qatādah, who said: He splits the grain and the date-stone to bring forth vegetation.

Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh transmitted from Mujāhid, who said: "the two halves that are in them."

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Abū Mālik something similar.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh transmitted from him regarding His saying: ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾, that he said: the palm-tree from the date-stone and the ear of grain from the grain; ﴿and brings forth the dead from the living﴾, that he said: the date-stone from the palm-tree and the grain from the ear.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Mujāhid: ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead and brings forth the dead from the living﴾, that he said: people, the living, from sperm-drops, and the sperm-drop is dead, coming out from living people; and likewise from livestock and plants.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿So how are you turned away?﴾ that it means: how then do you deny?

He also related from al-Hasan that he said: "How are you diverted?"

He also related from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿Splitter of the dawn﴾ that he said: "He created the night and the day."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he said: "By dawn (al-Isbah) is meant the light of the sun by day and the light of the moon by night."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid regarding ﴿Splitter of the dawn﴾ that he said: "The brightening of the dawn."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿Splitter of the dawn﴾, that he said: "Splitter of the morning (al-Subh)."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And He made the night a resting-place﴾, that he said: "Every bird and beast rests in it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And the sun and the moon as a reckoning﴾, that he said: "That is, the count of days, months and years."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And it is He who placed for you the stars that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of the land and the sea﴾, that he said: "A man may go astray while he is in darkness, and the path may be lost to him through deviation."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Khatib in his Book of the Stars related from Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "Learn from the stars what you are guided by on your land and your sea, then stop. By Allah, they were created only as an adornment for the heaven, as missiles against the devils, and as signs by which one is guided."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib related from Ibn Umar that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Learn from the stars what you are guided by in the darknesses of the land and the sea, then desist."
