Al-Farra' permitted that "al-jinn" be an appositive (badal) of "shuraka'" and its explanation (mufassir).

Al-Kisa'i permitted the nominative "al-jinn," meaning "they are the jinn," as if it was said, "Who are they?" and it was answered, "The jinn." Yazid ibn Abi Qutayb and Abu Hayyan recited it in the nominative. It was also recited in the genitive, with "shuraka'" in apposition to "al-jinn" for explanation (bayan).

The meaning is that they made partners for Allah and worshipped them as they worshipped Him, and glorified them as they glorified Him.

It was said that "al-jinn" here means the angels, because they are hidden (ijtinan), that is, concealed. They are the ones who said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah." It was also said that the verse was revealed concerning the heretics (zanadiqah) who said that Allah, the Exalted, and Iblis are brothers: Allah created people and animals, and Iblis created snakes, predators and scorpions.

This was narrated from al-Kalbi. Close to this is the view of the Magians, who said that the world has two creators, the Lord, glorified is He, and the devil (shaytan). Likewise are those who say that all good comes from light and all evil from darkness; they are the Manichaeans (al-Mانawiyyah).

His saying, ﴿and He created them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah) with "qad" implied: that is, "and they knew that Allah created them," or "created that which they made a partner of Allah."

His saying, ﴿and they invented for Him sons and daughters﴾: Nafi' recited it with the intensive form (tashdid), because the polytheists claimed that the angels are daughters of Allah, the Christians claimed that the Messiah is the son of Allah, and the Jews claimed that Uzayr is the son of Allah. Thus that (p-439) increased among their disbelief, so the verb was intensified to match the meaning. The rest recited it with the light form (takhfif).

It was also recited as "harrafu" (they distorted), from tahrif, that is, they falsified.

The lexicographers said: the meaning of "kharaqu" is that they fabricated, invented and lied. It is said: "He fabricated the lie (ikhtalaqa al-ifk), invented it (ikhtaraqahu) and forged it (kharaqahu)." Or its origin is from "kharaqa al-thawb," when he tore the garment, that is, they tore for Him sons and daughters.

His saying, ﴿without knowledge﴾ is connected to an implied element that is a circumstantial phrase (hal): that is, they were saying this without any knowledge, but rather they said that out of pure ignorance. Then, after relating this manifest error and this monstrous slander, of making the jinn partners of Allah and attributing sons and daughters to Him, He declared Himself free of it, saying, ﴿Glorified is He and exalted above what they describe﴾. The discussion of the meaning of "subhanahu" has already been given.

The meaning of "ta'ala" is that He is far removed and exalted above their false statement which they attribute to Him.

His saying, ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ means "its Originator (mubdi'uhuma)." So how could it be that ﴿He should have a son﴾, when "badi'" has frequently come in the sense of "mubdi'," just as "sami'" comes in the sense of "musmi'." From this is the saying of Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib:

"Does the caller Rayhanah, the one who hears, keep me awake, while my companions sleep?"

That is, "the one who makes hear." It was also said that it is from the construction of the attributive adjective (sifah mushabbahah) to its agent, and the original is "badi' samawatihi wa ardihi" (the originator of His heavens and His earth).

Al-Kisa'i permitted its genitive case as an adjective (na't) of Allah.

The apparent reading is that its nominative case is by an implied subject (mubtada'), or that it is a subject whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿how can He have a son﴾. It was also said that it is nominative as the agent of "ta'ala." It was recited in the accusative as praise (madh).

The interrogative in ﴿how can He have a son﴾ is for denial and remoteness: that is, how can one who has this description, namely that He is the Creator of the heavens, the earth and what is in them, have a son? He is one of His creatures, and how could He take as a son what He created? Then He stressed the negation of a son, saying, ﴿and He has no companion (sahibah)﴾, that is, how could He have a son when He has no consort? When a consort does not exist, the existence of a son is impossible.

The clause ﴿and He created everything﴾ serves to establish what precedes it, because whoever is the Creator of everything, it is impossible for Him to take one of His creatures as a son. ﴿And He is Knower of all things﴾ means nothing among His creatures is hidden from Him.

The demonstrative in His saying ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾ refers to the previous attributes. It is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and what follows is its predicate (khabar), which is the noble name. ﴿Allah, your Lord﴾ is an appositive (badal) of the demonstrative. Likewise, ﴿There is no deity except Him, the Creator of all things﴾ is the predicate of the subject. It is permitted that "Khaliq" be nominative with an implied subject, and al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' permitted its accusative case. ﴿So worship Him﴾: that is, whoever has these attributes is deserving of worship, so worship Him, and do not worship other than Him, of whom none has any of these great attributes.

His saying, ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾: "al-absar" is the plural of "basar," which is the faculty of sight. Perceiving (idrak) a thing is an expression for encompassing it.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, they do not reach the reality of His essence (kunh haqiqatihi). So what is negated is this perception, not mere seeing.

Moreover, it has been established by mutawatir hadiths (those transmitted by so many chains that there is no doubt or uncertainty about them), and no one is ignorant of this except one who is grossly ignorant of the pure Sunnah. Also, it has been established in the science of rhetoric (bayan) and logic (mizan) that the negation of a universal affirmative is a particular negative. So the meaning is that some vision does not perceive Him, namely the vision of the disbelievers. This is on the assumption that negating perception implies negating seeing, so the intended meaning is this specific seeing. The verse is a negation of comprehensiveness, not a comprehensive negation. The first (comprehensive negation) is replaced by the particular, and the meaning is: "All vision does not perceive Him, but some of it does," namely the vision of the believers.

Resorting to one of these two interpretations is necessary because of what we have made known to you regarding the mutawatir reports about the seeing in the Hereafter, and its support by His saying, ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22], and so on.

His saying, ﴿and He perceives the vision﴾: that is, He encompasses them and reaches their reality, nothing about them is hidden from Him. He specified "the visions" to match what precedes it.

Al-Zajjaj said: In this is evidence that created beings do not perceive vision, that is, they do not know the reality and nature of sight, or what it is by which a person sees with his two eyes and not with other limbs of his body. End quote.

﴿And He is the Subtle (al-Latif)﴾: that is, the Gentle with His servants. It is said: "Fulan lataffa bi-Fulan," that is, he was gentle with him. Gentleness (al-lutf) in action is kindness in it. Divine gentleness (al-lutf min Allah) is success (tawfiq) and protection (ismah). "Altaffahu bi-kadha" means he was kind to him. "Al-mulatafah" means being kind. This is what al-Jawhari and Ibn Faris said. And ﴿the All-Aware (al-Khabir)﴾ is the one who is tested (al-mukhtabar) in everything, such that nothing is hidden from Him.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying, ﴿And they made for Allah partners, the jinn, while He created them﴾, that he said: "Allah created them." ﴿And they invented for Him sons and daughters without knowledge﴾: he said, "They guessed (takharrasu)."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His saying, ﴿and they invented﴾, that he said, "They made (ja'alu)."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid that he said, "They lied."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Uqayli, Ibn Adi, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related with a weak chain from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, "from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning His saying, ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾, he said: 'If mankind, the jinn, the angels and the devils, from the time they were created until they perish, were arranged in one row, they would never encompass Allah.'"

al-Dhahabi said: "This is a munkar hadith." End quote.

In its chain is Atiyyah al-Awfi, who is weak.

al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih) and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Muhammad saw his Lord." Ikrimah said: "I said to him, 'Does not Allah say, ﴿No vision perceives Him, and He perceives the vision﴾?' He said: 'Woe to you! That is His light. When He manifests Himself with His light, nothing perceives Him.'" In another wording: "That is only when He manifests Himself in His modality, no sight can stand before Him."

Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: "No one's sight encompasses Allah."

Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi in Kitab al-Ru'yah related from al-Hasan concerning His saying, ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾, that he said: "In this world."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Isma'il ibn Ulayyah something similar.

This passage introduces another kind of their ignorance and error.

It was also said that the verse was revealed concerning the heretics (zanadiqah) who said that Allah, the Exalted, and Iblis are brothers: Allah created people and animals, and Iblis created snakes, predators and scorpions.

(p. 440) *Al-basa'ir* (insights, clear proofs) is the plural of *basira*, which originally means the light of the heart. Here it means the clear argument and the manifest proof. This speech is conveyed on the tongue of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), which is why He says at its end: ﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾. He describes the *basa'ir* as "coming" to magnify their status and to treat them as an absent thing whose arrival is expected, as one says: "Well-being has come, sickness has departed, good fortunes have approached, and misfortunes have turned away." ﴿So whoever sees, it is for his own self﴾, that is, whoever understands the proof, recognizes it, and submits to it, benefits himself, because by this sight he is saved from the punishment of the Fire. ﴿And whoever is blind﴾ to the proof, does not understand it, and does not submit to it, the harm falls upon his own self, because he exposes himself to the anger of God in this world, and his destination will be the Fire. ﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾: not a watcher who counts your deeds. I am only a messenger who conveys to you the messages of my Lord, and He is the Guardian over you.

Al-Zajjaj (ʿAbd al-Rahman) said: This was revealed before the obligation of fighting, and then he was commanded to prevent them by the sword from worshipping idols.

105. ﴿And thus We vary the verses﴾, that is, in the same wonderful variation We vary them in promise and threat, in admonition and warning.

His saying: ﴿and so that they may say, "You have studied"﴾ is coordinated with an implied element: that is, We vary the verses so that the proof may be established, and so that they may say "You have studied." Or it is a purpose-clause (ʿilla) for a verb that is implied and placed later: that is, "and so that they may say, 'You have studied,' We have varied them." In this case the lam is of consequence (al-ʿaqiba) or of outcome (al-sayrura).

The meaning is: in the same manner We vary the verses, and [the result is] that they say "You have studied." There is no concern with their words, nor any regard for them. So the meaning is a warning and a threat to them, and disregard for their words.

Al-Zajjaj has alluded to something similar.

Al-Nahhas said: There is another good opinion regarding the meaning, which is that "We vary the verses" means "We bring them one verse after another, so that they say 'You have studied' against us, and they are then reminded of the first by the last." This is the literal meaning. What Abu Ishaq (al-Zajjaj) said is metaphorical.

As for "darasta" (you have studied), there are readings. Abu ʿAmr and Ibn Kathir read *darasta* with an alif between the dal and the ra, like *faʿalta*. This is the reading of ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, ʿIkrima, and the people of Mecca. Its meaning: you studied with the People of the Book and they studied with you, that is, you debated with them and they debated with you. What supports this is the statement of God in the Noble Book about them: ﴿And another people helped him in it﴾ [al-Furqan: 4], meaning the Jews helped the Prophet (ﷺ) in the Qur'an. Similar is their saying: ﴿Fables of the ancients, which he has had written down, and they are dictated to him morning and evening﴾ [al-Furqan: 5], and their saying: ﴿Only a human is teaching him﴾.

On the second reading the meaning is: these verses have become old, faded, and ended, like their saying ﴿fables of the ancients﴾ [al-An'am: 25]. On the third reading the meaning is similar to the first reading.

Al-Akhfash said: It has the meaning of *darasta* except that it is more emphatic.

It is related from al-Mubarrad that he read *wa-liyaqulu* (with a sukun on the lam), so the meaning carries a threat: that is, "let them say whatever they wish, for the truth is clear."

In this word, the root is *darasa, yadrusu, dirasatan*, from *al-dars*, which is recitation. It is also said: from *darrastuhu*, meaning I made it easy through much recitation. Its original sense is *darasa al-taʿam*, meaning he threshed the grain. *Al-diyas* (threshing) is *al-dirasu* in the dialect of the people of al-Sham. It is also said: its origin is from *darastu al-thawba adrusuhu darsan*, meaning I wore it out. *Daratat al-mar'a darsan* means the woman menstruated. It is said that the vulva of a woman is referred to as *abu dirasin*, from menstruation. *Al-Dars* also means a hidden path.

Al-Asmaʿi related: a camel *lam yudras*, meaning it has not been ridden.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 109–113 (part 1 of 2):

His statement: ﴿They swore by God with the utmost of their oaths﴾. That is, the disbelievers in general, or the disbelievers of Quraysh specifically. *Jahd al-aymān* means the strongest of oaths: they swore by God with the strongest of their oaths, as far as their ability reached. They believed that God is the Greatest God, which is why they swore by Him. *Jahd* is in the accusative as a *maṣdar* (verbal noun, *maṣdar*) and, with a fatha on the *jīm*, means hardship, while with a ḍamma it means capacity. Some lexicographers treat the two as having one meaning. The meaning is that they proposed to the Prophet (ﷺ) a sign from among the signs they used to propose, and they swore that if this sign they had proposed came to them, ﴿they would surely believe in it﴾. Their aim was not faith. Rather, most of their intention was to dictate terms to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and to toy with the signs of God. So God, glorified is He, commanded him to answer them with His words: ﴿Signs are only with God﴾, this sign they propose and others, and I have no part in that. If He wills to send it down, He sends it down, and if He wills not to send it down, He does not send it down.

His statement: ﴿And what will make you realize that when they come they will not believe?﴾

Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Kathīr read *innahā* with a kasra on the *hamzah* (*inna*), and this is the reading of Mujāhid. This reading is supported by the reading of Ibn Masʿūd: *wa mā yushʿirukum idhā jāʾat lā yuʾminūn* (without *annahā*). Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd said: the address here is to the polytheists, meaning "and what will make you know," and then judgment is passed on them with His words: ﴿that when they come they will not believe﴾.

Al-Farrāʾ and others said: the address is to the believers, because the believers said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Messenger of God, if the sign were sent down, perhaps they would believe." Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And what will make you realize that when they come they will not believe﴾.

The people of Medina, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿annahā idhā jāʾat﴾ with a fatha on the *hamzah*. Al-Khalīl said: *annahā* here means *laʿallahā* (perhaps), as in the revelation: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾ [ʿAbasa: 3], meaning *annahu yazzakkā*, that he would purify himself. It is reported from the Arabs: *iʾti al-sūq annaka tashtarī lanā shayʾan*, meaning *laʿallaka* (perhaps you), "go to the market, perhaps you will buy something for us." From this is the verse of ʿAdī ibn Zayd:

"O my blamer, what will make you know that my death is (near) until an hour in the day or in the forenoon of tomorrow?"

Meaning: *laʿalla maniyyatī* (perhaps my death). From this is the verse of Durayd ibn al-Ṣimma:

"Show me a steed that died of emaciation, for I see what you see, or a miser made immortal."

Meaning: *laʿallanī* (perhaps I). And the verse of Abū al-Najm:

"I said to Shaybān: draw near to his meeting, for perhaps after today I shall be of his kind."

Meaning: *laʿallī* (perhaps I). And the verse of Jarīr:

"Will you turn aside with us, perhaps we may see the open plains or the traces of the tents?"

Meaning: *laʿallanā* (perhaps we). It occurs often in Arabic speech with the meaning of *laʿallahu*.

Al-Kisāʾī reported that it is written this way (*annahā*) in the codex of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb.

Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ also said: *anna* is redundant (*zāʾidah*, the particle *lā* is extra), and the meaning is: "And what will make you realize that when they come they will believe," so the *lā* was added, as it was added in His words: ﴿And it is forbidden to a town which We have destroyed that they will not return﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 95], and in His words: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 12]. Al-Zajjāj, al-Naḥḥās and others considered the addition of *lā* weak and said it is an error and a mistake.

Al-Naḥḥās and others mentioned that there is an ellipsis in the sentence, and the estimate is: *annahā idhā jāʾat lā yuʾminūn aw yuʾminūn* (that when they come they will not believe, or they will believe). Then this presumed part was omitted because the listener knows it.

His statement: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sights﴾ is coordinated with ﴿they will not believe﴾. It is said: the meaning is the turning of their hearts and sights on the Day of Resurrection over the flame of the fire and the heat of the embers, ﴿as they did not believe﴾ in the world, ﴿and We leave them﴾ in the world, that is, We give them respite and do not punish them. According to this view, part of the verse refers to the Hereafter and part to this world.

It is also said: the meaning is: We turn their hearts and their sights in this world, that is, We will hinder them from faith if that sign came to them, just as We hindered them from what you called them to at first, at the appearance of the miracle.

It is also said: there is inversion (*taqdīm wa taʾkhīr*) in the speech. The order is: *annahā idhā jāʾat lā yuʾminūn kamā lam yuʾminū*, and *nuqallibu afʾidatahum wa abṣārahum*, and *nadharuhum fī ṭughyānihim yaʿmahūn* (that when they come they will not believe as they did not believe, and We turn their hearts and sights, and We leave them in their rebellion wandering blindly), that is, they are bewildered. The *kāf* in ﴿as they did not believe﴾ is an adjective to an omitted *maṣdar*, and *mā* is a *maṣdariyyah* (verbal particle), and ﴿wandering blindly﴾ is in the accusative position as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause).

His statement: ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾, that is, they will not believe even if We had sent down to them the angels, as they proposed when they said: ﴿Why was not an angel sent down to him?﴾ [al-Anʿām: 8], ﴿and the dead spoke to them﴾, those they knew after We revived them for them, so they told them that this Prophet is truthful, sent from God, so believe in him, they would not believe. ﴿And We gathered against them every thing﴾ of what they asked for of signs, ﴿qubulan﴾, that is, as guarantors and as sureties, with the clear signs We brought them.

This is according to the reading of the one who reads ﴿qubulan﴾ with a ḍamma on the *qāf*, and this is the majority reading.

Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read *qibalan* with a kasra on the *qāf*, meaning "face to face" (*muqābalah*).

Muḥammad ibn Yazīd al-Mubarrad said: *qibalan* means "direction" (*nāḥiyah*), as you say: "to me so-and-so has property" (*qibala fulānin mālun*). So *qubulan* is in the accusative as an adverb of place (*ẓarf*). According to the first meaning, the words of God, exalted is He, are: ﴿or you bring God and the angels as a *qabīl*﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 92], that is, they stand surety. This is what al-Farrāʾ said.

Al-Akhfash said: it means *qabīl qabīl*, that is, group after group.

Abū Zayd reported: "I met so-and-so *qubulan*, and *muqābalatan*, and *qibalan*," all of which have one meaning, face to face. According to this, the ḍamma is like the kasra, and the two readings are equal.

*Al-ḥashr* means gathering. ﴿They would not believe except that God wills﴾, their faith. For what God wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. The exception is an exception of the "emptied" type (*mustathnā mufraghun*, where the exception has no explicit subject). ﴿But most of them are ignorant﴾, an ignorance that stands between them and the attainment of truth and reaching what is right.

His statement: 112. ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet﴾. This speech is to console the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and to remove the sorrow he felt because of their unbelief. That is, in the same manner of this appointment, ﴿We have appointed for every prophet an enemy﴾. The meaning is: just as We tested you with these people, We tested the prophets before you with a people of disbelievers, and We appointed for each of them an enemy from the disbelievers of their time. ﴿Devils of mankind and jinn﴾ is an apposition (*badal*) to "enemy." It is also said that it is the second object of *jaʿalnā*.

Al-Aʿmash read *al-Jinna wa al-Insa* with the *jinn* placed first. By "devils" is meant the rebellious ones of both groups. The genitive construction is either explanatory (*bayāniyyah*), or it is the genitive of an attribute to the thing qualified (*min idāfat al-ṣifah ilā al-mawṣūf*), and the original is "the mankind and jinn who are devils." The clause ﴿some of them inspire to others﴾ is in the accusative position as a *ḥāl*, that is, while one of them whispers to another. It is also said that the clause is a new resumptive sentence (*mustaʾnafah*) explaining the state of the enemy. It is called *waḥy* (inspiration) because it occurs only secretly between them. Their deception is described as "ornamented speech" because they make it attractive, and *zukhruf* means adornment; "the ornaments of water" are its patterns. ﴿Deceit﴾ is in the accusative as a *maṣdar*, because the meaning of "some of them inspire to others" is "they deceive them thereby, deception." It may also be in the position of a *ḥāl*, or be an object of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*). *Al-ghurūr* means falsehood.

His statement: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, they would not have done it﴾. The pronoun refers to what was mentioned earlier of the matters that the disbelievers did in his time and in the time of the prophets before him. That is, if your Lord had willed that what was mentioned not occur, they would not have done it or brought it about. It is also said: "they did not do the inspiring" which is implied by the verb. ﴿So leave them﴾, that is, abandon them. This command is a threat to the disbelievers, like His words: ﴿Leave Me with whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11]. ﴿And what they fabricate﴾: if *mā* is a *maṣdariyyah*, the estimate is: "leave them and their fabrication"; if it is a relative pronoun (*mawṣūlah*), the estimate is: "leave them and what they fabricate."

His statement: ﴿And that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it﴾. The *lām* in *li-taṣghā* is the *lām* of *kay* (in order that), so it indicates cause, like His words "inspire," and the estimate is: some of them inspire to others in order to deceive them and so that the hearts may incline. It is also said that it is attached to an omitted word that is placed later, that is, *li-taṣghā* ("so that it may incline") ﴿We have appointed for every prophet an enemy﴾. It is also said that the *lām* is the *lām* of command, and this is an error, because if it were the *lām* of command the verb would be jussive.

*Al-iṣghāʾ* means inclining. It is said: *ṣaghawtu aṣghū ṣaghwan*, and *ṣaghaytu uṣghī*. It is also said: *ṣaghaytu* with a kasra. It is said: *aṣghaytu al-ināʾ*, when I tilt the vessel so that what is in it gathers. Its original meaning is inclining toward a thing for some purpose. It is said: *ṣaghat al-nujūm* when the stars inclined toward setting, and *aṣghat al-nāqah* when the she-camel bent her head. From this is the verse of Dhū al-Rumma:

"She inclines when he tightens her with the saddle-bands, leaning, until, when he has settled in her stirrup and held firm."

The pronoun in "to it" refers to the ornamented speech, or to what was mentioned earlier of the ornamented speech and other things. That is, some of them inspired to others the ornamented speech in order to deceive them, ﴿and that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it﴾ among the disbelievers, ﴿and that they may be pleased with it﴾ for themselves after listening to it, ﴿and that they may commit what they are committing﴾ of sins. *Al-iqtirāf* means earning. It is said: "He went out to earn (*li-yaqtarifa*) for his family," that is, to earn for them. *Qāraffa fulānun hādhā al-amr* means he engaged in it. *Qaraffahu* means he accused him of doubt. *Iqtaraffa* means he lied. Its original meaning is cutting off a piece from a thing.

Abū al-Shaykh reported, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: ﴿And they swore by God with the utmost of their oaths﴾ was revealed concerning Quraysh, and ﴿And what will make you realize﴾ (p-443), O Muslims, ﴿that when they come they will not believe﴾.

Ibn Jarīr reported, from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) spoke with Quraysh, and they said: O Muhammad, you inform us that Mūsā had a staff with which he struck the stone, and that ʿĪsā used to revive the dead, and that Thamūd had a she-camel. So bring us signs so that we may believe you. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: What do you like that I bring to you? They said: Make Ṣafā gold for us. He said: If I do so, will you believe me? They said: Yes, by God, if you do so we will all follow you. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood up and began to supplicate, and Jibrīl came to him and said: If you wish, it will become gold, but if they do not believe at that point We will surely punish them. And if you wish, leave them until their repentant ones repent. He said: Rather, let their repentant ones repent. So God revealed: ﴿And they swore by God with the utmost of their oaths﴾ until His words ﴿they are ignorant﴾."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported, from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His words: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sights﴾, he said: When the polytheists denied what God had sent down, their hearts did not remain firm upon anything, and they were turned back from every matter.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir reported, from him, concerning ﴿And We gathered against them every thing, qubulan﴾, he said: face to face (*muʿāyanatan*). ﴿They would not believe﴾, that is, the people of wretchedness, ﴿except that God wills﴾, that is, the people of felicity, and those whom it had preceded in His knowledge that they would enter into faith.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Abū al-Shaykh reported, from Qatādah, concerning ﴿And We gathered against them every thing, qubulan﴾, that is, they saw that matter face to face.

Abū al-Shaykh reported, from Mujāhid, who said: "In groups, *qabīlan*."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported, from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His words: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy, devils of mankind and jinn﴾, he said: The jinn have devils who lead them astray, like the devils of mankind who lead them astray. The devil of mankind and the devil of the jinn meet, and this one says to that one: "Lead him astray with such-and-such, and I will lead him astray with such-and-such." So this is ﴿some of them inspire to others ornamented speech as deception﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbās also said: The jinn are the *jānn*, and they are not devils. The devils are the offspring of Iblīs, and they do not die except together with Iblīs, while the jinn die. Among them there are believers and among them there are disbelievers.

Abū al-Shaykh reported, from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: The soothsayers (*kahanah*) are the devils of mankind.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported, from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His words: ﴿some of them inspire to others﴾, he said: The devils of the jinn inspire to the devils of mankind, for God says: ﴿And indeed the devils inspire to their allies﴾ [al-Anʿām: 121].

ʿAbd al-Razzāq and Ibn al-Mundhir reported, from Qatādah, concerning the verse, he said: Among mankind there are devils, and among the jinn there are devils, some of them inspire to others.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verse 109–113 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿zukhrufa al-qawl﴾ (embellished speech), that he said: some of them beautify speech for others so that they may follow them in their deviation.

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani related from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Abu Dharr, seek refuge in Allah from the evil of the devils of the jinn and mankind." He said: "O Prophet of Allah, do mankind have devils?" He said: "Yes, ﴿the devils of mankind and jinn, who inspire one another with embellished speech as deception﴾."

Ahmad, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related from Abu Dharr, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), a similar report.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿wa-li-tasgha﴾ (and that it may incline), meaning: that it may incline.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from him: ﴿wa-li-tasgha﴾ means it turns aside; ﴿wa-liyaqtarifu﴾ means they may earn.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 109–113 (part 1 of 2):

His statement: ﴿They swore by God with the utmost of their oaths﴾. That is, the disbelievers in general, or the disbelievers of Quraysh specifically. *Jahd al-aymān* means the strongest of oaths: they swore by God with the strongest of their oaths, as far as their ability reached. They believed that God is the Greatest God, which is why they swore by Him. *Jahd* is in the accusative as a *maṣdar* (verbal noun, *maṣdar*) and, with a fatha on the *jīm*, means hardship, while with a ḍamma it means capacity. Some lexicographers treat the two as having one meaning. The meaning is that they proposed to the Prophet (ﷺ) a sign from among the signs they used to propose, and they swore that if this sign they had proposed came to them, ﴿they would surely believe in it﴾. Their aim was not faith. Rather, most of their intention was to dictate terms to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and to toy with the signs of God. So God, glorified is He, commanded him to answer them with His words: ﴿Signs are only with God﴾, this sign they propose and others, and I have no part in that. If He wills to send it down, He sends it down, and if He wills not to send it down, He does not send it down.

His statement: ﴿And what will make you realize that when they come they will not believe?﴾

Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Kathīr read *innahā* with a kasra on the *hamzah* (*inna*), and this is the reading of Mujāhid. This reading is supported by the reading of Ibn Masʿūd: *wa mā yushʿirukum idhā jāʾat lā yuʾminūn* (without *annahā*). Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd said: the address here is to the polytheists, meaning "and what will make you know," and then judgment is passed on them with His words: ﴿that when they come they will not believe﴾.

Al-Farrāʾ and others said: the address is to the believers, because the believers said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Messenger of God, if the sign were sent down, perhaps they would believe." Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And what will make you realize that when they come they will not believe﴾.

The people of Medina, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿annahā idhā jāʾat﴾ with a fatha on the *hamzah*. Al-Khalīl said: *annahā* here means *laʿallahā* (perhaps), as in the revelation: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾ [ʿAbasa: 3], meaning *annahu yazzakkā*, that he would purify himself. It is reported from the Arabs: *iʾti al-sūq annaka tashtarī lanā shayʾan*, meaning *laʿallaka* (perhaps you), "go to the market, perhaps you will buy something for us." From this is the verse of ʿAdī ibn Zayd:

"O my blamer, what will make you know that my death is (near) until an hour in the day or in the forenoon of tomorrow?"

Meaning: *laʿalla maniyyatī* (perhaps my death). From this is the verse of Durayd ibn al-Ṣimma:

"Show me a steed that died of emaciation, for I see what you see, or a miser made immortal."

Meaning: *laʿallanī* (perhaps I). And the verse of Abū al-Najm:

"I said to Shaybān: draw near to his meeting, for perhaps after today I shall be of his kind."

Meaning: *laʿallī* (perhaps I). And the verse of Jarīr:

"Will you turn aside with us, perhaps we may see the open plains or the traces of the tents?"

Meaning: *laʿallanā* (perhaps we). It occurs often in Arabic speech with the meaning of *laʿallahu*.

Al-Kisāʾī reported that it is written this way (*annahā*) in the codex of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb.

Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ also said: *anna* is redundant (*zāʾidah*, the particle *lā* is extra), and the meaning is: "And what will make you realize that when they come they will believe," so the *lā* was added, as it was added in His words: ﴿And it is forbidden to a town which We have destroyed that they will not return﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 95], and in His words: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 12]. Al-Zajjāj, al-Naḥḥās and others considered the addition of *lā* weak and said it is an error and a mistake.

Al-Naḥḥās and others mentioned that there is an ellipsis in the sentence, and the estimate is: *annahā idhā jāʾat lā yuʾminūn aw yuʾminūn* (that when they come they will not believe, or they will believe). Then this presumed part was omitted because the listener knows it.

His statement: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sights﴾ is coordinated with ﴿they will not believe﴾. It is said: the meaning is the turning of their hearts and sights on the Day of Resurrection over the flame of the fire and the heat of the embers, ﴿as they did not believe﴾ in the world, ﴿and We leave them﴾ in the world, that is, We give them respite and do not punish them. According to this view, part of the verse refers to the Hereafter and part to this world.

It is also said: the meaning is: We turn their hearts and their sights in this world, that is, We will hinder them from faith if that sign came to them, just as We hindered them from what you called them to at first, at the appearance of the miracle.

It is also said: there is inversion (*taqdīm wa taʾkhīr*) in the speech. The order is: *annahā idhā jāʾat lā yuʾminūn kamā lam yuʾminū*, and *nuqallibu afʾidatahum wa abṣārahum*, and *nadharuhum fī ṭughyānihim yaʿmahūn* (that when they come they will not believe as they did not believe, and We turn their hearts and sights, and We leave them in their rebellion wandering blindly), that is, they are bewildered. The *kāf* in ﴿as they did not believe﴾ is an adjective to an omitted *maṣdar*, and *mā* is a *maṣdariyyah* (verbal particle), and ﴿wandering blindly﴾ is in the accusative position as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause).

His statement: ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾, that is, they will not believe even if We had sent down to them the angels, as they proposed when they said: ﴿Why was not an angel sent down to him?﴾ [al-Anʿām: 8], ﴿and the dead spoke to them﴾, those they knew after We revived them for them, so they told them that this Prophet is truthful, sent from God, so believe in him, they would not believe. ﴿And We gathered against them every thing﴾ of what they asked for of signs, ﴿qubulan﴾, that is, as guarantors and as sureties, with the clear signs We brought them.

This is according to the reading of the one who reads ﴿qubulan﴾ with a ḍamma on the *qāf*, and this is the majority reading.

Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read *qibalan* with a kasra on the *qāf*, meaning "face to face" (*muqābalah*).

According to the first meaning, the words of God, exalted is He, are: ﴿or you bring God and the angels as a *qabīl*﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 92], that is, they stand surety. This is what al-Farrāʾ said.

Al-Akhfash said: it means *qabīl qabīl*, that is, group after group.

Abū Zayd reported: "I met so-and-so *qubulan*, and *muqābalatan*, and *qibalan*," all of which have one meaning, face to face. According to this, the ḍamma is like the kasra, and the two readings are equal.

*Al-ḥashr* means gathering. ﴿They would not believe except that God wills﴾, their faith. For what God wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. The exception is an exception of the "emptied" type (*mustathnā mufraghun*, where the exception has no explicit subject). ﴿But most of them are ignorant﴾, an ignorance that stands between them and the attainment of truth and reaching what is right.

That is, in the same manner of this appointment, ﴿We have appointed for every prophet an enemy﴾. The meaning is: just as We tested you with these people, We tested the prophets before you with a people of disbelievers, and We appointed for each of them an enemy from the disbelievers of their time. ﴿Devils of mankind and jinn﴾ is an apposition (*badal*) to "enemy." The clause ﴿some of them inspire to others﴾ is in the accusative position as a *ḥāl*, that is, while one of them whispers to another. It may also be in the position of a *ḥāl*, or be an object of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*). *Al-ghurūr* means falsehood.

His statement: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, they would not have done it﴾. The pronoun refers to what was mentioned earlier of the matters that the disbelievers did in his time and in the time of the prophets before him. That is, if your Lord had willed that what was mentioned not occur, they would not have done it or brought it about. It is also said: "they did not do the inspiring" which is implied by the verb. ﴿So leave them﴾, that is, abandon them. The people of Medina, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿annahā idhā jāʾat﴾ with a fatha on the *hamzah*. Al-Khalīl said: *annahā* here means *laʿallahā* (perhaps), as in the revelation: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾ [ʿAbasa: 3], meaning *annahu yazzakkā*, that he would purify himself. It is reported from the Arabs: *iʾti al-sūq annaka tashtarī lanā shayʾan*, meaning *laʿallaka* (perhaps you), "go to the market, perhaps you will buy something for us." From this is the verse of ʿAdī ibn Zayd:

"O my blamer, what will make you know that my death is (near) until an hour in the day or in the forenoon of tomorrow?"

Meaning: *laʿalla maniyyatī* (perhaps my death). From this is the verse of Durayd ibn al-Ṣimma:

"Show me a steed that died of emaciation, for I see what you see, or a miser made immortal."

Meaning: *laʿallanī* (perhaps I). And the verse of Abū al-Najm:

"I said to Shaybān: draw near to his meeting, for perhaps after today I shall be of his kind."

Meaning: *laʿallī* (perhaps I). And the verse of Jarīr:

"Will you turn aside with us, perhaps we may see the open plains or the traces of the tents?"

Meaning: *laʿallanā* (perhaps we). It occurs often in Arabic speech with the meaning of *laʿallahu*.

Al-Kisāʾī reported that it is written this way (*annahā*) in the codex of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb.

Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ also said: *anna* is redundant (*zāʾidah*, the particle *lā* is extra), and the meaning is: "And what will make you realize that when they come they will believe," so the *lā* was added, as it was added in His words: ﴿And it is forbidden to a town which We have destroyed that they will not return﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 95], and in His words: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 12]. Al-Zajjāj, al-Naḥḥās and others considered the addition of *lā* weak and said it is an error and a mistake.

Al-Naḥḥās and others mentioned that there is an ellipsis in the sentence, and the estimate is: *annahā idhā jāʾat lā yuʾminūn aw yuʾminūn* (that when they come they will not believe, or they will believe). Then this presumed part was omitted because the listener knows it.

His statement: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sights﴾ is coordinated with ﴿they will not believe﴾. It is said: the meaning is the turning of their hearts and sights on the Day of Resurrection over the flame of the fire and the heat of the embers, ﴿as they did not believe﴾ in the world, ﴿and We leave them﴾ in the world, that is, We give them respite and do not punish them. According to this view, part of the verse refers to the Hereafter and part to this world.

It is also said: the meaning is: We turn their hearts and their sights in this world, that is, We will hinder them from faith if that sign came to them, just as We hindered them from what you called them to at first, at the appearance of the miracle.

It is also said: there is inversion (*taqdīm wa taʾkhīr*) in the speech. The order is: *annahā idhā jāʾat lā yuʾminūn kamā lam yuʾminū*, and *nuqallibu afʾidatahum wa abṣārahum*, and *nadharuhum fī ṭughyānihim yaʿmahūn* (that when they come they will not believe as they did not believe, and We turn their hearts and sights, and We leave them in their rebellion wandering blindly), that is, they are bewildered. The *kāf* in ﴿as they did not believe﴾ is an adjective to an omitted *maṣdar*, and *mā* is a *maṣdariyyah* (verbal particle), and ﴿wandering blindly﴾ is in the accusative position as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause).

His statement: ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾, that is, they will not believe even if We had sent down to them the angels, as they proposed when they said: ﴿Why was not an angel sent down to him?﴾ [al-Anʿām: 8], ﴿and the dead spoke to them﴾, those they knew after We revived them for them, so they told them that this Prophet is truthful, sent from God, so believe in him, they would not believe. ﴿And We gathered against them every thing﴾ of what they asked for of signs, ﴿qubulan﴾, that is, as guarantors and as sureties, with the clear signs We brought them.

This is according to the reading of the one who reads ﴿qubulan﴾ with a ḍamma on the *qāf*, and this is the majority reading.

Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read *qibalan* with a kasra on the *qāf*, meaning "face to face" (*muqābalah*).

Muḥammad ibn Yazīd al-Mubarrad said: *qibalan* means "direction" (*nāḥiyah*), as you say: "to me so-and-so has property" (*qibala fulānin mālun*). So *qubulan* is in the accusative as an adverb of place (*ẓarf*). According to the first meaning, the words of God, exalted is He, are: ﴿or you bring God and the angels as a *qabīl*﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 92], that is, they stand surety. This is what al-Farrāʾ said.

Al-Akhfash said: it means *qabīl qabīl*, that is, group after group.

Abū Zayd reported: "I met so-and-so *qubulan*, and *muqābalatan*, and *qibalan*," all of which have one meaning, face to face. According to this, the ḍamma is like the kasra, and the two readings are equal.

*Al-ḥashr* means gathering. ﴿They would not believe except that God wills﴾, their faith. For what God wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. The exception is an exception of the "emptied" type (*mustathnā mufraghun*, where the exception has no explicit subject). ﴿But most of them are ignorant﴾, an ignorance that stands between them and the attainment of truth and reaching what is right.

His statement: 112. ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet﴾. This speech is to console the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and to remove the sorrow he felt because of their unbelief. That is, in the same manner of this appointment, ﴿We have appointed for every prophet an enemy﴾. The meaning is: just as We tested you with these people, We tested the prophets before you with a people of disbelievers, and We appointed for each of them an enemy from the disbelievers of their time. ﴿Devils of mankind and jinn﴾ is an apposition (*badal*) to "enemy." It is also said that it is the second object of *jaʿalnā*.

Al-Aʿmash read *al-Jinna wa al-Insa* with the *jinn* placed first. By "devils" is meant the rebellious ones of both groups. The genitive construction is either explanatory (*bayāniyyah*), or it is the genitive of an attribute to the thing qualified (*min idāfat al-ṣifah ilā al-mawṣūf*), and the original is "the mankind and jinn who are devils." The clause ﴿some of them inspire to others﴾ is in the accusative position as a *ḥāl*, that is, while one of them whispers to another. It is also said that the clause is a new resumptive sentence (*mustaʾnafah*) explaining the state of the enemy. It is called *waḥy* (inspiration) because it occurs only secretly between them. Their deception is described as "ornamented speech" because they make it attractive, and *zukhruf* means adornment; "the ornaments of water" are its patterns. ﴿Deceit﴾ is in the accusative as a *maṣdar*, because the meaning of "some of them inspire to others" is "they deceive them thereby, deception." It may also be in the position of a *ḥāl*, or be an object of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*). *Al-ghurūr* means falsehood.

His statement: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, they would not have done it﴾. The pronoun refers to what was mentioned earlier of the matters that the disbelievers did in his time and in the time of the prophets before him. That is, if your Lord had willed that what was mentioned not occur, they would not have done it or brought it about. It is also said: "they did not do the inspiring" which is implied by the verb. ﴿So leave them﴾, that is, abandon them. This command is a threat to the disbelievers, like His words: ﴿Leave Me with whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11]. ﴿And what they fabricate﴾: if *mā* is a *maṣdariyyah*, the estimate is: "leave them and their fabrication"; if it is a relative pronoun (*mawṣūlah*), the estimate is: "leave them and what they fabricate."

His statement: ﴿And that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it﴾. The *lām* in *li-taṣghā* is the *lām* of *kay* (in order that), so it indicates cause, like His words "inspire," and the estimate is: some of them inspire to others in order to deceive them and so that the hearts may incline. It is also said that it is attached to an omitted word that is placed later, that is, *li-taṣghā* ("so that it may incline") ﴿We have appointed for every prophet an enemy﴾. It is also said that the *lām* is the *lām* of command, and this is an error, because if it were the *lām* of command the verb would be jussive.

*Al-iṣghāʾ* means inclining. It is said: *ṣaghawtu aṣghū ṣaghwan*, and *ṣaghaytu uṣghī*. It is also said: *ṣaghaytu* with a kasra. It is said: *aṣghaytu al-ināʾ*, when I tilt the vessel so that what is in it gathers. Its original meaning is inclining toward a thing for some purpose. It is said: *ṣaghat al-nujūm* when the stars inclined toward setting, and *aṣghat al-nāqah* when the she-camel bent her head. From this is the verse of Dhū al-Rumma:

"She inclines when he tightens her with the saddle-bands, leaning, until, when he has settled in her stirrup and held firm."

The pronoun in "to it" refers to the ornamented speech, or to what was mentioned earlier of the ornamented speech and other things. That is, some of them inspired to others the ornamented speech in order to deceive them, ﴿and that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it﴾ among the disbelievers, ﴿and that they may be pleased with it﴾ for themselves after listening to it, ﴿and that they may commit what they are committing﴾ of sins. *Al-iqtirāf* means earning. It is said: "He went out to earn (*li-yaqtarifa*) for his family," that is, to earn for them. *Qāraffa fulānun hādhā al-amr* means he engaged in it. *Qaraffahu* means he accused him of doubt. *Iqtaraffa* means he lied. Its original meaning is cutting off a piece from a thing.

Abū al-Shaykh reported, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: ﴿And they swore by God with the utmost of their oaths﴾ was revealed concerning Quraysh, and ﴿And what will make you realize﴾ (p-443), O Muslims, ﴿that when they come they will not believe﴾.

Ibn Jarīr reported, from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) spoke with Quraysh, and they said: O Muhammad, you inform us that Mūsā had a staff with which he struck the stone, and that ʿĪsā used to revive the dead, and that Thamūd had a she-camel. So bring us signs so that we may believe you. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: What do you like that I bring to you? They said: Make Ṣafā gold for us. He said: If I do so, will you believe me? They said: Yes, by God, if you do so we will all follow you. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood up and began to supplicate, and Jibrīl came to him and said: If you wish, it will become gold, but if they do not believe at that point We will surely punish them. And if you wish, leave them until their repentant ones repent. He said: Rather, let their repentant ones repent. So God revealed: ﴿And they swore by God with the utmost of their oaths﴾ until His words ﴿they are ignorant﴾."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported, from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His words: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sights﴾, he said: When the polytheists denied what God had sent down, their hearts did not remain firm upon anything, and they were turned back from every matter.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir reported, from him, concerning ﴿And We gathered against them every thing, qubulan﴾, he said: face to face (*muʿāyanatan*). ﴿They would not believe﴾, that is, the people of wretchedness, ﴿except that God wills﴾, that is, the people of felicity, and those whom it had preceded in His knowledge that they would enter into faith.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Abū al-Shaykh reported, from Qatādah, concerning ﴿And We gathered against them every thing, qubulan﴾, that is, they saw that matter face to face.

Abū al-Shaykh reported, from Mujāhid, who said: "In groups, *qabīlan*."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported, from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His words: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy, devils of mankind and jinn﴾, he said: The jinn have devils who lead them astray, like the devils of mankind who lead them astray. The devil of mankind and the devil of the jinn meet, and this one says to that one: "Lead him astray with such-and-such, and I will lead him astray with such-and-such." So this is ﴿some of them inspire to others ornamented speech as deception﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbās also said: The jinn are the *jānn*, and they are not devils. The devils are the offspring of Iblīs, and they do not die except together with Iblīs, while the jinn die. Among them there are believers and among them there are disbelievers.

Abū al-Shaykh reported, from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: The soothsayers (*kahanah*) are the devils of mankind.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported, from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His words: ﴿some of them inspire to others﴾, he said: The devils of the jinn inspire to the devils of mankind, for God says: ﴿And indeed the devils inspire to their allies﴾ [al-Anʿām: 121].

ʿAbd al-Razzāq and Ibn al-Mundhir reported, from Qatādah, concerning the verse, he said: Among mankind there are devils, and among the jinn there are devils, some of them inspire to others.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verse 109–113 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿zukhrufa al-qawl﴾ (embellished speech), that he said: some of them beautify speech for others so that they may follow them in their deviation.

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani related from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Abu Dharr, seek refuge in Allah from the evil of the devils of the jinn and mankind." He said: "O Prophet of Allah, do mankind have devils?" He said: "Yes, ﴿the devils of mankind and jinn, who inspire one another with embellished speech as deception﴾."

Ahmad, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related from Abu Dharr, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), a similar report.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿wa-li-tasgha﴾ (and that it may incline), meaning: that it may incline.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from him: ﴿wa-li-tasgha﴾ means it turns aside; ﴿wa-liyaqtarifu﴾ means they may earn.

They believed that God is the Greatest God, which is why they swore by Him. *Jahd* is in the accusative as a *maṣdar* (verbal noun, *maṣdar*) and, with a fatha on the *jīm*, means hardship, while with a ḍamma it means capacity. It is also said that it is attached to an omitted word that is placed later, that is, *li-taṣghā* ("so that it may incline") ﴿We have appointed for every prophet an enemy﴾. It is also said that the *lām* is the *lām* of command, and this is an error, because if it were the *lām* of command the verb would be jussive.

*Al-iṣghāʾ* means inclining. It is said: *ṣaghawtu aṣghū ṣaghwan*, and *ṣaghaytu uṣghī*. It is also said: *ṣaghaytu* with a kasra. It is said: *aṣghaytu al-ināʾ*, when I tilt the vessel so that what is in it gathers. Its original meaning is inclining toward a thing for some purpose. It is said: *ṣaghat al-nujūm* when the stars inclined toward setting, and *aṣghat al-nāqah* when the she-camel bent her head. From this is the verse of Dhū al-Rumma:

"She inclines when he tightens her with the saddle-bands, leaning, until, when he has settled in her stirrup and held firm."

The pronoun in "to it" refers to the ornamented speech, or to what was mentioned earlier of the ornamented speech and other things. That is, some of them inspired to others the ornamented speech in order to deceive them, ﴿and that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it﴾ among the disbelievers, ﴿and that they may be pleased with it﴾ for themselves after listening to it, ﴿and that they may commit what they are committing﴾ of sins. *Al-iqtirāf* means earning. It is said: "He went out to earn (*li-yaqtarifa*) for his family," that is, to earn for them. *Qāraffa fulānun hādhā al-amr* means he engaged in it. *Qaraffahu* means he accused him of doubt. *Iqtaraffa* means he lied. Its original meaning is cutting off a piece from a thing.

Abū al-Shaykh reported, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: ﴿And they swore by God with the utmost of their oaths﴾ was revealed concerning Quraysh, and ﴿And what will make you realize﴾ (p-443), O Muslims, ﴿that when they come they will not believe﴾.

Ibn Jarīr reported, from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) spoke with Quraysh, and they said: O Muhammad, you inform us that Mūsā had a staff with which he struck the stone, and that ʿĪsā used to revive the dead, and that Thamūd had a she-camel. So bring us signs so that we may believe you. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: What do you like that I bring to you? They said: Make Ṣafā gold for us. He said: If I do so, will you believe me? They said: Yes, by God, if you do so we will all follow you. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood up and began to supplicate, and Jibrīl came to him and said: If you wish, it will become gold, but if they do not believe at that point We will surely punish them. And if you wish, leave them until their repentant ones repent. He said: Rather, let their repentant ones repent. So God revealed: ﴿And they swore by God with the utmost of their oaths﴾ until His words ﴿they are ignorant﴾."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported, from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His words: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sights﴾, he said: When the polytheists denied what God had sent down, their hearts did not remain firm upon anything, and they were turned back from every matter.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir reported, from him, concerning ﴿And We gathered against them every thing, qubulan﴾, he said: face to face (*muʿāyanatan*). ﴿They would not believe﴾, that is, the people of wretchedness, ﴿except that God wills﴾, that is, the people of felicity, and those whom it had preceded in His knowledge that they would enter into faith.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Abū al-Shaykh reported, from Qatādah, concerning ﴿And We gathered against them every thing, qubulan﴾, that is, they saw that matter face to face.

Abū al-Shaykh reported, from Mujāhid, who said: "In groups, *qabīlan*."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported, from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His words: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy, devils of mankind and jinn﴾, he said: The jinn have devils who lead them astray, like the devils of mankind who lead them astray. The devil of mankind and the devil of the jinn meet, and this one says to that one: "Lead him astray with such-and-such, and I will lead him astray with such-and-such." So this is ﴿some of them inspire to others ornamented speech as deception﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbās also said: The jinn are the *jānn*, and they are not devils. The devils are the offspring of Iblīs, and they do not die except together with Iblīs, while the jinn die. Among them there are believers and among them there are disbelievers.

Abū al-Shaykh reported, from Ibn Masʿūd, who said: The soothsayers (*kahanah*) are the devils of mankind.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported, from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His words: ﴿some of them inspire to others﴾, he said: The devils of the jinn inspire to the devils of mankind, for God says: ﴿And indeed the devils inspire to their allies﴾ [al-Anʿām: 121].

ʿAbd al-Razzāq and Ibn al-Mundhir reported, from Qatādah, concerning the verse, he said: Among mankind there are devils, and among the jinn there are devils, some of them inspire to others.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verse 109–113 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿zukhrufa al-qawl﴾ (embellished speech), that he said: some of them beautify speech for others so that they may follow them in their deviation.

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani related from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Abu Dharr, seek refuge in Allah from the evil of the devils of the jinn and mankind." He said: "O Prophet of Allah, do mankind have devils?" He said: "Yes, ﴿the devils of mankind and jinn, who inspire one another with embellished speech as deception﴾."

Ahmad, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related from Abu Dharr, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), a similar report.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿wa-li-tasgha﴾ (and that it may incline), meaning: that it may incline.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from him: ﴿wa-li-tasgha﴾ means it turns aside; ﴿wa-liyaqtarifu﴾ means they may earn.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 114–117:**

His saying: ﴿Shall I seek a judge other than Allah?﴾ The interrogative particle *al-istifham* (interrogation) is for denial (*inkar*), and the *fa'* is for coordination (*'atf*) upon an implied verb. The speech is on the intention of saying, and the estimate is: "Say to them, O Muhammad: How could I go astray and seek other than Allah as a judge?" *Ghayra* (غَيْرَ) is the object of *abtaghi* (أبْتَغِي), placed before it, and *hakaman* (حَكَمًا) is the second object, or vice versa.

It is permissible for *hakaman* (حَكَمًا) to be in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), and *al-hakam* (the judge) is more emphatic than *al-hakim* (the one who judges), as has been established regarding this kind of derived attribute.

Allah the Exalted commanded him to deny to them what they asked of him, namely that he should make between himself and them a judge concerning what they differed about. Indeed Allah is the just Judge between him and them. The clause ﴿And He it is who has sent down to you the Book, detailed﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state, meaning: how could I seek a judge other than Allah, when He is the One who has sent down to you the Qur'an, detailed, clarified, clear, comprehensive of every matter in detail? Then He informed His Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, that the People of the Book, although they manifest denial and obstinacy, they know that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah, by what the Books of Allah that were sent down, such as the Torah and the Gospel, indicate about it: that he is the Messenger of Allah and that he is the Seal of the Prophets. *Bil-haqq* (بِالحَقِّ, "with the truth") is linked to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial state: meaning, clothed with the truth about which there is no doubt and no ambiguity. Then He forbade him to be among the doubters regarding the fact that the People of the Book know that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah with the truth. Or He forbade him from doubt in general, and this would be an indirect address to his community, that none of them should doubt. Or the address is to everyone who is fit for it, meaning: let none of the people be among the doubters. This does not conflict with the fact that the address is to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, since his address is an address to his community.

His saying: (And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice.)

The people of Kufa read *kalimatun* (كَلِمَةً) in the singular, and the rest read it in the plural. *Al-kalimat* (الكَلِماتُ) means the expressions, or what relates to them of promise and threat.

The meaning: Allah has fulfilled His promise and His threat, so the truth became manifest and falsehood was effaced. It was also said: what is meant by *al-kalimah* or *al-kalimat* is the Qur'an. *Sidqan wa 'adlan* (صِدْقًا وعَدْلًا) are in the accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*) or as a circumstantial state, or as the attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: the perfection of truthfulness and justice. ﴿None can alter His words﴾: there is no failure in them and no changer of what He has decreed. The negated clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state, or it is an independent resumptive clause. ﴿And He is the Hearing﴾ of everything heard, ﴿the Knowing﴾ of everything known.

His saying: 116. ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you from the way of Allah.﴾ Allah the Exalted informed him that if he sought to obey most of those on earth, they would mislead him, because the truth is only in the hand of the few. Among them is the group that will remain upon the truth, and the opposition of those who oppose them will not harm them, as this was established from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. It was also said: what is meant by "the most" is the disbelievers. It was also said: (p-٤٤٤) what is meant by "the earth" is Mecca, meaning: most of the people of Mecca. Then the Exalted explained this by His saying: ﴿They follow not but assumption﴾, meaning they follow only the assumption that has no basis, which is their assumption that what they worship deserves worship and that it brings them near to Allah. ﴿And they are not but guessing﴾, meaning: they are only conjecturing and estimating. The root of *al-kharṣ* (الخَرْصُ, "guessing") is cutting off; from it comes *kharasa al-nakhl yakhursu* (خَرَصَ النَّخْلَ يَخْرُصُ), when one estimates the palm trees in order to take the zakat from them. So the estimator (*al-khariṣ*) asserts with certainty what it is not permissible to assert with certainty, since there is no certainty in it. If this is the state of most of those on earth, then true knowledge is with Allah. So follow what He has commanded you and leave aside the obedience of others. He is the Knower of who strays from His way and who is guided to it.

Some scholars of knowledge said: *a'lam* (أعْلَمُ) in both places has the meaning of *ya'lamu* (يَعْلَمُ, "knows"). He said: from it is the saying of Hatim al-Ta'i:

*So Tayy allied with a pact apart from us, and Allah knows we were not servants to them.*

The correct way of this interpretation is that the elative form (*af'al al-tafdil*) does not govern an apparent noun, so *man* (مَن) is in the accusative by the verb which the elative form was made to stand in place of. It was also said: the elative form is on its usual pattern and the accusative is by an omitted verb. It was also said: it is governed by the elative form, meaning: "Your Lord knows best who strays from His way." It was also said: it is in the accusative position by removal of the preposition, meaning: "with whom one strays," as said by some of the Basran grammarians. It was also said: it is in the genitive position by the elative form being put in construct with it.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah, concerning His saying ﴿detailed﴾, that he said: "clarified."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Qatadah, concerning His saying ﴿in truth and justice﴾, that he said: "Truthful in what He promised, and just in what He judged."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Abu Nasr al-Sijzi in *al-Ibanah* transmitted from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, concerning His saying ﴿None can alter His words﴾, that he said: "There is no alteration of anything He has said in this world and the Hereafter, by His saying: ﴿The word is not changed with Me﴾ [Qaf: 29]."

Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn al-Najjar transmitted from Anas, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, concerning His saying ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾, that he said: "There is no god but Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu al-Yaman Amir ibn Abd Allah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, entered the Sacred Mosque on the day of the Conquest of Mecca, and with him was a staff (*mikhsarah*). Every people had an idol that they worshipped. So he began to come to them, idol after idol, and he would strike the chest of the idol with the staff, then he would overturn it. Whenever he struck an idol, he would follow it with a blow of the bow, until they broke it and cast it outside the mosque, while the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, was saying: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice. None can alter His words. And He is the Hearing, the Knowing.﴾"

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 114–117:**

His saying: ﴿Shall I seek a judge other than Allah?﴾ The interrogative particle *al-istifham* (interrogation) is for denial (*inkar*), and the *fa'* is for coordination (*'atf*) upon an implied verb. The speech is on the intention of saying, and the estimate is: "Say to them, O Muhammad: How could I go astray and seek other than Allah as a judge?" *Ghayra* (غَيْرَ) is the object of *abtaghi* (أبْتَغِي), placed before it, and *hakaman* (حَكَمًا) is the second object, or vice versa.

It is permissible for *hakaman* (حَكَمًا) to be in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), and *al-hakam* (the judge) is more emphatic than *al-hakim* (the one who judges), as has been established regarding this kind of derived attribute.

Allah the Exalted commanded him to deny to them what they asked of him, namely that he should make between himself and them a judge concerning what they differed about. Indeed Allah is the just Judge between him and them. The clause ﴿And He it is who has sent down to you the Book, detailed﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state, meaning: how could I seek a judge other than Allah, when He is the One who has sent down to you the Qur'an, detailed, clarified, clear, comprehensive of every matter in detail? Then He informed His Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, that the People of the Book, although they manifest denial and obstinacy, they know that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah, by what the Books of Allah that were sent down, such as the Torah and the Gospel, indicate about it: that he is the Messenger of Allah and that he is the Seal of the Prophets. *Bil-haqq* (بِالحَقِّ, "with the truth") is linked to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial state: meaning, clothed with the truth about which there is no doubt and no ambiguity. Then He forbade him to be among the doubters regarding the fact that the People of the Book know that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah with the truth. Or He forbade him from doubt in general, and this would be an indirect address to his community, that none of them should doubt. Or the address is to everyone who is fit for it, meaning: let none of the people be among the doubters. This does not conflict with the fact that the address is to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, since his address is an address to his community.

His saying: (And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice.)

The people of Kufa read *kalimatun* (كَلِمَةً) in the singular, and the rest read it in the plural. *Al-kalimat* (الكَلِماتُ) means the expressions, or what relates to them of promise and threat.

The meaning: Allah has fulfilled His promise and His threat, so the truth became manifest and falsehood was effaced. It was also said: what is meant by *al-kalimah* or *al-kalimat* is the Qur'an. *Sidqan wa 'adlan* (صِدْقًا وعَدْلًا) are in the accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*) or as a circumstantial state, or as the attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: the perfection of truthfulness and justice. ﴿None can alter His words﴾: there is no failure in them and no changer of what He has decreed. The negated clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state, or it is an independent resumptive clause. ﴿And He is the Hearing﴾ of everything heard, ﴿the Knowing﴾ of everything known.

His saying: 116. ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you from the way of Allah.﴾ Allah the Exalted informed him that if he sought to obey most of those on earth, they would mislead him, because the truth is only in the hand of the few. Among them is the group that will remain upon the truth, and the opposition of those who oppose them will not harm them, as this was established from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. It was also said: what is meant by "the most" is the disbelievers. It was also said: (p-٤٤٤) what is meant by "the earth" is Mecca, meaning: most of the people of Mecca. Then the Exalted explained this by His saying: ﴿They follow not but assumption﴾, meaning they follow only the assumption that has no basis, which is their assumption that what they worship deserves worship and that it brings them near to Allah. ﴿And they are not but guessing﴾, meaning: they are only conjecturing and estimating. The root of *al-kharṣ* (الخَرْصُ, "guessing") is cutting off; from it comes *kharasa al-nakhl yakhursu* (خَرَصَ النَّخْلَ يَخْرُصُ), when one estimates the palm trees in order to take the zakat from them. So the estimator (*al-khariṣ*) asserts with certainty what it is not permissible to assert with certainty, since there is no certainty in it. If this is the state of most of those on earth, then true knowledge is with Allah. So follow what He has commanded you and leave aside the obedience of others. He is the Knower of who strays from His way and who is guided to it.

Some scholars of knowledge said: *a'lam* (أعْلَمُ) in both places has the meaning of *ya'lamu* (يَعْلَمُ, "knows"). He said: from it is the saying of Hatim al-Ta'i:

*So Tayy allied with a pact apart from us, and Allah knows we were not servants to them.*

The correct way of this interpretation is that the elative form (*af'al al-tafdil*) does not govern an apparent noun, so *man* (مَن) is in the accusative by the verb which the elative form was made to stand in place of. It was also said: the elative form is on its usual pattern and the accusative is by an omitted verb. It was also said: it is governed by the elative form, meaning: "Your Lord knows best who strays from His way." It was also said: it is in the accusative position by removal of the preposition, meaning: "with whom one strays," as said by some of the Basran grammarians. It was also said: it is in the genitive position by the elative form being put in construct with it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 118–120:

When the mention of what the disbelievers did with the cattle, from those jahiliyyah customs (sunan jahiliyyah), had preceded, God commanded the Muslims to eat from what the name of God has been mentioned over. It is said that it was revealed concerning a particular occasion, and it will come; but the consideration is with the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion. So whatever the slaughterer mentions God's name over is lawful, if it is among what God has permitted to eat.

And ʿAṭāʾ said: In this verse there is a command to mention God's name over drink, over slaughter, and over every food. The condition in ﴿if you are believers in His signs﴾ is for stirring up and inciting: that is, [believers] in His rulings, from among the commands and prohibitions, of which is the command to eat from what the name of God has been mentioned over.

The interrogation in ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not eat from what the name of God has been mentioned over﴾ is for denunciation (al-inkar): that is, what prevents you from eating what you have named God over, after God has permitted that to you? And the situation is that ﴿He has detailed for you what He has forbidden to you﴾, that is, He has made clear to you a detailed explanation that removes doubt and dispels suspicion, by His saying: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden...﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Anʿām: 145]. Then He made an exception, saying: ﴿except what you are compelled to﴾, that is, from all that He has forbidden to you, for necessity makes the forbidden lawful. Its verification has already been discussed in al-Baqarah.

Nāfiʿ and Yaʿqūb read ﴿He has detailed (faṣṣala) for you what He has forbidden to you﴾ with both verbs vowelled with fatḥah, on the form of the active voice, the subject being God, glorified is He.

Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Ibn Kathīr read both with ḍammah, on the form of the passive voice.

ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī read faṣala with the lightening (takhfīf), meaning: he made clear and manifested.

His saying: ﴿And indeed many lead astray by their desires without knowledge﴾ refers to the disbelievers who used to forbid the baḥīrah, the sāʾibah and the like. By these acts, founded on ignorance, they led people astray, so [people] followed them, and did not know that this was ignorance and error that goes back to no part of knowledge.

120 - ﴿And leave the outward and the inward of sin. Indeed those who earn sin will be recompensed for what they used to commit﴾. Then God commanded them to leave the outward and the inward of sin.

The outward is what appears, like the acts of the limbs; the inward is what does not appear, like the acts of the heart. It is said: what you make public and what you keep secret. It is also said: the open fornication and the concealed fornication.

He attributed the outward and the inward to sin because it is caused by them. Then He threatened those who earn sin with recompense, because of their fabricating against God, glorified is He.

Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī (who graded it ḥasan), al-Bazzār, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Abū al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "The Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'We eat what we kill, and we do not eat what God kills.' So God revealed: ﴿So eat from what the name of God has been mentioned over﴾ to His saying: ﴿And if you obey them, you are indeed polytheists﴾."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr regarding ﴿So eat from what the name of God has been mentioned over﴾: it is lawful; ﴿if you are believers in His signs﴾, meaning the Qur'an, believers, he said: those who affirm. ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not eat from what the name of God has been mentioned over﴾, meaning the slaughtered animals. ﴿And He has detailed for you what He has forbidden to you﴾, meaning what has been forbidden to you of carrion. ﴿And indeed many﴾, meaning of the polytheists of the Arabs, ﴿lead astray by their desires without knowledge﴾, meaning concerning the matter of slaughtered animals.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh transmitted from Qatādah, regarding His saying ﴿except what you are compelled to﴾: that is, of carrion, blood and pork.

Ibn Abī Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding ﴿And leave the outward of sin﴾, he said: it is marrying mothers and daughters; ﴿and its inward﴾, he said: it is (p-445) fornication.

Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, who said: The outward of it is ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married of women﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 22] and ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 23], to the end of the verse; and the inward is fornication.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Qatādah regarding the verse, he said: its openness and its secrecy.
