Al-ḥijr, with a kasra on its first letter and a sukūn on its second, is the reading of the majority (al-Jumhūr).

Abān ibn ʿUthmān read ḥujr with a ḍammah on the ḥāʾ and the jīm. Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah read it with a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ and a sukūn on the jīm. Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn al-Zubayr read ḥaraj, with the rāʾ placed before the jīm, and it is likewise in the codex of Ubayy. It derives from ḥaraj (constriction, narrowness), as in the saying: fulān yataḥarraj, meaning he narrows down on himself, refraining from entering into what is doubtful to him.

Al-ḥijr, according to the variant readings, is a masdar used in the sense of the passive participle: that is, maḥjūr (forbidden, prohibited). Its root meaning is prevention. So the meaning of the verse is: these are livestock and tilth that are forbidden (mamnūʿah), meaning that they are for their idols; none may eat from them except those whom they wish, according to their own claim, and they are the attendants of the idols.

The second category is their saying: ﴿and livestock whose backs have been forbidden﴾, which are the baḥīrah, the sāʾibah, and the ḥām. It has been said that this second category is also among what they designated for their gods.

The second category (in another sense) is livestock over which they do not mention the name of God; these are what they slaughter for their gods, for they slaughter them in the name of their idols, not in the name of God.

It has been said that the intended meaning is that they do not perform the pilgrimage (ḥajj) upon them, as fabrication against God, that is, for the purpose of fabricating against Him. ﴿He will repay them for what they used to fabricate﴾, that is, for their fabrication, or for that which they fabricate. It is permissible that ʿiftirāʾan (fabrication) be in the accusative as a masdar: that is, they fabricated a fabrication; or as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative): that is, fabricating. Its being in the accusative as a reason or cause (ʿillah) is more apparent.

Then God, glorified is He, explained another type of their ignorance, saying: ﴿And they say: what is in the bellies of these livestock﴾, meaning the baḥāʾir and the sawāʾib, of the fetuses, ﴿is exclusively for our males﴾, that is, lawful for them, ﴿and forbidden to our wives﴾, that is, to the category of wives, which are women, so that daughters, sisters, and the like are included in that. It has been said that it is the milk, which they made lawful for males and forbidden to females. The hāʾ in khāliṣah (exclusively) is for emphasis on exclusivity, like ʿallāmah and nassābah; this was said by al-Kisāʾī and al-Akhfash.

Al-Farrāʾ said: its feminine form is due to the feminine of al-anʿām (livestock).

This was refuted on the grounds that what is in the bellies of the livestock is not livestock. This refutation was countered: what is in the bellies of livestock is livestock, namely the fetuses, and mā is an expression referring to them. Thus the feminine of khāliṣah is in consideration of the meaning of mā, and the masculine of muḥarram is in consideration of its wording.

Al-Aʿmash read khāliṣ (masculine). Al-Kisāʾī said: the meaning of khāliṣ and khāliṣah is one, except that the hāʾ is for emphasis, as mentioned earlier from him.

Qatādah read khāliṣatan in the accusative, as a ḥāl from the pronoun in the complement of the adverbial phrase that is the ṣilah of mā, with the predicate of the subject omitted, like your saying: alladhī fi al-dār qāʾiman Zaydun (the one who is in the house, standing, is Zayd). This is the view of the Basrans.

Al-Farrāʾ said: it is in the accusative as a qaṭʿ (detachment, a separate predication).

Ibn ʿAbbās read khāliṣatin, with khāliṣ annexed to the pronoun, as a substitute (badal) for mā.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr read khāliṣan.

﴿And if it is dead﴾ has been read with the yāʾ and the tāʾ (both masculine and feminine forms): that is, if what is in the bellies of the livestock is dead, ﴿then they are partners in it﴾, that is, in what is in the bellies, the males and females eat from it together. ﴿He will repay them for their description﴾, that is, for their describing, and it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, and the meaning: He will repay them for their describing falsehood against God. It has been said the meaning is: He will repay them the recompense of their description.

Then God, glorified is He, explained another type of their ignorance, saying: ﴿Those who killed their children out of foolishness have certainly lost﴾, that is, their daughters, by burying them alive, which they used to do out of foolishness, that is, due to folly, which is levity and lightness, not for any rational or legal proof, whatever that may have been from them, ﴿without knowledge﴾ by which they could be guided.

His saying: ﴿And they forbade what God had provided them﴾ of the livestock which they named baḥīrah and sāʾibah, ﴿as fabrication against God﴾, that is, for the purpose of fabricating against Him, or they fabricated a fabrication against Him. ﴿They have certainly gone astray﴾ from the path of rectitude by these actions, ﴿and they were not guided﴾ to the truth, nor were they among those prepared for it.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: ﴿And they say: these are livestock and tilth, ḥijr﴾, he said: al-ḥijr is what they forbade of the waṣīlah, and the forbidding of what they forbade.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim transmitted from Mujāhid, regarding His saying: ﴿And they say: these are livestock and tilth, ḥijr﴾, he said: what they set aside for God and for their associates.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd transmitted from Qatādah, regarding ﴿and tilth, ḥijr﴾, he said: forbidden.

Ibn Abi Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Suddī, regarding the verse, he said: they say it is forbidden for the son to eat anything. ﴿And livestock whose backs have been forbidden﴾, he said: the baḥīrah, the sāʾibah, and the ḥāmī. ﴿And livestock over which they do not mention the name of God﴾ when they slaughter them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh transmitted from Abū Wāʾil regarding His saying: ﴿And livestock over which they do not mention the name of God﴾, he said: it was not made to be performed pilgrimage upon, and it is the baḥīrah.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding ﴿And they say: what is in the bellies of these livestock﴾ and the rest of the verse, he said: it is the milk.

These (compilers), except Ibn Jarīr, transmitted from Mujāhid regarding the verse, he said: the sāʾibah and the baḥīrah are forbidden to our wives: he said, the women. ﴿He will repay them for their description﴾, he said: their saying falsehood about that.

Abū al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding the verse, he said: when a ewe gave birth to a male, they slaughtered it, and it was for the men without the women; and if it was a female, they left it and did not slaughter it; and if it was dead, they were partners in it.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Bukhārī, Abū al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: If it pleases you to know the ignorance of the Arabs, then recite what is beyond the hundred and thirtieth verse of Surat al-Anʿām: ﴿Those who killed their children have certainly lost﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and they were not guided﴾.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abū al-Shaykh transmitted from ʿIkrimah regarding the verse, he said: it was revealed concerning those of Muḍar and Rabīʿah who used to bury their daughters alive.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh transmitted from Qatādah, regarding the verse, he said: this was the practice of the people of the Jāhiliyyah, where one of them would kill his daughter for fear of captivity and poverty, while feeding his dog. ﴿And they forbade what God had provided them﴾, he said: they made it baḥīrah, sāʾibah, waṣīlah, and ḥāmī, as arbitrary decree from Satan concerning their wealth.

This is an explanation of another type of their ignorance and misguidance.

So the meaning of the verse is: these are livestock and tilth that are forbidden (mamnūʿah), meaning that they are for their idols; none may eat from them except those whom they wish, according to their own claim, and they are the attendants of the idols.

The second category is their saying: ﴿and livestock whose backs have been forbidden﴾, which are the baḥīrah, the sāʾibah, and the ḥām. It has been said that this second category is also among what they designated for their gods.

The second category (in another sense) is livestock over which they do not mention the name of God; these are what they slaughter for their gods, for they slaughter them in the name of their idols, not in the name of God.

It has been said that the intended meaning is that they do not perform the pilgrimage (ḥajj) upon them, as fabrication against God, that is, for the purpose of fabricating against Him. ﴿He will repay them for what they used to fabricate﴾, that is, for their fabrication, or for that which they fabricate. It is permissible that ʿiftirāʾan (fabrication) be in the accusative as a masdar: that is, they fabricated a fabrication; or as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative): that is, fabricating. Its being in the accusative as a reason or cause (ʿillah) is more apparent.

Then God, glorified is He, explained another type of their ignorance, saying: ﴿And they say: what is in the bellies of these livestock﴾, meaning the baḥāʾir and the sawāʾib, of the fetuses, ﴿is exclusively for our males﴾, that is, lawful for them, ﴿and forbidden to our wives﴾, that is, to the category of wives, which are women, so that daughters, sisters, and the like are included in that. It has been said that it is the milk, which they made lawful for males and forbidden to females. The hāʾ in khāliṣah (exclusively) is for emphasis on exclusivity, like ʿallāmah and nassābah; this was said by al-Kisāʾī and al-Akhfash.

Al-Farrāʾ said: its feminine form is due to the feminine of al-anʿām (livestock).

This was refuted on the grounds that what is in the bellies of the livestock is not livestock. This refutation was countered: what is in the bellies of livestock is livestock, namely the fetuses, and mā is an expression referring to them. Thus the feminine of khāliṣah is in consideration of the meaning of mā, and the masculine of muḥarram is in consideration of its wording.

Al-Aʿmash read khāliṣ (masculine). Al-Kisāʾī said: the meaning of khāliṣ and khāliṣah is one, except that the hāʾ is for emphasis, as mentioned earlier from him.

Qatādah read khāliṣatan in the accusative, as a ḥāl from the pronoun in the complement of the adverbial phrase that is the ṣilah of mā, with the predicate of the subject omitted, like your saying: alladhī fi al-dār qāʾiman Zaydun (the one who is in the house, standing, is Zayd). This is the view of the Basrans.

Al-Farrāʾ said: it is in the accusative as a qaṭʿ (detachment, a separate predication).

Ibn ʿAbbās read khāliṣatin, with khāliṣ annexed to the pronoun, as a substitute (badal) for mā.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr read khāliṣan.

﴿And if it is dead﴾ has been read with the yāʾ and the tāʾ (both masculine and feminine forms): that is, if what is in the bellies of the livestock is dead, ﴿then they are partners in it﴾, that is, in what is in the bellies, the males and females eat from it together. ﴿He will repay them for their description﴾, that is, for their describing, and it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, and the meaning: He will repay them for their describing falsehood against God. It has been said the meaning is: He will repay them the recompense of their description.

Then God, glorified is He, explained another type of their ignorance, saying: ﴿Those who killed their children out of foolishness have certainly lost﴾, that is, their daughters, by burying them alive, which they used to do out of foolishness, that is, due to folly, which is levity and lightness, not for any rational or legal proof, whatever that may have been from them, ﴿without knowledge﴾ by which they could be guided.

His saying: ﴿And they forbade what God had provided them﴾ of the livestock which they named baḥīrah and sāʾibah, ﴿as fabrication against God﴾, that is, for the purpose of fabricating against Him, or they fabricated a fabrication against Him. ﴿They have certainly gone astray﴾ from the path of rectitude by these actions, ﴿and they were not guided﴾ to the truth, nor were they among those prepared for it.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: ﴿And they say: these are livestock and tilth, ḥijr﴾, he said: al-ḥijr is what they forbade of the waṣīlah, and the forbidding of what they forbade.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim transmitted from Mujāhid, regarding His saying: ﴿And they say: these are livestock and tilth, ḥijr﴾, he said: what they set aside for God and for their associates.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd transmitted from Qatādah, regarding ﴿and tilth, ḥijr﴾, he said: forbidden.

Ibn Abi Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Suddī, regarding the verse, he said: they say it is forbidden for the son to eat anything. ﴿And livestock whose backs have been forbidden﴾, he said: the baḥīrah, the sāʾibah, and the ḥāmī. ﴿And livestock over which they do not mention the name of God﴾ when they slaughter them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh transmitted from Abū Wāʾil regarding His saying: ﴿And livestock over which they do not mention the name of God﴾, he said: it was not made to be performed pilgrimage upon, and it is the baḥīrah.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding ﴿And they say: what is in the bellies of these livestock﴾ and the rest of the verse, he said: it is the milk.

These (compilers), except Ibn Jarīr, transmitted from Mujāhid regarding the verse, he said: the sāʾibah and the baḥīrah are forbidden to our wives: he said, the women. ﴿He will repay them for their description﴾, he said: their saying falsehood about that.

Abū al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding the verse, he said: when a ewe gave birth to a male, they slaughtered it, and it was for the men without the women; and if it was a female, they left it and did not slaughter it; and if it was dead, they were partners in it.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Bukhārī, Abū al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: If it pleases you to know the ignorance of the Arabs, then recite what is beyond the hundred and thirtieth verse of Surat al-Anʿām: ﴿Those who killed their children have certainly lost﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and they were not guided﴾.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abū al-Shaykh transmitted from ʿIkrimah regarding the verse, he said: it was revealed concerning those of Muḍar and Rabīʿah who used to bury their daughters alive.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh transmitted from Qatādah, regarding the verse, he said: this was the practice of the people of the Jāhiliyyah, where one of them would kill his daughter for fear of captivity and poverty, while feeding his dog. ﴿And they forbade what God had provided them﴾, he said: they made it baḥīrah, sāʾibah, waṣīlah, and ḥāmī, as arbitrary decree from Satan concerning their wealth.

This is an explanation of another type of their ignorance and misguidance.

Al-ḥijr, with a kasra on its first letter and a sukūn on its second, is the reading of the majority (al-Jumhūr).

This passage is a reminder of God's wondrous power and magnificent creation. "Anshaa" means He brought into being, and "al-jannat" means gardens. "Ma'rushat" means those raised up on trellises, and "ghayra ma'rushat" means those not raised on them. It was also said that "ma'rushat" refers to what spreads over the surface of the earth, such as the vine, crops and melons, while "ghayr al-ma'rushat" refers to what stands on a trunk, such as the date palm and the other trees. It was also said that "ma'rushat" is what people have planted and trellised, and "ghayr al-ma'rushat" is what grows in the wilds and mountains.

His words, ﴿wal-nakhla wal-zar'a﴾ ("and the date palm and the crops"), are coordinated with "jannat." He singled them out for mention, although they are included among the gardens, because of the excellence they possess. ﴿Mukhtalifan ukuluh﴾ means "its produce being diverse," that is, in its state of being diverse in taste, quality and inferiority.

Al-Zajjaj said: This is a difficult question in grammar, namely the accusative status of "mukhtalifan" as a circumstantial clause (hal), since one would say: He has brought them into being, yet their produce has not varied. The answer is that God, glory be to Him, brought them into being while ordaining diversity in them. Sibawayh explained this with his saying: "I passed by a man with a falcon, hunting with it tomorrow," meaning: intending to hunt with it tomorrow, just as you say: "You will certainly enter the house eating and drinking," meaning: intending that. This is the well-known "intended circumstance" (al-hal al-muqaddara) that the grammarians have recorded in their books of grammar.

He said ﴿mukhtalifan ukuluh﴾ and did not say "ukuluhuma" (their produce, in dual), being content with mentioning it in reference to one of them, as in His words ﴿wa-idha ra'aw tijaratan aw lahwan infaddu ilayha﴾ (62:11), or the pronoun is like a demonstrative: meaning, "the produce of that."

His words, ﴿wal-zaytun wal-rummana﴾ ("and the olive and the pomegranate"), are coordinated with "jannat." That is, He brought into being the olive and the pomegranate in a state of being similar and dissimilar. The explanation of this has already been given. ﴿Kulu min thamarihi﴾ ("eat of its fruit") means of the fruit of each of them, or of the fruit of that. ﴿Idha athmar﴾ ("when it bears fruit") means when fruit has appeared on it, even if it has not ripened or reached the time of harvest.

His words: ﴿wa-atu haqqahu yawma hasadihi﴾ ("and pay its due on the day of its harvest").

The scholars differed: Is this verse muhkam (definitive, not abrogated), or mansukh (abrogated), or to be understood as recommended (nadb)? Ibn Umar, Ata', Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr held that the verse is muhkam, and that the owner is obliged on the day of harvest to give to the poor who are present a handful (al-qabda) and a bundle (al-dighth) and the like.

Ibn Abbas, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, Tawus, Abu al-Sha'tha', Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Jurayj held that this verse has been abrogated (mansukha) by zakat.

Ibn Jarir chose this view, and it is supported by the fact that this verse is Meccan, while the verse of zakat is Medinan, in the second year after the Hijra. Most of the scholars, both among the early generations (al-salaf) and later ones (al-khalaf), went to this view.

A group of scholars said: The verse is to be understood as recommended, not obligatory.

His words, ﴿wa-la tusrifu﴾ ("and do not be extravagant"), mean in giving charity. The original meaning of "israf" in the language is error, and "israf" in spending means squandering. It was said: It is addressed to the rulers, telling them: Do not take more than your right. It was also said: The meaning is: Do not take a thing without its right and place it where it is not deserved.

His words, ﴿wa-min al-an'am hamulatan wa-farsha﴾ ("and of the livestock, beasts of burden and those for the floor"), are coordinated with "jannat." That is, He brought into being for you, from the livestock, beasts of burden and [what is] for fur. "Hamula" is what is carried upon, and it is specific to camels, so it is "fa'ula" in the sense of "fa'ila." "Farsh" is what is made from wool, fleece and hair as a bedding that people spread out. It was said: "Hamula" means camels, and "farsh" means sheep. It was also said: "Hamula" is every animal carried upon, including camels, cattle, horses, mules and donkeys, and "farsh" is sheep. This holds only if the term "an'am" is allowed to be applied to all of these mentioned items. It was also said: "Hamula" is what is ridden, and "farsh" is what its meat is eaten. ﴿Kulu mimma razaqakum﴾ ("eat of what He has provided you") from these things. ﴿Wa-la tattabi'u khutuwat al-shaytan﴾ ("and do not follow the footsteps of Satan"), as the polytheists did, by forbidding what God has not forbidden and permitting what God has not permitted. ﴿Innahu lakum aduwwun mubin﴾ ("indeed he is to you a clear enemy"): that is, manifestly hostile and openly showing enmity.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words ﴿wa-huwa alladhi ansha'a jannatin ma'rushatin﴾ (6:141), that he said: "Ma'rushat" is what people have trellised, and ﴿ghayra ma'rushat﴾ is what came out in the mountains and the wilderness of fruits.

Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatada, who said: "Ma'rushat" are those trellised with canes and reeds, and "ghayr ma'rushat" he said: those growing freely (al-dahi).

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning "ma'rushat," that he said: It is specifically the vine.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Nahhas, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, that the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His words ﴿wa-atu haqqahu yawma hasadihi﴾, said: "It is what falls from the ear of grain."

Abu Ubayd, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Nahhas, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Ibn Umar, concerning His words ﴿wa-atu haqqahu yawma hasadihi﴾, that he said: "They used to give to whoever was proud of them something other than charity."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi reported from Mujahid concerning the verse, that he said: "When you reap and the needy come to you, throw to them some of the ears of grain."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Maymun ibn Mihran and Yazid al-Asamm, who said: The people of Medina, when they cut the date palms, would bring the cluster and place it in the mosque, and the beggar would come and strike it with a stick, so that some of it would fall off. This is His words, ﴿wa-atu haqqahu yawma hasadihi﴾.

Ahmad and Abu Dawud in his Sunan reported from the hadith of Jabir ibn Abd Allah: "That the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered that from every eleven wasqs of dates there be a cluster hung in the mosque for the poor." Its chain of transmission is good.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Nahhas and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: ﴿wa-atu haqqahu yawma hasadihi﴾ was abrogated (nasakha-ha) by the tithe (al-'ushr) and half the tithe.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud in his book on abrogation (nasikhihi) and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Sudi something similar.

al-Nahhas, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ikrima something similar.

Abu Ubayd, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Dahhak something similar.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Sha'bi, who said: "Indeed in wealth there is a right besides zakat."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Abu al-Aliyah, who said: They did not used to give anything besides zakat. Then they hastened and were extravagant, so God revealed: ﴿wa-la tusrifu innahu la yuhibbu al-musrifin﴾ ("and do not be extravagant; indeed He does not love the extravagant").

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Jurayj, who said: It was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, who harvested a date palm and said: "No one will come to me today except that I will feed him." So he fed until evening and had not a single date left. So God revealed: ﴿wa-la tusrifu innahu la yuhibbu al-musrifin﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid, who said: If you spent the like of Abu Qubays in gold in obedience to God, it would not be extravagance; and if you spent a sa' in disobedience to God, it would be extravagance. Regarding this, the early generations (al-salaf) have lengthy discussions. (p-453)

al-Firyabi, Abu Ubayd, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, reported from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Hamula" is what is carried upon of the camels, and "farsh" are the young camels that do not carry loads.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Hamula" are the mature camels, and "farsh" are the young camels.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from him, who said: "Hamula" is what is carried upon, and "farsh" is what is eaten from it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him also, who said: "Hamula" are camels, horses, mules, donkeys and everything carried upon, and "farsh" is sheep.

Abd ibn Humayd reported from Abu al-Aliyah, who said: "Hamula" are camels and cattle, and "farsh" are sheep and goats.

This passage is a reminder of God's wondrous power and magnificent creation. "Anshaa" means He brought into being, and "al-jannat" means gardens. "Ma'rushat" means those raised up on trellises, and "ghayra ma'rushat" means those not raised on them. It was also said that "ma'rushat" refers to what spreads over the surface of the earth, such as the vine, crops and melons, while "ghayr al-ma'rushat" refers to what stands on a trunk, such as the date palm and the other trees. It was also said that "ma'rushat" is what people have planted and trellised, and "ghayr al-ma'rushat" is what grows in the wilds and mountains.

His words, ﴿wal-nakhla wal-zar'a﴾ ("and the date palm and the crops"), are coordinated with "jannat." He singled them out for mention, although they are included among the gardens, because of the excellence they possess. ﴿Mukhtalifan ukuluh﴾ means "its produce being diverse," that is, in its state of being diverse in taste, quality and inferiority.

Al-Zajjaj said: This is a difficult question in grammar, namely the accusative status of "mukhtalifan" as a circumstantial clause (hal), since one would say: He has brought them into being, yet their produce has not varied. The answer is that God, glory be to Him, brought them into being while ordaining diversity in them. Sibawayh explained this with his saying: "I passed by a man with a falcon, hunting with it tomorrow," meaning: intending to hunt with it tomorrow, just as you say: "You will certainly enter the house eating and drinking," meaning: intending that. This is the well-known "intended circumstance" (al-hal al-muqaddara) that the grammarians have recorded in their books of grammar.

He said ﴿mukhtalifan ukuluh﴾ and did not say "ukuluhuma" (their produce, in dual), being content with mentioning it in reference to one of them, as in His words ﴿wa-idha ra'aw tijaratan aw lahwan infaddu ilayha﴾ (62:11), or the pronoun is like a demonstrative: meaning, "the produce of that."

His words, ﴿wal-zaytun wal-rummana﴾ ("and the olive and the pomegranate"), are coordinated with "jannat." That is, He brought into being the olive and the pomegranate in a state of being similar and dissimilar. The explanation of this has already been given. ﴿Kulu min thamarihi﴾ ("eat of its fruit") means of the fruit of each of them, or of the fruit of that. ﴿Idha athmar﴾ ("when it bears fruit") means when fruit has appeared on it, even if it has not ripened or reached the time of harvest.

His words: ﴿wa-atu haqqahu yawma hasadihi﴾ ("and pay its due on the day of its harvest").

The scholars differed: Is this verse muhkam (definitive, not abrogated), or mansukh (abrogated), or to be understood as recommended (nadb)? Ibn Umar, Ata', Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr held that the verse is muhkam, and that the owner is obliged on the day of harvest to give to the poor who are present a handful (al-qabda) and a bundle (al-dighth) and the like.

Ibn Abbas, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, Tawus, Abu al-Sha'tha', Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Jurayj held that this verse has been abrogated (mansukha) by zakat.

Ibn Jarir chose this view, and it is supported by the fact that this verse is Meccan, while the verse of zakat is Medinan, in the second year after the Hijra. Most of the scholars, both among the early generations (al-salaf) and later ones (al-khalaf), went to this view.

A group of scholars said: The verse is to be understood as recommended, not obligatory.

His words, ﴿wa-la tusrifu﴾ ("and do not be extravagant"), mean in giving charity. The original meaning of "israf" in the language is error, and "israf" in spending means squandering. It was said: It is addressed to the rulers, telling them: Do not take more than your right. It was also said: The meaning is: Do not take a thing without its right and place it where it is not deserved.

His words, ﴿wa-min al-an'am hamulatan wa-farsha﴾ ("and of the livestock, beasts of burden and those for the floor"), are coordinated with "jannat." That is, He brought into being for you, from the livestock, beasts of burden and [what is] for fur. "Hamula" is what is carried upon, and it is specific to camels, so it is "fa'ula" in the sense of "fa'ila." "Farsh" is what is made from wool, fleece and hair as a bedding that people spread out. It was said: "Hamula" means camels, and "farsh" means sheep. It was also said: "Hamula" is every animal carried upon, including camels, cattle, horses, mules and donkeys, and "farsh" is sheep. This holds only if the term "an'am" is allowed to be applied to all of these mentioned items. It was also said: "Hamula" is what is ridden, and "farsh" is what its meat is eaten. ﴿Kulu mimma razaqakum﴾ ("eat of what He has provided you") from these things. ﴿Wa-la tattabi'u khutuwat al-shaytan﴾ ("and do not follow the footsteps of Satan"), as the polytheists did, by forbidding what God has not forbidden and permitting what God has not permitted. ﴿Innahu lakum aduwwun mubin﴾ ("indeed he is to you a clear enemy"): that is, manifestly hostile and openly showing enmity.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words ﴿wa-huwa alladhi ansha'a jannatin ma'rushatin﴾ (6:141), that he said: "Ma'rushat" is what people have trellised, and ﴿ghayra ma'rushat﴾ is what came out in the mountains and the wilderness of fruits.

Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatada, who said: "Ma'rushat" are those trellised with canes and reeds, and "ghayr ma'rushat" he said: those growing freely (al-dahi).

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Abbas, concerning "ma'rushat," that he said: It is specifically the vine.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Nahhas, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, that the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His words ﴿wa-atu haqqahu yawma hasadihi﴾, said: "It is what falls from the ear of grain."

Abu Ubayd, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Nahhas, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Ibn Umar, concerning His words ﴿wa-atu haqqahu yawma hasadihi﴾, that he said: "They used to give to whoever was proud of them something other than charity."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi reported from Mujahid concerning the verse, that he said: "When you reap and the needy come to you, throw to them some of the ears of grain."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Maymun ibn Mihran and Yazid al-Asamm, who said: The people of Medina, when they cut the date palms, would bring the cluster and place it in the mosque, and the beggar would come and strike it with a stick, so that some of it would fall off. This is His words, ﴿wa-atu haqqahu yawma hasadihi﴾.

Ahmad and Abu Dawud in his Sunan reported from the hadith of Jabir ibn Abd Allah: "That the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered that from every eleven wasqs of dates there be a cluster hung in the mosque for the poor." Its chain of transmission is good.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Nahhas and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: ﴿wa-atu haqqahu yawma hasadihi﴾ was abrogated (nasakha-ha) by the tithe (al-'ushr) and half the tithe.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud in his book on abrogation (nasikhihi) and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Sudi something similar.

al-Nahhas, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ikrima something similar.

Abu Ubayd, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Dahhak something similar.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from al-Sha'bi, who said: "Indeed in wealth there is a right besides zakat."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Abu al-Aliyah, who said: They did not used to give anything besides zakat. Then they hastened and were extravagant, so God revealed: ﴿wa-la tusrifu innahu la yuhibbu al-musrifin﴾ ("and do not be extravagant; indeed He does not love the extravagant").

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Jurayj, who said: It was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, who harvested a date palm and said: "No one will come to me today except that I will feed him." So he fed until evening and had not a single date left. So God revealed: ﴿wa-la tusrifu innahu la yuhibbu al-musrifin﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid, who said: If you spent the like of Abu Qubays in gold in obedience to God, it would not be extravagance; and if you spent a sa' in disobedience to God, it would be extravagance. Regarding this, the early generations (al-salaf) have lengthy discussions. (p-453)

al-Firyabi, Abu Ubayd, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, reported from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Hamula" is what is carried upon of the camels, and "farsh" are the young camels that do not carry loads.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Hamula" are the mature camels, and "farsh" are the young camels.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from him, who said: "Hamula" is what is carried upon, and "farsh" is what is eaten from it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him also, who said: "Hamula" are camels, horses, mules, donkeys and everything carried upon, and "farsh" is sheep.

Abd ibn Humayd reported from Abu al-Aliyah, who said: "Hamula" are camels and cattle, and "farsh" are sheep and goats.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 143–144:

There is disagreement about what *thamaniyata* (eight) is in the accusative case, depending on what it is governed by. Al-Kisa'i said it is governed by a implied verb, meaning "and He produced eight pairs."

Al-Akhfash Sa'id said it is in the accusative as a *badal* (substitution, or apposition) for *hamulatan wa farshan* ("for load-bearing and for flat-lying animals"). Al-Akhfash Ali ibn Sulayman said it is governed by *kulu* ("eat"), meaning "eat the meat of eight pairs." It was also said that it is in the accusative as a *badal* for *ma* in ﴿of what God has provided for you﴾ (al-An'am: 142).

The *zawj* (pair) is the opposite of the *fard* (single). One says *zawj* or *fard*, just as one says *shaf'* (even) or *witr* (odd). So His saying ﴿eight pairs﴾ means eight singles. The single was called a pair in this verse because each of the male and the female is a pair in relation to the other. The word *zawj* is also applied to a single individual, so one says "they two are a pair" and "he is a pair." One also says, "I bought two pairs of pigeons," meaning a male and a female.

The summary is that when a single individual stands alone, whether male or female, it is called *fard*. If a male is with a female of its kind, they are called a *zawj*, and each of them individually is also called a *zawj*. They may also be called *zawjan* (a pair, dual). From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So He made of him the two kinds, the male and the female﴾ (al-Qiyamah: 39).

His saying ﴿two of the sheep﴾ is a *badal* for *thamaniyata*, in the accusative governed by the same governing word, according to the earlier disagreement. *Al-Da'n* (sheep) are the woolly ones among the flock. It is the plural of *da'in*, and the female is called *da'inah*; the plural is *da'a'in*. It was also said that it is a plural with no singular. It was also said that its plural is *da'in*, like *abd* and *abid*.

Talhah ibn Musarrif read *al-Da'n* with a fatha on the hamza, and the rest read it with a sukun.

Aban ibn Uthman read: "of the sheep two, and of the goats two" with a raf' (nominative) as the beginning of the sentence.

His saying ﴿and of the goats two﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it and shares its ruling.

Ibn Amir, Abu Amr, Ibn Kathir and the people of Basra read *al-ma'z* with a fatha on the ayn. The rest read it with a sukun.

Al-Nahhas said: In the usage of the Arabs, the more common form is *al-ma'z* and *al-da'n* with a sukun. *Al-ma'z* is the goat, the opposite of the sheep, and they are the ones with hair and short tails. It is a collective noun. The singular of *al-ma'z* is *ma'iz*, like *sahb* and *sahib*, *rakb* and *rakib*, and *tajr* and *tajir*. The female is *ma'izah*.

The purpose of this verse is that God, Glorified is He, explained the state of the livestock and its details, up to the categories mentioned, to clarify the favor He bestowed upon His servants by them, and to refute what the pre-Islamic period (*al-Jahiliyyah*) claimed about making some of them lawful and forbidding some of them, inventing lies against God, Glorified is He, and fabricating against Him.

The *hamza* in ﴿Say: Has He forbidden the two males or the two females?﴾ is for denunciation. The intended meaning of "the two males" is the ram and the he-goat, and "the two females" is the ewe and the she-goat. The accusative of *al-dhakarayn* is governed by *harrama* (forbade), and *al-untayayn* is coordinated with it and in the accusative governed by the same governing word.

The meaning: it is a denunciation of the polytheists regarding the *bahirah* and what is mentioned with it, and their saying ﴿What is in the wombs of these livestock is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives﴾. That is, say to them: if He forbade the males, then every male is forbidden; if He forbade the females, then every female is forbidden; and if He forbade what the wombs of the two females contain, meaning of the sheep and the goats, then every offspring is forbidden, male or female, and all of them are offspring, so this entails that all of them are forbidden.

His saying ﴿Inform me with knowledge if you are truthful﴾ means: inform me with knowledge, not with ignorance, if you are truthful.

The purpose of this is rebuke and the establishing of proof against them, because He knows that they have no knowledge.

The same applies to His saying ﴿and of the camels two, and of the cattle two﴾ to the end of the verse.

His saying ﴿Or were you witnesses when God enjoined this upon you?﴾ The *am* here is the *munqati'ah* (disconnected) *am*, and the interrogation is for denial. It has the meaning of *bal* (rather) together with the *hamza*, that is: rather, were you present witnesses when God enjoined upon you this prohibition?

The purpose is rebuke and the establishing of proof, as preceded earlier.

His saying ﴿Who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God?﴾ means: no one is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God, forbidding something God did not forbid and attributing that to Him as a fabrication against Him, as the great leaders of the polytheists did. The *lam* in ﴿to mislead people without knowledge﴾ is for causation: that is, in order to mislead people through ignorance. It is connected to *iftara* (invented). ﴿Indeed God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is general, and those mentioned in the context are included in this first and foremost.

It is worth considering the reason for placing the goats and the sheep before the camels and the cattle, though the camels and the cattle are more beneficial, larger in body, and more useful, especially regarding the *hamulah* (load-bearing) and the *farsh* (flat-lying), from which the substitution was made, according to the clearest way of parsing *thamaniyata*.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported through several chains from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The eight pairs are of the camels, the cattle, the sheep, and the goats."

I wonder what the benefit is of quoting this statement from Ibn Abbas, from such imams, since no benefit attaches to it. That the eight pairs are those mentioned is stated plainly in the verse without any ambiguity.

Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatadah, who said: "The male and the female are a pair."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, (p-454) and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning His saying ﴿eight pairs﴾, who said: "It concerns what God forbade of the *bahirah* and the *sa'ibah*."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Layth ibn Abi Sulaym, who said: "The buffalo and the Bactrian camel are among the eight pairs."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported through several chains from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying ﴿eight pairs: of the sheep two, and of the goats two﴾, who said: "These are four." ﴿Say: Has He forbidden the two males, or the two females?﴾ He says: "I have not forbidden any of that." ﴿Or what the wombs of the two females contain?﴾ meaning: does the womb contain anything but a male or a female? Then why do they forbid some and permit some? ﴿Inform me with knowledge if you are truthful﴾ He says: "All of them are lawful," meaning what was mentioned earlier of what the people of the pre-Islamic period forbade.
