(p-457) His saying: ﴿Say: Come⟩ means: come forward.

Ibn al-Shajari said: The one commanded to come forward, in the original use of this verb, was seemingly seated, so it was said to him, "Ta'āl" — that is, raise your person by standing and come forward. Then they extended its usage until they made it for the one standing and the one walking.

Likewise al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: It is of the specific that became general. Its origin is that it was said by one who was in a high place to one who was lower than him; then it became frequent and extended until it became general.

His saying: ﴿I will recite what your Lord has forbidden⟩ — "I will recite" is the answer to the imperative, and "what" (mā) is a relative pronoun in the accusative position governed by it: that is, I will recite that which your Lord has forbidden to you.

The intended meaning of reciting what Allah has forbidden is reciting the verses that contain it. It is also permissible for "mā" to be a verbal noun (maṣdariyya): that is, I will recite the prohibition of your Lord. The meaning: what comprises the prohibition. It was said: It is also permissible for "mā" to be interrogative, that is, "I will recite which thing your Lord has forbidden", on the basis that recitation means saying; but this is very weak. As for "to you (ʿalaykum)": if it is connected to "I will recite", the meaning is: I will recite to you that which your Lord has forbidden. If it is connected to "has forbidden", the meaning is: I will recite that which your Lord has forbidden to you. This is preferable, because the context is the context of explaining what is forbidden to you, not the context of explaining what is forbidden absolutely. It was said: "to you" is for urging (ighrāʾ), and has no connection with what precedes it. The meaning: "Upon you is that you should not associate partners (with Him)," etc., that is: adhere to that, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Upon you is your own soul⟩ (al-Mā'ida: 105). This is weaker than what precedes it. And "that you not associate" (an lā tushrikū) is an explanatory clause for the verb of reciting. Al-Nahhas said: It is permissible for it to be in the position of accusative as a substitute for "mā": that is, I will recite to you the prohibition of associating. It was said: It is permissible for it to be in the position of nominative by supposing a subject: that is, what is recited is "that you not associate", and "shay'an" (anything) is either an object or a verbal noun, meaning: do not associate with Him anything of things, or anything of association.

His saying: ﴿And to parents, kindness⟩ — that is: be kind to both of them, and kindness to them is righteousness toward them and obedience to their commands and prohibitions.

This has already been discussed.

His saying: ﴿And do not kill your children out of poverty⟩ — when He mentioned the right of parents over children, He mentioned the right of children over parents, which is that they not kill them on account of poverty.

Imlāq (poverty) is destitution. The Jāhiliyya used to do this to males and females out of fear of poverty, and used to do it to females specifically out of fear of shame. Al-Naqqash related from Mu'arrij that imlāq means hunger in the dialect of Lakhm. Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Ballūṭī mentioned that imlāq means spending: it is said, "amlaqa mālahu," meaning he spent it.

The first meaning is the one upon which the leading lexicographers and the leading exegetes agree here. ﴿And do not approach the abominations⟩ — that is, the sins. From this is ﴿And do not approach fornication; indeed, it is an abomination⟩ (al-Isrā': 32). "Mā" in ﴿what is apparent⟩ is a substitute for "the abominations", and likewise "what is hidden".

What is meant by "what is apparent" is what is openly done of them, and "what is hidden" is what is secretly done.

This has already been mentioned. ﴿And do not kill the soul⟩ — the lām in "the soul" is for the genus, and ﴿which Allah has forbidden⟩ is a qualifier of "the soul": that is, do not kill any of the souls which Allah has forbidden ﴿except by right⟩, that is, except by what right requires. The exception is a "mufarragh" (open) exception: that is, do not kill him in any state except in the state of right; or do not kill them by any cause except by a cause of right. Among what is right is killing by way of retribution (qiṣāṣ), killing for the fornication of a married person, killing for apostasy, and similar causes that the Sharia has established. The indication with "that" (dhālikum) refers to what was mentioned before, what He recited to them; it is the subject, and ﴿He has enjoined you with it⟩ is its predicate: that is, He commanded you with it and made it obligatory upon you.

152. ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan⟩ — that is, do not meddle with it in any way except by the manner ﴿which is best⟩ over others, which is what brings about its good, its preservation, and its growth. This includes every way in which there is benefit to the orphan and increase in his property. It was said: What is meant by "that which is best" is trade. ﴿Until he reaches his maturity (ashuddahu)⟩ — that is, up to a limit which is that the orphan reaches his maturity. If he reaches that, then hand over his property to him, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you perceive in them maturity of judgment, then hand over to them their property⟩ (al-Nisā': 6).

The people of knowledge differed concerning ashudd. The people of Madina said: It is his reaching (puberty) and the perception of his maturity of judgment.

Abu Hanifa said: twenty-five years.

ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: It is puberty.

It was said: It is the end of middle age. From this is the saying of Suhaym al-Rabahi:

"The brother of fifty, my maturity has gathered, and in my speech is the turning of affairs."

The preferable view in establishing the attainment of ashudd is that it is reaching the age of legal responsibility together with the perception of maturity of judgment, which is that he is, in his dealings with his property, following the way of the sensible, not the way of the foolish and the wasteful. This is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He, in Surat al-Nisā': ﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age; then if you perceive in them maturity of judgment, hand over to them their property⟩ (al-Nisā': 6). So He made reaching the age of marriage, which is the age of legal responsibility, conditional upon the perception of maturity of judgment. Perhaps a discussion of this has already passed there. Ashudd is singular with no plural. It was said: its singular is shadd, like fals and aflus, and its origin is from "shadda al-nahar", meaning the day rose high.

Sibawayh said: its singular is shidda.

Al-Jawhari said: This is good in meaning, because it is said: "balagha al-kalam shiddatahu" (the speech reached its intensity), but the form fi'la is not pluralized as af'ul.

His saying: ﴿And give full measure and weight with justice⟩ — that is, with justice in taking and giving at the time of buying and selling. ﴿We do not burden any soul except to its capacity⟩ — that is, except to its ability, in every obligation of the obligations, and among that is the obligation to give full measure and weight, so the one in charge of them is not addressed with what cannot be avoided regarding excess or deficiency. ﴿And when you speak, be just⟩ — that is, when you say a statement in a report, or testimony, or in censure or commendation, then be just in it and seek the correct, and do not be partisan in that for a relative or against a distant one, nor incline toward a friend or against an enemy, but treat people equally, for that is part of the justice which Allah has commanded. The pronoun in ﴿even if it were⟩ refers to what "when you speak" implies, since speech necessarily has something spoken about or someone spoken to: that is, even if the one spoken about or the one spoken to is ﴿a near relative⟩, that is, a person of kinship to you. It was said: The meaning is: even if the right were upon the likes of your relatives. The first is preferable. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿Even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives⟩ (al-Nisā': 135).

His saying: ﴿And fulfill the covenant of Allah⟩ — that is, fulfill every covenant which Allah has made with you. Among what He has covenanted with you is what His Messenger recited to you by His command in this context. It is permissible that what is meant by it is every covenant, even if it is between created beings, because Allah, Exalted is He, when He commanded fulfilling it in many Qur'anic verses, that justified attributing it to Him. The indication with "that" refers to what was mentioned before: ﴿He has enjoined you with it⟩ — He commanded you with it as a emphatic command. ﴿That you may remember⟩ — so that you may be admonished by that.

His saying: ﴿And that this is My path, straight⟩ — "anna" is in the position of accusative: that is, and recite that this is My path. This was said by al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i.

Al-Farra' said: It is also permissible for it to be in the genitive: that is, He enjoined you with it, and with that this.

Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: The estimate is "and because this is My path, straight", as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And that the mosques are for Allah⟩ (al-Jinn: 18).

Al-A'mash, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "wa-inna hādhā" with a kasra on the hamza, as a resumption (istiʾnāf), the estimate being: "that which was mentioned in these verses is My path."

Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ya'qub read "wa-in hādhā ṣirāṭī" with lightening, on the estimate of the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n).

Al-A'mash read "hādhā ṣirāṭī". In the codex of ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud it is "wa-hādhā ṣirāṭu rabbikum", and in the codex of Ubayy it is "wa-hādhā ṣirāṭu rabbika". The ṣirāṭ is the way, and it is the way of the religion of Islam. "Mustaqīman" is in the accusative as a state (ḥāl). The mustaqīm is the even, which has no crookedness in it. Then He commanded them to follow it and forbade them from following the other paths: that is, the religions whose ways diverge, ﴿so that He scatters you⟩, that is, leads you astray, ﴿from His path⟩, that is, from the path of Allah, the straight one, which is the religion of Islam.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: These paths encompass Judaism, Christianity, Zoroastrianism, and all the other religious communities, and the people of innovations and misguidance from the people of desires and deviation in branches and other matters, and those who go to extremes in disputation and plunge into theological speculation. All of these are subject to slipping and are a cause of corrupt belief. The indication with "that" refers to what was mentioned before, and it is the subject, with ﴿He has enjoined you with it⟩ as its predicate: that is, He emphasized upon you the charge of it. ﴿That you may be mindful⟩ of what He has forbidden you.

Al-Tirmidhi related it and graded it as ḥasan, and Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh, from ʿUbada ibn al-Samit, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Which of you will pledge allegiance to me upon these three verses?" Then he recited ﴿Say: Come⟩ up to three verses, then said: "Whoever fulfills them, his reward is with Allah; and whoever falls short of any of them and Allah overtakes him in this world, that will be his punishment; and whoever has it deferred to the Hereafter, his affair is with Allah: if He wills, He will punish him, and if He wills, He will pardon him."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Dari's and Ibn al-Mundhir related, from Ka'b al-Ahbar, who said: The first thing sent down in the Torah was ten verses, and they are the ten which were sent down at the end of al-An'am: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you⟩ up to its end.

Abu al-Shaykh related, from ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAdi ibn al-Khiyar, who said: Ka'b heard a man reading ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you, that you associate not anything with Him, and to parents⟩, so Ka'b said: By Him in whose hand is Ka'b's soul, it is indeed the first verse in the Torah: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you⟩" up to the end of the verses. End of quote.

I say: These are the Ten Commandments in the Torah, the first of which is: "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. You shall have no other gods before me."

Among them: "Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which the LORD your God gives you. You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. You shall not covet your neighbor's house; you shall not covet your neighbor's wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor's." Perhaps this is the intent of Ka'b al-Ahbar. The Jews have a great concern with these commandments, and the People of the Psalms (Zabur) wrote them at the end of their Psalter, and the People of the Gospel at the beginning of their Gospel.

They are written on two tablets. We have omitted from them what relates to the Sabbath.

Abd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh related, from Qatada, regarding ﴿And do not kill your children out of poverty⟩, that he said: out of fear of destitution. He said: The people of the Jahiliyya would kill one of them his daughter out of fear of destitution for her and captivity. ﴿And do not approach the abominations, what is apparent of them and what is hidden⟩, he said: their secret and their public.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh related, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding ﴿And do not kill your children out of poverty⟩, that he said: out of fear of want. ﴿And do not approach the abominations, what is apparent of them and what is hidden⟩, he said: In the Jahiliyya they did not see any harm in fornication in secret, and they found it reprehensible in public, so Allah forbade fornication both in secret and in public.

Abd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh related, from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿And that this is My path, straight⟩, that he said: Know that the way is one way, the community of guidance, and its destination is Paradise; and that Iblis devised scattered paths, the community of misguidance, and their destination is the Fire.

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bazzar, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) drew a line with his hand, then said: 'This is the straight path of Allah.' Then he drew lines to the right and left of that line, and said: 'And these are the paths; there is not one of them except that upon it is a devil calling to it.' Then he recited: ﴿And indeed, this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow the [other] paths, lest they separate you from His way.﴾"

Ahmad, Ibn Majah, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated a similar report from the hadith of Jabir.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that a man asked him, "What is the straight path?" He said: "We left Muhammad (ﷺ) at its beginning, and its end is Paradise. To its right are byways, and to its left are byways, and there are men there calling whoever passes by them. Whoever takes one of those byways, it ends with him in the Fire, and whoever takes the straight path, it ends with him in Paradise." Then Ibn Mas'ud recited: ﴿And indeed, this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿and do not follow the paths﴾ that he said: "The misguidances."

[p. 459] This statement is a sequence given to establish the charge (tawṣiyah) that God enjoined upon His servants. The conjunction *thumma* (then) here has been questioned, since the story of Moses and His giving him the Book came before the thing it is joined to, namely His words ﴿That is what He has enjoined upon you﴾. It has been said that *thumma* here means the same as *wa* (and). It has also been said that the sentence is to be understood as: "Then, We had already given Moses the Book before We sent down the Qur'an upon Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace." It has been said that the meaning is: "Say: Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden to you. Then I will recite the giving of the Book to Moses." It has been said that the enjoining to which it is joined is ancient, and that every prophet has continued to enjoin it upon his community. It has been said that *thumma* indicates delay in the reporting, as when you say: "What you did today reached me, then what you did yesterday is more astonishing."

His words: ﴿tamāman (completely)﴾ is an object of purpose (*mafʿūl li-ajlihi*, an object indicating the reason for the action) or a verbal noun (*maṣdar*). The phrase ﴿ʿalā alladhī aḥsana (upon the one who did good)﴾ has been read with *raf'* (nominative), and this is the reading of Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar and Ibn Abī Isḥāq. In that case the *raf'* of *aḥsana* is by supposing an implied subject: that is, "upon the one who is best." From this is what Sībawayh reported from al-Khalīl, that he heard: *mā anā bi-alladhī qā'ilun laka shay'an* (I am not the one who will say anything to you).

The rest read it with *naṣb* (accusative), taking it as a past-tense verb according to the Basrans. Al-Farrā' and al-Kisā'ī permitted that it be a noun functioning as a qualifier (*naʿt*) of *alladhī*. This is impossible according to the Basrans, because it would be a qualifier of the noun before it is complete. The meaning according to them is: "completely upon whoever is good in accepting it and in carrying it out, whoever he may be." What supports this is that Ibn Masʿūd read: ﴿completely upon those who did good﴾. Al-Ḥasan said: "There were among them both a good-doer and a non-good-doer, so God sent down the Book completely upon the good-doers."

It has been said that the meaning is: We gave Moses the Torah as an addition to what Moses already knew well of what God had taught him before the Torah was sent down to him. It has been said that the meaning is: completely upon what God, the Mighty and Majestic, bestowed upon Moses of the message and other things. It has been said that the meaning is: completely upon Moses's good deeds in obedience to God, the Mighty and Majestic; this was said by al-Farrā'.

His words: ﴿and as a detailed explanation of everything﴾ are coordinated with *tamāman*, meaning: and for the sake of the detailed explanation of everything. Likewise, ﴿guidance and mercy﴾ are coordinated with it, meaning: and for guidance and mercy. The pronoun in ﴿la'allahum (so that they)﴾ refers to the Children of Israel, which is indicated by the mention of Moses. The *bāʾ* in ﴿bi-liqāʾi (with the meeting)﴾ is connected to *yu'minūn* (they believe).

His words: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed﴾: the demonstrative refers to the Qur'an. The demonstrative pronoun is the subject, and its predicate is *kitāb* (a Book). *Anzalnāhu* (We have sent it down) is a qualifier of *kitāb*, and *mubārak* (blessed) is another qualifier of it. The qualifier of sending down is placed first because the denial is connected to it. The *mubārak* is abundant in blessing, because of the worldly and religious benefits it contains. ﴿So follow it﴾: since it is from God and contains blessing, following it is binding upon you. ﴿And fear God [by avoiding opposing it and denying what is in it]﴾ so that ﴿perhaps you will receive mercy﴾ if you accept it and do not oppose it, through the mercy of God, glorified is He.

The *an* in ﴿lest you say﴾ is in the place of the accusative.

The Kufans said: "so that you do not say."

The Basrans said: "out of dislike that you say."

Al-Farrā' and al-Kisā'ī said: the meaning is: "so fear lest you say, O people of Mecca: ﴿The Book was sent down﴾, that is the Torah and the Gospel, ﴿upon two groups before us﴾, and they are the Jews and the Christians, and no Book was sent down upon us, ﴿and indeed we were unaware of their study﴾, that is, of the recitation of their books in their languages, that is, we do not know what is in them." What they intend is to establish the sending down of the two Books, together with an excuse for not following what is in them, by lack of understanding and unawareness of their meaning on their part.

His words: ﴿or [lest] you say: "If the Book had been sent down upon us, we would have been more guided than they"﴾ are coordinated with *taqūlū* (you say), meaning: or lest you say, "If the Book had been sent down upon us as it was sent down upon the two groups before us, ﴿we would have been more guided than them﴾ to the truth which God sought." This statement and this excuse of theirs are refuted by the sending of Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, to them, and by the sending down of the Qur'an upon him. For this reason He said: ﴿There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord﴾, that is, a Book which God sent down upon your Prophet, who is from among you, O company of Arabs. So do not offer excuses that are false, nor console yourselves with corrupt pretexts, for the dawn has become clear to one who has two eyes. ﴿And guidance and mercy﴾ are coordinated with *bayyina* (clear evidence), meaning: there has come to you clear evidence and the guidance by which everyone who desires guidance is guided, and mercy from God which includes everyone who seeks it and wishes to obtain it. But you have wronged yourselves by denying the signs of God and turning away from them, that is, by departing from them and diverting whoever wishes to approach them. ﴿So who is more wrong than one who denies the signs of God﴾ which are mercy and guidance for people ﴿and turns away from them﴾; so he goes astray by turning away from them, and he misguides others by diverting them from approaching them. ﴿We will repay those who turn away from Our signs with the worst punishment﴾, that is, the evil punishment, because of what they used to turn away. It has been said that the meaning of *ṣadafa* is "he turned away," and *yaṣdifūn* means "they turn away," which is close to the meaning of *ṣarf* (diverting). The meaning of this word has already been verified earlier. The interrogative in ﴿fa-man aẓlam (so who is more wrong)﴾ is for denial, meaning: denying that anyone could be more wrong than one who denies the signs of God and turns away from them, together with what this implies of rebuke for them.

Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Mujāhid regarding ﴿completely upon the one who did good﴾: he said, "upon the believing good-doers."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Abū Ṣakhr regarding ﴿completely upon the one who did good﴾: he said, "completely for what God had already done good."

He also reported from Ibn Zayd, who said: "completely for His blessing upon them and His goodness to them."

Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Qatādah, regarding His words ﴿And this is a Book﴾, he said: "It is the Qur'an which God sent down upon Muhammad." ﴿So follow it and fear God﴾: he said, "so follow what God has made lawful in it, and fear what He has forbidden."

These same narrators reported from Mujāhid regarding His words ﴿upon two groups before us﴾, he said: "The Jews and the Christians; he feared that Quraysh would say it."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "They are the Jews and the Christians." ﴿And indeed we were unaware of their study﴾, he said: "Their recitation."

Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Qatādah, regarding His words ﴿we would have been more guided than them﴾, he said: "This is the statement of the disbelievers of the Arabs."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from al-Suddī, regarding His words ﴿There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord﴾, he said: "There has come to you clear evidence: a clear Arabic tongue, when they did not know the study of the two groups."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His words ﴿and turned away from them﴾, he said: "He turned away from them."

Abd ibn Ḥumayd reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, regarding His words ﴿yaṣdifūn (they turn away)﴾, he said: "They turn away."

(p-460) That is: after We had established the proof against them, sent down the Book upon Our Messenger who was sent to them, and it did not benefit them and they did not turn back from their error by it, then nothing remains for them except that they are awaiting (yunzarun), i.e., they are waiting ﴿for the angels to come to them﴾, that is, the angels of death to take their souls. At that point, ﴿a soul will not benefit from its faith if it had not believed before﴾. ﴿Or your Lord comes﴾, O Muhammad, as they proposed when they said: ﴿Why were the angels not sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?﴾ (al-Furqan 25:21). It has been said that its meaning is: ﴿or the command of your Lord comes﴾ to destroy them. It has been said that the meaning is: ﴿or all the signs of your Lord come﴾, based on His saying: ﴿or some of the signs of your Lord come﴾. It has also been said that it is among the mutashabih (the ambiguous verses whose interpretation (ta'wil) none knows except Allah). The Qur'an frequently contains the omission of a modifier (hadhf al-mudaf), as in His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ (Yusuf 12:82), and His saying: ﴿and they were made to drink the calf into their hearts﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:93), meaning the love of the calf. It has also been said that the coming (ityan) of Allah is His coming on the Day of Resurrection to judge between His creation, as in His saying: ﴿and your Lord comes, and the angels rank upon rank﴾ (al-Fajr 89:22).

His saying: ﴿On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come﴾.

Ibn Umar and Ibn al-Zubayr read "yawma ta'ti" with the feminine ta' (fawqiyyah), while the rest read it with the masculine ya' (tahtiyyah).

Al-Mubarrad said: the feminine form is due to proximity to a feminine noun, not according to the original rule. From this is the saying of Jarir:

*When the news of al-Zubayr came, the walls of Madinah humbled themselves, and the humbled mountains.*

Ibn Sirin read "la tanfa'u" with the feminine ta'.

Abu Hatim said: this is an error attributed to Ibn Sirin.

People have said: in this there is a subtle point of grammar, mentioned by Nifthawayh: that both faith (al-iman) and the soul (al-nafs) each include the other, so he made "faith" feminine since it pertains to the soul.

Al-Nahhas said: there is another aspect, which is that "faith" is made feminine because it is a verbal noun (masdar), just as a feminine masdar is mentioned, as in His saying: ﴿So whoever receives an admonition from his Lord﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:275).

The meaning of ﴿On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come﴾ is: the day when the signs they proposed come, which are those that compel them to faith, ﴿a soul will not benefit from its faith﴾. Or it may be broader than that, so that what they are awaiting enters it. It has also been said that these are the signs that are the minor and major signs of the Hour mentioned in the authentic hadiths from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). These are the signs that, when they come, ﴿a soul will not benefit from its faith﴾.

His saying: ﴿had not believed before﴾ means: before the coming of some of the signs. As for the one who had believed before the coming of some of the signs, her faith benefits her.

The clause ﴿had not believed before﴾ is in the accusative position (mahall nasb) as a description (sifah) of "nafsan" (a soul).

His saying: ﴿or had earned good through its faith﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "amanat" (had believed), and the meaning is: a soul's faith does not benefit it when the signs are present, if it is described as not having believed before, or as having believed before but not having earned good through its faith. From this it results that nothing benefits except combining faith before the coming of some of the signs with earning good in faith. So whoever believed before only and did not earn good in his faith, or earned good but did not believe, that does not benefit him. This construction is like your saying: "I will not give to a man today who came to me, unless he did not come to me yesterday, or did not praise me for his coming to me yesterday." What is derived from this is that he does not deserve the gift except a man who came to him yesterday and praised him for his coming to him yesterday. Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded him to say to them: "Wait for what you desire to come; indeed we are waiting for it too." This is a severe threat and a great warning, and it strengthens what has been said in the interpretation of ﴿On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come﴾, that they are the signs they proposed, namely the coming of the angels and the coming of punishment to them from Allah, as has already been explained.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿Do they await anything but that the angels come to them﴾ that he said: at death. ﴿Or your Lord comes﴾, he said: on the Day of Resurrection.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah, regarding the interpretation of the verse, the same.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Muqatil regarding ﴿or your Lord comes﴾ that he said: on the Day of Resurrection, in canopies of clouds.

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd in his Musnad, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding His saying: ﴿On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come﴾, that he said: "The rising of the sun from its west."

Al-Tirmidhi said: it is gharib (a narration with a single or weak transmission line).

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Abd ibn Humayd narrated it from Abu Sa'id as a mawquf report (attributed to a Companion, not the Prophet).

al-Tabarani and Ibn Adi and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet).

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Nu'aym ibn Hammad and al-Tabarani narrated it from Ibn Mas'ud as a mawquf report.

When the elevation (raf') of this prophetic interpretation is established through a sound channel with no defect in it, then it has priority over every other interpretation and is binding to adopt. It is supported by what is established in the Two Sahihs and others, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Hour will not come until the sun rises from its west. When it rises and people see it, they will all believe, and that is the time when ﴿a soul will not benefit from its faith﴾," then he recited the verse.

Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others reported from Abu Dharr, as a marfu' report, something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas, as a marfu' report, something similar too.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddi regarding His saying: ﴿or had earned good through its faith﴾, that he said: it earned good in its affirmation by performing righteous deeds. As for these people of the qiblah (ahl al-qiblah, i.e., Muslims), even if it affirmed faith but had not done good before that, and then did good after it saw the sign, it will not be accepted from it. But if it did good before the sign, and then did good after the sign, it will be accepted from it.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Muqatil regarding His saying: ﴿or had earned good through its faith﴾ that he said: meaning the Muslim who did not do good in his faith and was persisting in major sins before the sign.

The signs that are the signs of the Hour have been described in many hadiths concerning their explanation and enumeration, and they are mentioned in the books of Sunnah.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 6, verses 159–160:**

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i (a recitation of Ali ibn Abi Talib) read ﴿فارَقُوا دِينَهم﴾ (*fāraqū dīnahum*, "they abandoned their religion"). Its meaning is: they left their religion and departed from it.

The rest of the readers read ﴿فَرَّقُوا﴾ (*farraqū*, "they divided") with the shaddah (doubled letter), except al-Nakha'i, who read it without the shaddah.

The meaning is that they made their religion divided: they took up some of it and abandoned some of it. It was said that the intended people are the Jews and the Christians.

Something with this meaning has come concerning the Jews, in the words of the Most High: ﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not divide except after the clear evidence had come to them﴾ (al-Bayyinah: 4). (p-461) It was also said that the intended people are the polytheists, some of whom worshipped idols and some of whom worshipped the angels. It was also said that the verse is general, covering all disbelievers and everyone who innovates and brings what Allah has not commanded. This is the correct view, because the wording conveys generality, so it includes groups of the People of the Book, groups of the polytheists, and others among the people of Islam who innovate.

The meaning of ﴿شِيَعًا﴾ (*shiya'an*, "sects") is factions and parties. It applies to every people whose affair in religion was once one and united, and then each group followed the opinion of a great man among their great ones that opposes the truth and departs from the right.

﴿لَسْتَ مِنهم في شَيْءٍ﴾ (*lasta minhum fī shay'in*, "you are not of them in anything") means: you are not part of their division, nor (are you responsible) for asking about the cause of their division or searching for the reason behind their factionalism, in any matter. Nothing of that is binding on you, and you are not addressed with it; your duty is only to convey. This is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever cheats us is not of us," meaning: we are free of him. The position of ﴿فِي شَيْءٍ﴾ (*fī shay'in*) is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl).

Al-Farra' said: it is by omission of a noun (muḍāf): i.e., you are not in any part of their punishment. You are only responsible for warning. Then Allah consoled him with His words: ﴿Their affair is only with Allah﴾, so He will recompense them according to what His will requires. The restriction by ﴿إنَّما﴾ (*innamā*, "only") here serves as a justification for what precedes it and as an emphasis on it. Then, on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿He will inform them﴾, i.e., He will tell them of what He will inflict on them of recompense, ﴿of what they used to do﴾ of deeds that oppose what Allah prescribed for them and made obligatory upon them. This verse is among those said to be abrogated (*mansūkh*) by the verse of the sword.

His words: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times its like﴾. When He threatened those who opposed Him with what He threatened, He then stated, immediately after that, the measure of the reward of those who act on what He commanded them and comply with what He prescribed: whoever brings one good deed from among the good deeds will have ten good deeds as reward. The implied sense is: he will have ten good deeds like it, so the attribute (ṣifah) took the place of the qualified noun.

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: the feminine form ﴿عَشْرُ﴾ (*ʿashru*) in ﴿عَشْرُ أمْثالِها﴾ is appropriate because ﴿أمْثال﴾ (*amthāl*) is in construct with a feminine noun, as in the expression ﴿ذَهَبَتْ بَعْضُ أصابِعِهِ﴾ (*dhahabat baʿḍu aṣābiʿihi*, "some of his fingers went").

al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and al-A'mash read ﴿فَلَهُ عَشْرُ أمْثالُها﴾ with both ﴿عَشْرُ﴾ and ﴿أمْثالُها﴾ in the nominative.

This doubling is established in the Sunnah through many hadiths. This doubling is the least that the doer of a good deed deserves.

The increase beyond this has come both generally and specifically. In the Qur'an there is His words: ﴿like a grain that grows seven ears﴾ (al-Baqarah: 261). Concerning some good deeds it has come that their doer will be rewarded without reckoning, and in the pure Sunnah there is the multiplication of reward to thousands upon thousands.

We have already examined this in two places in this tafsir, so let one refer to them.

﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, i.e., of evil deeds, ﴿will not be recompensed except with its like﴾, without any addition beyond its measure in lightness and gravity. The polytheist is recompensed for the evil of polytheism with eternal abiding in the Fire. The one among the Muslims who commits a sin is recompensed for it with its like from the punishments whose measure has been specified, as many hadiths explicitly state that whoever does such-and-such will have such-and-such. As for the sins for which no punishment has been specified, we should say: Allah will recompense him with its like, even though we do not know the exact nature of what he will be recompensed with. This applies if he does not repent. But if he repents, or if his good deeds outweigh his evil deeds, or if Allah covers him with His mercy and graciously pardons him, then there is no recompense. The evidence of the Book and the Sunnah explicitly state this in a way that leaves no doubt for the doubter. ﴿And they will not be wronged﴾, meaning those who bring a good deed and those who bring an evil deed, by a reduction in the reward of the good deeds of the doers of good, nor by an increase in the punishments of the evildoers.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: the Jews and the Christians differed before Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, and they split apart. When Muhammad was sent, this was revealed to him: ﴿Indeed, those who have divided their religion﴾, the verse.

al-Nahhas narrated from him in his book on abrogation (*nāsikh*): ﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion﴾ — he said: the Jews and the Christians abandoned Islam and the religion they were commanded to follow. ﴿And they became sects (shiya')﴾, i.e., factions, parties, different groups. ﴿You are not of them in anything﴾ — it was revealed in Makkah, and then it was abrogated by ﴿And fight the polytheists﴾ (al-Tawbah: 36).

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him concerning ﴿وكانُوا شِيَعًا﴾ (*wa-kānū shiyaʿan*): he said: various creeds.

al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah concerning His words: ﴿Indeed, those who have divided their religion﴾, the verse, that he said: they are in this community.

al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani, al-Shirazi in *al-Alqab*, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning the verse, that he said: "They are the people of innovations and whims from this community." In its chain is Abd ibn Kathir, who is abandoned in hadith (matrūk al-ḥadīth), and no one else raised it to the Prophet; all the others stopped it at Abu Hurayrah.

Abd ibn Humayd, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Umamah concerning the verse that he said: they are the Harūriyyah (Khawarij). It was also narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Nahhas, and Ibn Mardawayh from Abu Ghalib from Abu Umamah as a marfū' (attributed to the Prophet) report, but its raising to the Prophet is not sound.

al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Shahin, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah*, Abu Nasr al-Sijzi in *al-Ibanah*, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated from Umar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Aisha: "O Aisha, indeed those who divided their religion and became sects, they are the people of innovations, the people of whims, and the people of misguidance from this community. They have no repentance. O Aisha, indeed every person of sin has repentance, except the people of innovations and the people of whims; they have no repentance, and they are free of me."

Ibn Kathir said: it is strange, and its raising (to the Prophet) is not sound.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "When the verse ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ was revealed, a man from the Muslims said: O Messenger of Allah, is 'There is no god but Allah' a good deed? He said: 'Yes, it is the best of good deeds.'" This is a mursal report (its chain omits a companion), and we do not know how its chain reaches Sa'id.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* narrated from Ibn Mas'ud concerning ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed﴾ that he said: "There is no god but Allah."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas something similar.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu Hurayrah something similar as well.

We have already pointed out that sound hadiths have established the multiplication of a good deed to ten times its like, so we will not lengthen by mentioning them. Many hadiths have also come concerning increase beyond this measure, and the bounty of Allah (p-462) is vast, and His giving is abundant.

When Allah (Glorified is He) explained that the disbelievers had split into sects and formed factions, He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to them: ﴿Indeed, my Lord has guided me﴾, meaning He guided me by what He revealed to me, ﴿to a straight path﴾, which is the religion (millah) of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). The word dinan (religion) is in the accusative as a circumstantial construction (hal), according to Qutrub, or as the object of hadani (guided me), according to al-Akhfash. It was also said that it is accusative by a verb implied by hadani, because its meaning is "he informed me" (i.e., "he informed me of a religion"). It was said that it is a substitute (badal) for the place of "to a straight path," because its meaning is "he guided me to a straight path," like His saying: ﴿and guide you to a straight path﴾ (al-Fath: 20). It was also said that it is accusative by an implied verb, as if it were said: "Follow a religion."

His saying: "qiyaman" (upright). The Kufans and Ibn Amir read it with a kasra on the qaf and a light pronunciation with a fatha on the ya'. The rest read it with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the shadda-ed ya', and both are dialectal forms. Its meaning is the upright religion in which there is no crookedness. It is an adjective of dinan, described by it although it is a verbal noun, for emphasis. The accusative of ﴿millata Ibrahim﴾ (the religion of Ibrahim) is in apposition (atf bayan) to dinan. It may also be accusative by the implied "a'ni" (I mean). Hanifan (upright, inclining to truth) is accusative as a circumstantial construction from Ibrahim, as stated by al-Zajjaj.

Ali ibn Sulayman said: it is accusative by the implied "a'ni."

The hanif is one who inclines towards the truth, and its verification has already been discussed. ﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾ is in an accusative position as a conjoined phrase with hanifan, or it is an interjected sentence confirming what came before it.

His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed, my prayer﴾. Allah (Glorified is He) commanded him to say to them, with this statement, following His command to say to them the previous statement. It was said: the wisdom in this is that what the first statement contained refers to the fundamentals of religion, and this refers to its branches.

By prayer (salah) is meant its genus, so all its types are included. It was also said that what is meant here is the night prayer, and it was said: the Eid prayer.

Nusuk is the plural of nasikah, which is a sacrificial animal. So said Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others: meaning my sacrifice during Hajj and Umrah.

Al-Hasan said: my religion.

Al-Zajjaj said: my worship, from their saying "nasaka fulan," he is a nasik, when he worships. Several scholars also said this.

﴿And my life and my death﴾: meaning, what I do in my life and my death of good deeds. Among the good deeds at death is the bequest of charities and various kinds of acts of nearness to Allah. It was also said: the very life and the very death are for Allah.

Al-Hasan read "nusuki" with a sukun on the sin. The rest read it with a damma.

The people of Madinah read "mahyay" with a sukun on the ya'. The rest read it with a fatha, so that two sakins do not come together.

Al-Nahhas said: none of the grammarians permitted the sukun except Yunus, and he permitted it because the lengthening in the alif takes the place of the vowel.

Ibn Abi Ishaq, Isa ibn Umar and Asim al-Jahdari read "mahya" without an alif, and this is the dialect of the upper Mudar tribe. From this is the saying of the poet:

They outran my desires and bent their necks to their own passions, so they were cut off, and for every side there is a place of falling.

﴿For Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, meaning sincerely for Him, with no partner in it.

The reference of "dhalika" (that) is to what is conveyed by ﴿for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ and ﴿He has no partner﴾, namely sincerity in obedience and making it for Allah alone.

His saying: ﴿And I am the first of the Muslims﴾, meaning the first of the Muslims of his nation. It was also said: the first of all Muslims, because although he came later in prophethood, he is the first of them in creation. From this is His saying: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Nuh﴾ (al-Ahzab: 7), and so on. The first meaning is preferable.

Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: al-Shafi'i used this verse as evidence for the legitimacy of opening the prayer with this remembrance, since Allah commanded His Prophet with it and revealed it in His Book. Then he mentioned the hadith of Ali: "that the Prophet (ﷺ) when he stood to pray would say: 'I turned my face to the One who originated the heavens and the earth, as a hanif, and I am not of the polytheists,' up to his saying: 'And I am the first of the Muslims.'" I say: this is in Sahih Muslim in full, and it is one of the reported forms of the opening supplication. However, it is restricted to the night prayer as in the authentic narrations. The most authentic opening supplication, which the Prophet (ﷺ) constantly practiced and recommended, is: "O Allah, distance between me and my sins," to its end. We have explained this in our commentary on al-Muntaqa in a way that needs no addition here.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muqatil, regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, my prayer﴾, that he said: meaning the obligatory prayer. ﴿And my nusuk﴾: meaning the Hajj.

I said: "O Messenger of Allah, is this only for you and the people of your household specifically, or is it for the Muslims in general?" He said: "No, rather it is for the Muslims in general."

When Allah (Glorified is He) explained that the disbelievers had split into sects and formed factions, He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to them: ﴿Indeed, my Lord has guided me﴾, meaning He guided me by what He revealed to me, ﴿to a straight path﴾, which is the religion (millah) of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). The word dinan (religion) is in the accusative as a circumstantial construction (hal), according to Qutrub, or as the object of hadani (guided me), according to al-Akhfash. It was also said that it is accusative by a verb implied by hadani, because its meaning is "he informed me" (i.e., "he informed me of a religion"). It was said that it is a substitute (badal) for the place of "to a straight path," because its meaning is "he guided me to a straight path," like His saying: ﴿and guide you to a straight path﴾ (al-Fath: 20). It was also said that it is accusative by an implied verb, as if it were said: "Follow a religion."

His saying: "qiyaman" (upright). The Kufans and Ibn Amir read it with a kasra on the qaf and a light pronunciation with a fatha on the ya'. The rest read it with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the shadda-ed ya', and both are dialectal forms. Its meaning is the upright religion in which there is no crookedness. It is an adjective of dinan, described by it although it is a verbal noun, for emphasis. The accusative of ﴿millata Ibrahim﴾ (the religion of Ibrahim) is in apposition (atf bayan) to dinan. It may also be accusative by the implied "a'ni" (I mean). Hanifan (upright, inclining to truth) is accusative as a circumstantial construction from Ibrahim, as stated by al-Zajjaj.

Ali ibn Sulayman said: it is accusative by the implied "a'ni."

It was said: the wisdom in this is that what the first statement contained refers to the fundamentals of religion, and this refers to its branches.

By prayer (salah) is meant its genus, so all its types are included. It was also said that what is meant here is the night prayer, and it was said: the Eid prayer.

The people of Madinah read "mahyay" with a sukun on the ya'. The rest read it with a fatha, so that two sakins do not come together.

Al-Nahhas said: none of the grammarians permitted the sukun except Yunus, and he permitted it because the lengthening in the alif takes the place of the vowel.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 6, verses 164–165:

The interrogative in ﴿Ghayra Allahi abghi rabban?﴾ ("Shall I seek a lord other than Allah?") is for denial (li-l-inkar), and it is a reply to the polytheists when they invited him to worship other than Allah. That is: how could I seek a lord other than Allah, independent in lordship, and abandon the worship of Allah, or seek a partner with Allah so that I worship both together? The situation is that He is the Lord of everything, while the one you call me to worship is among those who are themselves lordly-governed (marbub), a created being like me, who has no power to benefit or to harm. In this speech there is a rebuke and reproach to them (p. 463) of an immeasurable degree. Ghayra is not governed by the verb that follows it, and rabban is either a specifier (tamyiz) or a second object, on the basis that the verb governs two objects.

His saying: ﴿And every soul earns only against itself﴾ means: no one is held accountable for the sin that another has committed or the disobedience that another has perpetrated. All of a soul's earnings of evil fall upon itself and do not extend beyond it to others. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It has what it earned, and against it is what it has earned﴾ (al-Baqarah: 286), and His saying: ﴿That every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ (Taha: 15).

His saying: ﴿And no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾. The origin of wizr (burden) is weight. From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾ (al-Sharh: 2), and here it means sin. ﴿And they bear their burdens upon their backs﴾ (al-An'am: 31).

Al-Akhfash said: it is said wuzira yuwzaru, and wazara yazir wizran, and izran is permissible. In this verse there is a rejection of what the Jahiliyyah practised: holding a relative accountable for the sin of his relative, and one member of a tribe accountable for the sin of another.

It has been said that the intended meaning of this verse is in the Hereafter, and likewise the verse before it, based on His saying: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike exclusively those of you who have wronged﴾ (al-Anfal: 25). Similar to this is the saying of Zaynab bint Jahsh: "O Messenger of Allah, shall we be destroyed while among us are the righteous?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness increases." The better approach is to take the verse according to its apparent meaning, namely its generality, and what has been reported of being held accountable for another's sin, such as the blood money (diyya) borne by the 'aqilah (paternal kin), and the like. It thus stands in the position of being specified by this generality, and this is established in its proper place. Nor does His saying, exalted is He, contradict this verse: ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ (al-'Ankabut: 13), for the burdens "along with their burdens" are the burdens of those whom they misled, as in the other verse: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge﴾ (al-Nahl: 25). ﴿Then to your Lord is your return﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿and He will inform you about that over which you used to differ﴾ in this world. At that point the truth of those who are right and the falsehood of those who are wrong will become manifest.

His saying: ﴿And it is He who has made you successors (khala'if) of the earth﴾. Khala'if is the plural of khalifah: that is, He made you successors of the past nations and bygone generations. Al-Shammakh said:

"I am struck by them while the calamities miss me, and I succeed in dwellings after dwellings."

Or the meaning is that some of them succeed others, or that this human species is the successors of Allah on His earth. ﴿And He has raised some of you above others in degrees﴾ in creation, provision, strength, virtue and knowledge. Darajat is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, meaning "to degrees." ﴿That He may test you in what He has given you﴾, that is, to examine you regarding those matters He has granted you, or that He may try some of you by means of others, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others﴾ (al-Furqan: 20). Then He warned them, saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is swift in penalty﴾. Although this pertains to the Hereafter, everything that is coming is near, as He said: ﴿And the matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye or even nearer﴾ (al-Nahl: 77). Then He encouraged those among the Muslims who deserve encouragement, saying: ﴿And indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, that is, abundant in forgiveness and mercy.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾, that he said: no one is held accountable for the sin of another.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿And it is He who has made you successors of the earth﴾, that he said: He destroyed the earlier generations, and then made us successors in it after them. ﴿And He has raised some of you above others in degrees﴾: he said, in provision.
